I just explained why I can’t do that.” He turned to Red-thumb and Luathas. “I even said I was a former slaver. Doesn’t that bother any of you?” “You do not understand,” Jian pressed. “ ey are not going. I am going.” “Wel … damn.” e blacksmith looked at Annev, his expression helpless. “ is wil probably bring us more trouble,” he said, lowering his voice to a whisper. “It’s not my rst choice,” Annev admitted, glancing sideways at their would-be Yomad companion. “Would denying the life debt bring us more trouble, though?” “Hard to say. Are you superstitious?” “Not especial y, though I might make an exception in Jian’s case.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.content: Sraon sighed. “Probably wise, given that he serves the God of Fate.” He leaned closer, his voice dropping to a whisper. “It just seems a little convenient, you know?” Annev held up a nger then turned his attention back to Red-thumb and the rest. “Excuse me. I’d like to discuss this proposal in private.” “Of course.” e knife-wielding juggler bowed, and the two groups separated a few dozen paces. “What’s convenient?” Annev asked once they were out of earshot. “Everything,” Sraon said, his face hard, his eyes grim. “I’ve seen setups like this before—even participated in a few. It’s common enough in the Empire.” “What is?” “ e game—the long con. It’s like they had us marked the moment we joined their audience. Probably as soon as they saw the provisions in our cart.” “You think they plan to rob us?” “At the very least. Just think back. Red-thumb marked erin during the show, probably to signal whom to target. en you gave him that coin and he turned his attention to you. He asked who our leader was, and a few minutes later …” Sraon clapped his hands in front of Annev’s face. Crack. Annev glanced sideways at Jian, Red-thumb and the rest. “You think they arranged the attack.” “I’m not even sure there was one. at Mad Cat fel ow would’ve had to move impossibly fast to stop that bolt—maybe he was holding the bolt the whole time. Jian shouts to get our attention and then —a quarrel sails over your head. Convenient, yes?” Annev nodded. “I never did see my attacker’s face—and Mad Cat could have pointed me in the wrong direction at the end.” He sco ed, feeling a fool. “ ey real y have been playing us. I bet Luathas isn’t even mute.” “I’m sure she reads lips,” Sraon countered, his back turning to face the woman. “Seems likely this group is exactly what they seem to be—a novelty act by performers and charlatans, the kind of rogues who prey on the charitable and the gul ible.” “And I nearly fel for it.” “We’re stil not out of the woods with them. at life debt nonsense puts us in a bind.” “Why not just say no?” Sraon hesitated. “Because it’s possible they’re tel ing the truth.” “But you just said—” “I know what I said, and I stil think I’m right. But I could be wrong—been wrong plenty o’ times before—and I’d hate to be wrong about this.” “Why? Wouldn’t it be safer just to assume?” “Aye, it would be, but you’l recal I have a history of treating Ilumites poorly, and I’m not proud of it. If they’re tel ing the truth—if they’re not just a bunch of rogues parroting the stereotypes—then I want to help. It’d go a smal way toward canceling my debt against their people.” “ en let’s be smart about it. Jian can come with us—just Jian—and we keep a close eye on him. Maybe he slips up and tel s us what Red-thumb is real y after. Or maybe he’s tel ing the truth and we help Jian locate their last contact.” Sraon considered it then nodded. “Agreed.” “Do we tel the others your suspicions?” “No, I don’t think so. One of them might try to take matters into their own hands.” “You mean Fyn.” “Wel , yes. I was trying to be tactful.” “Tact is wasted on Fyn.” Annev glanced toward the merrymakers. “Best to let them know our decision.” “Aye, better make it quick too. e others are returning.” Annev glanced up just as Brayan and the rest reached the apple cart. Each boy deposited an armload of supplies, and then the quartermaster handed out dried meat and apples. Fyn stared suspiciously at Annev. “Master Red-thumb,” Annev said, once he and Sraon rejoined Ilumites’ group. “Who is your contact in Luqura?” e leather-clad rogue smiled. “Another treasure hunter of sorts—a noblewoman.” “Do you have her name?” “Of sorts. My hooded friend here cal s her ‘the Raven’ or ‘the Sooted Rook.’ Makes me think ol’ Lady Fate can’t keep her corvids straight—that or Jian keeps mixing up the translation.” “ ere is no mixing up, Tesked.” Jian spoke without raising his pink eyes from the ground. “Al names are masks. ey are true and not true. Sometimes she is the Raven. Sometimes she is the Rook. She wears her names like di erent faces. Also, Fate is not a lady. He is Tacharan, the God of Doom.” “And now you see why I had wanted to bring everyone,” Red-thumb said to Annev. “Finding the missing members of my troupe is its own treasure hunt, especial y with this soothsayer leading us.” Annev nodded, remembering the cryptic way Kelga had spoken to him in the Brakewood, and the way Janak had spoken of the Oracle’s answers. “Prophecies aren’t always clear. I don’t trust them myself.” He glanced at the albino. “No o ense intended, Master Nikloss.” e soothsayer lifted his hooded face, a smal smile touching his lips. “I take no o ense. Fate is my master … but he is a cruel lord. Even to me, his face is masked.” “Hold on now,” Sraon said, lifting a hand. “Annev and I had agreed to let Master Nikloss join our caravan as payment for Annev’s life debt—and we’l do our best to keep him safe while we’re in Luqura—but I won’t agree to any faerie chasing.” He looked at the merrymaker. “Master Red-thumb, if you don’t know the name of your contact, then we can’t help you nd her. You can understand that, yes? Luqura is the second largest city in the Empire, and riddles about birds and noblewomen won’t get us any closer to—” “I know who she is,” Annev said, saying the words as he realized, with a shock, that he did know. “What’s this now?” Sraon said, al eyes turning to Annev. “How could you possibly know?” Annev peered at Jian Nikloss who stil wore his smal , knowing smile. “If I gave you her name, would you know if I was right?” “Names are masks. If the mask ts, it is right.” e soothsayer’s cryptic answer did not surprise Annev. In the Brakewood, Crag had tried to make the wood-witch speak plainly using both threats and talismans, and that had only been half successful. Fate, it seemed, would not be denied his riddles. “You seek Sodja Rocas, the daughter of the House of Rocas in Luqura.” He looked to the soothsayer and Jian nodded in con rmation. “Sodja is also a thief and a heartless kil er.” He glanced between Jian, Luathas, Mad Cat, and Red-thumb. “Why would you want her to join your troupe?” ere was an awkward silence. “Wanting and needing are almost never the same,” Red-thumb said, once more speaking for the others. “A good king does not want to burden his people with taxes, but he wil do so out of need. Our own need is no less great and requires us to seek out this Sodja woman—the Sooted Rook—so she can help us solve our puzzle.” “Al for a piece of a treasure?” Annev said, his tone mocking. Red-thumb didn’t take o ense. Instead his eyes gleamed with a erce passion. “ e best kind of treasure, Master Ainnevog. e kind they sing about in stories and wil remember for ages and ages to come.” Annev sni ed. “What treasure is that?” Red-thumb smiled, his roguish demeanor suddenly overcome by a beati c zeal. “We’re going to end the Silence of the Gods.” *** “I take it back,” Sraon boomed, his thick hands helping Brayan secure the supplies in the cart. “He’s not a charlatan or a con artist. He’s a mad man—a religious zealot.” “ at doesn’t explain the performance with the crossbow bolt.” “No,” Sraon admitted. “I won’t take it al back, then. ey’re stil performers—talented ones too—but they’re also zealots, and that makes them more dangerous than thieves. ey have an agenda—and I don’t doubt they’d justify any act that furthers their goal.” “Who’s this now?” erin asked, piping up from the other side of the cart. “Never you mind, lad. Just get the last o’ the foodstu s into the wagon.” Sraon surveyed the tidy cart and nodded. “ is should last us a week. More than enough for the short trip to the capital.” “Brayan says we might get there before nightfal tomorrow,” Titus added for Annev’s bene t. “It’d be faster if we al had horses, but two days is a modest pace with al of us walking. Do you know he’s been there twice on retrieval missions?” “Many years ago, Titus.” Brayan hand-fed the black mare from a bag of wild oats, his emptied hand stroking her neck after each mouthful. “Regardless, I think we should camp outside the city’s wal s when we arrive tomorrow. e capital is a big place, and evening is a poor time to get acquainted with it.” “I agree,” Sraon said. “Matter o’ fact, I was just talking with Annev about how it might be best for some of our group to stay here in Banok.” “What?” Titus’s face scrunched up with emotion. “You want to separate us? Won’t that make us more vulnerable?” “Not for those staying behind—you’d be safe, probably even get lodging with my smithing friend, Dolyn.” “You want me to stay behind?” Titus looked to Annev, his expression hurt. “Annev, you want me to come with you, right? Me and erin?” Annev glanced at erin whose attention was split between fol owing their discussion and eating a giant sugar apple. “Titus,” Annev said, “I don’t want to leave anyone behind—” “Good,” Titus said, as if that settled it. “—but I wil ,” Annev continued. “It’s not safe on the road or in the capital, and being around me is more than half the danger.” He lifted the gloved Hand of Keos, its size slightly out of proportion with the rest of his body. “Sraon’s friend Dolyn tried to help remove this. She tried—she tried very hard—but she failed, and she was hurt.” “She hurt herself?” Fyn asked, nal y breaking his silence. Annev xed the boy with a glare then stopped himself. “She was hurt because of me. e prosthetic hurt her because I couldn’t control it.” “Is she dead ?” erin asked, spitting out a piece of apple. “No! She just … her hands are burned, and she’s a smith so that’s a big deal. In fact, that’s another good reason for some of us to stay behind. Gwendolyn would probably appreciate the help while her hands heal.” “Did you say Gwendolyn?” Brayan rose to his ful height. “Gwendolyn Goldsmith?” Sraon nodded. “You know her, then?” e quartermaster shrugged, his cheeks reddening above his neckbeard. “Barely more than an acquaintance . . . but yes. Lost a few arm wrestling matches to her.” Sraon grunted, evidently unsurprised. “I’m stil coming with you, Annev,” Titus declared, his chubby face resolute. “I won’t abandon you. I promise.” His eyes traveled to the quartermaster. “You’l come too, won’t you, Brayan?” “I’m not sure,” Brayan said, eyeing rst Sraon and then Titus. “Annev and Sraon should be ne in the city—the blacksmith has been there more than I, it seems—but it sounds as if Gwendolyn could use our help.” “Annev needs our help.” Titus looked at erin. “You’re stil coming to Luqura, right, erin?” e scrawny boy pitched his apple core away. “I’m with you two—til Annev melts us al , anyway.” He laughed at his own joke, though no one else shared his mirth. “Okay,” Sraon said, resigned. “Brayan, wil you stay and help Dolyn?” “Certainly. Might be I can help with her forge work, and that’s not something the boys are apt to do.” “Good enough. ere’s one last issue to discuss, then. We’l be traveling with someone else—the soothsayer, Jian Nikloss, from the troupe of entertainers we saw earlier. Red-thumb has some business in Luqura. He can’t travel there himself, so we’re taking Jian in his stead.” “Why are we doing this?” Fyn asked, his hands resting on his sword belt. “Weren’t you just saying it’s dangerous to be around you?” “Yes,” Annev said, answering slowly, “but I don’t have much choice in the matter.” “Like hel you don’t.” “No, real y,” Annev said, his tone becoming more heated. “While you were with Brayan, someone tried to shoot me.” “What?” Titus dropped the reins he’d been hitching to the wagon. “Are you okay? What happened?” “So that’s what you two were talking about.” Fyn smirked as if he’d discovered some saucy secret. “So who was it? Did you kil them?” “Fyn,” Brayan rumbled. “ is isn’t the Academy. ere are di erent rules out here, and you need to learn them.” He looked at Annev. “So what did you do?” “Truthful y, not much,” Annev said, “ e shot came from over there.” He pointed to the al ey mouth just beyond the market square. “We chased them but could only nd their crossbow.” He stil wasn’t convinced the attack had been real, but he chose to fol ow Sraon’s advice and keep his suspicions to himself. “But why—” “Did you see—” “How did you—” Annev threw up his hands, halting their questions. “I’m ne—everything is ne. I knew someone would come after me. I just hoped it wouldn’t be til we reached the capital.” He looked at his companions puzzled faces and swore. “You al remember the monsters that destroyed Chaenbalu? ey were sent to the village by someone—by humans or maybe demigods, I don’t know—but they were meant to kil or capture me.” He waited another moment for that to sink in. “ e destruction of Chaenbalu hasn’t stopped the people who are after me. Today they sent a stranger with a crossbow. Tomorrow it could be poisoned potatoes, or an old woman with a knife, or some new devilry we’ve never seen before.” He paused, letting them see his sincerity. “When I nd out who’s hunting me, I’m going to end them. Til then, I’ve got assassins behind me, the godsdamned Hand of Keos hanging from my arm and a constant preoccupation with trying not to pick my nose or scratch my ass with it.” As a group, Annev’s companions stared at him in horror. Good, Annev thought. Give them something to think about. erin opened his mouth to say something then, and Fyn was just a heartbeat behind him, but Titus interjected before either boy could speak. “ at’s settled then. We’re de nitely not leaving you.” Fyn groaned and erin’s mouth snapped shut. Annev hoped to argue the point further, but he was then interrupted by a tug at his elbow. He turned and saw the gray-robed man standing just outside the circle of their discussion. It seemed he was stuck with the lot of them. “ is is Jian Nikloss,” Annev said, abandoning the argument. “Are you ready, Jian?” “Yes, Master Ainnevog.” He patted a black bag hanging from his waist and gestured to the larger drawstring knapsack slung over his shoulder. “I do not have a horse, but I wil not slow you down.” “He’s the Pale Man!” erin said, eyes widening. “ e Ghost Man with the dead eyes!” “ erin!” Sraon snapped. “Don’t be rude.” “It is not rude, Master Cheng.” Jian’s pink eyes slid to the blacksmith and then back to the wiry wide-eyed boy. “Avatar erin names me true. I am the Pale Man. e Ghost Man. I have other names and other masks too—Dead Eyes, Seer, Necromancer, Marrow-Lich—none of these names o end me, even when they are spoken in fear, hatred, or ignorance. ey are simply my names.” He looked at the rest of the group. “If I gave you names, would you fear or hate me? If I spoke the truths written on your faces, would you spit in mine?” He smiled, his teeth white as chalk. “Some would, I think—but I wil not say your names. Not unless you ask me to share them, or Master Ainnevog demands them.” Titus and erin exchanged looks with one another, neither one sure what to make of the soothsayer’s words. Sraon tugged on his eye patch and Fyn stayed silent, his hands rmly on his weapons belt. “Wel ,” Brayan said at last, breaking the silence, “I guess you’re the fel ow taking my place in the caravan.” e quartermaster extended his hand and Jian took it without hesitation, his blue-veined palm looking smal in the giant’s gentle grip. “ at is a new name,” Jian said, smiling broadly. “ ank you for bringing it to me.” “Er … you’re welcome.” Brayan glanced sideways at Sraon, one eyebrow raised, and nal y released the soothsayer’s hand and scratched his head. “Right then. I’l grab my war maul and, uh, maybe some supplies. at al right, Sraon?” e blacksmith nodded. “Wil you go straight to Dolyn’s?” “I think I might, yes. Feels strange walking the streets here—I’m used to skulking around at night, you know.” He shifted, his massive shoulders heaving in a bear-sized shrug. “I’m sure I’l get used to it.” He turned to Titus. “Take good care of the mare. You’re stil the Steward of Husbandry, after al .” Titus’s eyes were suddenly bright with tears. “We’l be back in a week, Brayan. We’l be quick.” “Sure,” Brayan said, sounding a little choked. “Just a week. Don’t worry if things stretch a bit, though. I’l be here waiting for you.” He forced a smile. “You’l nd Dolyn in the craftsmen’s district, Brayan. If you hurry, you might also run into those merrymakers Jian parted with. Seems they have business with her too.” “Do they now?” Brayan swiped his hammer and a sack from the wagon. “ at juggler puts on a good show. Wouldn’t mind seeing him perform some more—his sister too. Fastest ngers I’ve ever seen on a ute.” “Aye, better than Nikum, even!” Sraon winced as he spoke the dead carpenter’s name. In the silence that fol owed, Annev had the awkward sense that everyone was ghting not to stare at him. Because I’m to blame for everyone who died in Chaenbalu, he thought. It doesn’t matter that Nikum was murdered by the feurog or that I fought to protect him from the monsters. Somehow, they’re al my fault. e babes in the Academy’s nursery. e students and the witwomen. e farmers, masters, and ancients. ey’re al my fault … Instead of meeting their non-gazes, Annev looked beyond Jian, past the market and toward the city’s southern gates. e mil ing crowd l ed his vision, and he tried to banish his memories of the destruction he had caused. He blinked. at girl in the crowd … she looks familiar. en it dawned on him. She’s back. e ghost is back. “Odar’s bal s!” erin shouted, loud enough to spook the horse. “It’s Faith! Titus, are you seeing this?” e boy gestured at the girl Annev had seen: a young blond woman with a freckled nose and a ragged shift, a bundle clutched tightly in her arms. e light seemed to pass right through her, as her body did not obstruct Annev’s view of the market or of Banok’s town wal s. Titus shrieked. “She’s a ghost, erin! She fol owed us here from the woods.” “She’s stil carrying that dead baby,” Fyn said, his right hand shifting to his sword hilt. “Is she stil singing?” erin asked, his eyes locked on the shade now marching toward them. “She’s a ghost- witch!” Fyn snapped, his sword clearing his scabbard. “I bet she’s casting a hex now, to punish us for her death.” “Sraon,” Annev said, drawing the name out as he fought to keep the panic away. “Are you seeing this? She’s . . . glowing, right? And you can see right through her?” Faith’s specter stood just a score of paces away now, her eyes vacant, distant. e blacksmith nodded, his mouth agape. “Aye, lad. at’s what I’m seeing.” “How is this possible?” Sraon shook his head, eyes xed. “Dunno.” e girl’s clothes were torn and ragged. Her lips moved as she walked—as she stumbled—and Annev heard the rst echoes of a familiar tune. She’s de nitely holding a dead baby, Annev thought, unable to look away as she approached. And she’s singing the same song as before. Sad and sweet … about darkness and light. Somewhere on the opposite side of the square, a woman screamed and a clay jar shattered to the earth. In that same instant, the group’s trance seemed to break and the ghost gliding toward them winked out. Vanished. “Keos,” Fyn spat. “Is that ghost going to fol ow us al the way to the capital? I gured we’d left her in the Brake with al the other shadow magic.” Brayan was staring open-mouthed at the place the young woman had been standing, his grip white against the black wrapping of his maul. He licked his lips. “Right then. I’m o .” He shook as if trying to banish Faith’s ghost from his mind. “I’l , um … see you soon, Sraon.” e blacksmith’s eyes were tight. “Good luck, Master Brayan. Tel Gwennie I said hel o.” “Gwennie?” “Yeah. She loves that.” Brayan nodded absently, too distracted to catch the nature of Sraon’s joke. “I’l do that, Sraon. Safe travels.” He strode o , his sack of provisions forgotten on the ground where he’d dropped it. erin danced over, picked it up, and slung it back onto the cart. “Al right, boys! We’l need a brisk pace to get there. Master Nikloss, try and keep up, but do tel me if you need to ride. ese boys are al in their prime, so there’s no shame if you can’t match them.” “ ank you,” Jian said in his strange accent, his round eyes unblinking. “Are you also in your prime?” “Me? Oh, I do al my exercise with these.” Sraon exed his massive forearms and biceps. “I may not get winded easy, but my legs are my slowest part.” Jian’s pale lips pursed into a button of a smile. “No part of me is fast, but Fate propels my feet. I shal not slow your pace.” Sraon fel in front of the cart and took the horse’s reins. He clicked his tongue as he did so and the mare immediately fel into step with him, pul ing the wagon and its contents. Fyn strol ed beside the cart, and Titus and erin quickly fel in behind the wagon. Annev fol owed at a distance and Jian Nikloss soon trotted along beside him, his feet stepping quiet on the earth and cobblestones. “A strange vision,” Jian said once they had passed the gates and the trading post. “Who was the young woman?” “You saw her too? e blond girl with the torn dress?” “And the child,” Jian said, nodding. “ e poor babe sleeps deep. If it is not fed, I fear it wil die soon.” Annev’s steps faltered. “ e baby? You think it’s alive ?” “Without question.” Jian shifted his knapsack. “I have a talent of speaking with spirits, you wil remember, and the child wil become one soon. e girl too, if she does not let herself sleep.” “Can we help her? ere must be some way to reach her.” Jian shook his head. “Her path lies in another direction.” “But you say she’s on the brink of death?” “She has moved beyond death, Master Ainnevog. She has transcended, and your paths wil not cross again in this life.” Annev exchanged a look with erin, resigned. Faith was a ghost—they had al seen it—and Jian’s words did not help. “It would be lovely if she were stil alive,” erin said, his expression ful of mourning. “I know,” Annev said, placing a hand on the boy’s shoulder. “If I could, I’d bring them al back—al the innocents that died when the feurog attacked and the Academy fel ; al the infants from the nursery, and the acolyte children.” Annev glanced back at the city gates, half-believing their conversation would conjure the young woman’s ghost for a third time, forcing her spirit back into the ether. He peered through the thin cloud of dust rising behind them, but stil saw no one. As he returned his gaze to the road, though, he couldn’t shake the feeling that the witgirl’s dead eyes were lingering on his back, trailing them as their party fol owed the westbound road. CHAPTER TWELVE e sun had just passed its zenith when the group lost sight of Banok’s trading post, the rays warming their faces as they moved west along the East Road. Along the way, Annev took in the wide farmland and distant vil ages dotting the landscape, constantly searching for his rst glimpse of Luqura’s city wal s. He had seen the city from afar only once before, its parapets lit by lantern light and only barely visible from the top of the Brakewood’s tal est hil , and he was eager to repeat the experience. How long ago had that been? e last day of Regaleus had been Seventhday —the same night that he, Fyn, and Kenton had embarked on their mission to Banok—and though that seemed a lifetime ago, it had been less than two days. He had buried Sodar yesterday. Just a day ago the man had stil been alive. Sodar had died on the Firstday of Fourthmonth, and this week would have been the old man’s half-birthday. Annev let out a deep breath, al owing some of the pain of that loss to sink in. He had never stopped feeling it—not for a single minute since the priest had passed away—but he’d been ignoring it like a rotten tooth, too afraid to probe and see how deep the damage was. Maybe in a month or a year that pain would fade, but a day was nothing. Less than a blink in time, and every moment l ed with grief that he could not share or express. It choked him. He was surrounded by friends and companions, but he was also alone. Without Sodar, he would always feel alone. Annev slowed until he walked behind the dust cloud kicked up by the apple cart, then matched the cart’s brisk pace. Jian walked somewhere just ahead and to the side of him, as if uncertain whether to walk with Annev or join Titus and erin. As a result, he hung between the two, his pace faltering then picking up once more. Annev ignored him. He ignored the world rol ing by. e sounds of the road became muted and the conversations of his friends distant, as he remembered walking the Brakewood’s paths with Sodar, col ecting herbs, gathering rewood, and springing animal traps. He tried to think of the old man not as he wanted to remember him, but as he truly was. Surly. Always ready with his dry wit and his deep wisdom. Always trying to teach him something—especial y when he didn’t want to be taught. Annev knew he’d nd most of Sodar’s papers in the bottomless sack—not just his Speur Dún translation, but also the endless notes Sodar kept on every topic that interested him. Annev suspected not one of the priest’s lessons had disappeared when he died. In time, Annev would nd those notes and learn everything Sodar stil had to teach—he’d read every note, study every scribbled piece of chicken scratch—but not today. Today, Sodar’s lesson was one of mourning, and Annev feared it would be the hardest lesson the priest had taught him. “Sodar,” Annev breathed, saying the name just loud enough that only he could hear it. “I’m so angry at you. How can you be dead? You should be here, tel ing me how stupid I am without ever quite coming out and saying it. You should be here chiding me and pushing me … tel ing me how proud of me you are.” Annev pul ed his dragonscale cloak tight, the air around him feeling suddenly chil , and wiped a tear away. When he dropped his hand, he saw Jian was strol ing next to him once more. e Yomad was unsettlingly quiet. “It is di cult saying goodbye.” Annev didn’t care to explain. If the soothsayer truly spoke with spirits, he knew enough already. “You wil see him again.” “Excuse me?” “Your friend, with the strong heart and the wrinkled hands. You wil see him again.” Annev pressed his lips into a thin line, uncomfortable at Jian intruding on his grief. “I don’t think so, Master Nikloss. Sodar is with the Al -father now. I’l only see him again in dream, or in death.” Jian swept back his hood, nodding thoughtful y. “I heard spirits sometimes visit the dreams of the Kroserans. I did not know this was also true for your people. Have you seen him then? In dreams?” Annev shook his head. Jian nodded as if that were answer enough. “In my country, the dead do not visit us in dreams. We cal them to us in this physical life.” He gestured at the dirt road, the trees, the brown elds. “Our dead are al around us. We surround ourselves with death and gain strength from it.” “But you do not truly see your dead. ey are stil in the afterlife.” Jian shook his head. “Tacharan is not like the other Gods. He is not jealous of his treasures. He sends them to his children. We speak with our dead, we eat with them. ey are never far from us.” “ at’s . . . nice.” Annev fought to keep his tone neutral. “Your families must be quite large then. Lots of ghosts standing around, tel ing stories?” “In my household, yes, but this is rare. Fyn stepped up to Annev’s shoulder and whispered, “Don’t look now, but we’re being fol owed. Something—someone—has been trailing us through the orchards.” Annev fought the urge to turn his head. “How long?” “Since we left the estate.” Fyn gestured at the row of cherry trees marking the end of the Rocas Estate. “A pu of blossoms goes up, like something is throwing them in the air. Maybe running between the trees. Maybe jumping.” Annev felt sheepish not to have noticed it himself. “Where are they right now?” “About paral el with us. I think he or she aims to pass us, without being noticed. Keep an eye on that west orchard.” Annev did so, his eyes straining to peer sideways at the long rows of blooming peach trees that l ed the next noble family’s orchard. At rst he didn’t see anything, but as they moved past some owering fruit trees, Annev spotted a glimmer of green and brown rushing between the trunks of the orchard, its movement marked by the delicate pu of fal ing peach blossoms. He turned his head toward the movement, but as soon as he did, it stopped. “ ere,” Annev said, his voice low. “I can’t see it, though.” ey kept walking, erin trying to scare Titus with the imagined horrors they might encounter in the Low Quarter. Sraon punctuated the increasingly wild speculations with the reminder that the Ash Quarter and the Boneyard were in the northwestern corner of the city, whereas the Bottomless Cup lay to the south—but erin paid him no mind, describing charred ghouls, soot-blackened cannibals, and blood-spattered necromancers. Sraon cleared his throat at this last part, and it took erin a moment to realize Jian was smiling down at them from his horse, his pink eyes shining with silent amusement. “I … uh.” erin looked around for help but didn’t nd any. Final y, Jian saved him. “You are right to fear the Necromancer, Avatar erin, for those that deal in death rarely value life.” “But, um, aren’t you …” “A necromancer, yes.” “But you don’t, uh … you’re not that scary. I mean, you do look scary. Pale skin. Pink eyes. It’s creepy enough, right? But you don’t, uh . . . You just seem … I don’t know.” Jian nodded. “And if my mouth were covered in blood? Or a host of the undead fol owed, slaves eager to serve me, would you fear me then?” “Uh …” “Yes, I think you would—I know you would. Now understand, Avatar erin, that I value life and death equal y. I do not spend life easily, nor do I lightly cal upon those who have passed over to the realm of spirits. Life and death should both be respected.” Annev had one ear on the conversation while he watched for pu s of peach blossoms in the orchard to his left. He was fairly certain their tail was now ahead of them, for he no longer saw the uttering petals. e estates they were passing had begun to diminish in size and scope, and the brickwork road had transitioned back to cobblestones. Carriages had started to pass on either side of the road, and the city guard patrols had begun to give the group more careful inspections. Jian pul ed his hood close, once again taking on the role of a noblewoman with her retinue. ey had almost reached the plaza with the merfolk fountain when they were nal y chal enged, not by the city guard, but by a fat man wearing an open leather vest, its pockets festooned with heavy gold chains and oversized jewels. More than one chain snaked up from the man’s pierced nipples, their opposite ends tethered to his studded nose and bottom lip. “What is this rabble with an Ilumani slave on horseback?” e man shouted, waving his naked arms to gather the attention of both the nobility and the guard. “Rebels—no doubt! See how they hide their faces. How they carry their weapons in de ance of custom and conduct!” Annev frowned, noting that the speaker was himself wearing a sheathed scimitar and a pair of ornamental daggers. e man opened his vest wide, ngering the hilt of one dagger while his thumb stroked the chain piercing his esh. Annev wondered how he could hope to defend himself with such piercings, but then he noticed the caravan of warriors forming up behind the speaker and knew they would answer any cal s for violence. Like the chain-pierced warrior, these men were large, heavily muscled and carried scimitars of their own, but they were unencumbered by decorative piercings and chains of o ce. Instead, their swarthy skin was tattooed and their right shoulders were branded with the marks of their house and trade: a feral cat and a double-masted sailing vessel. Sraon stepped forward, his face dark as a storm cloud. “You dare to cal the Royal House of Cheng a rabble?” he barked. “On your knees, slaver!” e chain-festooned man hesitated. “I beg your pardon?” “You may not have it—on your knees!” Sraon spun, grabbed the hilt of the man’s scimitar and unsheathed the weapon in one uid motion. e guards that had been racing to answer their master’s summons came to an uncertain halt. “ is man has insulted the Royal House of Cheng. I demand an apology or I shal take his tongue.” e city guards looked at one another, as if convinced they were standing in front of a mad man. e Innistiul soldiers, however, seemed unsurprised by Sraon’s demand. Not one moved to unsheathe their swords. “Your lordship,” said one of the guards, “Not al of Innistiul’s customs are honored here. If you have a grievance with this man, you must take it up with the high judge or one of the local magistrates.” “Or the consulate,” Sraon said, straightening. “As this is a matter between slaving houses, Consul Anabo may resolve our dispute.” “ at would be … acceptable.” “Unless this man would like to apologize for his insult and withdraw his accusation. en he can keep his tongue and we can be on our way.” e slave captain sputtered. “Do you even know who I am? Why—” “Elar Kranak, Second Dan, Noble Lord of Innistiul.” e slaver’s mouth dropped open. “I … How do you know that?” “I am Sraon Cheng, First Dan, Archon of Innistiul.” He tapped the scimitar to the man’s jaw. “Now, on your knees and apologize, or I’l send these guards for the Lady Consul—and you know how that wil go.” Sraon stuck out his tongue and bit it. Elar paled and fel to his knees. “I am sorry, ah . . . Archon Cheng. Forgive me. I was told you were another.” He glanced at Jian who stil sat ahorse, eyes trained on the ground. “ is … foreigner you escort. May I ask—” “You may not.” Sraon threw the scimitar to the cobblestones in front of Elar. “I accept your apology and expect your tribute to make its way to our co ers. I wil let Magistrate Bliven know to expect it. Ten solari should be su cient.” Elar paused, halfway to his feet. “Ah … yes. Of course, Archon Cheng. Very gracious.” Sraon moved past the man, icking the gold chain attached to his left nipple and nostril. e slaver hissed in pain but said nothing, and the rest of the party fol owed Sraon through the plaza and then the Upper River District in silence. CHAPTER TWENTY Myjun woke to nd Oyru kneeling at her side, a mass of bloody black bandages heaped beside her. “Where am I?” she hissed, the mask seizing her emotions before she was ful y conscious. “South of the Brakewood. About a mile outside a town named Hentingsfort.” “ e Brakewood,” Myjun growled. “I was in the Vosgar … west.” “You were. And now you are here.” “But … the draken?” “A good question. I found your knife—what was left of it—but I do not think you kil ed the monster with it. Something else.” “It’s dead then.” She tried to relax and found the pain was too great. She forced herself to stand instead, and though it pained her more, she felt stronger for it. She thought of the blood drake, its snapping jaws clamping down and savaging her. She touched her bel y and was momentarily surprised to nd no scars, no sign of the damage the beast had done to her. “I kil ed it,” she whispered. “Yes.” “And it … kil ed me.” “Almost.” Oyru stood. “ e mask attempted to heal you, but the injuries were too great and its magic too slow. Your spirit entered the shadow realm and was prepared to move on to the World of Spirits. Instead, I brought your physical body to the shadow realm to reunite the two, and then I brought you back to the physical realm. Whole. Complete.” “How is that possible?” Oyru’s nger caressed her golden brow and temple. “ e mask’s power was not su cient to heal you, yet your body survived after your spirit had gone.” He tapped the gold mask. “Something else—some other power—was at work to heal you. While you were unconscious, I used the shadows to examine you and found a second piece of gold, embedded in your esh next to your eye.” Myjun raised a hand to the bridge of her nose, traced her left eye and touched her temple. “Metal,” she said, “in my head?” Oyru nodded. “It contained the blood of a Terran Inquisitor.” He stared at her. “Do you know how this shard found nd its way into you?” Myjun remembered her father standing between her and Annev, his arm held protectively in front of her as he blasted the one-armed keokum with his hel re wand. She recal ed her horror when Annev unleashed his fury on Tosan, his body suddenly consumed by liquid ame and demonic rage. Charred bits of her father’s hand and arm had blasted into her. She remembered the searing pain as her face ran hot with bloody re and the liquid metal of her father’s molten ring. Annev had scarred her—had ruined her—and then he had dropped her in that hole, sealing her away to be tortured by the monsters who had destroyed the vil age. “I was injured when the monsters captured me,” Myjun said, the hatred choking her throat. “ ey did something to my face—poured something on it.” “Aqlumera,” Oyru said, his voice neutral. “Liquid magic. It healed you and cursed you—but the Inquisitor blood came from somewhere else.” “My father,” she said, remembering the curse that he bore and the shame that she felt from it. “He had magic.” Oyru shook his head. “ is is di erent. You have an artifact buried in your skul , and it is augmenting the healing powers of your mask.” He stared at her, his eyes dark as waters beneath the new moon. “Where did the artifact come from?” “My father’s gold ring,” she said, the truth of it suddenly coming to her. “He claimed Odar had blessed him with the ability to sense when others were lying … but I suspected the ring might be an artifact. He was wearing it when Annev kil ed him.” “Could he also use the ring to heal himself?” “I don’t know,” Myjun said, swal owing the bile that rose in her throat. Speaking of Tosan brought back her father’s hypocrisy and his cursed blood. “My father believed artifacts could only be used by those with strong wil s and pure hearts. He said that he alone, the headmaster of the Academy, could be trusted to use them with prudence and piety.” She wanted to laugh, but instead she sneered. “He was a self-righteous, hypocritical bastard.” She spat, though without any saliva behind it—she had learned that lesson since donning her mask and she didn’t care to repeat it. “ at ring contained a blood-talent.” Oyru was unfazed by her anger. “And the aqlumera may have augmented that power.” “And the mask … ?” “Has augmented it further. Whatever your powers were before you became scarred, the combination of Inquisitor ring, aqlumera, and mask has made you something … exotic. Something unexpected.” “A monster—like you.” “You could say that.” Myjun sco ed. “It didn’t stop me from dying, though.” “You were only half dead—and that is an experience I can relate to.” He looked toward the elds at his left and then toward the Brakewood on his right. “It should not have been possible for you to slay the blood drake, not with its superior ability to heal. I am impressed.” He returned his gaze to Myjun. “Now for another test— three tests, actual y.” He twisted his ngers, icked his wrist and a bloody rag appeared in the palm of his hand. “I abducted a local farmer and hid him nearby. is belongs to him.” He tossed the rag to Myjun. “Hunt him down.” “ en what?” Myjun raised the cloth to her mask and inhaled. Even behind the gold metal, she could smel —could practical y taste—the blood. e coppery taste of rust. e bitter iron tang of life … and death. “Finding the farmer is the rst test. e second is to get answers from him.” “What questions would I ask a stupid farmer?” “You’l know when you nd him.” “And the third test?” “Something special—something that might explain how you kil ed that draken.” Myjun’s eyes narrowed. Her reaping clothes were blood-soaked, ragged and torn. Her body had healed, but the hunger and thirst she had felt while running through the Vosgar had been awakened once more. She ached for sustenance, for fuel … for pain. “I wil nd the farmer.” CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE Myjun studied the man tied to the chair, his face bruised, blood oozing from his scalp, shoulder, ribs, and arms. e hot, sticky scent of trickling blood left her feeling sick and horribly hungry. e desire for hot, dripping esh between her teeth made her tremble. She craved meat now more than she ever had. Something about its smel —the rawness of it—made her thrum with primal need. She had begun to suspect there was another way to feed herself, after she’d kil ed the dire wolves. She’d felt the rush of satisfaction, the barest al eviation of her hunger, and she’d become more certain while hunting the Vosgar’s other monsters. Myjun had to kil . Denying the urge was like refusing to eat. e mask’s magic could channel her hunger pains into its own sustenance, but that was weak broth when what she craved was red meat. e need to kil cal ed to her, tempting her with the promise of stolen strength. Myjun knew she wasn’t a vampyr . . . but she couldn’t deny that she was becoming a monster. e farmer’s legs and arms were bound by thick cords of shadow, their nethereal bers as strong as steel. He was gagged with the other half of the bloody cloth Oyru had given her to track him, and when Myjun tossed her scrap on the oor, the man’s attention icked to where she lurked in the shadows. His eyes searched the darkness for her, stopping when he saw the glint of the golden mask stained with bloody tears. He shed his own tears then. ey streaked down his cheeks, wetting his fuzzy white stubble. He sobbed, shoulders hunched, and a feeling of disgust bloomed in Myjun’s bel y. is man—this creature—was less than human. She saw that with clarity now; this farmer was as inferior as the prey that cowered before the hunter. “What …” he sobbed, unable to form the words. “Wha … what do you want?” Myjun watched him, the shadows lengthening inside the old barn. Chickens clucked outside and a horse snorted from a nearby stal . She caught the scent of a milk cow further down, its udders ful to bursting, and the man sobbed again. She remained silent. Truthful y, she had no answer for him, and even if she had, she doubted that she would have given it. She hated him for his weakness—hated him for reminding her of her own weaknesses. “Find out where his family is hiding.” Myjun had known he would come, had sensed his nearness—not quite a physical presence, but close enough that it did not matter. “You ask him.” e words cankered her mouth, her lips dry from lack of water. “No,” Oyru said, appearing beside her, “this is your second test.” Myjun stepped from the darkness into the square beam of light that shone through the barn’s open loft. “Tel me where your family is,” she hissed. “I don’t have any family. Just me.” His face was streaked with dirt, his cheekbones purple-black in the darkness. “I don’t believe you. Where is your family?” she repeated. “Gone.” “Gone where ?” She felt the heat rising behind her mask, her temper aring. “ ey are gone,” his voice quavered. “Please. Don’t hurt them.” Myjun studied him, seeing if the magic inside her would respond to his words. She felt nothing, though, and she turned the frustration of that failure upon the farmer. “You’re lying to me,” she said, stepping closer. “You try to save them—to protect them—but your lies only endanger them.” “Please, let me go. I’ve done nothing wrong!” “I don’t care,” Myjun said, surprised that she spoke the truth. “I don’t care if your hands are stained with the blood of a thousand women and children.” “I would never—” I don’t care,” she repeated, “if you are the world’s holiest saint. I don’t care if you’re a dutiful father and a loving husband.” She leaned forward, whispering into his ear. “I don’t care.” “ en why do this to me?” the man blubbered. “Why ask for them?” Myjun sni ed. She had asked because Oyru had told her to … which made her uncomfortable. Why did the assassin want to know about the farmer’s family? “Tel me where they are,” she repeated, “or I wil gut you like a sh and hang your bloody bits for them to nd when they return.” “No! Please, you can’t. My wife … my children.” He sobbed. She looked back at Oyru, then gestured in disgust at the wailing creature tied to the chair. “What is the point of this?” “Did he tel you the truth?” “He hasn’t told me anything.” “ en you are failing the test. You hunted him. Now catch the scent of the truth and track it down.” “It is not the same thing,” she growled. “Try harder. Find the truth.” Myjun studied the shadow mage’s dark silhouette. Find the truth, she thought, her anger with Oyru and the farmer growing hotter by the moment. Damn them both. I’l tear the truth from his bloody corpse. She turned back to the farmer, her green eyes smoldering. “Tel me where they are,” she urged, her voice near as cold as the assassin’s, “and I wil let you go.” “Wh-why are you doing this?” “Ah-ah.” She reached for the farmer’s throat, her ngernails tracing his jaw and jugular. “I ask the questions. Now tel me.” She paused. “Tel me … the name of your cow.” “ e what?” She raked her ngernails across his face. “No questions,” she hissed. “Just tel me … the name of your cow.” “G-G-Gertie,” he stuttered. “Her name. G-Gertie.” “Gertie,” Myjun repeated, her senses open to the truth he spoke. “ at’s a good name. I believe you … ?” “Da-David. e name’s David. Folks cal me Old Davey.” “Old Davey,” Myjun repeated. It seemed true enough, though she couldn’t say what made her sure of it—her gut, maybe. Or perhaps it was magic. “Old Davey,” she said again. “And you’re married?” “Y-yes.” True again. She was getting the sense of it now. “And you have children.” “Yes.” “ ank you for being honest, Davey. I hate it when people to lie to me. Bad things happen. You understand?” “Yes.” He seemed to be calmer now, the answers coming easier. “Excel ent. And their names, Davey.” “Sam, Palmer, Little Deidre … and Dawn.” True again, she thought, though it rankled not to know how or why she knew. Time for the tougher questions … Davey’s voice cracked and the pleading leaked back into his voice. “By the Gods, they’re just children. ey’ve done nothing— I’ve done nothing.” “Shhh.” She slid a nger down his lips, pressing them closed and fol owing her intuition. “Now tel me, Davey, this family you love so much. Did you save them, or did they abandon you? Did they run when my shadowy companion captured you?” e farmer sagged. “How do you know these things? Who are you?” Myjun slapped him. Hard. Davey’s head reeled, his eyes spinning. “I ask the questions,” she growled. “Forget again and I wil start spil ing guts over this barn. Understood?” “Yes, yes! Dear Gods, merciful Odar. Please, yes!” “Good,” she purred. “You see how easy it is to tel the truth?” “Yes,” he said, head lol ing as if drunk on his terror. “Yes. Yes, God—I see.” “Oh, I’m not your god, Davey. Your god, the Al -father, has abandoned you right now—but I am here, and I am very real.” She leaned close, her mask just inches from his face. “So tel me now—tel the truth. Where is your family?” e farmer hesitated—just for an instant—then shook his head. Myjun’s intuition screamed at her. He knows exactly where they are. e truth of it was clear to her, just as it had been clear when he was lying. “Tel me where you sent them! Which farmhouse are they hiding in? Which aunt did you send them to?” Davey’s eyes widened, but he said nothing. Myjun’s temper ared at his silence. She snatched up a pair of sheep shears, stepped back, and snipped o the man’s left nger. At his scream, she snipped more. Snip. Snip. Snip. Four ngers gone, and now he was choking on the tears and the pain. Myjun only stared at him, her anger stil hot, her rage stil rising. “Tel me now—and if you lie, I wil start on your other hand.” Despite al the blood, Myjun’s voice was level. “Where have they gone?” “My sister’s home,” he wept, “in Hentingsfort. Dear Gods, have mercy, please.” Myjun stared at him, her brow furrowed in concentration. e man had spoken the truth … but not the whole truth. Something was wrong. Something was missing. What was it? A truth and a lie perhaps? She drove back her anger at being lied to before she jammed the shears into his neck. Instead she steadied herself, forced him to look her in the eyes. “You lied to me.” “It’s the truth, I swear it!” False. Something about the man—a dim glow that seemed to pulse as he spoke—suggested he was lying to her stil . She gritted her teeth and shook her head. “ ey are with … the sister of your dead wife Charlyn—but they are not in Hentingsfort? ey are further east of us … along the Brakeroad.” “Witch,” the man breathed, his voice strangled, choked. “You’re a damn witch! Why do you care? What do you want from us!” She swung her arm back and drove the shears point- rst into Davey’s neck —or would have, had Oyru not caught her by the wrist and saved the farmer’s life. “He lied,” she hissed, pul ing her hand free, “and he disobeyed me.” “ e mask is making you act rashly. You must control your emotions.” She wanted to punch the shears into the assassin’s face. Instead, she stil ed her shaking hand and glanced at the farmer. “What do you care for him? He’s nothing— less than nothing.” “How did you know about Charlyn and Hentingsfort?” Myjun hesitated. “I don’t know,” she said, answering truthful y. Oryu studied her more closely then nodded. “How did you know he lied?” “ e light,” she said, unthinking. “It pulsed around him.” “Was the light there before he lied?” “I don’t know. Maybe.” She considered it. “Yes, but I had not noticed it.” “Look at him now. What do you see?” Myjun stared at the farmer, his mutilated hand bleeding onto the oor, his face pale, almost white. If his ngers weren’t tended to he could bleed to death. Myjun hu ed—he had lied to her—and she was about to look away when she noticed a icker of color around him. A silhouette of light she had thought was simply the glare from the sunbeam overhead. She squinted at it now, xed on it, trying to see it … but there was nothing to see. It was only an impression, an aura that she observed less with her eyes and more with … something else. She wasn’t sure what. “He’s glowing. ere’s some kind of aura surrounding him.” “Describe it.” “Yel ow? Maybe white. It has … streaks of blood in it. Red and pink.” “And when he lied?” She thought about it. She hadn’t real y seen colors—it was something she had felt more than saw. So what color did it feel like? What did it remind her of? “Not black … not purple,” she said at last. “Something between the two.” “You have a talent for auramancy,” Oyru said, nodding. “I cannot see it, but I feel the inverse of it. It is the opposite of shadow magic—the dark and the light.” “And?” “And,” Oyru continued, smoothly materializing so that his face became corporeal, a oating head amidst the darkness, “that means you have a talent for auramancy and soulriding—and, if the blood wyrm’s death is any indication, bladesinging. at is a rare combination. Very rare, when your father was only half Ilumite. You most likely possess the fourth Ilumite blood-talent as wel : lightslinging.” He pointed at the farmer. “It should be easy to execute him with your magic.”

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.content: Myjun sco ed. “What magic?” “You summoned soul re blades to kil the draken. It burned out its eyes.” He pointed at her. “With the ful Ilumite talent, you can conjure re and blades of light, you can throw lightning. You can bend the light around yourself—turn invisible—or you can re ect it and create il usions. Some of those skil s wil be hard to master and some wil come natural y, but as my apprentice you wil master them al .” She stared at the assassin. “I can’t do any of that. Not a damn piece of it. Besides,” she added, not caring in the slightest, “your farmer is dead. You let him bleed out.” Oyru shook his head. “Half dead is not truly dead.” And with that, he stuck his hand through the farmer’s chest and gave Old Davey’s heart a squeeze. e man’s eyes shot open and he screamed as if woken from a nightmare—except this was the nightmare, and Oyru would not let him leave it so easily. e Shadow Reborn slid his hand free then pointed at the terri ed farmer, the blood from Davey’s severed ngers slowly pooling at his feet. “Kil him,” he said, “using your magic. Use your soul re blades, or re, or lightning. I don’t care how, only that you do it.” “ is is the third test?” “Yes.” Myjun sni ed. “Fine.” She stomped over to the dazed farmer whose eyes were already drifting closed, and slapped him across his weather-beaten face. His eyes popped open once more, and he spat at her. In an instant rage, her hands reached for his throat. “ !” Myjun stopped, frozen by the intensity of Oyru’s voice. e cold apathy that always marked the man’s speech had vanished, replaced by a piercing anger. And then, quick as a summer storm, it disappeared. e iciness returned, harder than before. Colder. “Do not touch him. Feed your anger and frustration into him, al your pain and re. Lash him with it. Burn him with it.” Myjun stared at the dying farmer, his face bloodless, his body slack and unmoving. She felt little anger for the man—disgust and hatred, yes, but her rage had subsided as the man’s life-force ebbed away. She did feel frustration, though—a tiny ower of hatred that burned with the re of being unable to kil the man, of not being al owed to strangle him. She was angry at Oyru, angry that he believed she could do this, angry that he could compel her to do it. And yet … she had done it before. She tried to remember how, to draw out the memory. Blood and claws. Teeth and scales. Beetles gnawing at her esh, the acid-blood spewing from the draken’s mouth. Burning and pain, the frustration and anger as its jaws clamped down on her, piercing her esh. Myjun dug deeper, immersing herself in the pain of the moment—that moment when she longed to die but continued to live. She screamed, the sound ripping from her throat. She screamed and screamed … Light sparked in her hands—tiny ames, white-hot and incandescent—and then they winked out. Myjun panted with exertion, her voice raw with emotion. “Beautiful,” Oyru whispered, standing in the dark once again. “Absolutely beautiful.” “Pointless,” Myjun snapped. “A useless spark.” “Not so.” Oyru gestured at Old Davey who had fal en silent once again, the blood stil dripping from his severed ngers, but slower … slower … “Try taking his pain and fear—and using them to fuel your magic.” “I don’t . . .” Myjun stared at the farmer, watched the aura around him begin to dim. Could she do it? She knew pain fueled her mask and made her stronger, faster—but could she steal that same pain, those same emotions, from other people? Could she turn their pain into her strengths? A spark lit inside her, its intensity fueled by the possibility, by the need to try … To burn. To break. Myjun reached out to the dying farmer, al owing her emotions to feed o his. It was easy—easier than she expected. She felt the man’s aura peel away from him and Davey’s eyes ew open, more horror in his face than she had ever seen during her interrogation. He screamed at her, terri ed. “What are you doing!” Rage. Pain. Frustration. Disgust. Hatred. Al of his emotions were hers, channeled through her, strengthening her—and as her power grew, his fear grew too. Terror. Pain. Fear. Agony. Despair. An endless feedback loop that fed the spark inside her until it blossomed into a ame. at ame found its home in her arms, condensing, sharpening as twin points of light sprang from her palms—sharp white blades of pure spirit, an aura of emotion and re, light and energy. e blades grew into daggers … into swords. She realized she was screaming, was venting her pain with her ragged and intense voice, as sharp and piercing as any blade. Old Davey screamed too, his pale face l ed with a terror as pure as her hatred. en she struck, her soul re blades scissoring together to snip the farmer’s head from his shoulders. His skin burned as they slid into his esh, his eyes bursting into ame, an otherworldly light pouring from his mouth. e pain that l ed Myjun’s body, the hunger that penetrated her soul, suddenly evaporated in place of a sense of ful ness. e sensation startled her, awakening her senses to a world that had grown dul beneath the endless aches and pains. She was not hungry. She was not thirsty. She was … alive with the rush of life and a feeling of ful l ment, the thril of having taken a life and being given one. Beneath it al , she stil felt the in uence of the mask—the sharp need for pain and the malice that accompanied it—but these were distant now, their sharpness abated by the euphoria of the moment. And suddenly they were gone—the rush, the joy, the thril —al vanished. Her hunger and thirst were stil diminished, but alongside a void, a wide chasm of need … and a new kind of hunger that would not be satis ed by food or water. “You would be a Soulblade, I think—a Soulrider and a Bladesinger—but the aqlumera and the Inquisitor ring have tainted your magic.
