If true, this might have been the impetus for Kranak’s later betrayal of both the university and the city … but we shal leave such unfounded speculation to lesser scholars. What has been con rmed beyond doubt is Valdemar Kranak’s role in the destruction of the university, and the razing of Neven nan Su’ul and the province of Gorm Corsa. Terran propagandists have attempted to paint Kranak as a benevolent intel ectual who was later demonized by the Halcyon Knights, but public record and the eyewitness testimonies show he was instrumental in bringing the Terran Bloodlords to the city, precipitating the retreat of the Darite Empire from Gorm Corsa and the rest of Eastern Daroea (now New Terra). e evidence suggests Kranak began by fomenting unrest among the student populace around the beginning of the ird Age.† Having gained support among the university’s more radical students, Kranak began hosting nightly lectures questioning the accuracy of certain Darite history books, which were already disputed by Terran scholars. e content of these lectures became more and more occult, with at least one claiming that Neven nan Su’ul had been founded by the Terrans rather than the Darites. As the Terrans pressed further and further west, expanding beyond Terra Majora and into Eastern Daroea, Kranak’s lectures led to heated disagreements with other magisters which (in a few cases) escalated to physical blows. It is unclear when Valdemar Kranak’s lectures descended from genuine scholarship into Terran propaganda, but the surviving records of censure state the magister was brought before Arch Lector Gale-Dana’y and ordered to stop questioning the Empire’s doctrine. As ordered, Kranak disbanded his evening classes, only to be suspended when he was discovered meeting privately with students to further his pro-Terran agenda. On his return to the university fol owing his suspension, reports indicate Kranak was a changed man: his lectures had been sanitized of al their former in ammatory content and he publicly disavowed the arguments he had made in support of the Terran government. e change would be utterly remarkable, were it not for our own knowledge of Kranak’s later betrayal. Many scholars, including my col eague Alice Quenby, have argued that Valdemar Kranak was approached by Dortafola during his suspension, and invited to join what later became the Siänar. is is a persuasive argument, particularly as the dates of Kranak’s suspension align with what little we know of the Siänar’s rst creation. —“ e Siänar,” e Complete Histories of Luquatra by Kyartus Gairm † Kash Mikla, a survivor from the razing of Neven nan Su’ul, claims to have seen Kranak leading a cavalry of Bloodlords against the university’s own students (a testimony that has since been widely debunked as no mounts were used during either the city’s siege or the nal rout of its citizens); on the other hand, the folk poem “Vaul of the Fal ” describes Kranak as a scholar whose “love of the masses brought death to his classes when nechraict rose up from their graves,” suggesting that necromancy played an integral part in the city’s nal destruction. Final y, Crystal Gooden—one of my esteemed col eagues from Southmarch—has suggested Kranak used Terran shadow magic to in ltrate and attack the university, giving rise to his later moniker “ e Shadow.” It seems more likely, though, that Kranak’s nickname arose from his ability to silently pass through the university’s hal s (a common e ect produced by most Breathbreakers). CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO Fyn plucked the apple from the vendor’s cart without breaking stride and continued his strol along the River District’s promenade, a wide road that hid the underground canal connecting Luqura’s two rivers. Commerce was brisk here, and the guards were plentiful, but the opportunities for l ing his pockets vastly outnumbered his chances of getting caught. By contrast, the merchant and noble districts had too many eyes watching their vendor stal s and too many swords guarding the nobles’ purses. He’d noticed the mansions were less wel -guarded, though—and contained greater riches besides—so Fyn entertained himself with the idea he might rob the homes of Luqura’s upper class at night, while picking pockets and lifting goods from its lower class during the day. People in the Ash Quarter tended to carry their most valuable possessions on themselves, anyway—their burned hovels being too insecure to leave valuables unprotected and unmolested. Al Fyn needed was a base of operations, and a gang to speed his acquisition of wealth and power. Territory was easiest to take in the Ash Quarter—it was free, if he could keep and defend it—so he’d spent most of his rst two days scouting the Lower District for a good headquarters. He had found a promising corner that was wel away from the Boneyard and just a few blocks south of the unburned portions of the Lower District, and he was trying to settle on a tenement when he sensed someone—several someones from the sound of it—approaching from behind. Instead of turning or eeing, Fyn took his time eating his apple and continued his strol down the trash-littered street. At the rst blind al ey, he turned and ducked inside, knowing his pursuers would be close behind. As he melted into the shadows, he checked his weapons and waited for the expected ambush. He didn’t have to wait long. Six thugs appeared at the mouth of the al ey, their leader at the front, sni ng for blood. “Is it that same one you saw yesterday?” the largest one asked. He carried a heavy, rounded stick that resembled a battered rol ing pin, and his face looked almost cherubic in spite of his imposing gure. “Shh,” the leader hissed, his eyes darting around the al ey, searching for Fyn. “Don’t spook him, Siege.” “What’s to spook?” a third one said, a buxom woman as large as the man with the rol ing pin—probably bigger—carrying what looked to be a sherman’s ga . Of the three that hadn’t spoken, one hung back, presumably to guard the mouth of the al ey, and the other two shot forward, exploring the shadows and hoping to ank their prey. Fortunately for Fyn, he’d chosen this exact al ey yesterday with the purpose of anking them. He smiled from his hidden vantage point, circling behind the group and approaching the man they’d left as their lookout. Halfway into the darkened al ey, Siege gave a whoop as a snare tangled his foot and pul ed his legs out from under him. On cue, Fyn yanked a hidden rope and a sack ful of bricks dropped onto the woman with the ga , knocking her weapon from her hands and quite possibly knocking her out entirely. “It’s a trap!” the leader bel owed, doubling back to the al ey mouth. “Quinn! Way! Grab Siege and Poli and get the hel out of—” Fyn swatted the back of the man’s skul with an improvised slapjack and sent him sprawling atop the body of his unconscious lookout. “So you’re the infamous Fisher King,” Fyn said, leaning over the fal en gure, “the Serpent of South Ashes … the Terror of Tumbledown Street.” He gave a dry laugh then kicked the man between the legs—hard. “Oof!” Fisher doubled over on himself. Fyn glanced back down the al ey, his cold eyes meeting Quinn’s as she helped the larger woman, Poli, clamber out from beneath the bricks. Siege had nearly freed himself from his snare and was searching for his cudgel, which seemed to have rol ed away when he’d fal en. Meanwhile, the sneaky one— Way—had slipped a knife from his pocket and was slowly advancing in Fyn’s direction. “Should have thrown that at my back while I was kicking Fisher. Since you didn’t, either you don’t know how to throw, you have no intention of actual y kil ing me … or you’re scared shitless.” “I ain’t scared of a little chickenshit like you,” Way swore, stil advancing. “What are you? Twelve? Probably don’t even have hair on your fruits.” “Given the choice between my fruits and his …” Fyn kicked the Fisher King in the head, knocking him out cold. “I think I’l stick with mine—hairy or not.” “You got a mouth on you, don’tcha?” “Very observant—now let’s move this along.” Fyn nodded at Way’s weapon. “You gonna throw that or am I gonna take it from you?” e lithe man snickered, though he checked to make sure Siege and the others were backing him up. “I think I’l wait til you start running, then I’l throw it at you.” “You’d miss—and I’m not running.” “We outnumber you, boy. Poli’s got reach with her ga there, and you don’t want to mess with Sigs. Jol y sort, but he’s a kil er an’ no mistake. Arms like a bul . Crush your skul like an egg.” Fyn noticed the man didn’t mention their other associate, Quinn, who was scaling the rightmost building in an attempt to get behind him. Amateurs. “Bul s don’t have arms, asshole—and I’m getting bored.” He hurled his apple core at the man’s face, distracting him just as Quinn leapt from the shadows. He had expected a knife thrust, a hammer-blow or a hatchet-swing— he’d seen the crew use al three in the day and the night he’d been stalking them—but Quinn surprised him with heavy gloves ending in curved iron nails shaped to look like bear claws. Tekko-Kagi, Fyn realized, dodging the attack. Very interesting. Quinn swung again and Fyn stepped aside, placing the young woman between him and Way. When she swung a third time, he stepped into the attack, grabbed Quinn’s wrist and thrust his hips. e smal woman’s feet came o the ground and Fyn spun, slashing her other clawed hand at Way. e sneak cursed, stepped back and tried another angle. is time, Fyn tossed Quinn over his shoulder and into Way, sending both attackers sprawling. “You lot work for me now,” Fyn said, not even winded. “Your contract with the Fisher King has ended.” “Rot that,” Poli said, her ga hook extended. “I’m going to gut you like a sh, boy. No one drops bricks on me and walks away.” Instead of answering, Fyn reached down and plucked a smal purse from Fisher’s tunic. He jingled it in one hand then tossed it to Siege. “What’s your cut of the loot?” “Rule of quarters,” Siege answered, eyeing the sack in his hand with equal parts greed and suspicion. His rol ing pin disappeared into his tunic. “One-quarter for us. ree-quarters for Fisher. He says it’s for the guild—to pay them for the right to work the street.” “ at’s a new one,” Fyn said, snorting. “So who’s in on it? e city watch? e ieves Guild?” “Only one guild matters,” Poli said, lowering her ga . “ e Slavers Guild.” “You’re not from around here, are you?” Quinn said. “Like you can talk. Where’d you get those?” He gestured at the Tekko-Kagi. “You make them? Steal them?” e woman hissed at him in response, her black hair fal ing to cover half her face. “He’s de nitely not from around here,” Way said, slapping Quinn on the shoulder. “Ain’t you never seen the Pits?” he said, studying Fyn. “ ey put ’em on ghters al the time. Makes ’em look erce.” “Only they don’t know how to use them,” Quinn whispered. “And you do?” e woman nodded, her clawed hands crossed in front of her chest. Fyn studied the group, watching their body language for another attack. “You’re Quynh-Chi, though they keep cal ing you Quinn. My guess is you’re Kroseran, with the Tekko-Kagi. You brought here as a slave?” e woman didn’t respond, though she did lower her hands to her sides. “Ford Siegeman,” Fyn continued. “Siege—or Sigs. What’d you do before Fisher brought you into his gang? Work in a bakery or something?” Siege grinned. “Me and Poli worked the docks—I do like to bake, though. You ever eaten pizza pie?” Siege’s smile grew. “It’s Darter food—delicious.” “Maybe you can bake me one sometime.” “Heh. You nd me an oven and the right ingredients, I’l bake a score of ’em.” “What’s Darter food?” “Darite-Terran,” Way said, thumbing his chest. “I’m a Darter. David Sanhueza. People cal me Way.” “I had gured that’s ’cause you help Fisher nd the way into places.” Way shrugged. “I do that too. How long you been fol owing us? What do you want?” “Long enough—and I want to be your new crew leader.” e others shared a look, a few of them glancing at Fisher, who was starting to stir. Siege hefted the bag of coins, considering. “Why would we fol ow you?” He studied the maces, falchion, and other weapons strapped to Fyn’s body. “You cut a mean gure with al those blades, but you’re half Fisher’s age.” “I’m twenty,” Fyn lied. “And if he’s over forty, it’s time he started looking for softer work.” “Kil him,” Fisher coughed, rising to his knees and elbows. “Stop chatting the bastard up and kil him!” “ ey could try,” Fyn said, not bothering to look at the fal en crew chief. “Or I could tel them where you’re hiding that extra coin you claim is for the Slavers Guild.” Poli frowned, her grip tightening on the ga . “ at true, Fisher?” “He’s lying!” Fisher rose to his feet, slid a butcher knife from his coat and waved it at the rest of the group. “You know Neldon checks the books. He’d tel you if I wasn’t square.” “Would he?” Way asked, taking a step toward Fisher. “Neldon’s from your old crew. Maybe he’s in on the take. It’d be nice to ask him, only he seems to be sleeping on the job.” He nodded at the unconscious lookout then glanced at Fyn. “You kil him?” “I don’t kil people for doing their jobs—not even if they’re bad at it.” “What’s that supposed to mean?” Fisher said sharply, taking a step in Fyn’s direction. “People talk, Fisher.” Fyn had no idea what he was talking about—he’d only been in Luqura for a few days, and that wasn’t enough time to gather much more than gossip. He had a hunch, though, and he was fol owing it. “Wait for Neldon to wake up,” Fyn said, planting his feet. “He’l tel you what real y happened to the old gang. After that, I bet you won’t want to fol ow him.” Fisher charged, butcher-knife- rst. Fyn stepped wide of the blade, catching the crew leader’s wrist. He pul ed Fisher forward, carrying his momentum in an arc as he dipped his knee and guided the man’s knife up under his ribs and into his own chest cavity. e bald man coughed, eyes wide, as hot blood started to pump from his chest, his raggedy shirt soaked in sticky redness. Fyn let go and Fisher dropped to his knees, blood spurting from between his lips. He col apsed and the rest of the gang stared open-mouthed at their dead chief. “ e way I see it,” Fyn said, stepping smoothly away from the convulsing body, “you have three choices. One: you can attack me now—and when I’ve nished kil ing al of you, I’l look for another crew to become my gang. Two: you fol ow me, and I’l earn you more money than the Fisher King ever could.” “And the third option?” Way said, stil clutching his dagger. “ ree: you walk away—for now. I’l nd another gang and start claiming territory. Eventual y, though, we’l be back to one and two. You can join me now and get the early reward … or I can bury you and build my empire on your ashes.” Siege and Poli exchanged a look and Fyn knew he had them. Way would fol ow the majority—he seemed to be the cautious type—and Neldon didn’t get a vote since he was unconscious. at left Quinn. Fyn watched her, and she was studying him in turn, chewing her lip, her almond eyes icking to the anged maces on Fyn’s back. “Even shares for everyone in the crew?” “No. I get three shares, and my second gets a share and a half. Everyone else gets one.” “Who’s your second?” “One of you, I suppose. I’l let the ve of you decide whom you trust the most.” “Neldon,” Siege said, and Poli nodded her agreement. “ e lookout?” Fyn was skeptical. “He’s our medic,” Way said, sheathing his knife. “Used to be a scholar, a doctor. Something like that. Fel on hard times and ended up in the Ashes with the rest of us.” “Does he ght?” “If he needs to, he can throw a decent punch. Got a terrifying manubal ista he uses for bigger jobs. Usual y he keeps the books, though. Patches us up when we get hurt. Talks to the guild if Fisher’s busy.” “Al right,” Fyn said, wiping his hands on his trousers. “Neldon it is. Of my three shares, one goes into a strongbox for funding bigger jobs.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.content: Quinn frowned. “What about the guild?” “What about them? ey can go hang themselves.” e ve gang members looked at one another and sheathed their weapons. Quinn sco ed, spat, and went to check on Neldon. Fyn eyed them, feeling he’d missed something. “You don’t get it,” Way said, stepping close enough that Fyn kept an eye on the man’s hands. “ e guild controls most of what happens in the Ash Quarter, the Undercity, the Boneyard—even the Low Quarter and the River District. Everything except the Merchant and Noble Quarters—and they’re close to control ing them too. If you ignore the guild, they’l send the Watchers after you.” He shook his head. “You can keep your shares and your delusions. No one crosses the guild.” e rest of the group shouldered past, and Fyn realized he was losing them. He had to think quick. “You know the lizardman who works for the guild—some keokum freak? Me and my last crew nearly kil ed him.” e gang froze. Neldon was starting to wake and Siege helped him to his feet. “You’re blowing smoke and ashes,” Quinn said, her voice husky. “No one crosses the guild—and no one ghts Saltair and lives.” “Ask around. We cut o his tail and his hand. Might be you can even nd the pieces somewhere. I hear he can grow them back—but we stil got him.” He sucked at his teeth. “ ink about it. If you want to join my crew, be back here in three days and I’l tel you what I have in mind.” e gang bled away into the street with Neldon tottering between Siege and Poli. Way hung back, taking in Fyn’s weapons, his clothing and his face. Final y, he inclined his head. “ ree days?” “Yeah.” “And you’ve got a plan.” “I do.” Way grunted. “You got a name?” “Fyunai. People cal me Fyn.” “Fyn,” he said, trying the name on his lips. “Fyn the Feared … Fatal Fyn.” A queer smile quirked his lips. “I’l ask around about Saltair. If what you say is true … wel , then count me in.” Fyn inclined his head and the man slunk away, rejoining his gang. Once they were al gone, Fyn gave a deep sigh, looked down at Fisher’s body … and threw up. It wasn’t the sight of the corpse, nor did he feel guilty about murdering the crew chief—the way Fyn saw it, he’d had it coming. No, what made Fyn spray his lunch across the al ey was having no idea what to do about the Slavers Guild or their stranglehold on Luqura’s underworld . . . and he had exactly three days to create a workable plan. It almost made him wish Annev were stil in the city. Almost. Fyn wiped the vomit from his lips and steadied himself against the wal . A utter of movement caught his eye and he looked up to see a lithe gure in a raven mask staring down at him—watching. From the Slavers Guild? Fyn wondered, remembering Way mentioning their Watchers. But if the Raven worked for the guild, she gave no indication of it. Instead, she tilted her head, saluted him with two ngers, and slid the mask from her face. “ e hel ?” Fyn swore. e black-clad woman danced away across the roof of the building and disappeared from sight. Fyn watched her go in disbelief. He couldn’t imagine why she would be fol owing him—or why she’d have any interest in him after eeing Janak’s palace with the Rod of Compulsion. Yet he suspected he’d see Sodja Rocas again in the not-too-distant future—a thought that was not altogether unpleasant. CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE e stars were bright overhead as Sodja walked among the cherry trees surrounding her family’s estate. She reached the edge of the orchard and drifted over to the pool of super red arowana, the gleam of gold and copper scales beneath the water reminding her of the ames that had consumed Janak’s study during her escape with the Rod of Compulsion. Sodja touched that rod now—cool, slender, and heavy in her pocket—and she thought of her encounter with the three thieves who had started the re. at had been six days ago—and only four days since the thieves from the Brakewood had come back to Luqura to look for her. Sodja knew very little about the thieves’ mysterious organization. eir members were supposedly worshippers of Odar, though Sodja couldn’t say how con scating magic artifacts bene tted the God of Skywater. Sodja’s older brothers, Ketrit and Rista, had even encountered a few cultists while going about family business in Luqura, but Rista had been the only one to capture and interrogate one of the thieves, and the man had not long survived Rista’s ministrations. By contrast, the three cultists Sodja had encountered had been little more than boys—although the muscular one with the dreadlocks seemed a little older. Maybe even her age. Sodja smiled, remembering his poor attempt to track her back to Luqura. He’d been adorably angry when she’d used her shadow magic to disappear in front of him—and the string of curse words had been so malevolently creative, Sodja had been tempted to reappear just to let the fel ow give chase a bit longer. It didn’t hurt that he was easy on the eyes. At the time, Sodja guessed she would never see the young man again—he would hoof it back to the Brakewood, and that would be the end of it, despite her taunting the boys with her name, even encouraging them to retaliate against her family. eir arrival on her family’s doorstep had been a welcome complication … . . . and their leaving her family home without a lick of protest was an unwelcome surprise. No trouble at al for the Rocas family, despite her e orts. It was so frustrating—al that e ort to turn new enemies and former al ies against her family … for nothing. Sodja had been wondering if it was even worth fol owing them out of the High Quarter when Saltair had emerged from the mansion in pursuit and made the decision for her. Sodja watched him track the group into the Ash Quarter and attack them, watched him chase the boy with the glowing golden hand—the same one she’d left to die in Janak’s study—and then she’d watched that boy defeat rst Saltair and then Slavemaster Kranak. at reversal had been wonderful—exactly what Sodja had hoped for—but it had also left her with a hundred unanswered questions. Were the boys stil working for their Brakewood cult? Had the boy with the golden hand lost his arm in Janak’s burning study, and where did he get that obscenely powerful prosthetic? From Janak’s col ection? Sodja would have sought answers, but the one-armed boy and his companions vanished from the Boneyard, leaving only bodies in their wake . . . and abandoning the handsome boy with the dreadlocks. His actions suggested he had no intention of rejoining his companions. If anything, he seemed to be hoping to settle into Luqura. Another puzzle. Sodja kicked a loose pebble into the dragon sh pond. Red-gold scales ashed in the water. She sighed. It was late and she needed to nish her errand before the servants woke and guards changed their shift. Sodja walked on, passing the last of the ve pools and coming to a long row of hedges dividing the ornamental ponds and orchards from the grounds beyond the Rocas family’s keep. It was stil dark—closer to twilight than dawn—yet as Sodja approached the back of the mansion her eyes easily pierced the gloom, catching glimpses of the paths that ran right up to her family’s doorstep. Shaped like a giant wedge of cheese with a bite taken out of it, the Rocas Estate was narrow at the front, penetrating deep into the heart of Luqura’s High Quarter. As one moved away from the mansion’s entrance, though, the grounds ared out and opened into the gated hedges and orchards that her family privately cultivated. Sodja studied the street, seeing no carriages had been parked overnight at the front of her family’s home. at was good. No midnight visitors or urgent demands from the slavers. Al would be quiet inside with little chance of surprise, though Sodja always anticipated complications as a matter of personal and professional pride. Sodja ignored the front door and instead traced the path she would have to climb to reach her mother’s private balcony at the corner of the mansion. A col ection of chiseled gray eldstone formed the base of the keep, making it an easy ascent, but Sodja paused after taking a single step toward the wal . At the opposite corner of the mansion, Sodja spied a tal ow candle burning in the bedroom window just above a tal iron trel is. Her heart burning, Sodja steered away from the balcony and toward the window. A rose bush climbed the iron trel is, though the shrub had not been tended in years and its thorns were dry, impotent things. As she climbed, the familiar rusty metal dul y squeaked beneath her weight and the desiccated plant crumbled beneath her touch. When Sodja reached the window, she slipped a hand inside her shirt, grasped her lockpicking tools, then stopped to listen. From inside, Sodja could hear a woman’s strong voice. “Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is made, is unmade.” Sodja knew the litany. On a hunch, she moved her hand from her shirt and pushed on the glass. A sad smile touched her lips as the window swung inward, and she crept into the chambers as quiet as a breeze. Inside the room, a single candle made the shadows icker and lit the uid motions of an old woman sitting in front of it. ough her eyes were crinkled with crow’s-feet and her chin was no longer as rm as it once was, Sodja could see glimpses of the woman’s youth and beauty: high cheekbones, a pert nose in a heart-shaped face and raven-black hair that, though streaked with gray, stil retained most of its color. Her eyes were closed, though if she had opened them, Sodja knew those, too, would be beautiful—keen gray eyes with a hint of an almond shape to them. Sodja took a step forward and bowed her head in respect. “Hel o, grandmother.” e woman at the candle tilted her head in Sodja’s direction, as if acknowledging her presence. She did not open her eyes, though, nor did she address her grandchild. Instead, the Rocas family’s oldest matriarch bowed her head and continued her chanting. “Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free.” As Bel a spoke, her careful ngers guided a bone needle and black thread through the strips of tattered black-and-gray cloth sitting atop her lap. Sodja watched in fascination, though she had seen this many times in the past four months. Day and night, the woman sewed together rags while chanting gibberish to herself. She had to be coaxed to eat or drink, and Sodja regularly found the servants couldn’t be bothered. Cups of tepid water and bowls of uneaten food sat uncol ected beside the woman’s bed, inviting ies and other vermin. If not for Sodja’s nightly visits, she thought the woman would have died some months ago. “If the senile old biddy wants to starve herself while stitching rags together,” Tiana had said, “who am I to stop her?” Rista had laughed at that—he laughed at anything cruel—while Ketrit was silent. at hadn’t surprised her either. Sodja’s eldest brother rarely said anything, and while his visits to their grandmother hadn’t been as frequent as Sodja’s, the man stil saw her on occasion. And now Sodja had to visit Bel a in secret. Ever since running away from the mansion—ever since nding the ledger and discovering her mother’s secret —Sodja had been unable to visit her grandmother openly. It had been two months, and Sodja remained surprised that no one thought to wonder how Bel a stil survived when the servants and Sodja’s family rarely tended to her—a fact evinced by the acrid smel of an over owing chamber pot. Yet each group seemed to think the other must be privately tending to the old lady, for no one questioned how the dishes disappeared every night or why the chamber pot was magical y empty every morning. She couldn’t manage every day, true, but Sodja tried to keep her vigil, and so far she had evaded discovery. e young woman sighed and fol owed her nose to the vessel brimming with night soil. It hurt Sodja to think how sharp her grandmother had been—so vibrant and strong, reining in Rista’s cruel tendencies, keeping Tiana in her place—but then grandfather Gadish had died and Bel a had never been the same. Vintan died a year later, and though her father’s death had deeply wounded Sodja, it had broken her grandmother entirely. Sewing rags and chanting was something new, though. No one knew where her grandmother had found the fabric, but it materialized one day in Bel a’s room and thereafter never seemed to leave her hands. Always stitching, sewing, weaving. Binding grays to blacks, and blacks to deeper blacks. It would have been distressing enough to witness—to watch a woman so regal and dominant turn into a blathering recluse overnight—but the most disturbing part was that she stitched with her eyes closed. Every day and night, every stitch of needle and thread was done by touch. As if to il ustrate this, Bel a’s thin ngers set the bone needle down on her lap and searched for a nearly invisible scrap of black thread lying on the table beside the candle. e strand was as thin as the lament of a spider web, yet the woman stil guided it through the eye of her bone needle and resumed her stitching—al with her eyes closed. Her chanting resumed: “Keeper of truth. Warden of lies. Turn away light. Darken the skies. Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is unmade, is made. Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free. Warden of truth. Keeper of lies. Strengthen this shadow. Sharpen its eyes. Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is made, is unmade. Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free.” Sodja stayed as the woman began the litany again from the start, then respectful y backed out of the room, chamber pot in hand. Using one arm, she stealthily climbed back down the trel is, emptied the night soil in the cherry orchard and returned the vessel to Bel a’s room. When she returned, the old woman was sitting quietly in the corner, her hands folded in her lap, her eyes stil closed. Sodja looked between her grandmother and the sewing project that had so obsessed her. She crossed the room and softly placed one hand atop Bel a’s open palms. Using her other hand, she picked up the nearest cup of water and held it to the woman’s parched lips. For a while the cup sat there, moistening the woman’s dry skin without a drop being drunk. A minute passed then two. Final y, Bel a’s lips parted and the lukewarm water trickled into her mouth. She swal owed, coughed. Swal owed some more. Sodja l ed her mouth twice more before the woman turned her head aside. Why?” “ e same reason I asked you al to meet me here—and not to invite Aog.” Ather brushed back his trimmed coif of hair. “I’m afraid our dear Master Kenton has been manipulating us. Spying on us.” “How’s that?” Der crossed his arms. Edra knew that look—and the stance too. If the former Master of Stealth didn’t like Ather’s answer, he might fol ow up with a throwing star to the man’s throat. “I have suspected it for some time,” Ather drawled, unintimidated, “and I spent the last few weeks testing my theory. Whenever we’re wearing the amulets, Kenton knows where we are and, I believe, he can hear our thoughts. Unless he’s with Kiara in the Vault of Damnation. Whatever demon magic protects that place also interferes with the amulets. Kenton’s there right now with that witch, scrying or screwing or whatever the hel it is they do down there. at’s why he hasn’t come looking for us … yet.” “Damn me,” Denithal burped, his hands patting his chest for a blue vial that he quickly uncorked and chugged. “Sorry,” he said. “ e yel ow ones do wonders for my energy, but they give me some frightful indigestion.” “How did you learn this?” Edra asked, pointedly ignoring Denithal. Ather raised an eyebrow. “Did none of you think to try and identify the properties of the talismans? You simply took Kenton at his word?” e predatory popinjay snorted. “And I suppose none of you thought it odd those amulets were a matched set? e rst thing I did was sit down and properly identify each artifact—but you were al too eager to play with your new toys. You didn’t stop to think that young Master Kenton might be trying to control us?” Neither Der nor Denithal could meet his gaze. Edra at least had enough steel not to look sheepish, but Ather’s words rang painful y true. How long had he spent admiring his new leather armor and marveling at his new weapons? He’d never once in that time thought to second-guess their properties. Let the boy identify the artifacts and assign them, he had thought, and I’l make use of them. e former Master of Arms met Ather’s eyes. “Aye,” Edra said. “Seems we were a bit hasty in trusting the boy. What should we do then? We can’t put the amulets back on or he’l know we’ve gured out his secret.” “I mean to get out of here,” Ather said, nodding toward the road. “To leave Chaenbalu for good. Even if Kenton were being straight with us, you saw what Annev did to Elder Tosan—how he blew up the Academy and damn near kil ed us al . If we’re smart, we’l stay far, far away from that.” “But where can we go?” Der asked, looking pensive. “ e Academy … the vault and the magic?” He looked between the others. “What else is there for us?” Ather gave a dramatic sigh, dusted o a fal en tree, then sat down. “We should cal Murlach over. If you haven’t guessed yet, we aren’t ambushing any caravans today. I just needed an excuse to get us al together.” “And Aog?” Edra asked. “Why didn’t you invite him?” Ather peeled o one of his magic gloves and waved the garment at him. “ ese don’t work on Aog. I thought it was because of his armor, but he didn’t even respond when I touched his face. It’s like he’s … not there.” “ at’s nothing new,” Denithal said, snorting. “No,” Ather objected. “ is was di erent. Kenton’s done something to him, I think. Got him wrapped tighter than the rest of us, I’d wager. Haven’t you noticed? He keeps the Master of Punishment like some sort of pet. Has him digging those tunnels beneath the Academy’s ruins or running an errand of some sort. Aog’s never real y been the sycophantic type, and this reeks of magic.” He tapped Der on the shoulder with his gloved hand. “Go fetch Murlach?” Der nodded and sped away to col ect the monstrous Master of Engineering.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.content: Edra gave him a pointed look. “You just manipulated Der,” he accused. “How is that any di erent than what Kenton’s doing?” “Because,” Ather said, smiling wickedly, “I’m me and he’s not.” Edra sni ed but didn’t argue the point. Murlach and Der were back a minute later, the former frowning from within the nest of cables and wires surrounding his face and neck. “What’s al this about Kenton?” “He’s been spying on us,” Edra said, before Ather could o er a more garrulous explanation—Keos, that man could talk. “Ather gured out the amulets were involved somehow,” he continued. “You stil wearing yours?” A tentacled arm sprang to life at Murlach’s side, the pronged tip slithering into his armor. ere was a loud hissing sound and then his exoskeleton split open. “So,” he said, “you nal y gured it out.” “Figured what out?” Edra said, a moment before Der. “ e talismans.” Murlach’s tentacle retreated from his armor, its pincers drawing the amulet over his head before displaying the artifact for al to see. “I wondered how long it would take. Which of you was it?” Down the road, one of Murlach’s twiddlesnap contraptions clanked shut, eliciting a squeal as some poor animal was snapped and snared—but the rest of them gave it no mind. Edra pointed to Ather, head shaking as he said to Murlach, “If you’ve known this whole time, why would you wear it?” Murlach spun the talisman in front of Edra’s face so that he saw a peculiar drop of silver clinging to the amulet’s ruby. “What’s that?” Der asked, stepping forward to examine the artifact. “Some kind of … metal spider?” Edra grunted in agreement. e addition to the amulet did look like some sort of metal ic arachnid, with eight tiny legs and a blood-red thorax that matched the ruby beneath it. Murlach let each man see it in turn. “When we were down in the vault, I saw another half-dozen of these talismans sitting on a shelf at the back of the chamber—al with these metal spiders attached to them. at got me wondering, so I started poking around and found six unattached spiders sitting on the lower shelf. Didn’t take a genius to gure Kenton had modi ed ours, so I snatched one of the spider-amulets and gave it a closer look. Tried to gure out what kind of tricks our cursed leader was trying to pul on us.” “And?” Murlach’s silvery tentacle dropped the amulet back over his neck. “ e spiders alter the magic a bit. Instead of al owing Kenton to always hear my thoughts, they let me choose which ones to share and which to keep to myself.” “Why not tel the rest of us?” Der asked, his brow furrowed. Murlach shrugged. “I wanted to see how things played out—and I didn’t trust you lot to keep my secret.” He gestured at Ather with his pincers. “ at’s al moot now that Ather’s played our hands for us, though … so what’s the new plan?” He eyed the Master of Lies with unmasked contempt. “You going to confront him?” “After what he did to Master Carbad?” Ather said, his eyes widening with just a hint of terror. “Hel s no. I thought we could just leave—but rst I wanted to col ect some insurance.” “Which is?” “Aqlumera,” Ather said, his grin returning as he smoothed the thin line of his mustache. “Tosan didn’t like us entering the vault because he didn’t want people knowing we were sitting on an emperor’s ransom. Just a bottle of that stu would make us rich as kings—and I know folks who’d be more than eager to buy it. So imagine this: we hurry back to Chaenbalu before Kenton realizes we’ve discovered his secret. Murlach stays up here and uses his amulet to convince Kenton we’re al stil with him. When Kenton comes to investigate— and see why we’ve taken o our amulets—the rest of us wil break into the vault. We can grab some more artifacts, steal a few bottles of aqlumera and meet up with Murlach at the old mil . We circle south to the Brake Road and then we go east, away from Luqura and Banok and anywhere else Kenton might think to look for us. If we go to Port Caer, we’l have mountains of gold before the end of the month and can live out our lives in peace. Or we can turn mercenary and sel our services to the highest bidder. e point is we’l have options.” e others watched Murlach, who seemed to have become the de facto alternative to Ather’s leadership. “I don’t think there’s any reason for me to wait here,” Murlach said. “I can choose which thoughts Kenton sees, and I can do that as easily with you in Chaenbalu. And no need to regroup at the mil . We can just grab the aqlumera and get the hel out of these woods.” Der and Denithal glanced at Edra then, surprising him with their deference. e former Master of Arms waited just long enough to acknowledge their unasked question. “It has a certain attractiveness to it. Much better than waiting for Kenton to gure out what to do with us. I’m in.” Der and Denithal nodded—and that was that. One last theft, one nal betrayal, and they would be free of Chaenbalu forever. Murlach went to retrieve the trap he’d left on the road, and Der and Denithal replaced their masks, the former disappearing into an amorphous cloud of black smoke. “Hey, fel as!” Murlach cal ed back to them a minute later, his voice projected by some ingenious artifact inside his suit. “You need to come and look at this!” “What is it?” Ather shouted back, his nimble knee-high boots dancing him out of the tree line and down the slope leading onto the road. “You remember those metal monsters that attacked the Academy?” Murlach asked, a tremor in his voice. “ e twisted ones that ran o into the forest?” “Yes,” Edra said, feeling a cold prickle of fear creep up his neck. “Why? Did you nd one?” “Not sure,” Murlach said, his speaker clicking o as the group approached him from behind. “It looks a lot like one … but also not.” Edra nal y saw the beast caught in the jaws of Murlach’s enormous twiddlesnap: unlike the feral, mutated monsters that had attacked Chaenbalu, this creature seemed . . . wel , not like a creature at al ; more like a man wearing ful plate armor, his body segmented by overlapping metal plates. Metal and stone, Edra amended, slowing. en he realized. at’s not armor … that’s the creature’s esh! “Gods,” Denithal rasped from behind his white mask. “It is one of them!” Ather’s slender rapier hissed from its scabbard and Edra drew his own leaf-bladed long sword. Denithal dipped his hands under his bandolier and popped a red vial from his pocket, and while Edra couldn’t see Der’s gure amidst the cloud of smoke, he assumed the Master of Stealth was similarly preparing for battle. “You can put your pricks away, boys,” Murlach shouted back. “It’s dead.” “From the twiddlesnap?” Der asked amidst his cloud of smoke. “ ose aren’t lethal.” “ ey are when they’re big enough to crush a wagon wheel.” Murlach used his pincers to prod the metal man’s iron head and neck. “How in the name of the Gods does this magic work?” he wondered aloud. “Made of metal and stone … but not a machine. Is it a man … or a golem?” He shook his head, apparently more impressed by the arti cery than concerned by the dark omen of the creature’s presence. “Should we be worried that it was skulking about the East Road?” Edra asked. “No,” Ather said, any fear in his tone concealed beneath his usual veneer of vanity. “ is changes nothing. We go back to Chaenbalu, get the aqlumera, and head to Port Caer.” Murlach dropped the creature’s iron head and stood straight, his mechanized body nearly a foot tal er than without his suit. “We should keep an eye out for more of these buggers, though. If this ferruman is anything like the ones we saw in Chaenbalu, there’l be more—lots more.” Edra was suddenly anxious to get back to the questionable safety of Chaenbalu’s familiar ruins. “Let’s move.” CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN “Does she live?” Kenton asked, leaning dangerously close to the edge of the aqlumera pool. “Show me again. I have to know if she survived.” “She lives, Cursed One. She lives and wil yet live. As I promised, her life is only truly in peril when she returns here. You should not trouble yourself with these visions.” “Show me again, Kiara! I need to know what has happened to her.” e witmistress rubbed her temples then clasped her hands together. “Magic is not free, Kenton. Even when we use the aqlumera instead of the shadepools, there is a cost for scrying, and I do not spend it lightly.” “But those demons nearly kil ed her!” “ ose demons failed—as I foretold.” e Master of Curses ripped his blindfold away and stared into Kiara’s eyes, his own aring with demonic re, their light ickering at the edge of his vision. “Show. Her. Again.” “No.” Kenton’s cheek twitched and his hands shook as if he were about to strangle the woman. Instead, he spun away from the aqlumera cistern and smashed his st against the nearest shelf of artifacts. Magic ared from his Glove of Indomitability and the wood exploded into splinters. A heartbeat later, a catalogue of magic stones toppled to the oor, the rocks and pebbles scattering in al directions. Kiara frowned. “Tantrums do not persuade or inspire obedience. ey are a sign of weakness. A demonstration that you are incapable of leading.” She tucked a lock of hair behind her ear, the rest rmly secured in a neat bun. Since the Academy’s col apse, the other masters and ancients had started to relax, not seeking to impress one another, much less Kenton. Kiara had gone the opposite way, though, becoming even more formal, acting like a teacher in the midst of lecturing a student; her skirts were always clean and ironed, her face was always washed, her hair was always neat. Kenton, by contrast, was a haggard shadow of his former self who cared little for the company of others. e only exceptions were Kiara, whose magic al owed him to watch Myjun in the shadow realm, and Master Aog, whose wil he had entirely dominated. At the moment, the former Master of Punishment was digging a new tunnel from Chaenbalu’s lowest dungeon to the abandoned bakery at the perimeter of the vil age square—a secret tunnel, in case Kenton was ever trapped beneath the Academy again. Kenton had not yet admitted to anyone, not even himself, that he no longer wished to leave the Academy’s ruins. Its tunnels and its magic had become familiar to him, and he was becoming obsessed with the aqlumera pool and watching Myjun. He had no reason or desire to leave—not to wash, not to sleep, not even to eat—and the vault’s artifacts meant he never had to. “I could make you show me,” he growled. “I could force you.” “You can’t and you won’t. Harming me wil ensure you never see Myjun again. So you wil let me rest. You wil see the visions again when I am ready, not when you command. Is that clear?” Kenton’s lips puckered, his skin tightening as he felt his scarred face struggle to contain his scowl. “Quite clear,” he whispered, his voice so low it was almost impossible to hear. “She is not dead, Kenton. She is resting, and it wil take time for her wounds to heal.” “How long?” “Hours. Days. Not long, I suspect. Time passes more swiftly there, but while she is resting, we should rest.” Kenton stroked his scraggly beard. “I don’t like that half man. What he does … what he’s doing to her. He’s kil ing her. Maybe not her body, but her spirit.” “I’m not certain that girl ever real y had a spirit.” Kenton’s eyes ashed, their bril iance almost blinding, their light swel ing to throw back the shadows in the corners of the room. “You know nothing of Myjun.” “Don’t I? She was best friends with my apprentice, and the daughter of the headmaster. I knew her al too wel . Her little schemes, her vanity. I knew her mother too, before she died. Hel s, I practical y raised that girl with the other witwomen. If the Academy had lasted a few more years and her father hadn’t been an obstacle, we would have indoctrinated her into the Brides of Fate.” “Did you know she had magic?” “I did.” “How?” Kiara raised an eyebrow, her cool gray eyes inspecting him. “Come with me.” *** e witmistress’s bedchamber lay two oors above the vault, completely undisturbed by either the Academy’s col apse or the feurog attack, save for the narrow tunnel hidden behind Kiara’s bed. She had already explained how that single tunnel had al owed the feurog to enter the Academy, but she had been less forthcoming about why. “A clean slate,” she’d told him. “No witnesses to pursue us when we left with Annev. No survivors to guide any others to the village.” It had al seemed very cold to Kenton. “What did you want to show me?” he asked, sitting down in a padded rocking chair. “ is.” Kiara handed him a smal black book and Kenton ri ed through its pages. He saw dates, names and numbers—a chart of some kind—and a short description beside each name. In most cases, it also mentioned the parents’ names, or potential strains of magic. “ is is a logbook,” he said, ipping to the end. “A log of . . . stolen children?” “It was our job to locate and monitor infants who might become the Vessel. We abducted them from al over Greater Luqura and brought them here to be trained. One-armed infants were our rst priority, but none of them ever possessed the talent—none until Annev—so instead we kidnapped those likely to inherit the talent, thinking one might lose an arm during their training or an artifact retrieval mission … but it never happened. It was very vexing.” “What’s this?” Kenton asked, showing her an asterisk next to one boy’s name and the bright red letters NM. “Sage Lenka. Is this the Academy’s cook?” “Yes. ‘NM’ means nonmagical. Not every child had magic. Some were taken for political reasons.” “Hold on. ‘Lenka.’ Is that supposed to be King Lenka? As in the King of Greater Luqura.” Kiara nodded. “He had three children. e youngest boy was supposedly stil born, but he’s actual y been cooking the Academy’s meals for the past decade or more.” “You stole a prince?” he breathed. “Damn me. What for?” “Politics, mostly. We had our reasons.” Kenton ipped forward a few more pages and saw his reap mates. “Fyunai Harth … son of Janak Harth?” He looked up. “ at’s the merchant we kil ed in Banok!” “Just a strain of Ironborn in that one—nothing major—but Janak’s mercenary exploits let him amass too much power too quickly. Taking his son was meant to keep the bastard in line … but something went wrong at the reaping. Janak fought back. His wife was kil ed and he was crippled—but we stil managed to steal his son.” “Fyn,” Kenton breathed, head shaking in disbelief. “He kil ed his own father. at prick of a headmaster sent him to kil his own bloody father.” “It was no accident. Tosan was aware of his students’ parental lineage.” Kenton ipped to another page and found his own name. “Reotan NM,” he read beside his nameless father—and beside his unnamed mother . . . “Terran Arti cer?” He looked up. “I’m bloody Terran?” “Of course you are. Al Arti cers are Terran.” “But … I don’t look Terran.” “You have your father’s looks—like a Tir Reotan pirate—and your mother’s magic. She was an Arti cer.” “ ere are no names written here.” “No. We tended not to record the rapists, pirates, or whores.” Kenton’s mouth twitched, but he held his anger in check. “And I was stolen?” “You? No. Your father didn’t want a brat on his ship. Witwoman Kelga purchased you from your mother on the streets of Luqura.” Kenton wanted to ask more but his throat closed up. His nger drifted down the page until he found Annev’s name. “Ainnevog … but no number. No origin, no parentage.” He looked up. “Why not?” “Infants have their heels inked with numbers—to help us keep track of you al . Annev had no such number. My best guess is Sodar smuggled him into your reap.” Kenton snorted, nding some dark humor in it al . “So why show me this?” Kiara took the book and ipped to a group of pages he had missed. “ ese are our notes on the witapprentices. Only a few are stolen each year, though sometimes a witwoman wil get pregnant—in the case of us Brides, we select a mate with an a nity for prophetic magic. Myjun and her mother were both witchildren, but Myjun’s grandmother was a proper Bride of Fate . . . who married this man.” Kiara ipped to another page and tapped a spidery inscription next to an infant from the thirty-seventh reap. “Edwin,” Kenton read, taking back the book. “Son of Donald the Bard. Strong a nity for Ilumite magic.” He looked up. “ is is how you knew. You had your prophecies and the Academy’s training … and this.” “Yes. at’s how we knew Myjun would probably have the talent, though it was impossible to guess which strands would become dominant. Terran, Ilumite, Yomad. We never know until you reach an age where the magic is potent. We try to bring the girls into the Brides of Fate around then. For the young men . . . there’s usual y no harm in having a little of the talent, particularly if they’re never taught to use it. It makes them better avatars. And if some stumble upon how to use their magic … wel , avatars have such a high mortality rate.” “Did Duvarek have it?” Kenton asked, his voice sounding hol ow. “Is that why he was kil ed?” “Duvarek had it and I think he knew—it’s probably why he drank so much. But we didn’t kil him. at was al Janak’s fault.” “But Tosan had me kil him … because he got caught. at wasn’t your doing?” “No.” Kenton relaxed, suddenly aware he’d been on the point of violence. “ at’s good,” he said, his heart thudding heavily in his chest. He passed the logbook back. “I need to check in on Aog and the other masters.” “Are they giving you trouble?” “Not Aog. e slave ring keeps him completely docile—though he needs new commands every few hours or he’s liable to sit down in one of the tunnels and wait to be told what to do next.” “And the others?” Kiara asked, her tone implying something she knew that he did not. Kenton frowned. “Ather’s being a pain. He may have gured out the amulets.” “And if he has?” “ en I’l kil him.” Kiara nodded as though she’d expected as much. “You’re sure this isn’t motivated by your history with him?” “My history?” Kenton asked, tense once again. “Your scar,” she said, gesturing to the band of mottled esh that was now almost entirely hidden by the leathery, cal oused skin surrounding his lidless eyes. “No lingering resentments for that?” “Oh, of course,” Kenton said, his gloved hand gently scratching the smal patch of scarred esh, “but Ather has some subtlety that the others lack, so I’l overlook our past—so long as he stays in line. He recently stopped wearing his amulet, though, and I don’t think that’s an accident.” “He’s testing you,” Kiara said, her eyes glinting. “I think so, yes. And he keeps asking about the vault—keeps lingering whenever I enter or leave.” “ en make an example of him.” “I think he wants the aqlumera.” Kiara’s coy smile transformed into a frown. “He can’t take any of it. In the wrong hands, that magic could be catastrophic . . . not to mention you’ve trapped a demon down there.” “He’s not trapped,” Kenton said, his lips pressed into a rm line. “He’s waiting for another chance to escape.” “ en why hasn’t he tried to possess me?” Kenton smiled. “ at pin you wear in your hair. Did you not guess its enchantment?” Kiara’s frown deepened. “Identifying enchantments is not one of my strengths, Master Kenton.” Kenton led that information away for the future. “It protects the wearer from spectral possession. So long as you wear it, Elder Tosan can’t use you as a conduit.” “And do you wear a similar artifact?” “I do,” Kenton said, tapping the cu s of his Gloves of Indomitability. “ ese protect my hands and my soul.” Kiara nodded, seeming impressed. “You real y are a marvel with artifacts. I doubt anyone in the Academy’s history was so wel suited to be their keeper.” Kenton’s smile slipped and he turned from her then, choosing to busy himself checking on the masters. His eyes grew distant, and he located Aog in the dark tunnels of the Academy’s lowest levels. e brute was sluggishly carving away at the soil, his enchanted shovel simultaneously softening and hardening the earth that he cut away. He didn’t even need to cart away the dirt he excavated—it was simply vaporized. Kenton mental y told the man to dig for another hour and then come and eat, and then he checked on the other Sons of Damnation. “Something’s wrong,” he said, his brow furrowing. “ ey’ve taken o their amulets—al except Murlach.” “And where is he?” Kenton tried to glean the master’s location. “ e East Road … I think. But it doesn’t feel right. His thoughts are … chatty. He never thinks aloud this much.” “What’s he thinking?” “Something about robbing a caravan. It sounds like the others are with him.” He concentrated. “Oh shit.” “What?” Kiara asked, a touch of dread creeping into her voice. “ ey found something on the road. One of those feurog.” “Oh,” Kiara said, visibly relaxing. “You needn’t worry about them. Without someone to drive them, they’re little more than animals. at’s why Cruithear’s priests cast them out—and why we snatched them up. I admit they make hardy soldiers, but they prefer to hide from men. Besides, there aren’t many of them left. I’ve tried to recal the survivors but none have responded.” “No,” Kenton said, frowning. “ is one isn’t like your monsters—not exactly. Murlach … he’s cal ing it a ferruman. It’s not mutated like those others —not half-human, half-monster. It looks … Wel , damn. It looks like Janak Harth, after he drank that vial of magic.” Kiara’s nonchalance suddenly vanished. “Where did Murlach spot this ferruman?” “On the East Road. e golem got caught in one of his traps.” “It’s not a golem,” Kiara said, scowling. “If it looks like Janak Harth, then it’s human. A real man or woman, not a construct.” Kenton studied her, his magic revealing the aura of fear she fought to hide. “What aren’t you tel ing me?” e witmistress pursed her lips. “ e feurog were monsters—failed experiments of Cruithear—but the God of Minerals had some successes. Cruithear made those lucky enough not to become monsters into his elite soldiers—his Ironborn warriors. I suspect one of those is the ferruman Murlach saw.” “Why would one of those be here?” “Without scrying, I can only guess—but Cruithear is jealous of his elites. He hoards them like a miser with his coins … so if one is here, he means to attack someone, or something.” “What would be worth it, to him?” Kiara swore. “I haven’t asked the spirits … but Cruithear needs aqlumera to forge his warriors. e only reason he hasn’t made an army of them is because aqlumera is expensive, extremely limited, and di cult to locate—especial y untainted.” “Except here,” Kenton nished. “In the Vault of Damnation.” Kiara nodded. “Most of the feurog are mutants because the aqlumera that formed them was tainted—but if Cruithear discovered the existence of our fountain, and if he found one of Chaenbalu’s survivors and persuaded them to act as his guide …” “ en he’d bring his best soldiers here,” Kenton nished. “An army of ferrumen could be on their way to Chaenbalu now. ey could be just outside the village. Surrounding us. Looking for a way into the tunnels.” “ at is a possibility.” “And the masters are al north of the Brake. Al except Aog.” Kenton felt his adrenaline rising. “Blood and lth. How can we be sure?” e answer suddenly came to him and he let his eyes unfocus, sweeping his vision beyond Kiara’s bedroom and across the landscape around the Academy. He turned in a ful circle, his magic eyes piercing rock and stone, air and earth, and saw nothing alarming within the bounds of the vil age. He gave up after a minute of searching. “It seems we’re safe from … wait.” Kenton stopped, his eyes locking on to four warm bodies skulking near the edge of the vil age. Not ferrumen, but actual men. “I don’t think the masters are north of the Brake.” “What? Where are they?” “Just south of the village, near the old mil .” Kenton paused. “Why is Murlach thinking about robbing a caravan when he isn’t anywhere near the East Road?” he wondered aloud. “Something isn’t right.” Kiara tutted. “Focus on the ferrumen. If you must question your Sons of Damnation, do so—after they’ve helped you scout the Brake for more of Cruithear’s creatures.” Kenton quirked an eyebrow. “Is that advice … or a command?” Kiara snorted. “My days of commanding others died when the Brides of Fate perished. You are the Cursed Leader, Kenton of Chaenbalu. I only advise.” “So long as that advice bene ts you.” “So long as it bene ts us both.” “Very wel . I’l go round up the masters and scout the woods.” “And I wil return to the vault and scry from there—which wil take time, not to mention magic.” Kiara scratched her wrist and Kenton saw a patch of her skin had begun to turn ash-white, the cost of using her powers. “ is is important, Kenton,” she continued. “If Cruithear has sent any of his ferrumen to the surface, then they are coming for the aqlumera. He can’t be al owed to take possession of it.” “Because he’d use it to create more monsters?” “No! Because it would disrupt the lines of fate—Annev’s quest, Myjun’s arrival.
