A plume of black vapor trailed the injury and the assassin’s esh knitted itself back together. He climbed from the shadows then beckoned Myjun to fol ow, and they moved away from the Terran soldiers on the great wal , strol ing toward the eeing Yomads. “I do not ght for them,” Myjun snapped, nodding back at the towering wal that blocked the other end of the isthmus. “I ght for myself. I would kil them, too, if you would let me.” Oyru’s nger rose to trace the black scar that marked his missing eye. “ ose soldiers belong to the Legions of Keos, which makes them our al ies.” “I have no al ies.” “Not even me? Not after I risked my own life and sacri ced this for you?” Oyru tapped the withered eye socket, its esh puckered tight in contrast to the wide, unblinking eye pinning her with its soul ess glare. “ at was months ago—and I didn’t ask you to save me, you half-demon bastard.” e words hissed from her like steam from a kettle. “You’re not a savior or a rotting martyr. You’re a conjurer, a kil er, and a bloody liar. Al you do is torture me and tel me to kil , and delay ful l ing your promises.” Oyru shrugged as if her words meant nothing, which only enraged Myjun further. “I wil ful l my promises,” the Shadow Reborn said, resuming their walk. “We have made good progress these past few weeks.” “Months,” Myjun corrected. “It’s been ve months.” “Only if you reckon time by the blinks of Dorchnok’s Eye. Barely three weeks of traveling in the physical realm, and we have already reached the last leg of our journey.” e assassin gestured to the eld of ivory towers dotting the narrow isthmus of Lubree, a no-man’s-land that separated the continents of New and Old Terra. “Terra Minora lies just beyond the Neck, protected by the endless towers and the Spear of Tacharan. Once you are sated, we wil cross back into the shadow realm here in Lubree—at the Noose of the Neck—and from here pass into Takarania and Terra Minora.” He pointed to a speck on the horizon that could barely be seen above the heads of the innumerable towers ahead of them. “You see that lone tower? It is the Spear of Tacharan. It marks the end of the Neck of Lubree and the beginning of Takarania. Powerful magics protect it and the land surrounding it, preventing entry. Even sailors must avoid the isthmus and its shores and travel to Al tara in the south or Krosera in the north. We wil avoid its curse, though, by crossing the Neck in the shadow realm.” “And how much farther to Al tara?” Myjun asked, unable to conceal the venom in her tone. “Terra Minora is the home of three peoples: the Shalgarns of Al tara, the Yomads of Takarania, and my people in Krosera.” Oyru gestured past the isthmus. “Takarania lies at the center of Terra Minora and borders the Neck. It is a bu er between the shadowlands of Krosera and wildlands of Al tara, which we must pass through to reach the Iron Mountains and the trol clans. Doing so wil also bring us close to the obelisks that guard the House of Brass at the center of Takarania—perilous in either realm.” “So we must stil avoid them? Even after traveling into the shadow realm?” “We must, but for separate reasons. In this world, the Brazen Towers mark the borders of Takarania and are abutted by the mountains of Al tara. East of the mountains is the House of Brass, home to the priests who worship the God of Death. In the shadow realm, their temple overlaps the Heart of the Void— the center of Reocht na Skah.” “I thought you said it’s dangerous to go to Reocht na Skah—that we could get trapped there for eternity.” “Just so. To avoid both, we wil enter the shadows and cross beyond the Neck. at wil take us beyond the reach of the Spear of Tacharan. We wil then remain in the shadow realm and skirt the edge of Takarania to avoid entangling ourselves with the magic of Reocht na Skah. If we turn immediately southwest, that wil take us directly into the Al taran mountains and trol territory.” “To get my rotting armor.” “Yes.” “And then you wil take me back to the Empire to kil Annev.” “Yes.” “Fine. Let’s go.” Oyru gestured at the soldiers who had nal y reached the safety of their ivory towers. “You have satis ed your bloodlust?” He asked the question as though he were o ering her a nibble of a scone instead of the lives of a half-dozen men and women. “We wil not return to the physical world again—not til we reach Al tara—so you should take your l now.” “My hunger is never satis ed,” Myjun said, not bothering to hide her bitterness, “but I wil survive the trip.” Oyru nodded. “ e distance between here and Al tara would take a week to traverse over land—assuming we were unmolested by the Yomads and their magics. In the shadow realm it wil take a month or more … but time wil distort even more as we cross into Takarania. e greatest eidola also concentrate there, near the borders of Reocht na Skah, and that wil slow our pace further. at means it wil likely take us considerably longer than ve weeks to reach the trol mountains—at least, so long as we are traveling in the shadow realm.” “How much time wil al of this take in the physical realm?” “Stil a week by standard time, but we wil be stuck in the shadows for two months at least. And if we choose to venture nearer to southern Takarania— toward the heart of Reocht na Skah—it could be even longer.” “So why not return to the physical world once we are past the dangers of the Spear of Tacharan?” Oyru eyed her with his remaining black eye, its stare penetrating her to the core. “Because I believe the extra time and training would bene t you. You have grown much over these past ve months, but you stil lack ful control of your powers. You have not learned to bend or re ect the light as Bladesingers and Lightslingers do. You’ve learned to channel its baser elements—to summon your soulblades and channel the light re—but it seems the subtler arts are beyond you.” “And what do you know of the light, half man? You’re a master of the shadows. You couldn’t even teach me to summon the light, much less shape it. I learned that myself.” “Only because I forced you to.” He raised a hand to scratch the corner of his empty eye socket. Myjun sni ed. Perhaps he regretted his decision to save her, though if he did, Oyru never expressed it—and the omission hurt her more than any accusation. “I wil not delay my vengeance forever,” she asserted. “We should go west, straight into the mountains of Al tara. Reocht na Skah can keep its monsters and its secrets—and I would prefer we keep our current pace. If we stay in the shadow realm but keep close to the shoreline, that could be the fastest route of al .” Oyru said nothing, looking east—past the towers along the isthmus and toward a green coast that was almost entirely shrouded in mist. “We are close to Krosera now. If we crossed the Neck and went northeast instead of southwest, we would be in my homeland.” He looked wistful—and then he raised his face scarf and it was hidden. Myjun stared at him as if she’d just been slapped across the face. e man had been frowning—actual y frowning. “You don’t fear the death priests or the eidolons,” she said, accusing. “You’re not even afraid of spending a thousand years in the shadow of Reocht na Skah … but you are afraid of going home—and even then you tease yourself with it. Your words imply we might go there, yet you clearly wish to stay away. Why? What terrors do Krosera’s shadowlands hold for you?” Oyru turned to face her, his scarf fal ing away, his normal y stoic demeanor replaced by one of hatred and fear. “ e Kroserans and their impotent Shadow God can go to hel ,” Oyru said, his words colder than they had ever been. “We are bound for Al tara. I wil hasten our journey as you’ve requested—and you wil not speak of my homeland again.” As he said these last words, he covered his mouth and nose more completely, though the black fabric could not hide the tiny tear that trickled from the corner of the assassin’s eye. He dabbed it with his scarf, erasing the proof that he did indeed have a soul—but not before Myjun saw it. CHAPTER FIFTY-EIGHT “Why do you serve Keos instead of Dorchnok?” ey were back in the shadow realm and long past the Neck of Lubree. In their crossing, she had seen no evidence of the endless ivory towers that protected the isthmus, nor any shadow of the lone and awful Spear of Tacharan. She had instead seen black waves of smoke that l ed the depths of the Sauthron and Estron Seas. When she had later asked what happened to those that tried to sail those dark waters in the shadow realm, Oyru snorted, shook his head, and muttered something unintel igible about Voidweavers. e reaction seemed entirely out of character for the usual y stoic assassin, and the adjustment in her relationship with the Shadow Reborn left Myjun feeling adrift. At the same time, the assassin’s odd mood seemed to invite a more personal connection—something Myjun felt open to now they had left the physical world and the perpetual rage of her mask had been dimmed and dul ed. “I do not serve Keos,” Oyru said, morose. “I serve Dortafola and he serves Keos.” “Which is the same thing—and you did not answer my question. Why did you abandon your worship of Dorchnok?” “Are you not equal y impious? Did you not abandon your worship of Odar to fol ow me?” “ at’s di erent. I was damned—marked by Keos—and I had no choice. Not if I want to kil Annev.” Oyru said nothing for a long, long time. When he nal y did speak, it was with the measured words of someone who was unused to speech—as if the person behind the mask were speaking to her for the rst time. “I was betrayed once. Like you, I loved someone and was betrayed by them. She wasn’t Kroseran. She came from an Ilumite clan in Faer Fen and sailed across the Estron Sea to Northern Krosera. She pledged herself to me and then she wooed another Kroseran warrior—a warlord named Gevul the Terrible— and helped him destroy my house and my family. I kil ed Gevul, but not before he kil ed her . . . the woman I stil loved.” Oyru stared at the black waters, his face unreadable. “I tried to save her, I tried to bring her back—but Dorchnok would not heed my prayers. He did not save my family, he did not save her, and he could not save me.” e assassin turned south and pointed to the smoky horizon. “I ventured into Reocht na Skah. I thought that if I could reach into the Spirit World, I might persuade Oraqui to come back to me.” He xed his eye on Myjun. “She was a dualist—an Auramancer and a Lightslinger —but she could only do two things with her magic: she could manipulate others’ emotions and she could project il usions—re ections of the people and things nearby her. You have similar powers … sometimes you remind me of her.” He looked back to the horizon. “You entered Reocht na Skah,” Myjun said, her voice quiet. “I did.” “To the Heart of the Void.” “To the very center, yes.” Myjun swal owed. “How long were you gone? How long did you search for her?” “A week or two.” “A week or … in the Heart of the Void? When a day here is a thousand years there?” Oyru’s single eye shifted back to her, his usual stoic look back in place. “What made you leave? Or did you just give up?” She hadn’t meant it as a jab, though it came out that way. Stil , if Oyru was o ended he did not show it. “Dortafola came looking for me. Gevul had been one of his Siänar and when the man was kil ed … wel , he needed a replacement. Who better than the man who kil ed Gevul? He tracked me through the shadow realm to Reocht na Skah and promised that if I served him—that if I forsook my worship of Dorchnok and fol owed him—he would return Oraqui to me.” “And did he?” Oyru stared at her, his face a mask. “Maybe,” he said—and a chil went up her spine. *** “So you learned about Ilumite magic from her?” Oyru said nothing. He hadn’t spoken since their last conversation, two antumbras ago. Not a word. ey had turned southwest toward Al tara, keeping the black mists of the Sauthron Sea to their right and the endless gray plains to their left, and Myjun was tired of the shared silence. “She taught you about her magic, maybe even her people, and in return you taught her about Krosera and your magic.” Silence. “What made you think your master could bring her back?” More silence. “ is was hers, wasn’t it? is mask.” She tapped her gilded temple and forehead. “Did Gevul give it to her?” “Do not speak his name,” Oyru breathed, his voice as cold as ice—as cold as death. “Or what?” Myjun demanded, both relieved he had broken his silence and angry he had kept it for so long. “Wil you beat me? I wil drink the pain. Kil me? I don’t think so.” “I would leave you here,” Oyru said, his tone stil apathetic, though Myjun wondered if even his apathy was a mask. “I would leave you in the shadows, trapped here forever, and return to the physical world without you. You may have grown stronger, but you cannot traverse the planes of existence. You would be doomed to waste away until al life had left you and you became an eidolon.” “Is that what happened to you?” Myjun demanded. “Because you stayed so long in Reocht na Skah?” “Yes.” Myjun was satis ed. “ en I wil not speak that name again.” Oyru focused on a black xture that blanketed the horizon. “We are approaching the shadows of the Al taran mountains,” he said. “We are almost to our nal destination.” “We made good time, then.” Myjun stepped beside him, sharing the view. ough it seemed the land had been at for these many miles, she saw now that they had been climbing a long, gently rising hil . Al around them the ground gradual y fel away, the decline slow and steady behind them, almost imperceptible. Ahead, the slope grew more abrupt, rst fal ing and then rising again with greater height and severity. is pattern continued until the ground erupted in the black wal of mountains that stained the distant horizon.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.content: “How can these exist here?” Myjun asked, her eyes xed on the mountain range. “Near as I can tel , it re ects their proximity to Reocht na Skah. e power of the shadow realm lies thick on the mountains in the physical world, so their re ection in this world is more solid. It is the reason Al tara’s ironwood trees can be seen here and why another species grows in the hil s of Krosera—and why they cannot be cultivated anywhere else.” “Ironwood?” Myjun sni ed. “We have bushes of the stu in Western Daroea.” “A mongrel subspecies, no doubt transplanted by the Druids in Fertil Hedge. ey are not the same. Even the ironwood trees in Krosera are di erent from those here. Not worse—not mutated like your own shrubs—but di erent.” Myjun rol ed her eyes and let it drop, ready to move on. Oyru wasn’t. He pointed at the gray ring above their heads. “It is time to meditate. Also …” He tilted his head. “Something is hunting us.” Myjun spun, her eyes searching the horizon in every direction. From her vantage point, though, the plains looked empty. “Is there another waste nearby? I would have spotted—” “No waste. What hunts us is not so easily seen, nor is it attracted to the dreams and nightmares that bubble up from the cognitive realm.” “What is it then? An eidolon?” Oyru stood in silence for a long while, his eyes stil locked on the mountain range ahead of them. “You recal I said someone who was trapped here in the shadow realm would waste away and become eidola?” “Yes.” “ at was an oversimpli cation. People do not become shadow demons— not truly—they become something worse.” “Worse than shadow demons?” “Flesh wraiths … and witherkin.” “Wraiths and witherkin,” Myjun said, tasting the words. “Some kind of ghost? Something that eats our esh?” “Yes … and yes.” “And what hunts us?” “It is too soon to tel .” Myjun’s skin prickled with fear, and she found herself responding with anger. “So what the hel does it want? Why is it hunting us?” “Because,” Oyru said, his eye turning to face her, “I sent it here. I trapped it in the shadow realm when I attacked your vil age.” Myjun met Oyru’s gaze and the blood slowly drained from her face. “You mean a ghost is trying to kil us, and it’s somebody from Chaenbalu?” Oyru nodded. “It could not have fol owed us here without my noticing, but it might have used the aqlumera as a dimensional gate to Reocht na Skah.” “We can do that?” Oyru shook his head. “Not us. A Voidweaver or a Dark Lord could, but I am only a Shadowcaster.” “ en how … “ “I don’t know, tabibito. I only know it is someone from your vil age. A man, I think, or he was a man once.” “How long has he been fol owing us?” “Since the last umbra.” “And where is he now?” “Hiding. He seems to favor the deeper darkness of the umbra, so he stays out of sight of Dorchnok’s Eye. at is why we should meditate now, before the antumbra passes. Because when the umbra is here, I think we wil have a visitor—one that might crave our esh in addition to our spirits.” *** Myjun stared up at the black sky and wondered how any kind of light existed in this endless world of shadows. ere were no stars overhead, yet she felt as if she stood beneath the starlight of a moonless sky. And when the gray ring of Dorchnok’s Eye rose on the horizon, that starlight became more akin to moonlight. At the peak of the antumbra, when the eye stood directly above their heads, it was almost as bright as dawn or dusk in the physical world—yet there was no sun, moon, or star: the light simply was. Myjun had come to think of it as shadowlight, which softened the darkness of the shadow realm’s deeper blackness. Now, with Dorchnok’s Eye absent from the sky and the shadowlight faded to darkness, the umbral night possessed an alien intensity. Strangely, though, the black smoke of the Sauthron Sea seemed to sparkle more brightly during the umbra, as if its own luminescence increased when it did not have to compete with shadowlight or the Dorchnok’s antumbral eye. ey were camped near those shimmering waters now, its black vapors lapping at the gray land. Yet as Myjun turned her gaze across the wide, nethereal sea, it seemed more like a veil of stars. “He is coming,” Oyru said, rising from his meditative trance. “ e esh wraith?” Myjun asked. “Or the witherkin, yes. I glimpsed his form at the last umbra. I meant to kil him then, before he could hunt us, but he disappeared.” He pointed into the black vapors of the ocean. “And now he has returned.” Myjun stared into the night-black vapors and saw that where most of the waters stil sparkled with light, a space near the shore had lost its luminescence. Not long after that, she realized the darkness had the shape of a man and was coming toward them. “Do you know … before he was taken …” “Who he was?” Oyru shook his head. “I do not know the names nor do I recal the faces of the people the eidola stole from your vil age. I only wanted Annev.” e darkness drew closer and, as it did, Myjun saw more of the shade’s features revealed by the shadowlight: the broad forehead, the long nose and narrow eyes. It took her another moment, but then she knew the wraith’s identity for herself. “ at’s Yohan … the village chandler.” “A candlemaker. Interesting. His wil must have been strong to survive al this time.” Myjun remembered the chandler’s forceful personality, her anxiety rising. “Have you determined what he wants?” Oyru stared at the shade, his single eye squinting into the darkness. “Flesh wraiths crave life and take it in the form of esh. Witherkin want vengeance. ey have un nished business and won’t rest til it is ful l ed.” Oyru summoned his twin yssas and stepped purposeful y forward. “And this one is … ?” Myjun took a step back as the chandler’s ghost drew nearer. Oyru’s twin swords passed through the chandler’s shade, cutting the ghost neatly through the neck and chest. e blades passed through Yohan’s body without any resistance and then emerged out the other side. en the ghost’s eyes opened wide and shifted from night-black to pure white. “Witherkin!” Oyru said, dispel ing the blades. “Run!” Matching words to actions, the assassin bolted from their camp by the waters and ew straight as an arrow toward the dark mountains on the horizon. Myjun fol owed a heartbeat later, her soulblades screaming into existence in her hands. “Why are we running from a chandler’s ghost!” she shouted, not looking back to see if the witherkin was fol owing them. “ at is a spirit trapped in the cognitive realm,” Oyru bel owed. “ ey are to the shadow realm what the eidola are to the physical world: abominations. Nightmares. Void blades do not harm them, and they wil devour your mind and your somnumbra. ey are the wandering death of this land!” “You could have told me this before!” “Flesh wraiths are rare. Witherkin are almost nonexistent.” “Wel , this one seems pretty damn existent!” ey ran on in silence, their eet pace carrying them swiftly over the rol ing hil s toward the mountains. “Wil my soulblades kil it?” “Not likely. is stupid candlemaker is only partial y here. is is an echo of him; the rest has perished or moved on to the Spirit World.” “So how do we kil him?” “We don’t. He is dead already—but his mind wil not relent. If we give him what he wants, he may pass over.” Myjun ventured a glance back and saw the black ocean shore recede into the distance. ere was no sign of the witherkin. “Can we stop? I can’t see him.” “No. Witherkin are not tethered to this space, just as we are not temporal y tethered to space in the physical realm.” “Speak sense!” “He is not behind us because he is not actual y here.” “I said sense!” Oyru stopped abruptly and Myjun had to pivot to avoid crashing into him. He gestured at the rol ing hil s ahead of them and the sloping shores at their backs. “He is a shadow of the cognitive realm. His wil is causing him to manifest here, but he is not actual y here.” “ en why are we running from him!” Myjun shouted, her temper aring. As if in response to her question, a black shadow began to coalesce beside them, its glaring white eyes burning like the wrath of the sun. “Because of that,” Oyru said, and then he resumed his sprint. “How in the ve hel s can he do that!” “Nine Hel s,” Oyru said, not breaking stride. “But your question is stil valid. He’s not tethered to this plane, so as soon as we stop moving, he can shift to wherever we’ve run to.” “So,” Myjun said, gulping for breath, “we have to keep moving inde nitely?” “Until Dorchnok’s Eye rises and antumbra dawns … yes.” “Shit.” ey ran on in silence, neither one daring to look back, until Myjun slowed to a walk. Oyru ran on for a dozen paces, then turned. “What are you doing?” “If al we have to do is keep moving, we can walk. We don’t need to run.” Oyru stared at her blank-faced. en, as if realizing he had stopped moving, he jogged to catch up with Myjun and then kept pace beside her. ey walked in silence for a hundred paces, then Myjun snorted aloud. “I can’t believe you never thought to walk.” “ ey are not something I encounter often,” Oyru said, his voice strained. “What did you do last time? Run like an idiot?” e assassin peered sideways at her. “I am not usual y toting around a tabibito, much less one who cannot shift themselves to the physical world.” “So you run away … to another plane. You go to the physical world and hope it forgets about you?” Oyru exhaled. “Basical y.” Myjun laughed, her tone ful of spite. “You’re pathetic. You’re supposed to be this terrible, undying kil er who can pop out of the shadows and murder you—and here you are running from the ghost of a candlemaker.” “Witherkin,” Oyru said, his tone just shy of sul en. “He is not just a ghost. He is a witherkin.” Myjun slowed her pace even further then stopped. Oyru walked two more steps then stopped too. “What are you doing?” he asked. “Testing something.” She concentrated and summoned her soulblades. A moment later, the chandler’s shade appeared beside them, his black mouth yawning open in a silent scream. Myjun took a cautious step toward the specter and then rammed her daggers of light into the ghost’s eyes. e witherkin’s face contorted into a look of shock, then rage. His eyes ared, growing wider, brighter, and the chandler’s black hands reached out for her. Myjun stepped away, out of reach, then started walking. Oyru was just a step behind and, behind them, the witherkin’s eyes grew dim and his black form faded into the shadowlight. “I had to try,” Myjun said, dispel ing her soul re blades. “Obviously—and now you see why witherkin are not so easily vanquished.” Myjun grunted. “So are you witherkin?” “No. Maybe. Perhaps if I al owed one of the eidola to consume my soul, I would become one.” “Or a esh wraith?” “No. My body has grown too accustomed to somnumbra. I can survive on that alone … but that means I cannot stay in the physical world for too long. I am dependent on this world. I have become one of its denizens.” Myjun nodded, piecing it al together. “You had un nished business with Oraqui. You searched Reocht na Skah for her, for seven thousand years. Time warped and stretched and you became dependent on somnumbra … and you became a half shadow, half man.” Oyru kept pace beside her. “Annumbra,” he said. “Years in the shadow realm are cal ed annumbra … and I spent ten or twelve thousand of them in Reocht na Skah. Waiting. Searching. Praying for her to return to me.” “Do you regret it?” Myjun asked. “Sometimes,” he said, that single eye xed on the horizon, “I regret that I did not wait longer.” CHAPTER FIFTY-NINE Having passed their Tests of Ascendancy, erin and Titus established new routines with the journeymen and Dionachs from their respective castes. e most notable of these was Titus receiving instruction on the more nuanced arts of mindwalking, including how to enter an unguarded person’s mind and browse their dormant memories. e former steward was innately better at it than every journeyman in his caste, and that talent a rmed Dionach Holyoak’s decision to elevate him to ful Dionach. With that promotion, Brother Tym also began teaching Titus the principles of mind-leeching: drawing on another person’s thoughts and absorbing them, as if one’s own. Mind-leeching could also erase memories from a subject’s mind, but Dionach Holyoak and Brother Tym both agreed it would be prudent to master one aspect of the skil at a time. For erin, life at the Enclave had become far more interesting as a journeyman Breathbreaker. e skil s he practiced with Dionach Honeycutt and his fel ow journeymen weren’t altogether new, but their application required a new level of complexity, nuance, and creativity. He used vacuum bubbles to scale sheer wal s, cling to ceilings, and run up vertical surfaces. With the application of air and sound bubbles, he learned how to silence himself and those around him, how to create explosions with displaced air and how to propel himself with almost no friction or loss of momentum. He described his training in detail to Titus and Annev, thril ed by each new discovery and excited about combining them with the martial skil s he’d learned at the Academy. For Annev’s part, life at the Enclave had changed just as drastical y since the theft of the booby-trapped painting. Before the attack, he’d been determined to leave—to do anything except wait for Reeve to decide his future. But now he had a purpose again. He had a suspect, and he was tired of running from people who meant him harm. He’d tried to hide in Chaenbalu and they had sent the feurog and the Shadow Reborn. He’d gone to Banok and an assassin with a crossbow had tried to murder him. He’d ed to Luqura and been chased in turn by Elar Kranak and Saltair. Enough running. No longer content with simply leaving Quiri and returning to Luqura, Annev decided to go on the o ensive and begin hunting the people who were secretly hunting him. He told himself it would be cowardly to run and leave his friends to fend for themselves, and he had no intention of making them targets to save himself. Yet Annev held no il usions about what that meant for his own safety. Every day he took additional precautions against future attacks, and against any attempts to interfere with his belongings or his quarters. When his friends invited him to lunch, he was careful to eat food he had prepared himself. When he entered a new room or walked down a corridor, he slowed to study the wal s and furniture for subtle glyphs or wards. At night, he stopped sleeping in his room and instead rotated between the many empty chambers of the Enclave’s lowest oor. And then there were his experiments with the Rod of Arti cing. Once he had discovered that the Inquisitor ring al owed him to see the hundreds of invisible glyphs covering the wal s of the Enclave, Annev began to experiment, dismantling them. When he saw a rune or ward that looked potential y threatening, he took out his rod and tried to uncover which Dionach or journeyman had cast it. Sometimes the threads fel apart in his hands, but more often he was able to fol ow the ribbon of magic back to the caster. Sometimes Annev would then interrogate those Dionachs, using his codavora and Inquisitor rings, but his questions never yielded the answers he sought. at vigilance came with a cost, too, for as the days turned into weeks, he became increasingly morose, sleep-deprived, and paranoid. On the rare occasion that members of the Order came to speak with him, Annev refused to see them until he’d donned his entire arsenal of artifacts—including his dragonscale cloak and his amberge. He took the same precautions when walking around the Enclave, leading to some Dionachs whispering behind his back. He overheard himself described as Sodar’s unfortunate project—an oddity, a curio. Some brothers seemed to be afraid of him and his glowing golden hand—a fact con rmed by the auramancy of his codavora ring—which only pushed Annev further into depression. He struggled to be interested when his friends shared the exciting magics they were performing, and he convinced himself he couldn’t tel his friends what had happened. Gradual y, his silence transformed it into a secret. And Annev continued to search for his attacker. She became frenzied herself, her emotions further fueling her magic, speeding her beyond the reach of tooth and claw. She saw the anger in Kenton’s gaze and fought to dominate it. She saw the betrayal in Annev’s eyes after she’d discovered his missing limb, and she sought to blind him. Al around her, the trol s were fal ing, sprawling backward with their eyes burned out. One beast leapt atop her, surprising her as it wrestled her to the earth like an angry bear. It raked its claws down her back and she howled with both pleasure and pain. She twisted in his grasp, her sts slamming his armored skin, forcing the soul re blades into his chest. e iron trol convulsed … and died. Myjun gasped, crushed by the weight of the shaggy beast. With an e ort, she rol ed out from under the dead trol ’s bulk and blinked away the blood that stained her vision. ere were scores of monstrous corpses scattered about the clearing, and her body was already healing from the few wounds the trol s had in icted. She’d grown faster and stronger during their many months hunting eidolons—and though these trol s were fast, she was faster. Oyru stood over a trol that was stil moaning in the shadows. His yssas icked down, piercing its skul , and the thing shuddered and fel silent. With a grunt, the assassin yanked his narrow sword from the trol ’s eyes. e Shadow Reborn looked at her curiously. “You fought di erently tonight. Less angry. More . . . focused. It was almost a dance. Very beautiful.” He dispel ed his swords and walked close enough to her that Myjun could smel the hot blood on his clothes. “Have you gained control of your emotions, then?” he asked. “Have you discovered how to use the powers of the mask without letting it master you?” Myjun’s mind returned to her waking vision: she had never lain with Annev or Kenton, though she had come close with the latter, and the mask had centered her anger on that. She had been attracted to Kenton until the fool boy had been scarred. She’d never been able to look at him the same way after that. And then Annev had been worse. e deceptive one-armed bastard had been marked by Keos the whole time—and he’d kept it secret from her. He’d made her fal in love with him and then … What is wrong with me that everyone I love or care for is damaged or corrupted? Even my father. Even me. Everything I touch turns to ashes … and I am drawn to the darkness. She looked up and saw Oyru studying her, his pupil like a wide pool of inky blackness. He saw something in her and nodded his approval. “You are ready to face the test of ashes. Come with me to the re.” Myjun complied, feeling dazed and angry, only vaguely aware that she’d dispel ed her soulblades. She studied Oyru in turn, and when he beckoned her to sit, she did. Oyru extended his hand and wisps of smoke trailed behind his ngers. She half expected him to summon one of his yssas, but instead a pair of shadow-black tongs appeared in his hand. He stretched the tool into the re and plucked out one of the crumbling orange embers that glowed there. “Ironwood embers,” Oyru said, bringing the coal in front of him, “wil cool to resin and ash when they make contact with organic matter. e trol s eat them when there is only a touch of warmth remaining. To make your armor, though, the embers must be hot. Your blood wil cool them, and the mask wil heal your burns before they can scar … but it wil stil be painful.” Myjun nodded. “ e resin wil take about an hour to harden into plate armor. It wil be thin—like wearing a second skin—but it wil be tough as steel. Where you need more exibility, we wil use the residue from the ashes, which wil stil be stronger than any chainmail or leather you might wear—and protect you against magic, but it won’t be as strong as the resin. Even so, this is the most powerful and versatile armor in existence, and the best-kept secret of my long-dead family clan.” “Why do you not wear it then?” “ e magic does not bond with half-men.” “ en why didn’t you obtain it before you became a half man?” Myjun asked bluntly. Oyru hesitated, then placed the coal back in the re. “My father swore to bring me here and perform the ritual, but when he was kil ed that duty passed to my mother. She refused—for many years—because she disapproved of my choice of mate.” “Oraqui.” He nodded. “In the end, she won my mother over by o ering to take the test of ashes herself. She knew what it meant—both the pain, and that it would forever mark her as one of our clan. So my mother brought us both here, to these mountains. To the trol lairs. First she made me watch as she burned Oraqui’s esh … and then she made me help.” Oyru fel silent, no sign of emotion or weakness as he looked into the re. “I burned her with the ironwood resin and its ashes,” he continued, “but when it was my turn to take the test, there weren’t enough embers left. We swore to come back together—she would perform the ritual for me as I had for her—but then Oraqui betrayed me and brought Gevul down upon my household.” Myjun couldn’t hold her peace. “Why did you wait for her, after that? Why would you stil think she cared for you?” Oyru gestured to the re with his tongs. “Because Oraqui knew my family’s secret. She could have brought Gevul and his clan here and given our magic to them . . . but she never did. She kept her word. She helped Gevul kil my family, but she kept our greatest secret.” “Why would she do that?” He shrugged. “If I ever see her again, perhaps I wil ask.” “It makes no sense. She helped kil your family—why not betray that one secret?” Oyru hesitated. “Perhaps when we have hurt someone we love, it is natural to hold something in reserve, something to show we are not whol y monsters. Perhaps it is a cry for help or redemption.” e assassin plucked a fresh coal from its embers. “Or perhaps in a mad world, we cling to a single virtue so we can excuse the other atrocities we al ow ourselves to commit.” “I think it’s the latter.” e Shadow Reborn shrugged. “People are complicated.” “But you stil love her. Even though she kil ed your family, you stil love her.” “If you must ask that, you did not understand my story. Oraqui joined my family when I burned her with these coals. She became part of my clan.” He extended the ironwood ember toward Myjun. “I o er you the same.” Myjun stared at the orange coal then looked back to Oyru’s single eye. Without a word, she shed her clothes and stood, erce, before him. “I am ready.” “ en I wil bathe you in embers and ashes,” he whispered, and pressed the hot coal to her skin. Myjun hissed, just as the coal against her skin hissed, the latter glowing red with re and blood. e pain was bright and bril iant, almost overwhelming, and as it cooled it gave her clarity amidst the hazy vapors of charred ironwood. Oyru rol ed the ember over her and the pain ared anew, but when she looked down at her esh, she saw not bubbling burns, but a beautiful blue-black chitinous layer covering her esh. “ is wil transform me into a monster,” Myjun growled through gritted teeth. “I wil never be free of this—just like my mask.” “We are already monsters,” the assassin breathed in her ear, continuing the ritual, “and now our bodies match our hearts.” CHAPTER SIXTY-EIGHT Annev stared at Tym’s round face. “Dead?” he whispered. “But … I just saw him. He was alive.” Brother Tym’s eyebrows narrowed. “You mean . . . you saw him while mindwalking?” Annev nodded, earning a frown and a contemplative grunt from Misty and Tym respectively. “What did you see?” Tym asked, his expression neutral. Annev opened his mouth to answer, then he recal ed how his vision had ended: how blood had sprayed from Holyoak’s eyes, ears, and mouth. He remembered the mist. e gore. How it seemed he could taste the man’s blood on his lips. But none of that was real, Annev thought. We were mindwalking—we were in Holyoak’s mind, and I didn’t attack him. But was that true? Annev had used the Hand of Keos to break down Holyoak’s mind palace. Was that also an attack on the man’s literal mind? Had Annev’s actions inadvertently caused his death? “How did it happen?” Annev asked, reinforcing his own mental wal s. “You’d been under for a few hours,” Misty said, laying a hand on Tym’s shoulder. “Tym was monitoring you from outside the implanted memory and we were considering waking you but then something happened. You had … some kind of breakthrough?” “He found the quaire glyphs!” Tym interjected, unable to keep the excitement from his face. “It was bril iant. I never would have found them.” He turned to Annev. “But then you did something strange. You made the glyphs disappear … and then you disappeared.” “I dispel ed the quaire glyphs to see the trail of blood-talent and fol ow it to the traitor. Holyoak was at the other end—the forged memory must have led me into his mind. I spoke to him … and he admitted betraying the Enclave.” “We gathered that,” Misty said, her eyes ful of sympathy. “Tym couldn’t reach you, but you were mumbling. We caught pieces of what you were saying.” “I was talking in my sleep?” “Mindwalking is not sleep,” Tym corrected. “It looks near enough from the outside, though,” Misty said. “We heard enough of your accusations against Holyoak for Reeve to send some brothers to take him into custody.” “Did he ght back?” “He wasn’t even awake,” said Misty. Tym seemed about to say something, but a glare from her sti ed whatever objections he’d been about to raise. “ ere’s a time and a place for teaching mindwalking technique, dear.” Misty returned her gaze to Annev. “Holyoak was in a trance, like you, and nothing we did woke him. We worried that forcibly waking either of you might cause some mental or psychic damage, so we agreed not to wake either of you unless you became distressed. Holyoak was placed under close guard in a warded cel and you were kept in our bedroom.” Annev abruptly realized they were not currently in Misty and Tym’s bedchamber. e room was much smal er, and clearly unoccupied. He tensed when he noticed the tiny glyphs carved into the wal s. “ is is … one of the warded cel s?” Annev said, stating the obvious. Misty nodded then glanced sidelong at her husband. “Do you want to tel him?” “Might be better to show him,” Tym said, his hand gently fal ing on Annev’s shoulder. “Come on.” *** Not much was left in Tym and Misty’s bedroom: a badly charred bedspread, a soot-stained clothes chest, and scraps of smoky linens. e rest was gone—the bed, the books, the table and chairs—al burned to ash and cinders. Annev stood in the center of the room and swal owed, his throat dry from the lingering smoke and the bile that burned the back of his throat. His feet traced the curve of the melted stones beneath his feet and then he bowed his head in shame. “I’m sorry.” “It wasn’t your fault,” Misty said, immediately at Annev’s side. “You didn’t know what you were doing. You had no idea what was happening in the physical world.” “It’s my fault,” Tym said, his own head bowed with regret. “I should have moved you the moment you made contact with Holyoak— before then maybe— but I wanted to keep a close eye on you. I thought this was a good place, but . . . wel , it was my fault. I’m sorry.” e apology seemed as much for Misty as Annev. “It’s nobody’s fault,” Dionach McClanahan replied, her long arms draping over Tym’s shoulders. “It was an accident. No one could have predicted this.” Annev was less certain. He had wil ed the Hand of Keos to appear during his mindwalking trance: he had wanted it, summoned it—and then he had conjured its magic. He had brought the destructive ames into the cognitive realm, supposing they wouldn’t reach the physical world . . . and he’d been wrong. “How—” he croaked, his voice dry. He swal owed and tried again. “How did you stop it? How did you move me?” “As soon as the hand started glowing, we had some of the brothers come and try to contain the re with a shield spel ,” Tym said. “ at worked for a bit, until the ames . . . wel , they pushed the shield outward. I’m not sure how. I mean, it shouldn’t have been possible. But they couldn’t contain the re, and I couldn’t wake you, and the bed caught re and things were al a merry blaze for a bit. Reeve left Brother Honeycutt to watch Holyoak and dashed down here to help—he vented some of the re into that corner of the room, that’s how the bookcase caught ame—and things were stable enough that we were able to oat you down to the cel s. Got you tucked away nice and neat. Wel , mostly neat.” He looked around his ruined bedroom and shrugged. “It’s nothing that can’t be replaced. ere are copies of most of these books in the library—and the rest I can replace myself.” He tapped the side of his skul . “I’ve a pretty good memory.” Annev nodded, reminded of the chest of memories he’d recovered from Holyoak. “Did you get those memories back to Sraon? Wil he be okay?” “He’l be ne,” Misty said. “Tym passed me the stolen memories and I handled the transplant personal y. Reeve supervised. Sraon should make a ful recovery, but it wil stil take a few days before he feels like his old self.” Annev felt relieved until he returned his attention to the room’s destruction. “Al of this … How was I not injured?” “Good question,” Tym said. “Near as we can tel , the ames don’t harm you. Don’t understand why, but they don’t. Made our job a sight easier, in any case. We shielded you in a bal of skywater—ice, air, water—and that made the transport possible.” He chuckled. “Funny thing was, as soon as we got you to your cel , things began to quiet down. Turned the re o yourself, I think … but that’s when the trouble started up with Holyoak.” Annev studied the Mindwalker’s wary face. “What did happen to Holyoak?” Tym cleared his throat. “You remember how Honeycutt was left to watch Holyoak—when Reeve came dashing to help you?” “Yes,” Annev said, his eyebrows narrowing. “What happened?” “Honeycutt kil ed him.” Annev wasn’t sure he understood—then his eyes shot wide open. “Honeycutt kil ed Holyoak?” “Near as we can tel , yes.” “ e manner of death was consistent with a Breathbreaker attack,” Misty added. “And Brother Honeycutt has since ed the Enclave.” “But … why?” “We don’t know,” Misty said as Tym splayed his hands in the air. “ ere’s been some speculation that they were working together … and unfortunately that makes sense.” “If Honeycutt suspected Holyoak was talking to you,” Tym added, “he might have decided to eliminate him before he could be interrogated.” Annev nodded, imagining the Mindwalkers and Stormcal ers prying into Holyoak’s memories, sorting through his thoughts and exposing his secrets. “Has anyone else ed?” “No. Just him.” “Could there be other traitors hiding at the Enclave?” Tym sighed. “I had hoped you could answer that for us. I assume Holyoak didn’t tel you very much.” “No.” He gave a brief summary of what had transpired between him and Holyoak. When he had nished, both Tym and Misty seemed to be studying him with new eyes. “What is it?” Misty glanced at Tym, her eyes averted. “You pretended to be Keos?” “Wel … no, not exactly. I just intimidated him with the Hand and let him come to his own conclusions.” “So you pretended to be Keos,” she repeated, more forceful y. Annev winced. “I guess.” “And you told him to kneel?” is time there was no mistaking the look of disgust she tried to hide. “It seemed appropriate,” Annev said, wishing he’d omitted that detail. Tym’s eyes were twinkling. Misty shot him a look and he threw up his hands, defensive. “What? It was clever! He had to be convincing, didn’t he?” Dionach McClanahan sni ed then rol ed her eyes. “Men. Always quick to use the bluntest instrument in the room.” She turned back to Annev. “Did you get any inkling as to whether he had acted alone? Whether Honeycutt or anyone else had assisted him?” Annev thought about it. “He seemed surprised when I accused him of instigating the attack on my village and said he had only tried to kil me after I came to Quiri. But that can’t be true … can it?” “I don’t know, Annev. Why would he lie about that but admit being a servant of Keos? Why admit trying to kil you but deny the rest?” Annev thought for a long while. Final y, Tym broke the silence: “I worked closely with Holyoak, Annev—close enough to know when he left the Enclave. He was a bit of a recluse. He relied on messengers to communicate with distant members of our caste, and he rarely left Quiri.” “What about Saltair? Did Holyoak ever communicate with him?” “Not that I know of,” Tym said, chewing his lip, “but I doubt anyone at the Enclave would admit communicating with one of the Siänar.” “What about a merchant named Janak Harth?” “Janak who?” “Harth. He had a reputation for col ecting artifacts. Lived in Banok?” “I’ve heard of him,” Misty volunteered, “but how is he connected to the attack on your village?” “Honestly, I’m stil not sure, but he had planned to attack Chaenbalu. e feurog that nal y did destroy the village …” Annev shuddered, remembering them and the phantasmic shadow demons. “Maybe they weren’t connected— or maybe it was me. ey were al trying to get to me.” “ at may be true,” Tym said, “but so far as I know, Holyoak never had any contact with Janak Harth. In fact, the only suspicious thing I can identify is that he dispatched two of our Mindwalkers to visit the more distant Dionach chapter houses.” “Why is that suspicious?” “Because of those Dionachs who have traveled in the last year, al of them have been lost or kil ed, except for those two Dionachs—Chan and Davies, both Mindwalkers.” “And close associates of Brother Holyoak,” Misty said, her lips pursed. “ at does seem suspicious.” “Teiksim Chan and Rockford Davies? I can’t real y imagine any two Dionachs less suspicious. ey’re both dualists, like Holyoak, actual y.” Tym looked at Misty. “Do you think that’s signi cant?” She furrowed her brow. “Maybe … but we should be wary of prejudice. Mindcal ers and Stormpsychics have a history of being pro led as deviants. We can’t just assume their guilt, not even with Holyoak’s betrayal. And I doubt Rockford’s dualist nature is relevant. He’s a condenser, right?” “A Mindshear,” Tym supplied. “Half Mindwalker, half Shieldbearer.” Misty sni ed. “I can never keep those titles straight. Too many dualist names by half.” “One hundred and thirty-two among the prime mages,” Tym said, smiling, “and if you include the New Terran hybrids, you can have as many as—” “Please don’t.” “Four hundred and sixty-two,” he nished, stil grinning. “Makes my head hurt just thinking about it,” Misty said, pinching the bridge of her nose. “Anyway, I doubt it’s relevant. If Dionachs Chan and Davies are traitors, it wil be due to their proximity to Holyoak and his in uence, not because they are Mindwalker hybrids.” “So Chan and Davies are the only ones who survived recent trips abroad,” Annev pressed, not wanting to lose the thread of their discussion. “ ey’re both Mindwalkers with connections to Holyoak. at’s more than enough to investigate them.” “Dionach Chan’s proximity to the Empire’s border, on her mission, would have made her a perfect messenger, especial y since she and Holyoak were both Mindcal ers,” Misty added. “ ey could have passed messages freely between one another, and then Dionach Chan could have passed those messages on to their Terran al ies. She had the ability and the means to be invaluable to a spy network.” “What about Davies?” Annev asked. “Where was he stationed?” “His territory covered the southern half of the Empire,” Tym said, his expression darkening. “I don’t want to jump to any conclusions, but if Holyoak was orchestrating the assassinations of our missing members, Davies would have been perfect for the job. Mindwalking would have al owed him to spy on others, and his talents with skywater could make him a skil ed assassin.” He pursed his lips. “Blood and bile, I hope we’re wrong. Davies has always been a good friend to me. I can’t imagine him kil ing al those people. Dionach Kadmon, Brother Witherspoon, Sisters Rugebregt and Morgenstone . . . so many deaths, so many missing.” He clutched a hand to his mouth and muttered a quick apology before ducking out of the room. Annev and Misty both looked after him in sympathy, but when Misty turned back to Annev, he could see her steel. “We’ve tried to keep Holyoak’s death quiet, but with Honeycutt’s disappearance, rumors are going to spread. ey probably already have. If we’re going to track down Chan and Davies, we’l need to move fast.” “Agreed,” Annev said, grateful for the change in Misty’s attitude. “I don’t have much time to hunt down the traitors, and this recent debacle won’t encourage Reeve to extend my stay.” “Indeed not,” said a deep voice from the other end of the room. Annev turned and saw it was the Arch-Dionach himself, who entered with Brother Tym under his arm and a thunderous expression. “You wil leave the Enclave tomorrow.” “I hoped that—” “I am grateful for your work—but it doesn’t change this.” He gestured at the melted stones and charred furniture. “It’s too dangerous for you to stay here. at hasn’t changed, Annev. Holyoak is dead, so we have no one to question. Honeycutt is gone, and I can’t spare anyone to hunt him down with the threat of additional traitors hiding within the Order.” “We’ve been talking about that,” Annev said. “Dionachs Chan and Davies might be connected to Holyoak’s betrayal. Or even assisted him. If you quarantined them—” “Quarantined?” Reeve sni ed. “Boy, how many Dionachs do you think we have here at the Enclave? About two dozen. How many of those do you think I can trust? Odar’s beard, you think I’m worried about people running? I want them to run. I’m worried about whether I can keep control of the bloody place.” Annev blinked. “You’re worried about a coup?” Reeve nodded. “So . . . you’re not going to track him down? You’re going to let Honeycutt go?” “I don’t have a choice, Annev. e Order is in danger. e Enclave isn’t safe. I need to put my house in order before I start chasing down traitors and heretics. Frankly, I think we might have been overwhelmed already except we received some troubling news from the south just as this business with Holyoak happened.” He pul ed a creased letter from his robes, its seal broken. “Troubling news?” Annev said, his eyes brie y drawn to the letter. “Reeve, what could be more troubling than this? We need to act fast if we’re going to catch Honeycutt!” “You’re right … so take this.” He extended the letter to Annev. “Read it when you have the chance, and decide what you’d like to do.” Annev took it apprehensively. “What is it?”

chapters.title: Chapter 10
chapters.content: “For now, it’s just a distraction. Reports about a besieged city and a request from some traveling dreamers, when we need to focus on the traitors in our midst.” He nodded to the others. “Misty and Tym wil help me interrogate Davies and Chan, after we’ve questioned a few others of our brethren and con rmed their al egiance remains with Odar and the Dionachs Tobar.” “I could help, though,” Annev o ered, his st tightening. “I need to help. ese people . . . Reeve, this conspiracy may have been responsible for the attacks on my village. For Sodar’s death. I won’t just leave this investigation now.” “What makes you think they’re responsible, Annev? Holyoak knew nothing about Chaenbalu or Sodar’s mission. I alone knew Sodar’s location, and I only shared it with Brother Arnor.” He paused. “And he’s dead.” Annev considered this. “Would Arnor have told anyone else?” “Only his caste leader.” e group was silent as Reeve’s indignant, instinctive words slowly sank in. “Dammit,” Reeve swore. “Honeycutt knew.” e Arch-Dionach tugged his goatee. “Damn, this is al my fault.” Annev felt his st clench tighter. “No,” he said, his voice icy. “ is is Honeycutt’s fault. You made a mistake, but he pro ted from it. He’s de nitely part of this.” “… probably. But I can’t send anyone after him, Annev.” Annev’s wandering compass suddenly pointed resolutely in one direction, and he knew what he had to do. He could nal y leave the Enclave and continue his pursuit of the people who had attacked him and the vil agers of Chaenbalu. e certainty of it felt good—it felt right. Like he’d nal y found his purpose. “I’l go. You want me to leave anyway, so I may as wel hunt Honeycutt down and get answers out of him.” Reeve tutted his tongue against his teeth, his eyes shifting between the two silent Dionachs at his side. “I don’t like it … but you’re right. I can’t keep you here, and I can’t stop you.” He glanced meaningful y at Annev’s golden hand, which had begun to glow with a dul red luminescence. “Blood and ashes,” Annev swore, tucking the hand behind his back and trying to calm his emotions. “I’m sorry.” Reeve nodded, accepting the apology without drawing attention to it. “I had this made for you.” He tossed a black felt glove to Annev, its cu stitched with silver thread and its palm and ngers padded with … something. Annev slipped it on to his left hand and was immediately impressed by its t. “It’s got a few quaire glyphs woven into the lining—shields of air and water, something that might help quench an unintentional ame …” “It’s great,” Annev said, grateful to Reeve for saving the moment. “ ank you.” He nodded again. “Gather your things and go after Honeycutt if you must … but be careful. You’re resourceful and brave—you’ve been trained as an assassin and a thief—but you’re going up against a ful Dionach with over a thousand years of experience, and that puts you at a serious disadvantage. He might kil you or you might kil him, but you’re just as likely to blow up half the city. I hope that, if it comes down to letting Honeycutt go or destroying Quiri, you’l do the smart thing and save your revenge for another day. Another time and place.” “I’m not looking for revenge,” Annev protested, his cheeks ushed with anger and embarrassment. Reeve was unconvinced. “I know that look, Annev. I’ve worn it myself. You think you’re looking for answers—and you might nd them—but consider the cost before you do anything you may regret.” Annev remembered how close he had come to destroying Luqura and nodded. “Good.” Reeve patted Tym on the back. “Brother McClanahan, I’m sorry you are becoming the Mindwalkers’ leader under such sad circumstances—but I need your help. I’d be pleased if you and Misty would help me root out any remaining heretics. It’s time we nal y rid ourselves of the rot that’s been hiding under our noses. May Odar protect us … and may the Order survive our investigation.” CHAPTER SIXTY-NINE Annev’s goodbyes with Tym and Misty were quick, and accompanied with a promise to reconnect once their missions were complete. Even as he said the words, though, Annev doubted he’d return to the Order. ere was nothing for him here—he’d come to that conclusion long ago—and his presence endangered not only the Enclave, but his friends. He hastened to Titus and erin’s quarters to say his goodbyes but didn’t see either boy in their rooms, so he headed back down to col ect his few unburned possessions in preparation for his departure. Just as he reached the basement, he found them. “Annev, we’ve been looking for you!” “Titus, erin! I was—” “You heard the news about Dolyn and Brayan?” Titus continued. “Dolyn and …” Annev’s heart fel into the pit of his stomach. Was this related to the letter Reeve had given him? Annev had completely forgotten about the Orvanish blacksmith and the burly quartermaster. He hadn’t even sent word to Banok to let Brayan know the party had moved on from Luqura to Quiri. And I promised to return for them. Blood and ashes, I’m a horrible friend. at wasn’t al he had promised and forgotten. With painful clarity, Annev remembered swearing to Red-thumb that he would introduce Jian Nikloss to Sodja Rocas in Luqura and look after the albino necromancer. Annev hadn’t kept a single promise: he hadn’t returned to Banok, he had never found Sodja, and Jian had died to save him. Annev smothered his wave of guilt and made himself ask: “What news?” “ e whole damn town has been taken hostage!” erin said, his tone near hysterical. “We’ve been searching for you ever since we heard.” “Sorry, I’ve been a bit occupied.” He stopped. “Wait … so Brayan has been taken hostage?” Titus nodded. “Annev, I’m worried. ey aren’t letting anyone out.” Annev had an uneasy feeling sinking in his gut. “ is is in Banok?” ey nodded. “Do you know who’s doing it?” “A group cal ed the Sons of Damnation,” Titus said, looking concerned. “ ey aren’t Terran,” erin added. “ at’s been con rmed by the few who escaped before the gates were sealed.” Annev swal owed back bile, beginning to fear what was coming next. “How many?” “Just a handful, Reeve heard. Annev …” Titus wetted his lips. “Annev, they used artifacts. ey used magic to control the vil agers, but they’ve also been saying horrible things about anyone who might have a talent for magic—even a little. And I think … wel , I think they may be looking for you.” Rotting blood and ashes. Annev knees suddenly felt weak and his mouth had gone dry at this con rmation of his fears. “Why do you think they want me?” e boys shared a look and erin spoke. “ ey’ve made it clear they’re looking for someone with one arm or someone with a giant golden hand.” at sealed it then. e few masters left alive at Chaenbalu were the only group whose agenda might match Titus and erin’s description. Annev let out a long, slow breath and shook his head. “ ey didn’t seem like a threat. I thought they’d leave us alone … but they must have found a way to plunder the vault and come after us. Dammit. We should have kil ed them—made a clean slate of things.
