You see, the fth member of our party lies in the capital city, and Luqura has become altogether unwelcome toward the people of my culture.” “ at’s an understatement,” Sraon said, shifting his eye patch. “When was the last time you visited Luqura, Master Red-thumb?” e merrymaker smiled. “Ah, Master Sraon. is wil be my rst visit to your capital city.” “ en, for your own good, I suggest you postpone your visit . . . inde nitely.” “You are referring to the Ilumite slave trade, which has been imported from the north—from Innistiul.” “Yes,” Sraon hu ed. “I haven’t seen the capital in some time, but I’ve heard that King Cheng’s in uence has almost eclipsed King Lenka’s, even there, and I fear what wil happen when the old man passes, particularly with Innistiul’s hooks so rmly embedded in the city’s commerce. If you are intent on traveling to Luqura, you are likely to nd yourselves captured, branded, and enslaved.” He paused, glancing at the cat-eyed Shalgarn ranger and the pink-eyed albino soothsayer. “I expect the rest of your troupe wil meet a similar fate —worse, perhaps. If you openly walk the streets, they’l scoop you up and sel you o quicker than you can blink.” “Which is precisely why we need a chaperone in the city. Someone to vouchsafe for us while we track down the last member of our troupe.” Sraon shook his head. “I’ve already granted your boon, Master Red-thumb. I’ve told you where to nd Mistress Dolyn, and I’ve given you fair warning that you aren’t likely to persuade her. Best to give up this quest of yours before you endanger your life and that of your friends.” Red-thumb raised his open hands and arms. “ at I cannot do.” Sraon sni ed. “ en I wish you good health and good luck in your travels.” CHAPTER ELEVEN “Master Ainnevog stil owes a debt to me, yes?” e group turned to look at Jian, who had raised his hand in mild objection. Sraon frowned, scratching at his eye patch. “Could be. What do you want?” “To travel to Luqura … with you.” Sraon spat. “Come on, Jian. I just explained why I can’t do that.” He turned to Red-thumb and Luathas. “I even said I was a former slaver. Doesn’t that bother any of you?” “You do not understand,” Jian pressed. “ ey are not going. I am going.” “Wel … damn.” e blacksmith looked at Annev, his expression helpless. “ is wil probably bring us more trouble,” he said, lowering his voice to a whisper. “It’s not my rst choice,” Annev admitted, glancing sideways at their would-be Yomad companion. “Would denying the life debt bring us more trouble, though?” “Hard to say. Are you superstitious?” “Not especial y, though I might make an exception in Jian’s case.”

chunks.title: Final Section
chunks.content: He relived his last days with the priest in bright ashes, culminating in Sodar’s death at Elder Tosan’s hand. Alone, grief-stricken, Annev had unwittingly bonded the golden Hand of Keos to his stunted arm. He’d kil ed Tosan and half the Academy’s masters, then lanced the towering edi ce in half and col apsed it on itself. Last of al , he remembered Myjun, her betrayal and subsequent death. It had been an accident, but she’d stil died by his hand—by the Hand of Keos, which he had been wielding. Was it real y an accident? Annev wondered, his thoughts owing freely now. I wanted them al dead. I wanted to crush the Academy and destroy the vil age in rubble and ash. I turned the re toward her … toward that screaming … Sraon gasped behind him and Annev was startled back to the present. Gwendolyn’s eyes were wide and her hands raised as she stared down at Annev’s glowing prosthetic, which had now taken on a more lively light: instead of its dim yel ow glow, barely noticeable in the daylight, the hand shone with a bril iant orange re. Annev’s breath caught in his throat and he instinctively clenched the hand into a st. e orange glow ared, turning red. “Annev …” Sraon said, his tone measured, cautious. “Please don’t blow us al to bloody pieces.” In other circumstances Annev might have laughed, but there was nothing funny about the pulsing red ame shrouding his st. Instead he took a deep breath and slowly let it out, calming his mind. As he did, the re shrank, its light paling to yel ow and then sinking back into a soft white glow. Annev gently opened his hand and a tiny slip of smoke wafted up from his ngers. On his palm, the second half of the Terran inscription stil glowed with a dul orange re: NUMQUAM OBLIVISCI. Never forget. Annev blinked. Where had he learned that? He hadn’t. He shouldn’t have known the meaning of the inscription … yet there it was. Annev’s stomach twisted into a sour knot. He slowly turned the hand over and read the words on the other side: Aut inveniam viam aut faciam. is inscription was not glowing, and Annev hadn’t a clue what the words meant. e pit in his stomach slowly shrank and he began to breathe easier. “Interesting,” Dolyn said. “Maybe we should try a di erent tactic.” She eyed Annev, sizing him up. “What kind of art do you perform?” “Mm?” Dolyn waved a hand at the stil -glowing prosthetic. “Ignore that—and whatever you were thinking of when it started to glow like a forge re.” She shivered. “Tel me about you. Your magic. How did you access it before?” Annev thought about it. “Sodar trained me in Darite magic.” “Right, so what was he? ere are four elds: Breathbreaker, Stormcal er, Shieldbearer, Mindwalker.” “I’m not sure,” Annev said. “Sodar didn’t real y talk about magic like that. I overheard him talking to another artisan once. e other man cal ed him … a Breathbreaker, I think.” “So he never tried to nd your focus? Never tested your magic?” Annev laughed in spite of himself. “He tested it almost every day! But I was never good at accessing my powers. I didn’t manifest any kind of ability until a few days ago, and even then, it didn’t match the way Sodar said magic worked. It was …” Annev fel silent, remembering Sodar’s words. Like a keokum. “It wasn’t what he’d expected.” Dolyn studied him. “I guess that makes sense. You’d have to be special to get that thing to weld to you.” She frowned. “You’re a puzzle, Annev.” A long moment passed and then she smiled. “I like puzzles, though. Tel me. What were you doing when you rst accessed your magic? What happened?” “I was using an artifact—a Sword of Sharpness. I couldn’t get the glyph to work for me, though, so I . . .” He remembered how he had extended his awareness into the blade. He had sensed the weapon’s purpose, its essence. en he had shaped his own essence and pushed his wil into the sword, magnifying its power. Was Dolyn asking Annev to do something similar now—to extend himself into … himself? If he could get a rm grasp on that, if he could extend his mind and his wil to the edge of his being, perhaps … Annev emptied his mind of thought and emotion and settled his focus on his core, where his spirit dwelt. ese were abstract concepts for him, but he recal ed using Sodar’s sword, Mercy, to chop through Janak’s soldiers. He also remembered nding his ery amberge in the Vault of Damnation and using it to scythe through the metal limbs and stone skin of the monstrous feurog. He had sensed the source of that weapon’s power and magni ed its intensity until the heat was powerful enough to shear through iron and stone as easily as esh and bone. Annev’s arm began to tingle at the joint where the prosthetic joined his stunted forearm. He took note of it, recal ing the sensation as familiar but not paying it attention before. is was important. He wasn’t sure why or how, but there was something at work here, and while Annev couldn’t say what it was, it tickled at his memories. Annev relaxed, letting the memory go. He opened his eyes—surprised to nd he had closed them—and looked up at Dolyn. “I think I can feel it … that connection you spoke of. ere’s a twinge in my arm—a tingling. I’m not sure how to describe it.” He extended the gold arm toward Gwendolyn, open palm facing her. “What comes next?” Dolyn slowly reached out with both hands, taking his arm by the wrist and forearm for the third time. is time, though, she laid her left thumb on his palm and her right thumb at the seam of the prosthetic. “Keep your focus on that connection but relax your mind. I’m going to see if I can sense where you end and the arm begins.” She paused. “ is may be uncomfortable, so try not to ght it. Empty your mind—and please don’t bal your hand into a st. e prosthetic seems to respond to gestures used for dwimmer-crafting. I think there is some residual muscle-memory stored there from its last owner.” She trailed o , not daring to speak the name they were al thinking. Keos. What muscle memories had the god left behind in the golden artifact? What atrocities had he committed while wearing it? Worse yet, what acts could Annev inadvertently commit with the cursed prosthetic? If Dolyn’s warning had been intended to inspire calm, it had the opposite e ect. More than ever, Annev wanted to be rid of the damned thing. He couldn’t bear the thought of more destruction, like that in Chaenbalu. Another place burned, another friend dead or lost because of him and his glowing hand. “Do it,” Annev breathed, his teeth clenched. Dolyn closed her eyes. “Your spirit … it’s holding tight to the arm. Ease up, boy. Relax. You’re not ghting anyone, least of al me.” Annev nodded, forcing his muscles to unclench and redirecting his thoughts to more pleasant things. But it was like ghting a river current. e negative thoughts and emotions were always there, ebbing and owing around him. He tried to summon a positive memory, but he kept failing. inking of winning the stealth contest in the Academy’s nave made him think of kissing Myjun, and that made him think of her betrayal and death. inking of winning the Test of Judgment just reminded him how Tosan had unjustly stolen his victory and given it to erin. inking of Sodar … he couldn’t. Some wounds were stil too fresh. Annev startled as he felt a hand drop onto his shoulder—Sraon’s hand. “I’m here for you, Annev. Whatever happens. We al are.” at’s true, Annev thought, his anxiety easing slightly as Dolyn pressed at his esh. I have Sraon. And Titus and erin. Not to mention Fyn and Brayan. Annev smiled, remembering how the Academy’s former quartermaster had spoken for him in the village square when no one else had. How Brayan had stood up to Tosan and taken Annev’s side when al others were too afraid to do so. Fyn was another matter entirely. He’d been a bul y, a constant pain, and a gal ing irritation. He had also been a dangerous adversary during the Academy’s tests. But something had changed. Somehow, they had become reluctant al ies. It was a strange and thril ing shift in their relationship, and Annev stil wasn’t sure how he felt about it. “ ere it is,” Gwendolyn hissed through clenched teeth. “I can feel the connection, where the aqlumera has merged with your esh and spirit.” She slowly exhaled, her eyes half-lidded, then began to trace the surface of his skin with delicate invisible patterns. “Dwimmer-crafting,” she said between labored breaths, “requires motion of the body. Certain gestures, certain movements, cal on the magic inside us and the world around us.” e smith rose from her seat, her arms entwining Annev’s in a martial dance of owing movement that almost mirrored the patterns of the arabesques inscribed on the surface of the golden arm. “If I can persuade the metal ic elements that they aren’t part of you … if I can draw the aqlumera back into the arm itself …” Beads of perspiration had begun to dot the smith’s face. She clenched her jaw, head tilted to one side, and her elbows began to quiver. She drew her hands along the surface of the oversized arm, her ngers caressing the golden skin, drawing down to clutch the glowing hand in her rough palms. Annev jerked as he felt something yank at the marrow of his forearm. e sensation came from somewhere deep inside—deeper than esh or bone could possibly reach—and the pain that fol owed was like ery claws tearing at his soul. It transported Annev to another time and place. Instead of sitting in Dolyn’s underground kiln, he stood before a hel ish army of monsters, roaring with bloodlust. At the opposite end of the clearing, a young man with a glowing silver sta faced him. Lightning arced from the weapon, lancing Annev, fol owed by a rol ing wave of immolating re. Annev growled in frustration and pain, absorbing the magic and then attempting to hurl it back at his adversaries. e room shifted again and Annev gasped as arcs of bloodred lightning burst from his hand, throwing Dolyn against the wal . Al around them the air crackled with heat and the stench of burned esh. “Gods!” Sraon swore, dashing from Annev’s side to aid the fal en smith. “Gwen, are you al right?” e Orvane shuddered, her breath coming in deep, ragged gasps. She rose to her feet, though, which Annev took to be a good sign, and to his relief he didn’t see any visible injuries. And then Dolyn raised her hands, turning them, revealing the arabesques and inscriptions carved on Annev’s golden hand, which had somehow transferred themselves to hers, burning their likeness into the surface of her palms. He stared blankly at them, wisps of smoke stil rising from the charred outline of the war hammer oating above the smoking anvil. On the opposite hand, Annev could plainly read the mirrored letters of inscription on his palm: . . “I’m sorry,” Annev stammered. “I didn’t mean to—” Dolyn raised her burned palms between herself and Annev. “It’s my fault,” she said, wincing. “I found a thread and pul ed at it. e connection … it’s like nothing I’ve experienced—slippery as a sh but harder to grasp. e aqlumera has been forged into the shape of a golden arm but its spirit . . . it’s something else. Something wild and untamed.” She stared at her burned hands, ngers trembling. “It was beautiful,” she said, almost whispering, “like nothing I’ve ever held or forged. As ephemeral as re. Soft as silk, yet stronger than steel.” She shuddered, closing her eyes, and tears streaked down her face. “I’m sorry,” Dolyn said at last, her glistening eyes meeting Annev’s. “I cannot remove the hand.” CHAPTER FIVE e Shadow’s apprentice stalked among the sun-dappled shrubs of the Brakewood, her muscles tense, her green eyes sharp and shining beneath her gold mask. “When do we leave?” Myjun growled, her teeth gritted in pain. Oyru raised a single eyebrow. “Why would we leave?” Myjun’s breath quickened, her sts exing at her side, the cords of her neck tense with emotion. “To kil that bastard, Ainnevog! To avenge my father! You promised me blood, you kraik, and I want it.” “You have barely kil ed before,” Oyru said, matter of fact. “ e stench of death has not yet stained your soul. You have no experience.” “But I have kil ed. You saw it yourself in the tunnels.” Oyru stepped deeper into the glade, the shadows of the trees soothing him. “I saw you murder two mindless creatures—and you let the third escape. My other apprentices began as trained kil ers.” Oyru shrugged. “You are not ready to pursue your vengeance, let alone obtain it.” Myjun’s eyes remained erce beneath the blood-streaked golden mask. “You wish to test my commitment?” How quickly I forget, Oyru thought, that the Mask of Gevul’s Mistress makes its wearer an insu erable bitch. He would have laughed—or cursed, or sighed—if he cared enough. Instead, his thoughts were cold. Pragmatic. She must be humbled. Steel must be burned and beaten before it can be tempered and taught its shape. “I do wish to test your commitment … among other things.” Oyru raised his hand and drew on the void, channeling the energy of the shadow realm to forge a thin double-blade of nether in the palm of his hand. “ is is a shadow construct,” Oyru said, ipping the knife in his hand. “It is a physical manifestation of another plane of existence. One whose essence overlaps with this world but whose substance is anchored in another dimension of reality. I have drawn it into this world—summoned it from the nether—but its form is unstable.” Oyru ipped the knife high above him. It reached its arc and began to fal , the twin blades spinning lazily in the air. Oyru reached out as if to catch it, but before he could grasp the black shard, it evaporated into smoke and nothingness. Myjun stared at the assassin, her pale eyes stil erce and chal enging. “What is the point of this except to prove you’re a rotting conjurer?” She spat at Oyru’s boots, though the gesture was diminished by her saliva slapping against the inside of the golden mask. “I wil teach you how to nd your prey,” he said, unfazed. “I wil show you how to track him. How to capture and kil him. To do that, though, you must give heed to my instruction. You must learn to be as deadly as I am in the dark, if you wish to be equal y powerful in the light.” Myjun laughed, though there was no amusement in her voice. Instead, each spike of sound was like a needle driving into Oyru’s skul . “Teach me?” she sco ed. “I need learn nothing from you, demon. I have been trained by the greatest ghters in the Darite Empire. I am a warrior.” “Truly?” Oyru said, his face blank. “Truly.” Oyru icked his hand toward Myjun. A dark star of metal ew from his palm, its four points trailing wisps of ethereal smoke. e spinning construct thudded into Myjun’s shoulder, slicing deep into her ragged red dress and the esh beneath. Myjun’s hand ew up to clutch her injured shoulder. “You rotting kraik! Why’d you do that?” “You are a warrior, are you not?” Oyru gestured at Myjun’s injury and the black star of metal dissolved into smoke and nothingness, exposing the red wound further. “You attacked me!” Oyru forged three new shards of nether and casual y hurled a second vol ey at Myjun. She dodged to one side, throwing herself to the ground and evading the rst throw. A second trio of spikes fol owed them a heartbeat later, and Myjun inched as two plunged into the ground beside her. e last thudded into her calf and she screamed in pain. “Gods!” she cried out. “What in the hel s are you doing! Do you want to kil me?” “If I wanted you dead, you would be. e fact you are stil alive proves you had some martial training, but I wouldn’t cal you a warrior.” “ en you underestimate me,” Myjun said, her voice cracking beneath the pain. “I am a skil ed assassin, trained by the masters and witwomen of Chaenbalu.” “ at means little to me, especial y when your masters were so easily overrun by the feurog.” Oyru dismissed the ve throwing spikes in the dirt. e last spike, the one buried in Myjun’s calf, he left as a reminder of her weakness. “Why would you do this?” Myjun sobbed, prodding her injury. “What does this teach me? I can’t walk, and now Annev is going to get away!” She sni ed. Beneath the mask, her green eyes sparkled with tears. Could it be, Oyru marveled, stepping toward the injured woman, that I have misjudged this one so poorly? Could she truly be so weak? He began to kneel beside his apprentice, intending to remove the throwing spike. Before he could reach it, Myjun jerked the void-shard from her leg, spun around Oyru’s kneeling form, and jammed the shard into his left hamstring. She twisted hard, then pul ed savagely at his shade-bound esh. Oyru grunted, half in shock, half in pain. Before he could recover, Myjun plunged the spike into his back once. Twice. rice. en she swung her st sideways and slammed the nether-spike into his neck, just beneath his jaw. e assassin gurgled then coughed, blood dribbling from his lips. Myjun leaned over his shoulder and hissed in his ear, al trace of her former anguish gone. “I told you. I know how to kil .” Oyru reached up, his black-gloved hand patting the young woman’s, reaching for the spike. Myjun’s hand fel away and she hobbled backward, stil on her knees. She stared, incredulous, as Oyru grasped the twin-pointed shard . . . and ripped it free. A spray of blood pulsed from the wound, spattering his black rags, Myjun’s mask, and the shrubs on the forest oor. Oyru held up the spike, and the young woman gawked as Oyru casual y dismissed the construct back to the shadow realm. He forced a smile, teeth stained red, and saw Myjun’s eyes widen further. He knew what she was seeing; he could feel the nether streaming into him, the shadows swarming to l the gaps in his esh, healing what should have been several mortal wounds. He coughed again, but instead of spitting blood and bile, he felt the blood in his lungs shift into shadow-vapor and he exhaled a cloud of inky darkness, its essence spil ing from his lips like an airy waterfal , its mass somehow heavier than the surrounding air. “What are you?” Myjun asked, both disgusted and horri ed. “I am your master.” “ en what have I apprenticed myself to? e Lord of Shadows? To Keos himself?” Myjun shuddered, her disgust magnifying. “You are as foul as the one I hunt,” she breathed, ful of contempt. “I have no doubt that I am worse.” “ en why should I serve you? What makes you think I would be your apprentice?” “Because you already are. Because you are just as corrupted by magic. And …” He paused. “Because I am not the one who kil ed your father. I am not the one who betrayed you.” At these last words, a re seemed to kindle in Myjun’s emerald eyes. “He lied to me. Made me fal in love with him—a bloody keokum! I hate him. I hate everything he is—every lie he told me, every word he whispered to me. Death is too good for him … but his life is al I can take from him. He took my father from me. My beauty, my face, my life. He took everything. Annev,” she said, trembling with rage, “must die.” Oyru studied the young woman. e sharp edge to her voice was a contrast to the soft curves and al uring gaze of the cursed artifact. Its twin streaks of bloody tears were no less out of place, more sad than gruesome as they trailed down the mask’s perfectly crafted cheekbones. Oyru chided himself for letting the magic of the artifact lul him into seeing anything other than the dangerous girl beneath. Her anger made her feral. Bloodthirsty. ere was a cunningness to her eyes and a quickness to her movements—Myjun had not lied when she cal ed herself a warrior. She had indeed been trained to kil , though it was clear she had not much practiced the art, let alone perfected it. Stil , she had potential, more so than any of his previous apprentices. It had been over two decades since the last one had stabbed him … Larissa dan Karli, Oyru thought, remembering, and only when she had nearly nished her apprenticeship. He hadn’t even begun training Myjun, unless he counted stabbing her. She had good instincts. She reminded him of Oraqui. “You wil notice you moved faster the second time, and faster stil when you attacked me. is is the magic of the artifact—the Mask of Gevul’s Mistress. Your pain fuels it, gives it power. And it, in turn, feeds you. When you are injured, you wil move faster. When you feel pain, you wil strike harder. When you su er the most, you become the greatest threat. e mask wil also speed your healing and recovery, though that is not its primary function. It cannot make you invincible, though it might convince you that you are. But while it cannot save you from a mortal wound, whatever does not cripple you wil make you stronger.” Oyru rose to his feet, standing above Myjun. “ is is your rst lesson. Embrace your pain. Agony is your al y and su ering is your sword.” Oyru slapped Myjun’s gilded face, making the metal ring out. Myjun reeled, tumbling backward, rol ing awkwardly with the injuries to her shoulder and calf. “And this is your second lesson,” Oyru continued, his voice cold as Reotan ice. “I am not your friend. I am not your al y. I am your master and you are my apprentice—my servant. You wil obey me in al things and without question. If I tel you to plunge a dagger into your breast, you wil do so. If I tel you to sear your skin, you wil reach into the ames and press the coals to your esh. Do you understand?” Myjun hissed, climbing to unsteady feet. “You would make me a slave then. A whipping-maid for your cruel fancies.” “Yes. If I wish.” She growled, her injured leg unable to bear her ful weight, and rocked back, lowering herself to the earth once more. She paused. “But you wil help me kil my father’s murderer—my betrayer? You promise you wil help me nd and kil the demon that cal s itself Ainnevog?” “I wil .” Myjun nodded, her ragged breath beginning to slow. “ en it is worth it. Show me where he is that I may kil him.” Oyru sni ed. “You are not ready.” Myjun opened her mouth to protest but the assassin held up a single nger, forestal ing her objections. “I wil tel you when that time has come, and I say it is not that time. Your martial skil s are considerable, particularly when paired with the magic of your mask, but you are not perfect. You could not pluck my weapons from the air and hurl them back at me, much less evade my attacks.” Myjun sco ed. “You caught me by surprise and hit me twice—in the shoulder and the leg. I stabbed you ve times, and three of those blows would have kil ed you if you weren’t some Keos-be-damned shadow-spawn.” She was right, of course. Not just about who had bested whom, but about his damnation and his otherworldly powers. True, he hadn’t been trying to kil her in earnest, and she had surprised him, but he had been incautious because of his certainty that she couldn’t harm him—not permanently. He never would have been so careless, so reckless, if he had felt he was in any real danger. It was refreshing, after decades of training obedient apprentices. Oyru had given her the mask and then provoked her into fueling it with her pain. He had injured her, and then left her the nether-spike instead of dismissing it. He had given her the opening, the training, and the means … and she had taken it. She had baited him then gutted him like a sh. He should have expected her attack, should have been waiting for it. He would have to be more careful. Especial y as she had bested him. “You are right,” Oyru said at last. “You are not without skil , and the mask enhances it. You surprised me, and that is no smal thing.” How many times had he done this? With how many apprentices? He had lost track of the faces and the names. e gilded mask had replaced them al , erased as surely as if they had never existed before putting on the mask. And when he looked at them, he thought of only one face. One name. Oraqui. It was strange to feel nothing when thinking of her—no pain or anger, no regret or sorrow, no longing or love. Time could do that. It could not “heal al injuries” as the poet Nilanteska had oft asserted, yet it was stil the only balm to give him a clip of relief. Not wine or women. Not murder or self- agel ation —not even his own death had eased it. Time was the only remedy, it seemed, and even that could not have quenched his anguish without the second ingredient in his secret salve. Obsession. Oyru could never bring Oraqui back, just as he could never fol ow her. But he could craft a new Oraqui. He molded each new apprentice into Oraqui’s replacement, shaped her into something better than the original. And if he failed—if the duplicate proved inferior to the original or no longer pleased him—he could break her and start anew. He had done it hundreds of times, and each time he felt a little more relief, a little more distance. It was as if each of their deaths deadened him further. He felt so little now it was sometimes di cult to rise above his own apathy and fol ow his master’s instructions. Capture the Vessel. Bring him to me. Alive. It seemed such a simple task, and yet Oyru had lost the boy. He had never failed before. He had never needed to report to the First Vampyr with the reasons for his failure. Oyru wasn’t even sure what he would say to Dortafola. Much better to treat his mission as incomplete than failed. An ongoing task with an inde nite timetable. Dortafola could always correct him of that assumption. Til then, Oyru’s mission to capture Ainnevog had not changed. He would bring him to Fala Tuir, as instructed, and to hel with his promise to help Myjun. But she needn’t know that, and he would not tel her. He needed al ies. Something more formidable than a corrupted wood-witch or the perverse creatures that served her. He had his eidolons, of course—the shadow demons that begged to be released into this world—but that wasn’t enough, he realized, not if he was going to remain in the physical realm for this long. To capture this particular quarry, he needed an al y who could ght in the sunlight as easily as he could ght in the shadows. He needed someone like Oraqui to keep his own demons at bay. For the rst time in decades, Oyru needed an apprentice. He needed an al y who was dangerous enough to aid him but not enough to be a threat to him. “You are not ready,” Oyru repeated, studying Myjun, “but I wil teach you. I wil nish the education begun by your witwomen and witmistress, and you wil begin your second school of study.” He waited, knowing she would ask. “Studies? e only thing I want from you is Annev.” “I do not know where to nd him.” “But you said—” “ at I would teach you how to nd him.” “And kil him,” Myjun added, her eyes inty behind the static mask. Oyru al owed his silence to speak the lie for him. “You have much to learn, apprentice. I can teach you so much about pain, and survival … and betrayal.” He watched her, but the maiden behind the mask didn’t inch. Good. “But you have already learned some of these things. Today I want to discover the extent of your a nity for magic.” Myjun sco ed. “I don’t have magic. I’m not cursed like you.” “Aren’t you? You are scarred. You were betrayed and abandoned. You wear a cursed mask.” e apprentice shook her head. “But I am not a aming keokum.” Oyru stepped toward the young woman, his eyes gleaming. “You don’t understand. at mask only bonded to you because you possess magic. e only question that remains is what kind.” He tilted his head, a thought occurring to him. “Your father wielded that obsidian wand. Something smal and dark ew over Annev’s head. “Gods!” Sraon swore, pushing Annev to the ground. “Stay down, boy!” e smith fel atop him in a heap, but Annev was quick to regain his feet. e albino stood beside him along with Red-thumb and his mute sister. “ ere!” e merrymaker shouted, pointing. “Down that al ey!” e group turned and Annev spotted a silhouetted gure eeing down an al ey mouth. e ranger holstered his tonfa and dashed after the assailant, both disappearing into the shadows. Beside Annev, the albino swept back his gray cowl, revealing hair as bone-white as his skin, though his smooth skin and sharp eyes suggested he was nearly the same age as Sraon. He stooped to the earth, picked something up, and held it for al to see: a crossbow quarrel. e albino studied rst the quarrel and then Annev with intense pink eyes. “You are hurt, Master Ainnevog?” Instead of responding, Annev dashed o after the ranger and the would-be assassin, hurtling past tents and stal s crowded with hawkers and customers. “Annev!” Sraon shouted. “Wait!” But Annev was already gone, having cal ed on the magic of his Boots of Speed. Within seconds, he reached the al ey where the ranger had disappeared, barely catching a glimpse of him as the eeing assassin dashed behind a row of vendor stal s with the Al taran in close pursuit. Annev took another step and nearly tripped over a heavy crossbow. He left it where it lay and hurried after the ranger, catching him as he reached Banok’s city wal . “ ere!” e Al taran pointed to a cluster of booths sel ing woven rugs and artful tapestries. “Behind that red wal hanging!” Annev reached the stal three steps ahead of the ranger and tore the hanging aside, chagrined to nd only a blank stone wal behind the drape. “Where did he go?” e ranger inhaled deeply. “I swear he was here.” e man tilted his head to the side, inhaling. “ e attacker’s scent lingers. He was here. He should stil be here.” e foreigner pressed his nose to the city wal , smel ing its bricks. “I don’t understand it. It’s as if he vanished into the rock.” Annev looked up at the looming city wal , his hand pressed to the stone, and tried to imagine his attacker scaling it unnoticed. He swore. Just like Faith, Annev thought. Vanished into thin air … unless the assassin went through the wal ? “Are you al right?” Annev turned to see the ranger studying him. “I’m ne. Just upset we didn’t catch him.” “You’re not even winded,” the ranger said, obviously impressed. “Few, even among my countrymen, can match my speed.” “Ah,” Annev said, understanding. “I did not truly best you.” He hesitated, wondering if he should say more, then decided he could probably trust the ranger with one of his secrets. He lowered his voice: “My boots are enchanted.” “Excuse me!” e pair turned to nd a sweaty merchant glowering at them. “You gonna buy that?” he asked, pointing at the tapestry stil gripped in the ranger’s hand. e Al taran stared blankly at him. “ en get the hel out of my stal ! You’re scaring away my customers.” Annev doubted that, but he and the ranger complied al the same, returning the way they had come. “ ank you for saving my life,” Annev said, extending a hand. “My name is Annev.” “Wel met.” ey shook hands. “I am Corentin, a Shalgarn from Al tara, though my companions cal me Mad Cat.” “Mad Cat?” Annev repeated. “ at’s a strange—” He saw the man’s eyes for the rst time: yel ow with black, oval pupils, the same shape as a cat’s. “Not so strange,” Mad Cat said with a grin. “Oh!” Annev said, surprised. “Yes … I see why.” e Shalgarn walked to the fal en crossbow, picked it up, and o ered it to Annev. “Are these common in your country?” Annev took the heavy weapon. e stock was made from metal and the string of braided wire. “I’ve never seen its like,” he marveled. “I can’t imagine being strong enough to load it without assistance.” “Expensive too,” Mad Cat agreed. “ at’s the tool of a master assassin. At a distance, it could probably punch through plate mail.” “How did you knock that quarrel out of the air?” “I almost missed it. My eyes and re exes gave me an advantage—similar to your boots, I think.” “You mean … an enchantment?” “A blessing,” Mad Cat corrected, “though the e ect is the same.” “Annev!” Sraon cal ed, running across the market square to join them as they emerged from the crowded row of booths. “What were you thinking, running o like that?” “I was thinking someone had tried to kil me and I didn’t want them to get away.” Annev handed Sraon the crossbow to examine. “I’m not sure how he eluded us. We chased him straight to the city wal and then he just . . . disappeared.” “Are you injured?” Sraon asked, drawing them back toward the group stil surrounding the apple cart. “No,” Annev said, speaking to the entire group. “ e bolt didn’t even graze me.” “ at’s a relief,” Red-thumb said, and Luathas was quick to nod her assent. “It’s a ne thing Corentin and Jian were here, else your journey might have ended here.” “Jian?” Annev said, looking toward the hooded albino. “You shouted the warning, yes?” e pale-skinned man bowed his head. “As you say, Master Ainnevog. It was foreseen.” “And you knew my name,” Annev continued. “My ful name … though we’ve never met.” e pale man inclined his head again. He glanced to Red-thumb for assistance but Sraon interjected before the merrymaker could speak. “We had just nished our introductions. e pale fel ow is Jian Nikloss, a Yomad from Terra Majora.” Jian bowed a third time, his hands clasped in front of him. “A pleasure.” “Master Nikloss possesses a talent for sensing what cannot be seen by the common man,” Red-thumb explained, twisting his mustache. “It grants him limited precognition of people and future events. It’s also been a popular trick among the smal villages … but I sense Jian has not showed us the ful extent of his talents.” Annev stared openly at the white-skinned man, half in disbelief and half in suspicion. “You mean … you can see the future?” e Yomad made a strange gesture with his hands and shook his head. When he spoke again, Annev noticed he spoke with a slight accent. “Like seeing,” Jian said, “but not seeing. Smal window to see the world. Short time to see and hear.” Annev tried to process this. “Did your magic tel you my name then—and save me from that crossbow bolt?” Jian bowed again. “As you say, Master Ainnevog.” Annev touched the hem of his smithing glove, a re churning in his gut. First Dolyn … and then the Ilumites, the Shalgarn, and the Yomad. In one day I’ve met the worshipers of Cruithear, Lumea, Sealgair, and Tacharan. at can’t be a coincidence—and the wood-witch said I would be hunted by the Younger Gods, which means someone here probably has ulterior motives. Annev frowned at the soothsayer, unnerved by his appearance. “You wonder about my other talents,” Jian said, teeth ashing. “I have many,” he continued before Annev could answer. “Seeing. Speaking. Summoning. Not common to have these al .” “What do Speaking and Summoning entail?” Annev asked. “I talk to …” Jian searched for the word. “People who go to holy lands,” he said at last. “I cal them and hear them. Sometimes they speak. Sometimes I speak.” “You speak with the dead?” Annev ventured. Jian made the strange gesture again, once more shaking his head. “Not dead. Lumen and quaire move to holy lands. ey live. T’rasang remains in this world. T’rasang is dead.” He hesitated. “But I can speak to t’rasang too. Sometimes it answers. Sometimes it no answers.” Mad Cat cleared his throat and al eyes turned to him. “Your pardon, but your leader has admitted to owing me a life debt.” e ranger indicated Annev. “I would claim it, but I have already promised my aid to these two Ilumani.” Mad Cat pointed to Red-thumb and Luathas. “Because I have pledged myself to them, his life debt is transferred to them as wel .” e ranger nodded as if he had completed some formal contract. “ at is al .” “Life debt?” Annev asked, turning rst to Sraon and then to Red-thumb. e former swore under his breath while the latter merely stroked the patch of hair beneath his bottom lip. “Mad Cat is Shalgarn,” Jian said, nodding sagely. “Life debts are common in Al tara.” He held up a nger. “But I also have claim to your life. I shouted the warning to you, and I had told Mad Cat to protect you from ying harm.” “You foresaw the crossbow bolt,” Annev said, l ing in the gaps in the soothsayer’s broken Darite. “You had a vision that I would be attacked, and you told Mad Cat to save me.” “You are wise,” Jian said, bowing his head once more. “Our party is bound for Luqura on a mission of grave importance,” Sraon said testily. “We cannot be waylaid by life debts and strange customs.” He inclined his head slightly toward Luathas. “No o ense intended, mistress.” Mad Cat frowned. “I am confused. You cannot mean you wil shirk your debts.” “No,” Sraon said again, “but we have commitments we must keep, just as you have yours.” “Ah yes. is I understand.” Mad Cat looked between Red-thumb and Jian Nikloss. “A favor, then. It is customary to exchange a favor in such cases as these.” He turned back to Annev. “You wil grant us a boon, yes?” Annev then saw the game for what it was. is was probably what the foreigners had been after al along. Just another way to trap me, he guessed, suspicious. “Am I permitted to ask the nature of the boon before it is requested?” Red-thumb gave a smile that was al teeth. “I think we can al ow it.” e merrymaker gestured to his group. “I am seeking additional members of our troupe.” “Stop right there,” Sraon interrupted. “Not a one of us wil be joining your clan. We have our own mission to ful l .” Red-thumb laughed, his hands waving in front of him. “No, no. We are seeking speci c members. My Yomad friend here has even divined some of their names.” e merrymaker raised two ngers. “We are seeking a Druid from Fertil Hedge and an Orvane named Dolyn. We came here looking for Dolyn, but Jian’s magics have failed to unearth him.” “If we can direct you to Dolyn, wil that ful l my debt to Mad Cat?” Annev asked. Red-thumb looked at him gravely. “Might do.” “Dolyn is a woman,” Sraon interjected, “who has been absent from the village these past few days … but I doubt she’l join your troupe. She runs a very successful smithing operation in the Gold District. Deals in ne metals mostly, but she can work damn near anything.” He shrugged. “Find her if you like, but don’t discuss her heritage in mixed company. You seem cosmopolitan enough, Master Red-thumb, but not al folks are so accepting of foreigners.” Mad Cat whispered something to his white-skinned companion, and Jian tugged his gray cowl back to cover his hair and face. “Indeed,” Red-thumb said, nodding in agreement. “And that is why I seek your help. You see, the fth member of our party lies in the capital city, and Luqura has become altogether unwelcome toward the people of my culture.” “ at’s an understatement,” Sraon said, shifting his eye patch. “When was the last time you visited Luqura, Master Red-thumb?” e merrymaker smiled. “Ah, Master Sraon. is wil be my rst visit to your capital city.” “ en, for your own good, I suggest you postpone your visit . . . inde nitely.” “You are referring to the Ilumite slave trade, which has been imported from the north—from Innistiul.” “Yes,” Sraon hu ed. “I haven’t seen the capital in some time, but I’ve heard that King Cheng’s in uence has almost eclipsed King Lenka’s, even there, and I fear what wil happen when the old man passes, particularly with Innistiul’s hooks so rmly embedded in the city’s commerce. If you are intent on traveling to Luqura, you are likely to nd yourselves captured, branded, and enslaved.” He paused, glancing at the cat-eyed Shalgarn ranger and the pink-eyed albino soothsayer. “I expect the rest of your troupe wil meet a similar fate —worse, perhaps. If you openly walk the streets, they’l scoop you up and sel you o quicker than you can blink.” “Which is precisely why we need a chaperone in the city. Someone to vouchsafe for us while we track down the last member of our troupe.” Sraon shook his head. “I’ve already granted your boon, Master Red-thumb. I’ve told you where to nd Mistress Dolyn, and I’ve given you fair warning that you aren’t likely to persuade her. Best to give up this quest of yours before you endanger your life and that of your friends.” Red-thumb raised his open hands and arms. “ at I cannot do.” Sraon sni ed. “ en I wish you good health and good luck in your travels.” CHAPTER ELEVEN “Master Ainnevog stil owes a debt to me, yes?” e group turned to look at Jian, who had raised his hand in mild objection. Sraon frowned, scratching at his eye patch. “Could be. What do you want?” “To travel to Luqura … with you.” Sraon spat. “Come on, Jian. I just explained why I can’t do that.” He turned to Red-thumb and Luathas. “I even said I was a former slaver. Doesn’t that bother any of you?” “You do not understand,” Jian pressed. “ ey are not going. I am going.” “Wel … damn.” e blacksmith looked at Annev, his expression helpless. “ is wil probably bring us more trouble,” he said, lowering his voice to a whisper. “It’s not my rst choice,” Annev admitted, glancing sideways at their would-be Yomad companion. “Would denying the life debt bring us more trouble, though?” “Hard to say. Are you superstitious?” “Not especial y, though I might make an exception in Jian’s case.”

chunks.content: He relived his last days with the priest in bright ashes, culminating in Sodar’s death at Elder Tosan’s hand. Alone, grief-stricken, Annev had unwittingly bonded the golden Hand of Keos to his stunted arm. He’d kil ed Tosan and half the Academy’s masters, then lanced the towering edi ce in half and col apsed it on itself. Last of al , he remembered Myjun, her betrayal and subsequent death. It had been an accident, but she’d stil died by his hand—by the Hand of Keos, which he had been wielding. Was it real y an accident? Annev wondered, his thoughts owing freely now. I wanted them al dead. I wanted to crush the Academy and destroy the vil age in rubble and ash. I turned the re toward her … toward that screaming … Sraon gasped behind him and Annev was startled back to the present. Gwendolyn’s eyes were wide and her hands raised as she stared down at Annev’s glowing prosthetic, which had now taken on a more lively light: instead of its dim yel ow glow, barely noticeable in the daylight, the hand shone with a bril iant orange re. Annev’s breath caught in his throat and he instinctively clenched the hand into a st. e orange glow ared, turning red. “Annev …” Sraon said, his tone measured, cautious. “Please don’t blow us al to bloody pieces.” In other circumstances Annev might have laughed, but there was nothing funny about the pulsing red ame shrouding his st. Instead he took a deep breath and slowly let it out, calming his mind. As he did, the re shrank, its light paling to yel ow and then sinking back into a soft white glow. Annev gently opened his hand and a tiny slip of smoke wafted up from his ngers. On his palm, the second half of the Terran inscription stil glowed with a dul orange re: NUMQUAM OBLIVISCI. Never forget. Annev blinked. Where had he learned that? He hadn’t. He shouldn’t have known the meaning of the inscription … yet there it was. Annev’s stomach twisted into a sour knot. He slowly turned the hand over and read the words on the other side: Aut inveniam viam aut faciam. is inscription was not glowing, and Annev hadn’t a clue what the words meant. e pit in his stomach slowly shrank and he began to breathe easier. “Interesting,” Dolyn said. “Maybe we should try a di erent tactic.” She eyed Annev, sizing him up. “What kind of art do you perform?” “Mm?” Dolyn waved a hand at the stil -glowing prosthetic. “Ignore that—and whatever you were thinking of when it started to glow like a forge re.” She shivered. “Tel me about you. Your magic. How did you access it before?” Annev thought about it. “Sodar trained me in Darite magic.” “Right, so what was he? ere are four elds: Breathbreaker, Stormcal er, Shieldbearer, Mindwalker.” “I’m not sure,” Annev said. “Sodar didn’t real y talk about magic like that. I overheard him talking to another artisan once. e other man cal ed him … a Breathbreaker, I think.” “So he never tried to nd your focus? Never tested your magic?” Annev laughed in spite of himself. “He tested it almost every day! But I was never good at accessing my powers. I didn’t manifest any kind of ability until a few days ago, and even then, it didn’t match the way Sodar said magic worked. It was …” Annev fel silent, remembering Sodar’s words. Like a keokum. “It wasn’t what he’d expected.” Dolyn studied him. “I guess that makes sense. You’d have to be special to get that thing to weld to you.” She frowned. “You’re a puzzle, Annev.” A long moment passed and then she smiled. “I like puzzles, though. Tel me. What were you doing when you rst accessed your magic? What happened?” “I was using an artifact—a Sword of Sharpness. I couldn’t get the glyph to work for me, though, so I . . .” He remembered how he had extended his awareness into the blade. He had sensed the weapon’s purpose, its essence. en he had shaped his own essence and pushed his wil into the sword, magnifying its power. Was Dolyn asking Annev to do something similar now—to extend himself into … himself? If he could get a rm grasp on that, if he could extend his mind and his wil to the edge of his being, perhaps … Annev emptied his mind of thought and emotion and settled his focus on his core, where his spirit dwelt. ese were abstract concepts for him, but he recal ed using Sodar’s sword, Mercy, to chop through Janak’s soldiers. He also remembered nding his ery amberge in the Vault of Damnation and using it to scythe through the metal limbs and stone skin of the monstrous feurog. He had sensed the source of that weapon’s power and magni ed its intensity until the heat was powerful enough to shear through iron and stone as easily as esh and bone. Annev’s arm began to tingle at the joint where the prosthetic joined his stunted forearm. He took note of it, recal ing the sensation as familiar but not paying it attention before. is was important. He wasn’t sure why or how, but there was something at work here, and while Annev couldn’t say what it was, it tickled at his memories. Annev relaxed, letting the memory go. He opened his eyes—surprised to nd he had closed them—and looked up at Dolyn. “I think I can feel it … that connection you spoke of. ere’s a twinge in my arm—a tingling. I’m not sure how to describe it.” He extended the gold arm toward Gwendolyn, open palm facing her. “What comes next?” Dolyn slowly reached out with both hands, taking his arm by the wrist and forearm for the third time. is time, though, she laid her left thumb on his palm and her right thumb at the seam of the prosthetic. “Keep your focus on that connection but relax your mind. I’m going to see if I can sense where you end and the arm begins.” She paused. “ is may be uncomfortable, so try not to ght it. Empty your mind—and please don’t bal your hand into a st. e prosthetic seems to respond to gestures used for dwimmer-crafting. I think there is some residual muscle-memory stored there from its last owner.” She trailed o , not daring to speak the name they were al thinking. Keos. What muscle memories had the god left behind in the golden artifact? What atrocities had he committed while wearing it? Worse yet, what acts could Annev inadvertently commit with the cursed prosthetic? If Dolyn’s warning had been intended to inspire calm, it had the opposite e ect. More than ever, Annev wanted to be rid of the damned thing. He couldn’t bear the thought of more destruction, like that in Chaenbalu. Another place burned, another friend dead or lost because of him and his glowing hand. “Do it,” Annev breathed, his teeth clenched. Dolyn closed her eyes. “Your spirit … it’s holding tight to the arm. Ease up, boy. Relax. You’re not ghting anyone, least of al me.” Annev nodded, forcing his muscles to unclench and redirecting his thoughts to more pleasant things. But it was like ghting a river current. e negative thoughts and emotions were always there, ebbing and owing around him. He tried to summon a positive memory, but he kept failing. inking of winning the stealth contest in the Academy’s nave made him think of kissing Myjun, and that made him think of her betrayal and death. inking of winning the Test of Judgment just reminded him how Tosan had unjustly stolen his victory and given it to erin. inking of Sodar … he couldn’t. Some wounds were stil too fresh. Annev startled as he felt a hand drop onto his shoulder—Sraon’s hand. “I’m here for you, Annev. Whatever happens. We al are.” at’s true, Annev thought, his anxiety easing slightly as Dolyn pressed at his esh. I have Sraon. And Titus and erin. Not to mention Fyn and Brayan. Annev smiled, remembering how the Academy’s former quartermaster had spoken for him in the village square when no one else had. How Brayan had stood up to Tosan and taken Annev’s side when al others were too afraid to do so. Fyn was another matter entirely. He’d been a bul y, a constant pain, and a gal ing irritation. He had also been a dangerous adversary during the Academy’s tests. But something had changed. Somehow, they had become reluctant al ies. It was a strange and thril ing shift in their relationship, and Annev stil wasn’t sure how he felt about it. “ ere it is,” Gwendolyn hissed through clenched teeth. “I can feel the connection, where the aqlumera has merged with your esh and spirit.” She slowly exhaled, her eyes half-lidded, then began to trace the surface of his skin with delicate invisible patterns. “Dwimmer-crafting,” she said between labored breaths, “requires motion of the body. Certain gestures, certain movements, cal on the magic inside us and the world around us.” e smith rose from her seat, her arms entwining Annev’s in a martial dance of owing movement that almost mirrored the patterns of the arabesques inscribed on the surface of the golden arm. “If I can persuade the metal ic elements that they aren’t part of you … if I can draw the aqlumera back into the arm itself …” Beads of perspiration had begun to dot the smith’s face. She clenched her jaw, head tilted to one side, and her elbows began to quiver. She drew her hands along the surface of the oversized arm, her ngers caressing the golden skin, drawing down to clutch the glowing hand in her rough palms. Annev jerked as he felt something yank at the marrow of his forearm. e sensation came from somewhere deep inside—deeper than esh or bone could possibly reach—and the pain that fol owed was like ery claws tearing at his soul. It transported Annev to another time and place. Instead of sitting in Dolyn’s underground kiln, he stood before a hel ish army of monsters, roaring with bloodlust. At the opposite end of the clearing, a young man with a glowing silver sta faced him. Lightning arced from the weapon, lancing Annev, fol owed by a rol ing wave of immolating re. Annev growled in frustration and pain, absorbing the magic and then attempting to hurl it back at his adversaries. e room shifted again and Annev gasped as arcs of bloodred lightning burst from his hand, throwing Dolyn against the wal . Al around them the air crackled with heat and the stench of burned esh. “Gods!” Sraon swore, dashing from Annev’s side to aid the fal en smith. “Gwen, are you al right?” e Orvane shuddered, her breath coming in deep, ragged gasps. She rose to her feet, though, which Annev took to be a good sign, and to his relief he didn’t see any visible injuries. And then Dolyn raised her hands, turning them, revealing the arabesques and inscriptions carved on Annev’s golden hand, which had somehow transferred themselves to hers, burning their likeness into the surface of her palms. He stared blankly at them, wisps of smoke stil rising from the charred outline of the war hammer oating above the smoking anvil. On the opposite hand, Annev could plainly read the mirrored letters of inscription on his palm: . . “I’m sorry,” Annev stammered. “I didn’t mean to—” Dolyn raised her burned palms between herself and Annev. “It’s my fault,” she said, wincing. “I found a thread and pul ed at it. e connection … it’s like nothing I’ve experienced—slippery as a sh but harder to grasp. e aqlumera has been forged into the shape of a golden arm but its spirit . . . it’s something else. Something wild and untamed.” She stared at her burned hands, ngers trembling. “It was beautiful,” she said, almost whispering, “like nothing I’ve ever held or forged. As ephemeral as re. Soft as silk, yet stronger than steel.” She shuddered, closing her eyes, and tears streaked down her face. “I’m sorry,” Dolyn said at last, her glistening eyes meeting Annev’s. “I cannot remove the hand.” CHAPTER FIVE e Shadow’s apprentice stalked among the sun-dappled shrubs of the Brakewood, her muscles tense, her green eyes sharp and shining beneath her gold mask. “When do we leave?” Myjun growled, her teeth gritted in pain. Oyru raised a single eyebrow. “Why would we leave?” Myjun’s breath quickened, her sts exing at her side, the cords of her neck tense with emotion. “To kil that bastard, Ainnevog! To avenge my father! You promised me blood, you kraik, and I want it.” “You have barely kil ed before,” Oyru said, matter of fact. “ e stench of death has not yet stained your soul. You have no experience.” “But I have kil ed. You saw it yourself in the tunnels.” Oyru stepped deeper into the glade, the shadows of the trees soothing him. “I saw you murder two mindless creatures—and you let the third escape. My other apprentices began as trained kil ers.” Oyru shrugged. “You are not ready to pursue your vengeance, let alone obtain it.” Myjun’s eyes remained erce beneath the blood-streaked golden mask. “You wish to test my commitment?” How quickly I forget, Oyru thought, that the Mask of Gevul’s Mistress makes its wearer an insu erable bitch. He would have laughed—or cursed, or sighed—if he cared enough. Instead, his thoughts were cold. Pragmatic. She must be humbled. Steel must be burned and beaten before it can be tempered and taught its shape. “I do wish to test your commitment … among other things.” Oyru raised his hand and drew on the void, channeling the energy of the shadow realm to forge a thin double-blade of nether in the palm of his hand. “ is is a shadow construct,” Oyru said, ipping the knife in his hand. “It is a physical manifestation of another plane of existence. One whose essence overlaps with this world but whose substance is anchored in another dimension of reality. I have drawn it into this world—summoned it from the nether—but its form is unstable.” Oyru ipped the knife high above him. It reached its arc and began to fal , the twin blades spinning lazily in the air. Oyru reached out as if to catch it, but before he could grasp the black shard, it evaporated into smoke and nothingness. Myjun stared at the assassin, her pale eyes stil erce and chal enging. “What is the point of this except to prove you’re a rotting conjurer?” She spat at Oyru’s boots, though the gesture was diminished by her saliva slapping against the inside of the golden mask. “I wil teach you how to nd your prey,” he said, unfazed. “I wil show you how to track him. How to capture and kil him. To do that, though, you must give heed to my instruction. You must learn to be as deadly as I am in the dark, if you wish to be equal y powerful in the light.” Myjun laughed, though there was no amusement in her voice. Instead, each spike of sound was like a needle driving into Oyru’s skul . “Teach me?” she sco ed. “I need learn nothing from you, demon. I have been trained by the greatest ghters in the Darite Empire. I am a warrior.” “Truly?” Oyru said, his face blank. “Truly.” Oyru icked his hand toward Myjun. A dark star of metal ew from his palm, its four points trailing wisps of ethereal smoke. e spinning construct thudded into Myjun’s shoulder, slicing deep into her ragged red dress and the esh beneath. Myjun’s hand ew up to clutch her injured shoulder. “You rotting kraik! Why’d you do that?” “You are a warrior, are you not?” Oyru gestured at Myjun’s injury and the black star of metal dissolved into smoke and nothingness, exposing the red wound further. “You attacked me!” Oyru forged three new shards of nether and casual y hurled a second vol ey at Myjun. She dodged to one side, throwing herself to the ground and evading the rst throw. A second trio of spikes fol owed them a heartbeat later, and Myjun inched as two plunged into the ground beside her. e last thudded into her calf and she screamed in pain. “Gods!” she cried out. “What in the hel s are you doing! Do you want to kil me?” “If I wanted you dead, you would be. e fact you are stil alive proves you had some martial training, but I wouldn’t cal you a warrior.” “ en you underestimate me,” Myjun said, her voice cracking beneath the pain. “I am a skil ed assassin, trained by the masters and witwomen of Chaenbalu.” “ at means little to me, especial y when your masters were so easily overrun by the feurog.” Oyru dismissed the ve throwing spikes in the dirt. e last spike, the one buried in Myjun’s calf, he left as a reminder of her weakness. “Why would you do this?” Myjun sobbed, prodding her injury. “What does this teach me? I can’t walk, and now Annev is going to get away!” She sni ed. Beneath the mask, her green eyes sparkled with tears. Could it be, Oyru marveled, stepping toward the injured woman, that I have misjudged this one so poorly? Could she truly be so weak? He began to kneel beside his apprentice, intending to remove the throwing spike.
