chunks.content: Sraon sighed. “Probably wise, given that he serves the God of Fate.” He leaned closer, his voice dropping to a whisper. “It just seems a little convenient, you know?” Annev held up a nger then turned his attention back to Red-thumb and the rest. “Excuse me. I’d like to discuss this proposal in private.” “Of course.” e knife-wielding juggler bowed, and the two groups separated a few dozen paces. “What’s convenient?” Annev asked once they were out of earshot. “Everything,” Sraon said, his face hard, his eyes grim. “I’ve seen setups like this before—even participated in a few. It’s common enough in the Empire.” “What is?” “ e game—the long con. It’s like they had us marked the moment we joined their audience. Probably as soon as they saw the provisions in our cart.” “You think they plan to rob us?” “At the very least. Just think back. Red-thumb marked erin during the show, probably to signal whom to target. en you gave him that coin and he turned his attention to you. He asked who our leader was, and a few minutes later …” Sraon clapped his hands in front of Annev’s face. Crack. Annev glanced sideways at Jian, Red-thumb and the rest. “You think they arranged the attack.” “I’m not even sure there was one. at Mad Cat fel ow would’ve had to move impossibly fast to stop that bolt—maybe he was holding the bolt the whole time. Jian shouts to get our attention and then —a quarrel sails over your head. Convenient, yes?” Annev nodded. “I never did see my attacker’s face—and Mad Cat could have pointed me in the wrong direction at the end.” He sco ed, feeling a fool. “ ey real y have been playing us. I bet Luathas isn’t even mute.” “I’m sure she reads lips,” Sraon countered, his back turning to face the woman. “Seems likely this group is exactly what they seem to be—a novelty act by performers and charlatans, the kind of rogues who prey on the charitable and the gul ible.” “And I nearly fel for it.” “We’re stil not out of the woods with them. at life debt nonsense puts us in a bind.” “Why not just say no?” Sraon hesitated. “Because it’s possible they’re tel ing the truth.” “But you just said—” “I know what I said, and I stil think I’m right. But I could be wrong—been wrong plenty o’ times before—and I’d hate to be wrong about this.” “Why? Wouldn’t it be safer just to assume?” “Aye, it would be, but you’l recal I have a history of treating Ilumites poorly, and I’m not proud of it. If they’re tel ing the truth—if they’re not just a bunch of rogues parroting the stereotypes—then I want to help. It’d go a smal way toward canceling my debt against their people.” “ en let’s be smart about it. Jian can come with us—just Jian—and we keep a close eye on him. Maybe he slips up and tel s us what Red-thumb is real y after. Or maybe he’s tel ing the truth and we help Jian locate their last contact.” Sraon considered it then nodded. “Agreed.” “Do we tel the others your suspicions?” “No, I don’t think so. One of them might try to take matters into their own hands.” “You mean Fyn.” “Wel , yes. I was trying to be tactful.” “Tact is wasted on Fyn.” Annev glanced toward the merrymakers. “Best to let them know our decision.” “Aye, better make it quick too. e others are returning.” Annev glanced up just as Brayan and the rest reached the apple cart. Each boy deposited an armload of supplies, and then the quartermaster handed out dried meat and apples. Fyn stared suspiciously at Annev. “Master Red-thumb,” Annev said, once he and Sraon rejoined Ilumites’ group. “Who is your contact in Luqura?” e leather-clad rogue smiled. “Another treasure hunter of sorts—a noblewoman.” “Do you have her name?” “Of sorts. My hooded friend here cal s her ‘the Raven’ or ‘the Sooted Rook.’ Makes me think ol’ Lady Fate can’t keep her corvids straight—that or Jian keeps mixing up the translation.” “ ere is no mixing up, Tesked.” Jian spoke without raising his pink eyes from the ground. “Al names are masks. ey are true and not true. Sometimes she is the Raven. Sometimes she is the Rook. She wears her names like di erent faces. Also, Fate is not a lady. He is Tacharan, the God of Doom.” “And now you see why I had wanted to bring everyone,” Red-thumb said to Annev. “Finding the missing members of my troupe is its own treasure hunt, especial y with this soothsayer leading us.” Annev nodded, remembering the cryptic way Kelga had spoken to him in the Brakewood, and the way Janak had spoken of the Oracle’s answers. “Prophecies aren’t always clear. I don’t trust them myself.” He glanced at the albino. “No o ense intended, Master Nikloss.” e soothsayer lifted his hooded face, a smal smile touching his lips. “I take no o ense. Fate is my master … but he is a cruel lord. Even to me, his face is masked.” “Hold on now,” Sraon said, lifting a hand. “Annev and I had agreed to let Master Nikloss join our caravan as payment for Annev’s life debt—and we’l do our best to keep him safe while we’re in Luqura—but I won’t agree to any faerie chasing.” He looked at the merrymaker. “Master Red-thumb, if you don’t know the name of your contact, then we can’t help you nd her. You can understand that, yes? Luqura is the second largest city in the Empire, and riddles about birds and noblewomen won’t get us any closer to—” “I know who she is,” Annev said, saying the words as he realized, with a shock, that he did know. “What’s this now?” Sraon said, al eyes turning to Annev. “How could you possibly know?” Annev peered at Jian Nikloss who stil wore his smal , knowing smile. “If I gave you her name, would you know if I was right?” “Names are masks. If the mask ts, it is right.” e soothsayer’s cryptic answer did not surprise Annev. In the Brakewood, Crag had tried to make the wood-witch speak plainly using both threats and talismans, and that had only been half successful. Fate, it seemed, would not be denied his riddles. “You seek Sodja Rocas, the daughter of the House of Rocas in Luqura.” He looked to the soothsayer and Jian nodded in con rmation. “Sodja is also a thief and a heartless kil er.” He glanced between Jian, Luathas, Mad Cat, and Red-thumb. “Why would you want her to join your troupe?” ere was an awkward silence. “Wanting and needing are almost never the same,” Red-thumb said, once more speaking for the others. “A good king does not want to burden his people with taxes, but he wil do so out of need. Our own need is no less great and requires us to seek out this Sodja woman—the Sooted Rook—so she can help us solve our puzzle.” “Al for a piece of a treasure?” Annev said, his tone mocking. Red-thumb didn’t take o ense. Instead his eyes gleamed with a erce passion. “ e best kind of treasure, Master Ainnevog. e kind they sing about in stories and wil remember for ages and ages to come.” Annev sni ed. “What treasure is that?” Red-thumb smiled, his roguish demeanor suddenly overcome by a beati c zeal. “We’re going to end the Silence of the Gods.” *** “I take it back,” Sraon boomed, his thick hands helping Brayan secure the supplies in the cart. “He’s not a charlatan or a con artist. He’s a mad man—a religious zealot.” “ at doesn’t explain the performance with the crossbow bolt.” “No,” Sraon admitted. “I won’t take it al back, then. ey’re stil performers—talented ones too—but they’re also zealots, and that makes them more dangerous than thieves. ey have an agenda—and I don’t doubt they’d justify any act that furthers their goal.” “Who’s this now?” erin asked, piping up from the other side of the cart. “Never you mind, lad. Just get the last o’ the foodstu s into the wagon.” Sraon surveyed the tidy cart and nodded. “ is should last us a week. More than enough for the short trip to the capital.” “Brayan says we might get there before nightfal tomorrow,” Titus added for Annev’s bene t. “It’d be faster if we al had horses, but two days is a modest pace with al of us walking. Do you know he’s been there twice on retrieval missions?” “Many years ago, Titus.” Brayan hand-fed the black mare from a bag of wild oats, his emptied hand stroking her neck after each mouthful. “Regardless, I think we should camp outside the city’s wal s when we arrive tomorrow. e capital is a big place, and evening is a poor time to get acquainted with it.” “I agree,” Sraon said. “Matter o’ fact, I was just talking with Annev about how it might be best for some of our group to stay here in Banok.” “What?” Titus’s face scrunched up with emotion. “You want to separate us? Won’t that make us more vulnerable?” “Not for those staying behind—you’d be safe, probably even get lodging with my smithing friend, Dolyn.” “You want me to stay behind?” Titus looked to Annev, his expression hurt. “Annev, you want me to come with you, right? Me and erin?” Annev glanced at erin whose attention was split between fol owing their discussion and eating a giant sugar apple. “Titus,” Annev said, “I don’t want to leave anyone behind—” “Good,” Titus said, as if that settled it. “—but I wil ,” Annev continued. “It’s not safe on the road or in the capital, and being around me is more than half the danger.” He lifted the gloved Hand of Keos, its size slightly out of proportion with the rest of his body. “Sraon’s friend Dolyn tried to help remove this. She tried—she tried very hard—but she failed, and she was hurt.” “She hurt herself?” Fyn asked, nal y breaking his silence. Annev xed the boy with a glare then stopped himself. “She was hurt because of me. e prosthetic hurt her because I couldn’t control it.” “Is she dead ?” erin asked, spitting out a piece of apple. “No! She just … her hands are burned, and she’s a smith so that’s a big deal. In fact, that’s another good reason for some of us to stay behind. Gwendolyn would probably appreciate the help while her hands heal.” “Did you say Gwendolyn?” Brayan rose to his ful height. “Gwendolyn Goldsmith?” Sraon nodded. “You know her, then?” e quartermaster shrugged, his cheeks reddening above his neckbeard. “Barely more than an acquaintance . . . but yes. Lost a few arm wrestling matches to her.” Sraon grunted, evidently unsurprised. “I’m stil coming with you, Annev,” Titus declared, his chubby face resolute. “I won’t abandon you. I promise.” His eyes traveled to the quartermaster. “You’l come too, won’t you, Brayan?” “I’m not sure,” Brayan said, eyeing rst Sraon and then Titus. “Annev and Sraon should be ne in the city—the blacksmith has been there more than I, it seems—but it sounds as if Gwendolyn could use our help.” “Annev needs our help.” Titus looked at erin. “You’re stil coming to Luqura, right, erin?” e scrawny boy pitched his apple core away. “I’m with you two—til Annev melts us al , anyway.” He laughed at his own joke, though no one else shared his mirth. “Okay,” Sraon said, resigned. “Brayan, wil you stay and help Dolyn?” “Certainly. Might be I can help with her forge work, and that’s not something the boys are apt to do.” “Good enough. ere’s one last issue to discuss, then. We’l be traveling with someone else—the soothsayer, Jian Nikloss, from the troupe of entertainers we saw earlier. Red-thumb has some business in Luqura. He can’t travel there himself, so we’re taking Jian in his stead.” “Why are we doing this?” Fyn asked, his hands resting on his sword belt. “Weren’t you just saying it’s dangerous to be around you?” “Yes,” Annev said, answering slowly, “but I don’t have much choice in the matter.” “Like hel you don’t.” “No, real y,” Annev said, his tone becoming more heated. “While you were with Brayan, someone tried to shoot me.” “What?” Titus dropped the reins he’d been hitching to the wagon. “Are you okay? What happened?” “So that’s what you two were talking about.” Fyn smirked as if he’d discovered some saucy secret. “So who was it? Did you kil them?” “Fyn,” Brayan rumbled. “ is isn’t the Academy. ere are di erent rules out here, and you need to learn them.” He looked at Annev. “So what did you do?” “Truthful y, not much,” Annev said, “ e shot came from over there.” He pointed to the al ey mouth just beyond the market square. “We chased them but could only nd their crossbow.” He stil wasn’t convinced the attack had been real, but he chose to fol ow Sraon’s advice and keep his suspicions to himself. “But why—” “Did you see—” “How did you—” Annev threw up his hands, halting their questions. “I’m ne—everything is ne. I knew someone would come after me. I just hoped it wouldn’t be til we reached the capital.” He looked at his companions puzzled faces and swore. “You al remember the monsters that destroyed Chaenbalu? ey were sent to the village by someone—by humans or maybe demigods, I don’t know—but they were meant to kil or capture me.” He waited another moment for that to sink in. “ e destruction of Chaenbalu hasn’t stopped the people who are after me. Today they sent a stranger with a crossbow. Tomorrow it could be poisoned potatoes, or an old woman with a knife, or some new devilry we’ve never seen before.” He paused, letting them see his sincerity. “When I nd out who’s hunting me, I’m going to end them. Til then, I’ve got assassins behind me, the godsdamned Hand of Keos hanging from my arm and a constant preoccupation with trying not to pick my nose or scratch my ass with it.” As a group, Annev’s companions stared at him in horror. Good, Annev thought. Give them something to think about. erin opened his mouth to say something then, and Fyn was just a heartbeat behind him, but Titus interjected before either boy could speak. “ at’s settled then. We’re de nitely not leaving you.” Fyn groaned and erin’s mouth snapped shut. Annev hoped to argue the point further, but he was then interrupted by a tug at his elbow. He turned and saw the gray-robed man standing just outside the circle of their discussion. It seemed he was stuck with the lot of them. “ is is Jian Nikloss,” Annev said, abandoning the argument. “Are you ready, Jian?” “Yes, Master Ainnevog.” He patted a black bag hanging from his waist and gestured to the larger drawstring knapsack slung over his shoulder. “I do not have a horse, but I wil not slow you down.” “He’s the Pale Man!” erin said, eyes widening. “ e Ghost Man with the dead eyes!” “ erin!” Sraon snapped. “Don’t be rude.” “It is not rude, Master Cheng.” Jian’s pink eyes slid to the blacksmith and then back to the wiry wide-eyed boy. “Avatar erin names me true. I am the Pale Man. e Ghost Man. I have other names and other masks too—Dead Eyes, Seer, Necromancer, Marrow-Lich—none of these names o end me, even when they are spoken in fear, hatred, or ignorance. ey are simply my names.” He looked at the rest of the group. “If I gave you names, would you fear or hate me? If I spoke the truths written on your faces, would you spit in mine?” He smiled, his teeth white as chalk. “Some would, I think—but I wil not say your names. Not unless you ask me to share them, or Master Ainnevog demands them.” Titus and erin exchanged looks with one another, neither one sure what to make of the soothsayer’s words. Sraon tugged on his eye patch and Fyn stayed silent, his hands rmly on his weapons belt. “Wel ,” Brayan said at last, breaking the silence, “I guess you’re the fel ow taking my place in the caravan.” e quartermaster extended his hand and Jian took it without hesitation, his blue-veined palm looking smal in the giant’s gentle grip. “ at is a new name,” Jian said, smiling broadly. “ ank you for bringing it to me.” “Er … you’re welcome.” Brayan glanced sideways at Sraon, one eyebrow raised, and nal y released the soothsayer’s hand and scratched his head. “Right then. I’l grab my war maul and, uh, maybe some supplies. at al right, Sraon?” e blacksmith nodded. “Wil you go straight to Dolyn’s?” “I think I might, yes. Feels strange walking the streets here—I’m used to skulking around at night, you know.” He shifted, his massive shoulders heaving in a bear-sized shrug. “I’m sure I’l get used to it.” He turned to Titus. “Take good care of the mare. You’re stil the Steward of Husbandry, after al .” Titus’s eyes were suddenly bright with tears. “We’l be back in a week, Brayan. We’l be quick.” “Sure,” Brayan said, sounding a little choked. “Just a week. Don’t worry if things stretch a bit, though. I’l be here waiting for you.” He forced a smile. “You’l nd Dolyn in the craftsmen’s district, Brayan. If you hurry, you might also run into those merrymakers Jian parted with. Seems they have business with her too.” “Do they now?” Brayan swiped his hammer and a sack from the wagon. “ at juggler puts on a good show. Wouldn’t mind seeing him perform some more—his sister too. Fastest ngers I’ve ever seen on a ute.” “Aye, better than Nikum, even!” Sraon winced as he spoke the dead carpenter’s name. In the silence that fol owed, Annev had the awkward sense that everyone was ghting not to stare at him. Because I’m to blame for everyone who died in Chaenbalu, he thought. It doesn’t matter that Nikum was murdered by the feurog or that I fought to protect him from the monsters. Somehow, they’re al my fault. e babes in the Academy’s nursery. e students and the witwomen. e farmers, masters, and ancients. ey’re al my fault … Instead of meeting their non-gazes, Annev looked beyond Jian, past the market and toward the city’s southern gates. e mil ing crowd l ed his vision, and he tried to banish his memories of the destruction he had caused. He blinked. at girl in the crowd … she looks familiar. en it dawned on him. She’s back. e ghost is back. “Odar’s bal s!” erin shouted, loud enough to spook the horse. “It’s Faith! Titus, are you seeing this?” e boy gestured at the girl Annev had seen: a young blond woman with a freckled nose and a ragged shift, a bundle clutched tightly in her arms. e light seemed to pass right through her, as her body did not obstruct Annev’s view of the market or of Banok’s town wal s. Titus shrieked. “She’s a ghost, erin! Myjun only stared at him, her anger stil hot, her rage stil rising. “Tel me now—and if you lie, I wil start on your other hand.” Despite al the blood, Myjun’s voice was level. “Where have they gone?” “My sister’s home,” he wept, “in Hentingsfort. Dear Gods, have mercy, please.” Myjun stared at him, her brow furrowed in concentration. e man had spoken the truth … but not the whole truth. Something was wrong. Something was missing. What was it? A truth and a lie perhaps? She drove back her anger at being lied to before she jammed the shears into his neck. Instead she steadied herself, forced him to look her in the eyes. “You lied to me.” “It’s the truth, I swear it!” False. Something about the man—a dim glow that seemed to pulse as he spoke—suggested he was lying to her stil . She gritted her teeth and shook her head. “ ey are with … the sister of your dead wife Charlyn—but they are not in Hentingsfort? ey are further east of us … along the Brakeroad.” “Witch,” the man breathed, his voice strangled, choked. “You’re a damn witch! Why do you care? What do you want from us!” She swung her arm back and drove the shears point- rst into Davey’s neck —or would have, had Oyru not caught her by the wrist and saved the farmer’s life. “He lied,” she hissed, pul ing her hand free, “and he disobeyed me.” “ e mask is making you act rashly. You must control your emotions.” She wanted to punch the shears into the assassin’s face. Instead, she stil ed her shaking hand and glanced at the farmer. “What do you care for him? He’s nothing— less than nothing.” “How did you know about Charlyn and Hentingsfort?” Myjun hesitated. “I don’t know,” she said, answering truthful y. Oryu studied her more closely then nodded. “How did you know he lied?” “ e light,” she said, unthinking. “It pulsed around him.” “Was the light there before he lied?” “I don’t know. Maybe.” She considered it. “Yes, but I had not noticed it.” “Look at him now. What do you see?” Myjun stared at the farmer, his mutilated hand bleeding onto the oor, his face pale, almost white. If his ngers weren’t tended to he could bleed to death. Myjun hu ed—he had lied to her—and she was about to look away when she noticed a icker of color around him. A silhouette of light she had thought was simply the glare from the sunbeam overhead. She squinted at it now, xed on it, trying to see it … but there was nothing to see. It was only an impression, an aura that she observed less with her eyes and more with … something else. She wasn’t sure what. “He’s glowing. ere’s some kind of aura surrounding him.” “Describe it.” “Yel ow? Maybe white. It has … streaks of blood in it. Red and pink.” “And when he lied?” She thought about it. She hadn’t real y seen colors—it was something she had felt more than saw. So what color did it feel like? What did it remind her of? “Not black … not purple,” she said at last. “Something between the two.” “You have a talent for auramancy,” Oyru said, nodding. “I cannot see it, but I feel the inverse of it. It is the opposite of shadow magic—the dark and the light.” “And?” “And,” Oyru continued, smoothly materializing so that his face became corporeal, a oating head amidst the darkness, “that means you have a talent for auramancy and soulriding—and, if the blood wyrm’s death is any indication, bladesinging. at is a rare combination. Very rare, when your father was only half Ilumite. You most likely possess the fourth Ilumite blood-talent as wel : lightslinging.” He pointed at the farmer. “It should be easy to execute him with your magic.”

chunks.content: Myjun sco ed. “What magic?” “You summoned soul re blades to kil the draken. It burned out its eyes.” He pointed at her. “With the ful Ilumite talent, you can conjure re and blades of light, you can throw lightning. You can bend the light around yourself—turn invisible—or you can re ect it and create il usions. Some of those skil s wil be hard to master and some wil come natural y, but as my apprentice you wil master them al .” She stared at the assassin. “I can’t do any of that. Not a damn piece of it. Besides,” she added, not caring in the slightest, “your farmer is dead. You let him bleed out.” Oyru shook his head. “Half dead is not truly dead.” And with that, he stuck his hand through the farmer’s chest and gave Old Davey’s heart a squeeze. e man’s eyes shot open and he screamed as if woken from a nightmare—except this was the nightmare, and Oyru would not let him leave it so easily. e Shadow Reborn slid his hand free then pointed at the terri ed farmer, the blood from Davey’s severed ngers slowly pooling at his feet. “Kil him,” he said, “using your magic. Use your soul re blades, or re, or lightning. I don’t care how, only that you do it.” “ is is the third test?” “Yes.” Myjun sni ed. “Fine.” She stomped over to the dazed farmer whose eyes were already drifting closed, and slapped him across his weather-beaten face. His eyes popped open once more, and he spat at her. In an instant rage, her hands reached for his throat. “ !” Myjun stopped, frozen by the intensity of Oyru’s voice. e cold apathy that always marked the man’s speech had vanished, replaced by a piercing anger. And then, quick as a summer storm, it disappeared. e iciness returned, harder than before. Colder. “Do not touch him. Feed your anger and frustration into him, al your pain and re. Lash him with it. Burn him with it.” Myjun stared at the dying farmer, his face bloodless, his body slack and unmoving. She felt little anger for the man—disgust and hatred, yes, but her rage had subsided as the man’s life-force ebbed away. She did feel frustration, though—a tiny ower of hatred that burned with the re of being unable to kil the man, of not being al owed to strangle him. She was angry at Oyru, angry that he believed she could do this, angry that he could compel her to do it. And yet … she had done it before. She tried to remember how, to draw out the memory. Blood and claws. Teeth and scales. Beetles gnawing at her esh, the acid-blood spewing from the draken’s mouth. Burning and pain, the frustration and anger as its jaws clamped down on her, piercing her esh. Myjun dug deeper, immersing herself in the pain of the moment—that moment when she longed to die but continued to live. She screamed, the sound ripping from her throat. She screamed and screamed … Light sparked in her hands—tiny ames, white-hot and incandescent—and then they winked out. Myjun panted with exertion, her voice raw with emotion. “Beautiful,” Oyru whispered, standing in the dark once again. “Absolutely beautiful.” “Pointless,” Myjun snapped. “A useless spark.” “Not so.” Oyru gestured at Old Davey who had fal en silent once again, the blood stil dripping from his severed ngers, but slower … slower … “Try taking his pain and fear—and using them to fuel your magic.” “I don’t . . .” Myjun stared at the farmer, watched the aura around him begin to dim. Could she do it? She knew pain fueled her mask and made her stronger, faster—but could she steal that same pain, those same emotions, from other people? Could she turn their pain into her strengths? A spark lit inside her, its intensity fueled by the possibility, by the need to try … To burn. To break. Myjun reached out to the dying farmer, al owing her emotions to feed o his. It was easy—easier than she expected. She felt the man’s aura peel away from him and Davey’s eyes ew open, more horror in his face than she had ever seen during her interrogation. He screamed at her, terri ed. “What are you doing!” Rage. Pain. Frustration. Disgust. Hatred. Al of his emotions were hers, channeled through her, strengthening her—and as her power grew, his fear grew too. Terror. Pain. Fear. Agony. Despair. An endless feedback loop that fed the spark inside her until it blossomed into a ame. at ame found its home in her arms, condensing, sharpening as twin points of light sprang from her palms—sharp white blades of pure spirit, an aura of emotion and re, light and energy. e blades grew into daggers … into swords. She realized she was screaming, was venting her pain with her ragged and intense voice, as sharp and piercing as any blade. Old Davey screamed too, his pale face l ed with a terror as pure as her hatred. en she struck, her soul re blades scissoring together to snip the farmer’s head from his shoulders. His skin burned as they slid into his esh, his eyes bursting into ame, an otherworldly light pouring from his mouth. e pain that l ed Myjun’s body, the hunger that penetrated her soul, suddenly evaporated in place of a sense of ful ness. e sensation startled her, awakening her senses to a world that had grown dul beneath the endless aches and pains. She was not hungry. She was not thirsty. She was … alive with the rush of life and a feeling of ful l ment, the thril of having taken a life and being given one. Beneath it al , she stil felt the in uence of the mask—the sharp need for pain and the malice that accompanied it—but these were distant now, their sharpness abated by the euphoria of the moment. And suddenly they were gone—the rush, the joy, the thril —al vanished. Her hunger and thirst were stil diminished, but alongside a void, a wide chasm of need … and a new kind of hunger that would not be satis ed by food or water. “You would be a Soulblade, I think—a Soulrider and a Bladesinger—but the aqlumera and the Inquisitor ring have tainted your magic. Forged it into something new. Something wonderful. You aren’t spel singing. You are … soul-shrieking.” A queer smile touched the corner of Oyru’s mouth then—an emotion so foreign, so out of place, that it sickened Myjun to see it. “A Soulscreamer. Light-bending and soulriding may be chal enging for you —certainly more di cult than for a ful -blooded Ilumite—but that jagged edge … that raw power.” His expression morphed into a sadistic grin. “Oh, yes. You are my sharp little knife. My bloody Oraqui.” Behind them, the husk of the dead man slumped forward, his skin and bones as dry and brittle as burned charcoal. When his soul ess body hit the ground, there was a faint crackle of light, a soft sigh, and then silence. “Come,” Oyru continued, not missing a beat. “ e people of Hentingsfort await us.” “What’s in Hentingsfort?” Myjun might have been angered to ask before, but her feelings stil oated beneath the memory of her soulfeasting. She hungered for more—more blood, more death, more soul-sucking. She craved it, needed it like a lusty lover or starving mendicant. “Another test,” Oyru said, beckoning toward the door. “ e last before I take you beyond Reocht na Skah and the heart of the shadow realm.” “You wil take me … into the shadows?” e assassin led her outside, into the sunlight and then the deep shade of the Brakewood. “Yes, but Hentingsfort rst. You’ve only just discovered your power, and the shadows are far more dangerous than an old farmer tied to a chair. Hentingsfort is a village, with its own town council and militia. A few hundred people.” “And what wil we do when we get there?” “What else? We wil ght and kil . We wil sup on the souls of the weak. Drink the darkness and the light.” Myjun shivered in anticipation, eager for the taste of blood and the thril of the hunt. She would dine on death—she would slake her unquenchable thirst and satisfy her insatiable hunger. She shuddered at the thought of it and fol owed the assassin into the woods. CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO Tosan’s spirit fought Kenton, as precise and relentless as a mason chipping at a block of stone. At the same time, Kenton felt fragments of himself being washed away, drawn inexorably downward into the aqlumera. He felt disoriented, as though he were spinning into an abyss. Kenton reached out, grasping for any anchor, and seized on his love for Myjun and his hatred for Annev. An instant later, Tosan loomed over him, and it was as though they wrestled at the edge of some spiritual void. “My daughter is dead!” the former headmaster shouted, his attacks pushing Kenton toward oblivion. “If you had kept Annev in his cel ,”— push—“she would stil be alive!” Push. Shove. Kenton’s spirit stood at the brink of the aqlumera. His grasp on himself slipped and he felt his feelings for and memories of Myjun grow faint . . . distant. Tosan shoved again, threatening to tumble him into the yawning abyss. “I had wondered whether you had helped him—whether you had freed that monster from his cel —but then I saw you were just inept. Unable to save yourself, unable to save my daughter.” Push. Shove. “Her death is as much your fault as his!” Tosan struck, his blows hard enough to shake Kenton to his core . . . yet Kenton’s grip on his twin loves and hatreds remained, and he clung ferociously to his life and control of his body … and, by so doing, he learned how to ght back. Entangled with the man’s psyche, Kenton sensed Tosan’s own doubts and fears—his weaknesses, the things he loved and most wanted to protect. e former headmaster truly cared about very little, but two things stood out: his dead daughter and the ruined Academy. “You couldn’t protect the Academy! You blame Annev and me for its destruction, but you were the one who struck the rst blow. It was your magic —your hel re wand—that sparked the tinder. Everybody in Chaenbalu died because of you!” “No!” Tosan roared, his grip slipping. “It was that boy—that one-armed keokum took everything I loved—everything you loved!” Kenton wavered, struggling to regain control. Annev had destroyed Kenton’s life … but it was Tosan’s fault too. Kenton had been trapped in the prison cel , unable to ght. Tosan had been above ground, ghting the monsters. He’d been trying to protect his daughter—and he’d succeeded … right up until he’d attacked Annev. And then Kenton saw the headmaster’s weakness . . . his most terrible secret. e truth of it hit Kenton like a bolt of thunder. “You let him kil her.” Tosan stumbled, shaken to his core, and they stood on equal ground once again. “No, I tried to save her! You weren’t even there!” e headmaster clawed at Kenton’s psyche, trying to regain control. “I died trying to protect her.” “I can see into your memories, Tosan. You thought Annev wouldn’t hurt you so long as Myjun stayed by your side. You used her as a shield, to protect yourself, and she died ! ” Tosan faltered, his doubts creeping in, pul ing his certainties apart, and when he stumbled again Kenton shoved—hard. e vengeful spirit reeled back, his psyche tipping backward into the void of aqlumera. “No! ” But it was too late. Kenton ung the old man away, forcing him out of his body, and Tosan’s spirit tumbled back into the magical abyss, his essence swal owed by the liquid magic. Kenton took a shuddering a breath, in possession of himself once again. He was alive, but pieces of his psyche had been splintered, their pieces swept away by the battle with Tosan. Kenton had clung tightly to major things—aspects of himself that he most identi ed with, the things that anchored him—but smal er details had been torn away, pul ed down into the consuming void of aqlumera. He tried to recal the names of his favorite poisons, his preferred weapons, or his companions at the Academy … but they were hazy. He was surprised to remember that he favored ghting with the tachi—a piece of himself that had nearly been lost—but he could not recal if he had a favorite color or food. As Kenton quietly gathered himself, he found other splinters that were decidedly not his memories. His thoughts of Annev and Myjun remained, but they were tainted by a feeling that was almost patriarchal. His thoughts and impressions of the Academy were similarly possessive, and rooms he had never entered now felt familiar. Kenton lay on his back, his ery glass orbs staring sightlessly at the curved ceiling of the vault chamber. Cautiously, he eased himself into a sitting position, then rose to stand in front of the pool of aqlumera once more. is time he did not peer into its depths; he would not tempt fate or give Tosan a second chance to possess him. Instead, Kenton reached into his Cloak of Secrets and withdrew a long black scarf—an artifact that made its wearer more commanding, more likely to be fol owed. He wrapped it around his head and tied it tight over his lidless eyes, hoping it might lend some protection against further attacks to his soul. It didn’t impede his supernatural vision, and Kenton turned his back on the glowing font, returning to the trap door. I have to try one more time, he thought. e cloak is too risky, and with these new artifacts I should be able to forge a way out of here. Kenton cautiously navigated the fal en stone and broken rock and returned to the broken cel door, ignoring the col apsed tunnel he had dug with Mercy. Once safely free of the cel , he renewed his exploration of the Academy’s subterranean passages, hoping he might nd a new, unexplored path to the surface. He had little hope, yet after wandering the gloom for just a few minutes his sharpened vision led him to a new section of tunnels. He started to fol ow the twists and turns as if on instinct, rst warily and then with increasing con dence, as if he knew these tunnels. A moment’s re ection revealed the truth: he did remember them, but they were Tosan’s memories. One of the fragments the Eldest of Ancients had inadvertently left within him. Sel sh prick, Kenton swore, not for the rst time. Trying to cheat death by stealing my body … my life. He sni ed, the irony not lost on him. And now I’m using his memories to escape. e notion brought a smile to his face, though it was quickly tempered by the thought that Myjun was stil dead, and that Annev had been the one to kil her. It reignited his sorrow and rage, though his feelings were dul ed too. Kenton no longer felt like himself, and he worried about the long-term consequences of his struggle with Tosan. It was dusk when Kenton nal y emerged, led by his vision and Tosan’s memories, and saw a ickering camp re between the town wel and the Academy’s stables. A group of men whispered there, and it wasn’t long before Kenton recognized the varied voices of Master Carbad, Ancient Denithal, and the other surviving teachers from the Academy. Kenton watched in silence, trying to decide whether to approach and announce himself or sneak away and leave Chaenbalu forever. As he listened, though, a plan slowly began to form, one that might utilize Tosan’s stolen memories and increase Kenton’s chances of taking his revenge. *** Edra surveyed the haggard men surrounding the camp re. ey were a pitiful lot, made worse by squabbling between themselves. Like a pack of dogs ghting over a soup bone. But this soup has lost its savor. e former Ancient in the Art of Warcraft looked at the ruins of the Academy. It had been his home. With its towering gray wal s and stout wooden doors, the Academy was more than a building: for the infants that were brought through those wooden doors it was a nursery; for the boys tutored there it was both a school and a sanctuary; for the men that survived their training and lived to go on retrieval missions, the Academy was a comfortable home and a familiar friend. e one constant in an otherwise bleak life. And it had been sheared in half in a matter of seconds, tumbled to the ground and melted to so much slag and cinders. It was a crushed husk of its former glory. e stained glass windows that once rivaled the greatest cathedrals of Luqura were al shattered when the edi ce col apsed. e Academy’s familiar dark rooms and narrow hal s had caved in, forming an impossible, impenetrable warren of tunnels—Edra knew, because he had tried to get through. It was a tomb now, a crypt for both his fal en brethren and the monsters that had invaded their smal vil age. Edra shuddered, recal ing their grotesque corpses: feral men with twisted metal woven through their bodies, stone clubs for limbs and teeth led to razor-sharp spikes. Edra felt the bile rise in his throat as he remembered the mangled bodies of both friend and foe. Broken limbs, sheared torsos, shattered faces. More than once, he’d tried to move a stone blocking his path, only to discover it was not a stone at al , but a monster’s severed limb. It had been dangerous work, trying to explore. Bringing a torch into the con ned spaces often led to the smoke forcing Edra back out after a few minutes of searching, yet without light it was near impossible to navigate the maze of fal en stone. Some paths suddenly dead-ended. Others spiraled upward. Sometimes the ground itself would tremble—an aftershock from the earth-rending battle between Ancient Tosan and Annev—and the paths would either shift or col apse in on themselves. Edra’s home—the only place he ever felt safe and at peace—had become a death trap. “We should leave. is place is dead and so are the vil agers. You are talking nonsense, Carbad.” Edra glanced up at Ather, the slender Master of Lies, and nodded in agreement. e man’s words echoed his own thoughts, and it was the rst thing remotely resembling wisdom he had heard from the lot of former masters. Unfortunately, Master Carbad was deaf to it. “We must rebuild, Master Ather. For the good of the Order, the Vault of Damnation must be exhumed, its foundations rebuilt, and its wal s reclaimed.” e spindly Master of Operations twisted his ash-stained robes. “ e Academy must rise again.” “It can’t be done,” said Murlach, the Master of Engineering. “ e foundation is unstable. e Academy was built atop that grotto centuries ago, and that fool boy must have blasted a hole down to its core.” He ran a hand through his greasy black hair, drawing attention to the shock of white that now graced his forehead. “If the Academy must be rebuilt, it would be better to start work on a solid foundation—preferably one far away from here—instead of atop some shifting hole that is bound to give way and swal ow up our e orts.” Ancient Denithal shook his head in disagreement. “We cannot build the Academy somewhere else. e Vault of Damnation is unique. It protects the artifacts from detection—it is the only reason the Academy was built here in the rst place! e aqlumera is also irreplaceable—if unstable—so we cannot simply build another Academy, let alone another vault.” “Which is why we must stay,” Carbad declared, seizing hold of the conversation once again. “I’m certain that with Master Murlach’s ingenuity we can safely excavate the building.” “Even if it were possible, I would need a hundred laborers just to dig out the foundations,” Murlach snapped. “We don’t have the resources to—” “We can nd the resources,” Carbad said, his cheeks ushing. “We can bring scores of villagers from Banok and Luqura and force them to rebuild. We wil take farmers from their elds and bring them and their families to til the ground and reestablish—” “You’re insane.” Al eyes turned to Aog, the brooding Master of Punishment. Despite his towering stature, the stony-faced man had always been soft-spoken and solitary. As the Academy’s de facto executioner, he was also adept at silencing other men with an almost casual indi erence. Since the Academy’s destruction, he had not spoken a word. It seemed tting to Edra that he chose to speak now, to say what the others had been thinking but were afraid to articulate. Carbad sputtered, wanting to object but unable to nd the words. Edra smiled at that; it was uncharacteristic for Tosan’s former lapdog to be speechless, and it was even rarer for Aog to nd words where Carbad could not. “Cut o a man’s head. He dies.” Aog jerked his head at the Academy. “Tosan is dead. So is the Academy.” “I can replace Tosan. I managed the Academy and the vil age while Tosan was in charge, and I assisted Ancient Windsor for almost a decade!” Denithal sputtered, rising from his seat next to the low-burning re. “You aren’t even an Ancient, Carbad, let alone Eldest of Ancients. If anyone were to replace Tosan, it should be me.” Edra spat into the re in disgust, and al turned and looked up at him. His hands had drifted down to the sword sheathed at his hip. “No more of this garbage,” Edra said, forcing his hand away from the comforting hilt. He felt the veins bulging on his neck, the tightness of his clenched jaw, and tried to relax. His body was aching for a ght—but this was not the ght he wanted. “We’ve been retreading this argument for two days, and you seem intent to drown us al in it.” He punctuated his accusation by pointing a nger at the grandfatherly Denithal. “You’re twice as old as any of us here, Den. You were two decades older than Tosan. You were passed over for the title of Ancient for years because you’re an alchemist. You’re not a leader. No one has ever asked you to be one and no one wants to fol ow you. So stick to your potions and stop pretending we care what you think.” Denithal blustered, patting his robes as if searching for some defense against Edra’s words—but they were true, and the other masters knew it. Edra wasn’t nished. He turned to Carbad, saw the smug smile on the man’s face, and slapped him. e Master of Operations’ hand ew to his mouth and he drew it away bloodied, eyes wide with shock. “How dare you—” Edra slapped him again. is time Carbad kept his mouth shut, though his eyes gleamed with hatred. Edra nodded. “Aog is right. e Academy is dead—and you’re an idiot, Carbad. We can’t rebuild this. We can’t even salvage the artifacts trapped in the vault. Even if we could get down there, what would we do? Trade artifacts for food or gold in Luqura, after spending our lifetimes col ecting and safeguarding them?” Edra heaved a great breath. “Chaenbalu is dead,” he repeated. “Brayan was right to leave for Luqura, and I wish I’d had the sense to go with him.” e Master of Arms looked around at the six other men surrounding the re and saw Der, Ather, and Murlach nodding in agreement. Aog ran a hand over his shaved head, letting his silence speak for him. “It’s settled, then.” “Not quite.” Edra raised an eyebrow, surprised to hear a voice of dissent coming from the direction of the Academy. He turned, prepared to clout whomever it was until he saw the man climbing out of the Academy’s ruins. e newcomer wore long robes the color of ash and thunder clouds, with a black cloak over his shoulders and thick cloth wrapped around his eyes. A dazzling array of jewelry adorned his neck, forearms, and gloved hands. Edra’s eyes locked on a particularly entrancing gold-and-ruby amulet. As the gure walked toward them, Edra couldn’t help but feel there was something familiar about the stranger … about the way he walked … “Tosan?” Edra asked, taking a step forward to see the man emerging from the rubble more clearly. With the setting sun shining behind his head, it took Edra a second to realize the truth. “Kenton?” e newly raised Master of Curses continued to pick his way between the stones, and when his blind gaze fel upon Edra, he felt his blood run cold. Something was di erent. Edra blinked, trying to shake the chil he felt when he looked at the shrouded young man. “We thought you were kil ed in the attack,” he said. “We tried to search the Academy for survivors, but …” “But you failed to nd me.” Kenton stopped in front of Edra and looked the Master of Arms up and down, as if he could see through the thick blindfold that covered half his face. Edra shivered in spite of himself. Had the boy grown tal er? When had he become so intimidating? And what had happened to his eyes? “Yes …” he said slowly. “It’s been two days since the Academy fel … and we’ve searched but we seem to be the only survivors. We were just discussing what to do.” “You’ve been debating for days,” Kenton said, managing to glower through his blindfold at each man around the re, “and you haven’t done a damn thing but sit here.” Master Carbad stumbled forward, apparently wil ing to stand up to Kenton despite having crumpled before Edra. “Who the hel do you think you are, whelp? You’re barely raised from an acolyte—and then only because the real masters were too drunk to raid Janak’s keep, which you failed to do anyway. Tosan made you Master of Curses because he was so embarrassed of you.” He paused, suddenly horri ed. “Is that where you got that clothing? at jewelry? Did you plunder the vault?” Edra had wondered the same thing. Kenton seemed to be dressed head to toe in cursed artifacts. He licked his lips, appreciating how dangerous Kenton might be if those items real y had come from the vault. As if Kenton could hear Edra’s thoughts, the former Master of Curses raised his hands and gently removed his blindfold. Edra gasped and Carbad stumbled backward, tripping on his robes: instead of eyes, tongues of rainbow re burned inside the boy’s skul , giving him the appearance of both demon and angel; it was as if his eyes had been burned away, replaced by orbs of re, and their gaze pierced Edra to his very soul. Keos, he thought, biting his cheek to keep from uttering the curse aloud. e boy is a ghost … or a demon? He’s like those wraiths that attacked the vil age. As Edra watched, the ames dancing inside the boy’s eye sockets seemed to shift from orange-red to purple-black. He swal owed hard. e young man let his eyes meet that of every man at the re pit, matching them glare for glare, daring anyone else to chal enge him. “Yes, I plundered the vault—and you should too. Every one of you.” Kenton paused, turning to Carbad. “Except for you, Master Carbad. As you possess no magical a nity, you are of no use to me.” “What? Of course I can’t use magic. None of us can! We aren’t bloody keokum.” Kenton gestured at Edra, Denithal, and the rest of the masters, excluding Carbad. “Each of these men possesses magic, though they may not know it. I can see it burning inside them. It has shaped their natural abilities. Pushed them into the roles they now possess. Stealth, deception, engineering, alchemy, arms …” He studied Aog. “And the administration of death.” Edra squinted at the former Master of Curses, trying to reconcile the quiet, dark-haired boy he remembered with this powerful, con dent man. e side of his face was stil scarred from when Master Ather had beaten the boy bloody, but instead of hiding the dis gurement behind his long dark hair as he used to do, Kenton seemed to be displaying the scar. Displaying it … and his eyes. is was not the same boy that Tosan sent to apprentice with Master Narach. He was stronger . . . and Kenton knew it. ose eyes, Edra thought, shying away from Kenton’s uncovered gaze. She has entered the shadow realm, a plane of existence that overlaps our own but which remains distant and alien.” “Like the Spirit World?” “ ey are similar. e World of Spirits is farther stil , though it overlaps in much the same way.” “She is dead then.” “No.” Kiara waved her hand at the shadepool and the darkness shifted, forming images of overlapping gray discs, some dark and some light. “We inhabit the physical realm, ruled by the Elder Gods and the Younger Gods of Plants, Minerals, and Animals.” Kiara gestured at the pool again and a spinning white disc separated itself from the others. “Overlapping our world are the other three planes of existence: the Plane of Shadows, the World of Dreams, and the Spirit World. Our actions here cast shadows, silhouettes of reality, in the shadow realm. When we sleep, our consciousness touches the World of Dreams—and when we die, our spirits travel to the Spirit World.” ree gray discs rose from the shadepool, their edges overlapping with each other and the white disc. “Al three parts of our soul—mind, body, and spirit—converge here and anchor us in the physical realm, yet it is possible to travel to the other planes if you possess a special connection to skywater, earthblood, or light re.” “And Myjun is in the shadow realm. She’s there physical y?” “Correct.” Kiara waved her hand once more and the shadows reformed into the hazy image of the woman in the golden mask and the man in black armor. “Why?” Kiara grunted. “Some secrets remain secrets. But”—she held up a nger —“I can give you three vital pieces of information. First, Myjun wil return here —to this very shadepool—in less than a year’s time. Second, she wil be coming to hunt Annev as wel . ird, if you are not here to stop her—if you are not here to save her—then she wil be kil ed.” Kenton stared at Kiara, unable to deduce the woman’s motives. If she was lying, it was an elaborate lie—and one that placed the blame for Chaenbalu’s destruction squarely on her own shoulders. If she was tel ing the truth, though … “Why are you tel ing me this?” “Because your current mission runs counter to my own. You seek to nd Annev and kil him. I seek to use the Vessel for another purpose—a purpose I cannot achieve if he is already dead. But now perhaps our desires run paral el to one another. You sought vengeance because you believed Annev had kil ed the headmaster’s daughter—your would-be lover—but those motives were misplaced.” Kenton was grateful that the darkness hid his reddening cheeks from the witmistress. He wondered how many of the Academy’s witgirls and witwomen had known about Kenton and Myjun’s short courtship. It doesn’t matter a whit now, though. According to Kiara, they’re al dead … and Myjun is alive. “Maybe. But if Myjun wil be here in a year that stil gives me plenty of time to nd Annev.” “Less than a year—and you don’t need to nd him. He wil be here too.” “Why wait when I can nd him sooner?” Kiara shook her head. “If Annev is not here then Myjun wil not be here either. She wil be lost to you forever.” Kenton’s hand drifted to the bone dagger at his hip. He felt a powerful urge to kil this woman, not just because she was manipulating him, but for destroying the village, the Academy, and everything they represented— everything Kenton had been working toward. In some twisted way, Annev’s escape from prison, the loss of his eyes, and Myjun’s death were her fault. She had brought the monsters here; their attack had drawn Tosan away and led to Kenton being alone with Annev. But no. Kenton had chosen to stay in that cel . He had al owed Annev to goad him, and then blind him. Kenton’s hand stopped. “So I wait for Annev—a few weeks or months, maybe a year. en what? What am I saving Myjun from?” “From death. From the shadows. From herself.” Kenton frowned. “From the man she was with?” “Half man—he is a shadow reborn—and he is her master.” “Master?” Kenton’s lip curled. “Myjun has no master.” “She is as much a captive to herself as to him. at is why she needs you to save her— not to interfere with Ainnevog. Do you understand? If she kil s him, she wil be kil ed. If you kil him, you wil never see her again.” “ at’s no guarantee she wil want to see me—or that she wants to be saved.” “Some mysteries we must solve for ourselves.” “I suppose.” He paused. “Why do you want Annev so much? You and your Brides of Fate destroyed the village … for what?” Kiara gave a sly grin. “You do not seem too upset by my part in Chaenbalu’s destruction.” Kenton sni ed. “I didn’t much like the people who lived here … and they didn’t care for me. Why should I care now that they’re dead? e only person I cared about is in the shadow realm.” Kenton looked back to the shadepool and the images that oated there. “Very wel . If it wil save Myjun then I wil play my part.” Kiara nodded. “ en our paths have momentarily aligned.” She gestured at the shadepool. “So long as you remain here with me, I can show you Myjun’s location. You wil know when she is about to return.” “And what is your path, Witmistress?” Kiara waved at the shadepool and the image of Myjun and her master faded into darkness. “For many decades now, the purpose of the reap has been to nd babies with the potential for magic and bring them back to the Academy.” She cocked her head at Kenton, sensing his surprise. “What? You thought you and Annev were the only ones?” “Why?” She sighed, head shaking. “It al comes from fear, I suppose. e Academy was founded many centuries ago, when a sect of preachers claimed the priesthood had been corrupted and that al magic, including artifacts, was evil. ey persecuted any who believed otherwise, and soon left the Church to form their own sect in the heart of the Brakewood. When they left, they stole many of the Church’s treasures, including artifacts of legend such as the Hand of Keos. e heretics believed it was their sacred duty to either guard or destroy such magic. Ironic then that they chose to hide in Chaenbalu, home to a radiant fountain of pure aqlumera.” “ e vault,” Kenton interrupted. “You’re talking about that liquid in the vault.” “Just so. e vault was built atop the fountain, the Academy was built to protect the vault, and it trained young zealots to l it with other stolen artifacts—but not al of the founders were true believers. One among them, Pomela Witsom, was a Bride of Fate, fol owing a prophecy that the Vessel of Keos would be raised among these heretics. So she joined the group before they splintered, married Elder Cornett—who would become Chaenbalu’s rst headmaster—and she in turn became the rst witwoman. On the surface, Pomela took charge of delivering infants for the Academy and the vil age. en she began training other witwomen to assist her in “saving” other untainted children from the world. ey were midwives initial y, but gradual y Pomela found women gifted with the blood-talent. A handful were like her—Yomad priestesses with Darite complexions, already Brides of Fate. e rest were brought in one at a time and indoctrinated.” “Indoctrinated,” Kenton repeated, turning the word over in his mouth. “ ey al joined your cult then?” Kiara stared at him—not quite a glare, but close. “ ose with too little magic or too little sense remained regular witwomen. rough our work, those without magic have been winnowed out of the Academy, and the ones con scating magic—the ones that are taught to hate it more fervently—are also the ones carrying the blood-talent.” “ at’s perverse.” Kenton paused, considering. “So are you a Darite orphan or a New Terran in ltrator?” is time Kiara did glare. “I am a Yomad from New Terra.” “But aren’t you al stolen from Darite vil ages, like the avatars?” “In every reap we bring in a few infants from Al tara or Old Terra, to keep the old blood alive and to be sure we are thorough in our search for the Vessel. None of us had imagined he would be born in Chaenbalu, let alone to an Ilumite mother … but such is the chal enge of prophecy. We see the future, but only darkly.” “And that’s why it took so long to realize Annev was your Vessel.” “ at, and that meddling priest, Sodar.” Kenton studied the old witmistress, her iron-gray hair and piercing eyes. She stil hadn’t revealed why she wanted Annev, and he was of a mind to discover her secrets. But if she was right—if Myjun real y was alive and would need his help—then he had no reason to leave. He could even stil send the Sons of Damnation on ahead to search Annev out. His connection to their amulets would keep him appraised of their actions, and he could remain here and keep an eye on Myjun through Kiara’s magic scrying. Until she was of no further use to him. “Very wel , Witmistress. I’l spare Annev … for now. In exchange, you wil tel me more about your order—these Brides of Fate. Tel me who they are—or were—and why they exist.” “Mm … and you wil not harm Annev? Neither directly nor indirectly?” “So long as Myjun remains alive and you can show her to me … yes.” “Bargain struck, then.” e gray woman o ered her palm. Kenton hesitated, then he shook it. As he did so, the air in the room seemed to shudder, the magic in his eyes ared, and for an instant it seemed as though he were holding the bony hand of a aming skeleton. PART THREE e origins of the Six are shrouded in myth and mystery. Such tales—involving monsters, traitors, and keokum being directed by the merciless vampyr Dortafola—are often greatly exaggerated, though on occasion the truth seems more fantastic than ction. One case that is frequently misrepresented is that of Valdemar Kranak, the rst Darite to abandon his cal ing as a priest and scholar so that he might instead support Dortafola and his Siänar’s malign designs. According to the surviving records, Kranak was born toward the end of the Age of Kings and was raised as one of the Dionachs Tobar. He made the ageless covenant with an unknown Terran priest at the turn of the century and leveraged his longevity at the University of Neven nan Su’ul to become a Magister of the First Order. It has been rumored that Kranak lobbied for the position of Arch Lector and was denied the coveted role, possibly due to his sympathies with Terran scholarship. If true, this might have been the impetus for Kranak’s later betrayal of both the university and the city … but we shal leave such unfounded speculation to lesser scholars. What has been con rmed beyond doubt is Valdemar Kranak’s role in the destruction of the university, and the razing of Neven nan Su’ul and the province of Gorm Corsa. Terran propagandists have attempted to paint Kranak as a benevolent intel ectual who was later demonized by the Halcyon Knights, but public record and the eyewitness testimonies show he was instrumental in bringing the Terran Bloodlords to the city, precipitating the retreat of the Darite Empire from Gorm Corsa and the rest of Eastern Daroea (now New Terra). e evidence suggests Kranak began by fomenting unrest among the student populace around the beginning of the ird Age.† Having gained support among the university’s more radical students, Kranak began hosting nightly lectures questioning the accuracy of certain Darite history books, which were already disputed by Terran scholars. e content of these lectures became more and more occult, with at least one claiming that Neven nan Su’ul had been founded by the Terrans rather than the Darites. As the Terrans pressed further and further west, expanding beyond Terra Majora and into Eastern Daroea, Kranak’s lectures led to heated disagreements with other magisters which (in a few cases) escalated to physical blows. It is unclear when Valdemar Kranak’s lectures descended from genuine scholarship into Terran propaganda, but the surviving records of censure state the magister was brought before Arch Lector Gale-Dana’y and ordered to stop questioning the Empire’s doctrine. As ordered, Kranak disbanded his evening classes, only to be suspended when he was discovered meeting privately with students to further his pro-Terran agenda. On his return to the university fol owing his suspension, reports indicate Kranak was a changed man: his lectures had been sanitized of al their former in ammatory content and he publicly disavowed the arguments he had made in support of the Terran government. e change would be utterly remarkable, were it not for our own knowledge of Kranak’s later betrayal. Many scholars, including my col eague Alice Quenby, have argued that Valdemar Kranak was approached by Dortafola during his suspension, and invited to join what later became the Siänar. is is a persuasive argument, particularly as the dates of Kranak’s suspension align with what little we know of the Siänar’s rst creation. —“ e Siänar,” e Complete Histories of Luquatra by Kyartus Gairm † Kash Mikla, a survivor from the razing of Neven nan Su’ul, claims to have seen Kranak leading a cavalry of Bloodlords against the university’s own students (a testimony that has since been widely debunked as no mounts were used during either the city’s siege or the nal rout of its citizens); on the other hand, the folk poem “Vaul of the Fal ” describes Kranak as a scholar whose “love of the masses brought death to his classes when nechraict rose up from their graves,” suggesting that necromancy played an integral part in the city’s nal destruction. Final y, Crystal Gooden—one of my esteemed col eagues from Southmarch—has suggested Kranak used Terran shadow magic to in ltrate and attack the university, giving rise to his later moniker “ e Shadow.” It seems more likely, though, that Kranak’s nickname arose from his ability to silently pass through the university’s hal s (a common e ect produced by most Breathbreakers). CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO Fyn plucked the apple from the vendor’s cart without breaking stride and continued his strol along the River District’s promenade, a wide road that hid the underground canal connecting Luqura’s two rivers. Commerce was brisk here, and the guards were plentiful, but the opportunities for l ing his pockets vastly outnumbered his chances of getting caught. By contrast, the merchant and noble districts had too many eyes watching their vendor stal s and too many swords guarding the nobles’ purses. He’d noticed the mansions were less wel -guarded, though—and contained greater riches besides—so Fyn entertained himself with the idea he might rob the homes of Luqura’s upper class at night, while picking pockets and lifting goods from its lower class during the day. People in the Ash Quarter tended to carry their most valuable possessions on themselves, anyway—their burned hovels being too insecure to leave valuables unprotected and unmolested. Al Fyn needed was a base of operations, and a gang to speed his acquisition of wealth and power. Territory was easiest to take in the Ash Quarter—it was free, if he could keep and defend it—so he’d spent most of his rst two days scouting the Lower District for a good headquarters. He had found a promising corner that was wel away from the Boneyard and just a few blocks south of the unburned portions of the Lower District, and he was trying to settle on a tenement when he sensed someone—several someones from the sound of it—approaching from behind. Instead of turning or eeing, Fyn took his time eating his apple and continued his strol down the trash-littered street. At the rst blind al ey, he turned and ducked inside, knowing his pursuers would be close behind. As he melted into the shadows, he checked his weapons and waited for the expected ambush. He didn’t have to wait long. Six thugs appeared at the mouth of the al ey, their leader at the front, sni ng for blood. “Is it that same one you saw yesterday?” the largest one asked. He carried a heavy, rounded stick that resembled a battered rol ing pin, and his face looked almost cherubic in spite of his imposing gure. “Shh,” the leader hissed, his eyes darting around the al ey, searching for Fyn. “Don’t spook him, Siege.” “What’s to spook?” a third one said, a buxom woman as large as the man with the rol ing pin—probably bigger—carrying what looked to be a sherman’s ga . Of the three that hadn’t spoken, one hung back, presumably to guard the mouth of the al ey, and the other two shot forward, exploring the shadows and hoping to ank their prey. Fortunately for Fyn, he’d chosen this exact al ey yesterday with the purpose of anking them. He smiled from his hidden vantage point, circling behind the group and approaching the man they’d left as their lookout. Halfway into the darkened al ey, Siege gave a whoop as a snare tangled his foot and pul ed his legs out from under him. On cue, Fyn yanked a hidden rope and a sack ful of bricks dropped onto the woman with the ga , knocking her weapon from her hands and quite possibly knocking her out entirely. “It’s a trap!” the leader bel owed, doubling back to the al ey mouth. “Quinn! Way! Grab Siege and Poli and get the hel out of—” Fyn swatted the back of the man’s skul with an improvised slapjack and sent him sprawling atop the body of his unconscious lookout. “So you’re the infamous Fisher King,” Fyn said, leaning over the fal en gure, “the Serpent of South Ashes … the Terror of Tumbledown Street.” He gave a dry laugh then kicked the man between the legs—hard. “Oof!” Fisher doubled over on himself. Fyn glanced back down the al ey, his cold eyes meeting Quinn’s as she helped the larger woman, Poli, clamber out from beneath the bricks. Siege had nearly freed himself from his snare and was searching for his cudgel, which seemed to have rol ed away when he’d fal en. Meanwhile, the sneaky one— Way—had slipped a knife from his pocket and was slowly advancing in Fyn’s direction. “Should have thrown that at my back while I was kicking Fisher. Since you didn’t, either you don’t know how to throw, you have no intention of actual y kil ing me … or you’re scared shitless.” “I ain’t scared of a little chickenshit like you,” Way swore, stil advancing. “What are you? Twelve? Probably don’t even have hair on your fruits.” “Given the choice between my fruits and his …” Fyn kicked the Fisher King in the head, knocking him out cold. “I think I’l stick with mine—hairy or not.” “You got a mouth on you, don’tcha?” “Very observant—now let’s move this along.” Fyn nodded at Way’s weapon. “You gonna throw that or am I gonna take it from you?” e lithe man snickered, though he checked to make sure Siege and the others were backing him up. “I think I’l wait til you start running, then I’l throw it at you.” “You’d miss—and I’m not running.” “We outnumber you, boy. Poli’s got reach with her ga there, and you don’t want to mess with Sigs. Jol y sort, but he’s a kil er an’ no mistake. Arms like a bul . Crush your skul like an egg.” Fyn noticed the man didn’t mention their other associate, Quinn, who was scaling the rightmost building in an attempt to get behind him. Amateurs. “Bul s don’t have arms, asshole—and I’m getting bored.” He hurled his apple core at the man’s face, distracting him just as Quinn leapt from the shadows. He had expected a knife thrust, a hammer-blow or a hatchet-swing— he’d seen the crew use al three in the day and the night he’d been stalking them—but Quinn surprised him with heavy gloves ending in curved iron nails shaped to look like bear claws. Tekko-Kagi, Fyn realized, dodging the attack. Very interesting. Quinn swung again and Fyn stepped aside, placing the young woman between him and Way. When she swung a third time, he stepped into the attack, grabbed Quinn’s wrist and thrust his hips. e smal woman’s feet came o the ground and Fyn spun, slashing her other clawed hand at Way. e sneak cursed, stepped back and tried another angle. is time, Fyn tossed Quinn over his shoulder and into Way, sending both attackers sprawling. “You lot work for me now,” Fyn said, not even winded. “Your contract with the Fisher King has ended.” “Rot that,” Poli said, her ga hook extended. “I’m going to gut you like a sh, boy. No one drops bricks on me and walks away.” Instead of answering, Fyn reached down and plucked a smal purse from Fisher’s tunic. He jingled it in one hand then tossed it to Siege. “What’s your cut of the loot?” “Rule of quarters,” Siege answered, eyeing the sack in his hand with equal parts greed and suspicion. His rol ing pin disappeared into his tunic. “One-quarter for us. ree-quarters for Fisher. He says it’s for the guild—to pay them for the right to work the street.” “ at’s a new one,” Fyn said, snorting. “So who’s in on it? e city watch? e ieves Guild?” “Only one guild matters,” Poli said, lowering her ga . “ e Slavers Guild.” “You’re not from around here, are you?” Quinn said. “Like you can talk. Where’d you get those?” He gestured at the Tekko-Kagi. “You make them? Steal them?” e woman hissed at him in response, her black hair fal ing to cover half her face. “He’s de nitely not from around here,” Way said, slapping Quinn on the shoulder. “Ain’t you never seen the Pits?” he said, studying Fyn. “ ey put ’em on ghters al the time. Makes ’em look erce.” “Only they don’t know how to use them,” Quinn whispered. “And you do?” e woman nodded, her clawed hands crossed in front of her chest. Fyn studied the group, watching their body language for another attack. “You’re Quynh-Chi, though they keep cal ing you Quinn. My guess is you’re Kroseran, with the Tekko-Kagi. You brought here as a slave?” e woman didn’t respond, though she did lower her hands to her sides. “Ford Siegeman,” Fyn continued. “Siege—or Sigs. What’d you do before Fisher brought you into his gang? Work in a bakery or something?” Siege grinned. “Me and Poli worked the docks—I do like to bake, though. You ever eaten pizza pie?” Siege’s smile grew. “It’s Darter food—delicious.” “Maybe you can bake me one sometime.” “Heh. You nd me an oven and the right ingredients, I’l bake a score of ’em.” “What’s Darter food?” “Darite-Terran,” Way said, thumbing his chest. “I’m a Darter. David Sanhueza. People cal me Way.” “I had gured that’s ’cause you help Fisher nd the way into places.” Way shrugged. “I do that too. How long you been fol owing us? What do you want?” “Long enough—and I want to be your new crew leader.” e others shared a look, a few of them glancing at Fisher, who was starting to stir. Siege hefted the bag of coins, considering. “Why would we fol ow you?” He studied the maces, falchion, and other weapons strapped to Fyn’s body. “You cut a mean gure with al those blades, but you’re half Fisher’s age.” “I’m twenty,” Fyn lied. “And if he’s over forty, it’s time he started looking for softer work.” “Kil him,” Fisher coughed, rising to his knees and elbows. “Stop chatting the bastard up and kil him!” “ ey could try,” Fyn said, not bothering to look at the fal en crew chief. “Or I could tel them where you’re hiding that extra coin you claim is for the Slavers Guild.” Poli frowned, her grip tightening on the ga . “ at true, Fisher?” “He’s lying!” Fisher rose to his feet, slid a butcher knife from his coat and waved it at the rest of the group. “You know Neldon checks the books. He’d tel you if I wasn’t square.” “Would he?” Way asked, taking a step toward Fisher. “Neldon’s from your old crew. Maybe he’s in on the take. It’d be nice to ask him, only he seems to be sleeping on the job.” He nodded at the unconscious lookout then glanced at Fyn. “You kil him?” “I don’t kil people for doing their jobs—not even if they’re bad at it.” “What’s that supposed to mean?” Fisher said sharply, taking a step in Fyn’s direction. “People talk, Fisher.” Fyn had no idea what he was talking about—he’d only been in Luqura for a few days, and that wasn’t enough time to gather much more than gossip. He had a hunch, though, and he was fol owing it. “Wait for Neldon to wake up,” Fyn said, planting his feet. “He’l tel you what real y happened to the old gang. After that, I bet you won’t want to fol ow him.” Fisher charged, butcher-knife- rst. Fyn stepped wide of the blade, catching the crew leader’s wrist. He pul ed Fisher forward, carrying his momentum in an arc as he dipped his knee and guided the man’s knife up under his ribs and into his own chest cavity. e bald man coughed, eyes wide, as hot blood started to pump from his chest, his raggedy shirt soaked in sticky redness. Fyn let go and Fisher dropped to his knees, blood spurting from between his lips. He col apsed and the rest of the gang stared open-mouthed at their dead chief. “ e way I see it,” Fyn said, stepping smoothly away from the convulsing body, “you have three choices. One: you can attack me now—and when I’ve nished kil ing al of you, I’l look for another crew to become my gang. Two: you fol ow me, and I’l earn you more money than the Fisher King ever could.” “And the third option?” Way said, stil clutching his dagger. “ ree: you walk away—for now. I’l nd another gang and start claiming territory. Eventual y, though, we’l be back to one and two. You can join me now and get the early reward … or I can bury you and build my empire on your ashes.” Siege and Poli exchanged a look and Fyn knew he had them. Way would fol ow the majority—he seemed to be the cautious type—and Neldon didn’t get a vote since he was unconscious. at left Quinn. Fyn watched her, and she was studying him in turn, chewing her lip, her almond eyes icking to the anged maces on Fyn’s back. “Even shares for everyone in the crew?” “No. I get three shares, and my second gets a share and a half. Everyone else gets one.” “Who’s your second?” “One of you, I suppose. I’l let the ve of you decide whom you trust the most.” “Neldon,” Siege said, and Poli nodded her agreement. “ e lookout?” Fyn was skeptical. “He’s our medic,” Way said, sheathing his knife. “Used to be a scholar, a doctor. Something like that. Fel on hard times and ended up in the Ashes with the rest of us.” “Does he ght?” “If he needs to, he can throw a decent punch. Got a terrifying manubal ista he uses for bigger jobs. Usual y he keeps the books, though. Patches us up when we get hurt. Talks to the guild if Fisher’s busy.” “Al right,” Fyn said, wiping his hands on his trousers. “Neldon it is. Of my three shares, one goes into a strongbox for funding bigger jobs.”

chunks.content: Myjun sco ed. “What magic?” “You summoned soul re blades to kil the draken. It burned out its eyes.” He pointed at her. “With the ful Ilumite talent, you can conjure re and blades of light, you can throw lightning. You can bend the light around yourself—turn invisible—or you can re ect it and create il usions. Some of those skil s wil be hard to master and some wil come natural y, but as my apprentice you wil master them al .” She stared at the assassin. “I can’t do any of that. Not a damn piece of it. Besides,” she added, not caring in the slightest, “your farmer is dead. You let him bleed out.” Oyru shook his head. “Half dead is not truly dead.” And with that, he stuck his hand through the farmer’s chest and gave Old Davey’s heart a squeeze. e man’s eyes shot open and he screamed as if woken from a nightmare—except this was the nightmare, and Oyru would not let him leave it so easily. e Shadow Reborn slid his hand free then pointed at the terri ed farmer, the blood from Davey’s severed ngers slowly pooling at his feet. “Kil him,” he said, “using your magic. Use your soul re blades, or re, or lightning. I don’t care how, only that you do it.” “ is is the third test?” “Yes.” Myjun sni ed. “Fine.” She stomped over to the dazed farmer whose eyes were already drifting closed, and slapped him across his weather-beaten face. His eyes popped open once more, and he spat at her. In an instant rage, her hands reached for his throat. “ !” Myjun stopped, frozen by the intensity of Oyru’s voice. e cold apathy that always marked the man’s speech had vanished, replaced by a piercing anger. And then, quick as a summer storm, it disappeared. e iciness returned, harder than before. Colder. “Do not touch him. Feed your anger and frustration into him, al your pain and re. Lash him with it. Burn him with it.” Myjun stared at the dying farmer, his face bloodless, his body slack and unmoving. She felt little anger for the man—disgust and hatred, yes, but her rage had subsided as the man’s life-force ebbed away. She did feel frustration, though—a tiny ower of hatred that burned with the re of being unable to kil the man, of not being al owed to strangle him. She was angry at Oyru, angry that he believed she could do this, angry that he could compel her to do it. And yet … she had done it before. She tried to remember how, to draw out the memory. Blood and claws. Teeth and scales. Beetles gnawing at her esh, the acid-blood spewing from the draken’s mouth. Burning and pain, the frustration and anger as its jaws clamped down on her, piercing her esh. Myjun dug deeper, immersing herself in the pain of the moment—that moment when she longed to die but continued to live. She screamed, the sound ripping from her throat. She screamed and screamed … Light sparked in her hands—tiny ames, white-hot and incandescent—and then they winked out. Myjun panted with exertion, her voice raw with emotion. “Beautiful,” Oyru whispered, standing in the dark once again. “Absolutely beautiful.” “Pointless,” Myjun snapped. “A useless spark.” “Not so.” Oyru gestured at Old Davey who had fal en silent once again, the blood stil dripping from his severed ngers, but slower … slower … “Try taking his pain and fear—and using them to fuel your magic.” “I don’t . . .” Myjun stared at the farmer, watched the aura around him begin to dim. Could she do it? She knew pain fueled her mask and made her stronger, faster—but could she steal that same pain, those same emotions, from other people? Could she turn their pain into her strengths? A spark lit inside her, its intensity fueled by the possibility, by the need to try … To burn. To break. Myjun reached out to the dying farmer, al owing her emotions to feed o his. It was easy—easier than she expected. She felt the man’s aura peel away from him and Davey’s eyes ew open, more horror in his face than she had ever seen during her interrogation. He screamed at her, terri ed. “What are you doing!” Rage. Pain. Frustration. Disgust. Hatred.
