She stil hadn’t revealed why she wanted Annev, and he was of a mind to discover her secrets. But if she was right—if Myjun real y was alive and would need his help—then he had no reason to leave. He could even stil send the Sons of Damnation on ahead to search Annev out. His connection to their amulets would keep him appraised of their actions, and he could remain here and keep an eye on Myjun through Kiara’s magic scrying. Until she was of no further use to him. “Very wel , Witmistress. I’l spare Annev … for now. In exchange, you wil tel me more about your order—these Brides of Fate. Tel me who they are—or were—and why they exist.” “Mm … and you wil not harm Annev? Neither directly nor indirectly?” “So long as Myjun remains alive and you can show her to me … yes.” “Bargain struck, then.” e gray woman o ered her palm. Kenton hesitated, then he shook it. As he did so, the air in the room seemed to shudder, the magic in his eyes ared, and for an instant it seemed as though he were holding the bony hand of a aming skeleton. PART THREE e origins of the Six are shrouded in myth and mystery. Such tales—involving monsters, traitors, and keokum being directed by the merciless vampyr Dortafola—are often greatly exaggerated, though on occasion the truth seems more fantastic than ction. One case that is frequently misrepresented is that of Valdemar Kranak, the rst Darite to abandon his cal ing as a priest and scholar so that he might instead support Dortafola and his Siänar’s malign designs. According to the surviving records, Kranak was born toward the end of the Age of Kings and was raised as one of the Dionachs Tobar. He made the ageless covenant with an unknown Terran priest at the turn of the century and leveraged his longevity at the University of Neven nan Su’ul to become a Magister of the First Order. It has been rumored that Kranak lobbied for the position of Arch Lector and was denied the coveted role, possibly due to his sympathies with Terran scholarship. If true, this might have been the impetus for Kranak’s later betrayal of both the university and the city … but we shal leave such unfounded speculation to lesser scholars. What has been con rmed beyond doubt is Valdemar Kranak’s role in the destruction of the university, and the razing of Neven nan Su’ul and the province of Gorm Corsa. Terran propagandists have attempted to paint Kranak as a benevolent intel ectual who was later demonized by the Halcyon Knights, but public record and the eyewitness testimonies show he was instrumental in bringing the Terran Bloodlords to the city, precipitating the retreat of the Darite Empire from Gorm Corsa and the rest of Eastern Daroea (now New Terra). e evidence suggests Kranak began by fomenting unrest among the student populace around the beginning of the ird Age.† Having gained support among the university’s more radical students, Kranak began hosting nightly lectures questioning the accuracy of certain Darite history books, which were already disputed by Terran scholars. e content of these lectures became more and more occult, with at least one claiming that Neven nan Su’ul had been founded by the Terrans rather than the Darites. As the Terrans pressed further and further west, expanding beyond Terra Majora and into Eastern Daroea, Kranak’s lectures led to heated disagreements with other magisters which (in a few cases) escalated to physical blows. It is unclear when Valdemar Kranak’s lectures descended from genuine scholarship into Terran propaganda, but the surviving records of censure state the magister was brought before Arch Lector Gale-Dana’y and ordered to stop questioning the Empire’s doctrine. As ordered, Kranak disbanded his evening classes, only to be suspended when he was discovered meeting privately with students to further his pro-Terran agenda. On his return to the university fol owing his suspension, reports indicate Kranak was a changed man: his lectures had been sanitized of al their former in ammatory content and he publicly disavowed the arguments he had made in support of the Terran government. e change would be utterly remarkable, were it not for our own knowledge of Kranak’s later betrayal. Many scholars, including my col eague Alice Quenby, have argued that Valdemar Kranak was approached by Dortafola during his suspension, and invited to join what later became the Siänar. is is a persuasive argument, particularly as the dates of Kranak’s suspension align with what little we know of the Siänar’s rst creation. —“ e Siänar,” e Complete Histories of Luquatra by Kyartus Gairm † Kash Mikla, a survivor from the razing of Neven nan Su’ul, claims to have seen Kranak leading a cavalry of Bloodlords against the university’s own students (a testimony that has since been widely debunked as no mounts were used during either the city’s siege or the nal rout of its citizens); on the other hand, the folk poem “Vaul of the Fal ” describes Kranak as a scholar whose “love of the masses brought death to his classes when nechraict rose up from their graves,” suggesting that necromancy played an integral part in the city’s nal destruction. Final y, Crystal Gooden—one of my esteemed col eagues from Southmarch—has suggested Kranak used Terran shadow magic to in ltrate and attack the university, giving rise to his later moniker “ e Shadow.” It seems more likely, though, that Kranak’s nickname arose from his ability to silently pass through the university’s hal s (a common e ect produced by most Breathbreakers). CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO Fyn plucked the apple from the vendor’s cart without breaking stride and continued his strol along the River District’s promenade, a wide road that hid the underground canal connecting Luqura’s two rivers. Commerce was brisk here, and the guards were plentiful, but the opportunities for l ing his pockets vastly outnumbered his chances of getting caught. By contrast, the merchant and noble districts had too many eyes watching their vendor stal s and too many swords guarding the nobles’ purses. He’d noticed the mansions were less wel -guarded, though—and contained greater riches besides—so Fyn entertained himself with the idea he might rob the homes of Luqura’s upper class at night, while picking pockets and lifting goods from its lower class during the day. People in the Ash Quarter tended to carry their most valuable possessions on themselves, anyway—their burned hovels being too insecure to leave valuables unprotected and unmolested. Al Fyn needed was a base of operations, and a gang to speed his acquisition of wealth and power. Territory was easiest to take in the Ash Quarter—it was free, if he could keep and defend it—so he’d spent most of his rst two days scouting the Lower District for a good headquarters. He had found a promising corner that was wel away from the Boneyard and just a few blocks south of the unburned portions of the Lower District, and he was trying to settle on a tenement when he sensed someone—several someones from the sound of it—approaching from behind. Instead of turning or eeing, Fyn took his time eating his apple and continued his strol down the trash-littered street. At the rst blind al ey, he turned and ducked inside, knowing his pursuers would be close behind. As he melted into the shadows, he checked his weapons and waited for the expected ambush. He didn’t have to wait long. Six thugs appeared at the mouth of the al ey, their leader at the front, sni ng for blood. “Is it that same one you saw yesterday?” the largest one asked. He carried a heavy, rounded stick that resembled a battered rol ing pin, and his face looked almost cherubic in spite of his imposing gure. “Shh,” the leader hissed, his eyes darting around the al ey, searching for Fyn. “Don’t spook him, Siege.” “What’s to spook?” a third one said, a buxom woman as large as the man with the rol ing pin—probably bigger—carrying what looked to be a sherman’s ga . Of the three that hadn’t spoken, one hung back, presumably to guard the mouth of the al ey, and the other two shot forward, exploring the shadows and hoping to ank their prey. Fortunately for Fyn, he’d chosen this exact al ey yesterday with the purpose of anking them. He smiled from his hidden vantage point, circling behind the group and approaching the man they’d left as their lookout. Halfway into the darkened al ey, Siege gave a whoop as a snare tangled his foot and pul ed his legs out from under him. On cue, Fyn yanked a hidden rope and a sack ful of bricks dropped onto the woman with the ga , knocking her weapon from her hands and quite possibly knocking her out entirely. “It’s a trap!” the leader bel owed, doubling back to the al ey mouth. “Quinn! Way! Grab Siege and Poli and get the hel out of—” Fyn swatted the back of the man’s skul with an improvised slapjack and sent him sprawling atop the body of his unconscious lookout. “So you’re the infamous Fisher King,” Fyn said, leaning over the fal en gure, “the Serpent of South Ashes … the Terror of Tumbledown Street.” He gave a dry laugh then kicked the man between the legs—hard. “Oof!” Fisher doubled over on himself. Fyn glanced back down the al ey, his cold eyes meeting Quinn’s as she helped the larger woman, Poli, clamber out from beneath the bricks. Siege had nearly freed himself from his snare and was searching for his cudgel, which seemed to have rol ed away when he’d fal en. Meanwhile, the sneaky one— Way—had slipped a knife from his pocket and was slowly advancing in Fyn’s direction. “Should have thrown that at my back while I was kicking Fisher. Since you didn’t, either you don’t know how to throw, you have no intention of actual y kil ing me … or you’re scared shitless.” “I ain’t scared of a little chickenshit like you,” Way swore, stil advancing. “What are you? Twelve? Probably don’t even have hair on your fruits.” “Given the choice between my fruits and his …” Fyn kicked the Fisher King in the head, knocking him out cold. “I think I’l stick with mine—hairy or not.” “You got a mouth on you, don’tcha?” “Very observant—now let’s move this along.” Fyn nodded at Way’s weapon. “You gonna throw that or am I gonna take it from you?” e lithe man snickered, though he checked to make sure Siege and the others were backing him up. “I think I’l wait til you start running, then I’l throw it at you.” “You’d miss—and I’m not running.” “We outnumber you, boy. Poli’s got reach with her ga there, and you don’t want to mess with Sigs. Jol y sort, but he’s a kil er an’ no mistake. Arms like a bul . Crush your skul like an egg.” Fyn noticed the man didn’t mention their other associate, Quinn, who was scaling the rightmost building in an attempt to get behind him. Amateurs. “Bul s don’t have arms, asshole—and I’m getting bored.” He hurled his apple core at the man’s face, distracting him just as Quinn leapt from the shadows. He had expected a knife thrust, a hammer-blow or a hatchet-swing— he’d seen the crew use al three in the day and the night he’d been stalking them—but Quinn surprised him with heavy gloves ending in curved iron nails shaped to look like bear claws. Tekko-Kagi, Fyn realized, dodging the attack. Very interesting. Quinn swung again and Fyn stepped aside, placing the young woman between him and Way. When she swung a third time, he stepped into the attack, grabbed Quinn’s wrist and thrust his hips. e smal woman’s feet came o the ground and Fyn spun, slashing her other clawed hand at Way. e sneak cursed, stepped back and tried another angle. is time, Fyn tossed Quinn over his shoulder and into Way, sending both attackers sprawling. “You lot work for me now,” Fyn said, not even winded. “Your contract with the Fisher King has ended.” “Rot that,” Poli said, her ga hook extended. “I’m going to gut you like a sh, boy. No one drops bricks on me and walks away.” Instead of answering, Fyn reached down and plucked a smal purse from Fisher’s tunic. He jingled it in one hand then tossed it to Siege. “What’s your cut of the loot?” “Rule of quarters,” Siege answered, eyeing the sack in his hand with equal parts greed and suspicion. His rol ing pin disappeared into his tunic. “One-quarter for us. ree-quarters for Fisher. He says it’s for the guild—to pay them for the right to work the street.” “ at’s a new one,” Fyn said, snorting. “So who’s in on it? e city watch? e ieves Guild?” “Only one guild matters,” Poli said, lowering her ga . “ e Slavers Guild.” “You’re not from around here, are you?” Quinn said. “Like you can talk. Where’d you get those?” He gestured at the Tekko-Kagi. “You make them? Steal them?” e woman hissed at him in response, her black hair fal ing to cover half her face. “He’s de nitely not from around here,” Way said, slapping Quinn on the shoulder. “Ain’t you never seen the Pits?” he said, studying Fyn. “ ey put ’em on ghters al the time. Makes ’em look erce.” “Only they don’t know how to use them,” Quinn whispered. “And you do?” e woman nodded, her clawed hands crossed in front of her chest. Fyn studied the group, watching their body language for another attack. “You’re Quynh-Chi, though they keep cal ing you Quinn. My guess is you’re Kroseran, with the Tekko-Kagi. You brought here as a slave?” e woman didn’t respond, though she did lower her hands to her sides. “Ford Siegeman,” Fyn continued. “Siege—or Sigs. What’d you do before Fisher brought you into his gang? Work in a bakery or something?” Siege grinned. “Me and Poli worked the docks—I do like to bake, though. You ever eaten pizza pie?” Siege’s smile grew. “It’s Darter food—delicious.” “Maybe you can bake me one sometime.” “Heh. You nd me an oven and the right ingredients, I’l bake a score of ’em.” “What’s Darter food?” “Darite-Terran,” Way said, thumbing his chest. “I’m a Darter. David Sanhueza. People cal me Way.” “I had gured that’s ’cause you help Fisher nd the way into places.” Way shrugged. “I do that too. How long you been fol owing us? What do you want?” “Long enough—and I want to be your new crew leader.” e others shared a look, a few of them glancing at Fisher, who was starting to stir. Siege hefted the bag of coins, considering. “Why would we fol ow you?” He studied the maces, falchion, and other weapons strapped to Fyn’s body. “You cut a mean gure with al those blades, but you’re half Fisher’s age.” “I’m twenty,” Fyn lied. “And if he’s over forty, it’s time he started looking for softer work.” “Kil him,” Fisher coughed, rising to his knees and elbows. “Stop chatting the bastard up and kil him!” “ ey could try,” Fyn said, not bothering to look at the fal en crew chief. “Or I could tel them where you’re hiding that extra coin you claim is for the Slavers Guild.” Poli frowned, her grip tightening on the ga . “ at true, Fisher?” “He’s lying!” Fisher rose to his feet, slid a butcher knife from his coat and waved it at the rest of the group. “You know Neldon checks the books. He’d tel you if I wasn’t square.” “Would he?” Way asked, taking a step toward Fisher. “Neldon’s from your old crew. Maybe he’s in on the take. It’d be nice to ask him, only he seems to be sleeping on the job.” He nodded at the unconscious lookout then glanced at Fyn. “You kil him?” “I don’t kil people for doing their jobs—not even if they’re bad at it.” “What’s that supposed to mean?” Fisher said sharply, taking a step in Fyn’s direction. “People talk, Fisher.” Fyn had no idea what he was talking about—he’d only been in Luqura for a few days, and that wasn’t enough time to gather much more than gossip. He had a hunch, though, and he was fol owing it. “Wait for Neldon to wake up,” Fyn said, planting his feet. “He’l tel you what real y happened to the old gang. After that, I bet you won’t want to fol ow him.” Fisher charged, butcher-knife- rst. Fyn stepped wide of the blade, catching the crew leader’s wrist. He pul ed Fisher forward, carrying his momentum in an arc as he dipped his knee and guided the man’s knife up under his ribs and into his own chest cavity. e bald man coughed, eyes wide, as hot blood started to pump from his chest, his raggedy shirt soaked in sticky redness. Fyn let go and Fisher dropped to his knees, blood spurting from between his lips. He col apsed and the rest of the gang stared open-mouthed at their dead chief. “ e way I see it,” Fyn said, stepping smoothly away from the convulsing body, “you have three choices. One: you can attack me now—and when I’ve nished kil ing al of you, I’l look for another crew to become my gang. Two: you fol ow me, and I’l earn you more money than the Fisher King ever could.” “And the third option?” Way said, stil clutching his dagger. “ ree: you walk away—for now. I’l nd another gang and start claiming territory. Eventual y, though, we’l be back to one and two. You can join me now and get the early reward … or I can bury you and build my empire on your ashes.” Siege and Poli exchanged a look and Fyn knew he had them. Way would fol ow the majority—he seemed to be the cautious type—and Neldon didn’t get a vote since he was unconscious. at left Quinn. Fyn watched her, and she was studying him in turn, chewing her lip, her almond eyes icking to the anged maces on Fyn’s back. “Even shares for everyone in the crew?” “No. I get three shares, and my second gets a share and a half. Everyone else gets one.” “Who’s your second?” “One of you, I suppose. I’l let the ve of you decide whom you trust the most.” “Neldon,” Siege said, and Poli nodded her agreement. “ e lookout?” Fyn was skeptical. “He’s our medic,” Way said, sheathing his knife. “Used to be a scholar, a doctor. Something like that. Fel on hard times and ended up in the Ashes with the rest of us.” “Does he ght?” “If he needs to, he can throw a decent punch. Got a terrifying manubal ista he uses for bigger jobs. Usual y he keeps the books, though. Patches us up when we get hurt. Talks to the guild if Fisher’s busy.” “Al right,” Fyn said, wiping his hands on his trousers. “Neldon it is. Of my three shares, one goes into a strongbox for funding bigger jobs.”

chunks.content: Myjun sco ed. “What magic?” “You summoned soul re blades to kil the draken. It burned out its eyes.” He pointed at her. “With the ful Ilumite talent, you can conjure re and blades of light, you can throw lightning. You can bend the light around yourself—turn invisible—or you can re ect it and create il usions. Some of those skil s wil be hard to master and some wil come natural y, but as my apprentice you wil master them al .” She stared at the assassin. “I can’t do any of that. Not a damn piece of it. Besides,” she added, not caring in the slightest, “your farmer is dead. You let him bleed out.” Oyru shook his head. “Half dead is not truly dead.” And with that, he stuck his hand through the farmer’s chest and gave Old Davey’s heart a squeeze. e man’s eyes shot open and he screamed as if woken from a nightmare—except this was the nightmare, and Oyru would not let him leave it so easily. e Shadow Reborn slid his hand free then pointed at the terri ed farmer, the blood from Davey’s severed ngers slowly pooling at his feet. “Kil him,” he said, “using your magic. Use your soul re blades, or re, or lightning. I don’t care how, only that you do it.” “ is is the third test?” “Yes.” Myjun sni ed. “Fine.” She stomped over to the dazed farmer whose eyes were already drifting closed, and slapped him across his weather-beaten face. His eyes popped open once more, and he spat at her. In an instant rage, her hands reached for his throat. “ !” Myjun stopped, frozen by the intensity of Oyru’s voice. e cold apathy that always marked the man’s speech had vanished, replaced by a piercing anger. And then, quick as a summer storm, it disappeared. e iciness returned, harder than before. Colder. “Do not touch him. Feed your anger and frustration into him, al your pain and re. Lash him with it. Burn him with it.” Myjun stared at the dying farmer, his face bloodless, his body slack and unmoving. She felt little anger for the man—disgust and hatred, yes, but her rage had subsided as the man’s life-force ebbed away. She did feel frustration, though—a tiny ower of hatred that burned with the re of being unable to kil the man, of not being al owed to strangle him. She was angry at Oyru, angry that he believed she could do this, angry that he could compel her to do it. And yet … she had done it before. She tried to remember how, to draw out the memory. Blood and claws. Teeth and scales. Beetles gnawing at her esh, the acid-blood spewing from the draken’s mouth. Burning and pain, the frustration and anger as its jaws clamped down on her, piercing her esh. Myjun dug deeper, immersing herself in the pain of the moment—that moment when she longed to die but continued to live. She screamed, the sound ripping from her throat. She screamed and screamed … Light sparked in her hands—tiny ames, white-hot and incandescent—and then they winked out. Myjun panted with exertion, her voice raw with emotion. “Beautiful,” Oyru whispered, standing in the dark once again. “Absolutely beautiful.” “Pointless,” Myjun snapped. “A useless spark.” “Not so.” Oyru gestured at Old Davey who had fal en silent once again, the blood stil dripping from his severed ngers, but slower … slower … “Try taking his pain and fear—and using them to fuel your magic.” “I don’t . . .” Myjun stared at the farmer, watched the aura around him begin to dim. Could she do it? She knew pain fueled her mask and made her stronger, faster—but could she steal that same pain, those same emotions, from other people? Could she turn their pain into her strengths? A spark lit inside her, its intensity fueled by the possibility, by the need to try … To burn. To break. Myjun reached out to the dying farmer, al owing her emotions to feed o his. It was easy—easier than she expected. She felt the man’s aura peel away from him and Davey’s eyes ew open, more horror in his face than she had ever seen during her interrogation. He screamed at her, terri ed. “What are you doing!” Rage. Pain. Frustration. Disgust. Hatred. Al of his emotions were hers, channeled through her, strengthening her—and as her power grew, his fear grew too. Terror. Pain. Fear. Agony. Despair. An endless feedback loop that fed the spark inside her until it blossomed into a ame. at ame found its home in her arms, condensing, sharpening as twin points of light sprang from her palms—sharp white blades of pure spirit, an aura of emotion and re, light and energy. e blades grew into daggers … into swords. She realized she was screaming, was venting her pain with her ragged and intense voice, as sharp and piercing as any blade. Old Davey screamed too, his pale face l ed with a terror as pure as her hatred. en she struck, her soul re blades scissoring together to snip the farmer’s head from his shoulders. His skin burned as they slid into his esh, his eyes bursting into ame, an otherworldly light pouring from his mouth. e pain that l ed Myjun’s body, the hunger that penetrated her soul, suddenly evaporated in place of a sense of ful ness. e sensation startled her, awakening her senses to a world that had grown dul beneath the endless aches and pains. She was not hungry. She was not thirsty. She was … alive with the rush of life and a feeling of ful l ment, the thril of having taken a life and being given one. Beneath it al , she stil felt the in uence of the mask—the sharp need for pain and the malice that accompanied it—but these were distant now, their sharpness abated by the euphoria of the moment. And suddenly they were gone—the rush, the joy, the thril —al vanished. Her hunger and thirst were stil diminished, but alongside a void, a wide chasm of need … and a new kind of hunger that would not be satis ed by food or water. “You would be a Soulblade, I think—a Soulrider and a Bladesinger—but the aqlumera and the Inquisitor ring have tainted your magic. Forged it into something new. Something wonderful. You aren’t spel singing. You are … soul-shrieking.” A queer smile touched the corner of Oyru’s mouth then—an emotion so foreign, so out of place, that it sickened Myjun to see it. “A Soulscreamer. Light-bending and soulriding may be chal enging for you —certainly more di cult than for a ful -blooded Ilumite—but that jagged edge … that raw power.” His expression morphed into a sadistic grin. “Oh, yes. You are my sharp little knife. My bloody Oraqui.” Behind them, the husk of the dead man slumped forward, his skin and bones as dry and brittle as burned charcoal. When his soul ess body hit the ground, there was a faint crackle of light, a soft sigh, and then silence. “Come,” Oyru continued, not missing a beat. “ e people of Hentingsfort await us.” “What’s in Hentingsfort?” Myjun might have been angered to ask before, but her feelings stil oated beneath the memory of her soulfeasting. She hungered for more—more blood, more death, more soul-sucking. She craved it, needed it like a lusty lover or starving mendicant. “Another test,” Oyru said, beckoning toward the door. “ e last before I take you beyond Reocht na Skah and the heart of the shadow realm.” “You wil take me … into the shadows?” e assassin led her outside, into the sunlight and then the deep shade of the Brakewood. “Yes, but Hentingsfort rst. You’ve only just discovered your power, and the shadows are far more dangerous than an old farmer tied to a chair. Hentingsfort is a village, with its own town council and militia. A few hundred people.” “And what wil we do when we get there?” “What else? We wil ght and kil . We wil sup on the souls of the weak. Drink the darkness and the light.” Myjun shivered in anticipation, eager for the taste of blood and the thril of the hunt. She would dine on death—she would slake her unquenchable thirst and satisfy her insatiable hunger. She shuddered at the thought of it and fol owed the assassin into the woods. CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO Tosan’s spirit fought Kenton, as precise and relentless as a mason chipping at a block of stone. At the same time, Kenton felt fragments of himself being washed away, drawn inexorably downward into the aqlumera. He felt disoriented, as though he were spinning into an abyss. Kenton reached out, grasping for any anchor, and seized on his love for Myjun and his hatred for Annev. An instant later, Tosan loomed over him, and it was as though they wrestled at the edge of some spiritual void. “My daughter is dead!” the former headmaster shouted, his attacks pushing Kenton toward oblivion. “If you had kept Annev in his cel ,”— push—“she would stil be alive!” Push. Shove. Kenton’s spirit stood at the brink of the aqlumera. His grasp on himself slipped and he felt his feelings for and memories of Myjun grow faint . . . distant. Tosan shoved again, threatening to tumble him into the yawning abyss. “I had wondered whether you had helped him—whether you had freed that monster from his cel —but then I saw you were just inept. Unable to save yourself, unable to save my daughter.” Push. Shove. “Her death is as much your fault as his!” Tosan struck, his blows hard enough to shake Kenton to his core . . . yet Kenton’s grip on his twin loves and hatreds remained, and he clung ferociously to his life and control of his body … and, by so doing, he learned how to ght back. Entangled with the man’s psyche, Kenton sensed Tosan’s own doubts and fears—his weaknesses, the things he loved and most wanted to protect. e former headmaster truly cared about very little, but two things stood out: his dead daughter and the ruined Academy. “You couldn’t protect the Academy! You blame Annev and me for its destruction, but you were the one who struck the rst blow. It was your magic —your hel re wand—that sparked the tinder. Everybody in Chaenbalu died because of you!” “No!” Tosan roared, his grip slipping. “It was that boy—that one-armed keokum took everything I loved—everything you loved!” Kenton wavered, struggling to regain control. Annev had destroyed Kenton’s life … but it was Tosan’s fault too. Kenton had been trapped in the prison cel , unable to ght. Tosan had been above ground, ghting the monsters. He’d been trying to protect his daughter—and he’d succeeded … right up until he’d attacked Annev. And then Kenton saw the headmaster’s weakness . . . his most terrible secret. e truth of it hit Kenton like a bolt of thunder. “You let him kil her.” Tosan stumbled, shaken to his core, and they stood on equal ground once again. “No, I tried to save her! You weren’t even there!” e headmaster clawed at Kenton’s psyche, trying to regain control. “I died trying to protect her.” “I can see into your memories, Tosan. You thought Annev wouldn’t hurt you so long as Myjun stayed by your side. You used her as a shield, to protect yourself, and she died ! ” Tosan faltered, his doubts creeping in, pul ing his certainties apart, and when he stumbled again Kenton shoved—hard. e vengeful spirit reeled back, his psyche tipping backward into the void of aqlumera. “No! ” But it was too late. Kenton ung the old man away, forcing him out of his body, and Tosan’s spirit tumbled back into the magical abyss, his essence swal owed by the liquid magic. Kenton took a shuddering a breath, in possession of himself once again. He was alive, but pieces of his psyche had been splintered, their pieces swept away by the battle with Tosan. Kenton had clung tightly to major things—aspects of himself that he most identi ed with, the things that anchored him—but smal er details had been torn away, pul ed down into the consuming void of aqlumera. He tried to recal the names of his favorite poisons, his preferred weapons, or his companions at the Academy … but they were hazy. He was surprised to remember that he favored ghting with the tachi—a piece of himself that had nearly been lost—but he could not recal if he had a favorite color or food. As Kenton quietly gathered himself, he found other splinters that were decidedly not his memories. His thoughts of Annev and Myjun remained, but they were tainted by a feeling that was almost patriarchal. His thoughts and impressions of the Academy were similarly possessive, and rooms he had never entered now felt familiar. Such tales—involving monsters, traitors, and keokum being directed by the merciless vampyr Dortafola—are often greatly exaggerated, though on occasion the truth seems more fantastic than ction. One case that is frequently misrepresented is that of Valdemar Kranak, the rst Darite to abandon his cal ing as a priest and scholar so that he might instead support Dortafola and his Siänar’s malign designs. According to the surviving records, Kranak was born toward the end of the Age of Kings and was raised as one of the Dionachs Tobar. He made the ageless covenant with an unknown Terran priest at the turn of the century and leveraged his longevity at the University of Neven nan Su’ul to become a Magister of the First Order. It has been rumored that Kranak lobbied for the position of Arch Lector and was denied the coveted role, possibly due to his sympathies with Terran scholarship. If true, this might have been the impetus for Kranak’s later betrayal of both the university and the city … but we shal leave such unfounded speculation to lesser scholars. What has been con rmed beyond doubt is Valdemar Kranak’s role in the destruction of the university, and the razing of Neven nan Su’ul and the province of Gorm Corsa. Terran propagandists have attempted to paint Kranak as a benevolent intel ectual who was later demonized by the Halcyon Knights, but public record and the eyewitness testimonies show he was instrumental in bringing the Terran Bloodlords to the city, precipitating the retreat of the Darite Empire from Gorm Corsa and the rest of Eastern Daroea (now New Terra). e evidence suggests Kranak began by fomenting unrest among the student populace around the beginning of the ird Age.† Having gained support among the university’s more radical students, Kranak began hosting nightly lectures questioning the accuracy of certain Darite history books, which were already disputed by Terran scholars. e content of these lectures became more and more occult, with at least one claiming that Neven nan Su’ul had been founded by the Terrans rather than the Darites. As the Terrans pressed further and further west, expanding beyond Terra Majora and into Eastern Daroea, Kranak’s lectures led to heated disagreements with other magisters which (in a few cases) escalated to physical blows. It is unclear when Valdemar Kranak’s lectures descended from genuine scholarship into Terran propaganda, but the surviving records of censure state the magister was brought before Arch Lector Gale-Dana’y and ordered to stop questioning the Empire’s doctrine. Since you didn’t, either you don’t know how to throw, you have no intention of actual y kil ing me … or you’re scared shitless.” “I ain’t scared of a little chickenshit like you,” Way swore, stil advancing. “What are you? Twelve? Probably don’t even have hair on your fruits.” “Given the choice between my fruits and his …” Fyn kicked the Fisher King in the head, knocking him out cold. “I think I’l stick with mine—hairy or not.” “You got a mouth on you, don’tcha?” “Very observant—now let’s move this along.” Fyn nodded at Way’s weapon. “You gonna throw that or am I gonna take it from you?” e lithe man snickered, though he checked to make sure Siege and the others were backing him up. “I think I’l wait til you start running, then I’l throw it at you.” “You’d miss—and I’m not running.” “We outnumber you, boy. Poli’s got reach with her ga there, and you don’t want to mess with Sigs. Jol y sort, but he’s a kil er an’ no mistake. Arms like a bul . Crush your skul like an egg.” Fyn noticed the man didn’t mention their other associate, Quinn, who was scaling the rightmost building in an attempt to get behind him. Amateurs. “Bul s don’t have arms, asshole—and I’m getting bored.” He hurled his apple core at the man’s face, distracting him just as Quinn leapt from the shadows. He had expected a knife thrust, a hammer-blow or a hatchet-swing— he’d seen the crew use al three in the day and the night he’d been stalking them—but Quinn surprised him with heavy gloves ending in curved iron nails shaped to look like bear claws. Tekko-Kagi, Fyn realized, dodging the attack. Very interesting. Quinn swung again and Fyn stepped aside, placing the young woman between him and Way. When she swung a third time, he stepped into the attack, grabbed Quinn’s wrist and thrust his hips. e smal woman’s feet came o the ground and Fyn spun, slashing her other clawed hand at Way. e sneak cursed, stepped back and tried another angle. is time, Fyn tossed Quinn over his shoulder and into Way, sending both attackers sprawling. “You lot work for me now,” Fyn said, not even winded. “Your contract with the Fisher King has ended.” “Rot that,” Poli said, her ga hook extended. “I’m going to gut you like a sh, boy. No one drops bricks on me and walks away.” Instead of answering, Fyn reached down and plucked a smal purse from Fisher’s tunic. He jingled it in one hand then tossed it to Siege. “What’s your cut of the loot?” “Rule of quarters,” Siege answered, eyeing the sack in his hand with equal parts greed and suspicion. His rol ing pin disappeared into his tunic. “One-quarter for us. ree-quarters for Fisher. He says it’s for the guild—to pay them for the right to work the street.” “ at’s a new one,” Fyn said, snorting. “So who’s in on it? e city watch? e ieves Guild?” “Only one guild matters,” Poli said, lowering her ga . “ e Slavers Guild.” “You’re not from around here, are you?” Quinn said. “Like you can talk. Where’d you get those?” He gestured at the Tekko-Kagi. “You make them? Steal them?” e woman hissed at him in response, her black hair fal ing to cover half her face. “He’s de nitely not from around here,” Way said, slapping Quinn on the shoulder. “Ain’t you never seen the Pits?” he said, studying Fyn. “ ey put ’em on ghters al the time. Makes ’em look erce.” “Only they don’t know how to use them,” Quinn whispered. “And you do?” e woman nodded, her clawed hands crossed in front of her chest. Fyn studied the group, watching their body language for another attack. “You’re Quynh-Chi, though they keep cal ing you Quinn. My guess is you’re Kroseran, with the Tekko-Kagi. You brought here as a slave?” e woman didn’t respond, though she did lower her hands to her sides. “Ford Siegeman,” Fyn continued. “Siege—or Sigs. What’d you do before Fisher brought you into his gang? Work in a bakery or something?” Siege grinned. “Me and Poli worked the docks—I do like to bake, though. You ever eaten pizza pie?” Siege’s smile grew. “It’s Darter food—delicious.” “Maybe you can bake me one sometime.” “Heh. You nd me an oven and the right ingredients, I’l bake a score of ’em.” “What’s Darter food?” “Darite-Terran,” Way said, thumbing his chest. “I’m a Darter. David Sanhueza. People cal me Way.” “I had gured that’s ’cause you help Fisher nd the way into places.” Way shrugged. “I do that too. How long you been fol owing us? What do you want?” “Long enough—and I want to be your new crew leader.” e others shared a look, a few of them glancing at Fisher, who was starting to stir. Siege hefted the bag of coins, considering. “Why would we fol ow you?” He studied the maces, falchion, and other weapons strapped to Fyn’s body. “You cut a mean gure with al those blades, but you’re half Fisher’s age.” “I’m twenty,” Fyn lied. “And if he’s over forty, it’s time he started looking for softer work.” “Kil him,” Fisher coughed, rising to his knees and elbows. “Stop chatting the bastard up and kil him!” “ ey could try,” Fyn said, not bothering to look at the fal en crew chief. “Or I could tel them where you’re hiding that extra coin you claim is for the Slavers Guild.” Poli frowned, her grip tightening on the ga . “ at true, Fisher?” “He’s lying!” Fisher rose to his feet, slid a butcher knife from his coat and waved it at the rest of the group. “You know Neldon checks the books. He’d tel you if I wasn’t square.” “Would he?” Way asked, taking a step toward Fisher. “Neldon’s from your old crew. Maybe he’s in on the take. It’d be nice to ask him, only he seems to be sleeping on the job.” He nodded at the unconscious lookout then glanced at Fyn. “You kil him?” “I don’t kil people for doing their jobs—not even if they’re bad at it.” “What’s that supposed to mean?” Fisher said sharply, taking a step in Fyn’s direction. “People talk, Fisher.” Fyn had no idea what he was talking about—he’d only been in Luqura for a few days, and that wasn’t enough time to gather much more than gossip. He had a hunch, though, and he was fol owing it. “Wait for Neldon to wake up,” Fyn said, planting his feet. “He’l tel you what real y happened to the old gang. After that, I bet you won’t want to fol ow him.” Fisher charged, butcher-knife- rst. Fyn stepped wide of the blade, catching the crew leader’s wrist. He pul ed Fisher forward, carrying his momentum in an arc as he dipped his knee and guided the man’s knife up under his ribs and into his own chest cavity. e bald man coughed, eyes wide, as hot blood started to pump from his chest, his raggedy shirt soaked in sticky redness. Fyn let go and Fisher dropped to his knees, blood spurting from between his lips. He col apsed and the rest of the gang stared open-mouthed at their dead chief. “ e way I see it,” Fyn said, stepping smoothly away from the convulsing body, “you have three choices. One: you can attack me now—and when I’ve nished kil ing al of you, I’l look for another crew to become my gang. Two: you fol ow me, and I’l earn you more money than the Fisher King ever could.” “And the third option?” Way said, stil clutching his dagger. “ ree: you walk away—for now. I’l nd another gang and start claiming territory. Eventual y, though, we’l be back to one and two. You can join me now and get the early reward … or I can bury you and build my empire on your ashes.” Siege and Poli exchanged a look and Fyn knew he had them. Way would fol ow the majority—he seemed to be the cautious type—and Neldon didn’t get a vote since he was unconscious. at left Quinn. Fyn watched her, and she was studying him in turn, chewing her lip, her almond eyes icking to the anged maces on Fyn’s back. “Even shares for everyone in the crew?” “No. I get three shares, and my second gets a share and a half. Everyone else gets one.” “Who’s your second?” “One of you, I suppose. I’l let the ve of you decide whom you trust the most.” “Neldon,” Siege said, and Poli nodded her agreement. “ e lookout?” Fyn was skeptical. “He’s our medic,” Way said, sheathing his knife. “Used to be a scholar, a doctor. Something like that. Fel on hard times and ended up in the Ashes with the rest of us.” “Does he ght?” “If he needs to, he can throw a decent punch. Got a terrifying manubal ista he uses for bigger jobs. Usual y he keeps the books, though. Patches us up when we get hurt. Talks to the guild if Fisher’s busy.” “Al right,” Fyn said, wiping his hands on his trousers. “Neldon it is. Of my three shares, one goes into a strongbox for funding bigger jobs.”

chunks.title: Chapter 7
chunks.content: Quinn frowned. “What about the guild?” “What about them? ey can go hang themselves.” e ve gang members looked at one another and sheathed their weapons. Quinn sco ed, spat, and went to check on Neldon. Fyn eyed them, feeling he’d missed something. “You don’t get it,” Way said, stepping close enough that Fyn kept an eye on the man’s hands. “ e guild controls most of what happens in the Ash Quarter, the Undercity, the Boneyard—even the Low Quarter and the River District. Everything except the Merchant and Noble Quarters—and they’re close to control ing them too. If you ignore the guild, they’l send the Watchers after you.” He shook his head. “You can keep your shares and your delusions. No one crosses the guild.” e rest of the group shouldered past, and Fyn realized he was losing them. He had to think quick. “You know the lizardman who works for the guild—some keokum freak? Me and my last crew nearly kil ed him.” e gang froze. Neldon was starting to wake and Siege helped him to his feet. “You’re blowing smoke and ashes,” Quinn said, her voice husky. “No one crosses the guild—and no one ghts Saltair and lives.” “Ask around. We cut o his tail and his hand. Might be you can even nd the pieces somewhere. I hear he can grow them back—but we stil got him.” He sucked at his teeth. “ ink about it. If you want to join my crew, be back here in three days and I’l tel you what I have in mind.” e gang bled away into the street with Neldon tottering between Siege and Poli. Way hung back, taking in Fyn’s weapons, his clothing and his face. Final y, he inclined his head. “ ree days?” “Yeah.” “And you’ve got a plan.” “I do.” Way grunted. “You got a name?” “Fyunai. People cal me Fyn.” “Fyn,” he said, trying the name on his lips. “Fyn the Feared … Fatal Fyn.” A queer smile quirked his lips. “I’l ask around about Saltair. If what you say is true … wel , then count me in.” Fyn inclined his head and the man slunk away, rejoining his gang. Once they were al gone, Fyn gave a deep sigh, looked down at Fisher’s body … and threw up. It wasn’t the sight of the corpse, nor did he feel guilty about murdering the crew chief—the way Fyn saw it, he’d had it coming. No, what made Fyn spray his lunch across the al ey was having no idea what to do about the Slavers Guild or their stranglehold on Luqura’s underworld . . . and he had exactly three days to create a workable plan. It almost made him wish Annev were stil in the city. Almost. Fyn wiped the vomit from his lips and steadied himself against the wal . A utter of movement caught his eye and he looked up to see a lithe gure in a raven mask staring down at him—watching. From the Slavers Guild? Fyn wondered, remembering Way mentioning their Watchers. But if the Raven worked for the guild, she gave no indication of it. Instead, she tilted her head, saluted him with two ngers, and slid the mask from her face. “ e hel ?” Fyn swore. e black-clad woman danced away across the roof of the building and disappeared from sight. Fyn watched her go in disbelief. He couldn’t imagine why she would be fol owing him—or why she’d have any interest in him after eeing Janak’s palace with the Rod of Compulsion. Yet he suspected he’d see Sodja Rocas again in the not-too-distant future—a thought that was not altogether unpleasant. CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE e stars were bright overhead as Sodja walked among the cherry trees surrounding her family’s estate. She reached the edge of the orchard and drifted over to the pool of super red arowana, the gleam of gold and copper scales beneath the water reminding her of the ames that had consumed Janak’s study during her escape with the Rod of Compulsion. Sodja touched that rod now—cool, slender, and heavy in her pocket—and she thought of her encounter with the three thieves who had started the re. at had been six days ago—and only four days since the thieves from the Brakewood had come back to Luqura to look for her. Sodja knew very little about the thieves’ mysterious organization. eir members were supposedly worshippers of Odar, though Sodja couldn’t say how con scating magic artifacts bene tted the God of Skywater. Sodja’s older brothers, Ketrit and Rista, had even encountered a few cultists while going about family business in Luqura, but Rista had been the only one to capture and interrogate one of the thieves, and the man had not long survived Rista’s ministrations. By contrast, the three cultists Sodja had encountered had been little more than boys—although the muscular one with the dreadlocks seemed a little older. Maybe even her age. Sodja smiled, remembering his poor attempt to track her back to Luqura. He’d been adorably angry when she’d used her shadow magic to disappear in front of him—and the string of curse words had been so malevolently creative, Sodja had been tempted to reappear just to let the fel ow give chase a bit longer. It didn’t hurt that he was easy on the eyes. At the time, Sodja guessed she would never see the young man again—he would hoof it back to the Brakewood, and that would be the end of it, despite her taunting the boys with her name, even encouraging them to retaliate against her family. eir arrival on her family’s doorstep had been a welcome complication … . . . and their leaving her family home without a lick of protest was an unwelcome surprise. No trouble at al for the Rocas family, despite her e orts. It was so frustrating—al that e ort to turn new enemies and former al ies against her family … for nothing. Sodja had been wondering if it was even worth fol owing them out of the High Quarter when Saltair had emerged from the mansion in pursuit and made the decision for her. Sodja watched him track the group into the Ash Quarter and attack them, watched him chase the boy with the glowing golden hand—the same one she’d left to die in Janak’s study—and then she’d watched that boy defeat rst Saltair and then Slavemaster Kranak. at reversal had been wonderful—exactly what Sodja had hoped for—but it had also left her with a hundred unanswered questions. Were the boys stil working for their Brakewood cult? Had the boy with the golden hand lost his arm in Janak’s burning study, and where did he get that obscenely powerful prosthetic? From Janak’s col ection? Sodja would have sought answers, but the one-armed boy and his companions vanished from the Boneyard, leaving only bodies in their wake . . . and abandoning the handsome boy with the dreadlocks. His actions suggested he had no intention of rejoining his companions. If anything, he seemed to be hoping to settle into Luqura. Another puzzle. Sodja kicked a loose pebble into the dragon sh pond. Red-gold scales ashed in the water. She sighed. It was late and she needed to nish her errand before the servants woke and guards changed their shift. Sodja walked on, passing the last of the ve pools and coming to a long row of hedges dividing the ornamental ponds and orchards from the grounds beyond the Rocas family’s keep. It was stil dark—closer to twilight than dawn—yet as Sodja approached the back of the mansion her eyes easily pierced the gloom, catching glimpses of the paths that ran right up to her family’s doorstep. Shaped like a giant wedge of cheese with a bite taken out of it, the Rocas Estate was narrow at the front, penetrating deep into the heart of Luqura’s High Quarter. As one moved away from the mansion’s entrance, though, the grounds ared out and opened into the gated hedges and orchards that her family privately cultivated. Sodja studied the street, seeing no carriages had been parked overnight at the front of her family’s home. at was good. No midnight visitors or urgent demands from the slavers. Al would be quiet inside with little chance of surprise, though Sodja always anticipated complications as a matter of personal and professional pride. Sodja ignored the front door and instead traced the path she would have to climb to reach her mother’s private balcony at the corner of the mansion. A col ection of chiseled gray eldstone formed the base of the keep, making it an easy ascent, but Sodja paused after taking a single step toward the wal . At the opposite corner of the mansion, Sodja spied a tal ow candle burning in the bedroom window just above a tal iron trel is. Her heart burning, Sodja steered away from the balcony and toward the window. A rose bush climbed the iron trel is, though the shrub had not been tended in years and its thorns were dry, impotent things. As she climbed, the familiar rusty metal dul y squeaked beneath her weight and the desiccated plant crumbled beneath her touch. When Sodja reached the window, she slipped a hand inside her shirt, grasped her lockpicking tools, then stopped to listen. From inside, Sodja could hear a woman’s strong voice. “Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is made, is unmade.” Sodja knew the litany. On a hunch, she moved her hand from her shirt and pushed on the glass. A sad smile touched her lips as the window swung inward, and she crept into the chambers as quiet as a breeze. Inside the room, a single candle made the shadows icker and lit the uid motions of an old woman sitting in front of it. ough her eyes were crinkled with crow’s-feet and her chin was no longer as rm as it once was, Sodja could see glimpses of the woman’s youth and beauty: high cheekbones, a pert nose in a heart-shaped face and raven-black hair that, though streaked with gray, stil retained most of its color. Her eyes were closed, though if she had opened them, Sodja knew those, too, would be beautiful—keen gray eyes with a hint of an almond shape to them. Sodja took a step forward and bowed her head in respect. “Hel o, grandmother.” e woman at the candle tilted her head in Sodja’s direction, as if acknowledging her presence. She did not open her eyes, though, nor did she address her grandchild. Instead, the Rocas family’s oldest matriarch bowed her head and continued her chanting. “Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free.” As Bel a spoke, her careful ngers guided a bone needle and black thread through the strips of tattered black-and-gray cloth sitting atop her lap. Sodja watched in fascination, though she had seen this many times in the past four months. Day and night, the woman sewed together rags while chanting gibberish to herself. She had to be coaxed to eat or drink, and Sodja regularly found the servants couldn’t be bothered. Cups of tepid water and bowls of uneaten food sat uncol ected beside the woman’s bed, inviting ies and other vermin. If not for Sodja’s nightly visits, she thought the woman would have died some months ago. “If the senile old biddy wants to starve herself while stitching rags together,” Tiana had said, “who am I to stop her?” Rista had laughed at that—he laughed at anything cruel—while Ketrit was silent. at hadn’t surprised her either. Sodja’s eldest brother rarely said anything, and while his visits to their grandmother hadn’t been as frequent as Sodja’s, the man stil saw her on occasion. And now Sodja had to visit Bel a in secret. Ever since running away from the mansion—ever since nding the ledger and discovering her mother’s secret —Sodja had been unable to visit her grandmother openly. It had been two months, and Sodja remained surprised that no one thought to wonder how Bel a stil survived when the servants and Sodja’s family rarely tended to her—a fact evinced by the acrid smel of an over owing chamber pot. Yet each group seemed to think the other must be privately tending to the old lady, for no one questioned how the dishes disappeared every night or why the chamber pot was magical y empty every morning. She couldn’t manage every day, true, but Sodja tried to keep her vigil, and so far she had evaded discovery. e young woman sighed and fol owed her nose to the vessel brimming with night soil. It hurt Sodja to think how sharp her grandmother had been—so vibrant and strong, reining in Rista’s cruel tendencies, keeping Tiana in her place—but then grandfather Gadish had died and Bel a had never been the same. Vintan died a year later, and though her father’s death had deeply wounded Sodja, it had broken her grandmother entirely. Sewing rags and chanting was something new, though. No one knew where her grandmother had found the fabric, but it materialized one day in Bel a’s room and thereafter never seemed to leave her hands. Always stitching, sewing, weaving. Binding grays to blacks, and blacks to deeper blacks. It would have been distressing enough to witness—to watch a woman so regal and dominant turn into a blathering recluse overnight—but the most disturbing part was that she stitched with her eyes closed. Every day and night, every stitch of needle and thread was done by touch. As if to il ustrate this, Bel a’s thin ngers set the bone needle down on her lap and searched for a nearly invisible scrap of black thread lying on the table beside the candle. e strand was as thin as the lament of a spider web, yet the woman stil guided it through the eye of her bone needle and resumed her stitching—al with her eyes closed. Her chanting resumed: “Keeper of truth. Warden of lies. Turn away light. Darken the skies. Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is unmade, is made. Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free. Warden of truth. Keeper of lies. Strengthen this shadow. Sharpen its eyes. Absence. Periphery. Shadow and shade. Smoke and vapor. What is made, is unmade. Bone of my bone. Shadow of me. Blood of my blood. Shadow of thee. Absence. Periphery. Walk and be free.” Sodja stayed as the woman began the litany again from the start, then respectful y backed out of the room, chamber pot in hand. Using one arm, she stealthily climbed back down the trel is, emptied the night soil in the cherry orchard and returned the vessel to Bel a’s room. When she returned, the old woman was sitting quietly in the corner, her hands folded in her lap, her eyes stil closed. Sodja looked between her grandmother and the sewing project that had so obsessed her. She crossed the room and softly placed one hand atop Bel a’s open palms. Using her other hand, she picked up the nearest cup of water and held it to the woman’s parched lips. For a while the cup sat there, moistening the woman’s dry skin without a drop being drunk. A minute passed then two. Final y, Bel a’s lips parted and the lukewarm water trickled into her mouth. She swal owed, coughed. Swal owed some more. Sodja l ed her mouth twice more before the woman turned her head aside. Sodja slid a brown piece of apple between the woman’s lips, but the fruit hung there for a second and fel to the oor. “Not hungry today?” Sodja whispered, her heart aching, wondering how long the woman could survive like this. Bel a said nothing, did not even open her eyes. It was as though she had fal en asleep in her chair, though Sodja suspected she was stil awake. Listening. Waiting. Perhaps she enjoyed the company. Perhaps she knew it was Sodja who took care of her, who kept her alive when others had left her to die. If that was true, though, her grandmother gave no indication of it. She sat in silence, her knobby hands clutching Sodja’s for several minutes, and then the old woman squeezed Sodja’s hand, picked her sewing needle back up and resumed her chant. “Keeper of Truth. Warden of Lies. Turn away light. Darken the skies.” Sodja carried the dishes down to the servants’ quarters, then crept back upstairs and stealthily moved toward her original objective: the bedchamber of Matron Tiana. Outside the temple vault, it was the safest and most secure location in the mansion, and while it was possible Tiana kept her nancial ledgers in the vault itself, Sodja knew her mother wel enough to guess she would keep the record book on her person at al times. It was the only way she could promise the Slavers Guild their records were kept safe, and thus the only way Tiana could keep using the Rocas family’s temple as the banking house for the foreign slavers of Innistiul. It was also the only evidence Sodja had to prove Tiana had kil ed her husband and Sodja’s father, Vintan Rocas. An accidental peek at the woman’s nancial ledgers some months ago was the rst thing that had tipped Sodja o . She hadn’t understood what she was seeing at rst, but as she’d ipped through the pages and read her mother’s notes, the reality of the situation had become clear: Tiana Rocas and the Slavers Guild had come to a mutual agreement to permanently remove Vintan and the ieves Guild from Luquran politics. Vintan had already stepped down as the guild’s master thief—relinquishing that position to his rst lieutenant, Tymmit Blank—but that didn’t matter to Matron Rocas or the Slavers; Tiana had made certain that Vintan’s death was included in the arrangement, Blank and his other lieutenants were murdered, and the ieves Guild was driven out of the city—and Sodja’s mother had been paid for arranging al of it. It was al there in the ledgers—a record of their communications, an accounting of payments made and debts owed, receipts, and depository notes. Tiana had kept track of al of it, her merchant instincts strong as ever, and she’d been handsomely rewarded for her work. e vault inside the Temple of Dorchnok was ful to bursting, and the Slavers Guild had virtual y taken control of the city. With King Lenka’s health in decline and no heir apparent, it seemed likely Tiana was positioning herself to make a bid for the throne of Greater Luqura. But not if Sodja got hold of that ledger—the ledger she had stupidly left behind when her mother caught her reading the damnable thing. Tiana had been quick to reclaim the book, and Sodja had been just as quick to ee the mansion. ey had both made a mistake in letting the other go. Now Tiana sought to silence Sodja, and Sodja sought to reclaim the ledger so she could publish the truth of the Rocas family’s dealings—legal and il egal—with Innistiul. Doing so would cast a shadow on her family’s ambitions for the crown and, with luck, it might even turn the tide against the foreign powers hoping to control the Luquran throne. Sodja approached her mother’s bedchamber, her heart thudding in her chest. As she reached for the lock, though, she felt a chil pass over her and turned to see Ketrit standing behind her in the hal way. “Hel o, sister.” Sodja waited a breath. en another. “Aren’t you going to cal the guards?” “I suspect you would be long gone before they arrived.” “Not if you caught me rst.” “True enough.” He gestured at the door. “It’s not in there, you know—and she’s expecting you to come looking for it.” “Traps?” Ketrit nodded. “Why do you keep coming back?” “Why haven’t you stopped me?” “For our grandmother. I know you’ve been visiting her—even if the rest are too stupid to realize it. I’ve even covered for you a few times.” “But why? Why not have Rista waiting to ambush me? Why not end this?” “I told you. For Bel a. She seems to do better after your visits—at least she used to. ese past few weeks I haven’t noticed much of a di erence. I think … maybe it’s her way of letting us know she’s ready to move on.” “You don’t real y think—?” “I do think. I love Grandma Bel a, Sodja. Not as much as you, maybe … but I’ve cared for her. Cared enough to sit while she ate, to check on her a few times a day … but that’s my limit. I can’t empty her chamber pots or be her ful -time caretaker—and I certainly can’t stand between her and Mother.” He sni ed, studied Sodja from head to toe. “Tiana wanted me to marry you, you know. Just like Aunt Daunia and Uncle Pyodr.” Sodja turned her eyes to the oor, knowing Ketrit was only half right. Like the rest of the Saevors, Tiana placed high value on maintaining a pure Kroseran bloodline—but Sodja had never been intended for Ketrit. He was supposed to be the noble sacri ce, the one who married into the royal family and secured ultimate power in Luqura. “Don’t worry,” Ketrit added, sensing Sodja’s unease, “you’re not my type.” Sodja snorted. “Don’t fancy your sister?” “I don’t fancy women.” Sodja paused at that. She had known her brother was picky when it came to love interests, and she had guessed at his preferences, but he’d never con ded them to her—not in her whole life at the estate. She wondered what made him tel her now. “Have you told Mother?” is time Ketrit snorted. “Wouldn’t matter if I did. She’s got her eye on a crown, and she wil keep putting noble women in my bed til I seed one of them.” Ketrit was right about that. And clearly knew what Tiana planned for her youngest two children. “You should come with me,” Sodja protested, hoping she could convince him. “Fight back.” “No,” Ketrit said, resigned. “We both know how that wil end. Tiana gets what she wants, and she destroys anyone who stands in her way.” ere was a warning there—possibly a threat. “Besides,” he continued, “there are perks to sitting a throne. After a decade or three, Mother might even pass into shadow and shade, and I could rule.” “Unless you die early and Rista takes your place.” “Perhaps,” Ketrit said. “I’l take my chances, though.” Sodja hu ed and turned away, thinking that was al to be said.
