Denithal’s white mask turned to look at Der’s smoky gure, though how either of them could see the other’s expression was beyond Edra. e black mists around Der wavered and a gloved hand appeared in the fog, dissipating the magic smoke. e former Master of Stealth had taken o his mask—a black face wrap that completely molded to his skin, similar to the fabric that wrapped the rest of his lean, muscled body—and he squinted meaningful y at Denithal, who perched the rigid white shel of his own mask atop his wizened head. e elderly alchemist looked pointedly at Edra. “Ather said not to invite him,” the former ancient rasped. “He didn’t say why. I didn’t ask.” “He said the same to me—and to leave our amulets behind.” Edra frowned. “What’s that about?” Der shrugged. “I left mine too … but it seems odd not wearing it. I mean, it’s supposed to protect us. So why leave them?” “I left mine by accident once,” Edra said, distracted by Murlach’s distant gure dragging traps into place, preparing for another ambush. Even from that distance, he could hear the soft whir and click of the contraptions covering the man’s body—more like some monstrous insect than a human, his limbs and torso covered in wire tentacles, spindly metal arms and clacking pincers. “I forgot it,” Edra continued, “and didn’t think anything of it. A few hours later Kenton found me and handed it back. Told me I should always keep it on me —so it could protect me. Damned if I know how he knew I wasn’t wearing it.” “But you left it today, didn’t you?” e trio turned to see Ather, the former Master of Lies, step out nimbly from behind a gnarled oak. “You each left your amulets in Chaenbalu as I instructed, did you not?” Edra slowly nodded and, to his relief, so did Der and Denithal. “I can’t imagine why we’d listen to a serpent like you,” Denithal croaked, wiping saliva from his lips, “but here we are.” Ather waggled the ngers of his powder-blue Gloves of Persuasion. “Blood and lth,” Edra swore. “You tricked us. Why?” “ e same reason I asked you al to meet me here—and not to invite Aog.” Ather brushed back his trimmed coif of hair. “I’m afraid our dear Master Kenton has been manipulating us. Spying on us.” “How’s that?” Der crossed his arms. Edra knew that look—and the stance too. If the former Master of Stealth didn’t like Ather’s answer, he might fol ow up with a throwing star to the man’s throat. “I have suspected it for some time,” Ather drawled, unintimidated, “and I spent the last few weeks testing my theory. Whenever we’re wearing the amulets, Kenton knows where we are and, I believe, he can hear our thoughts. Unless he’s with Kiara in the Vault of Damnation. Whatever demon magic protects that place also interferes with the amulets. Kenton’s there right now with that witch, scrying or screwing or whatever the hel it is they do down there. at’s why he hasn’t come looking for us … yet.” “Damn me,” Denithal burped, his hands patting his chest for a blue vial that he quickly uncorked and chugged. “Sorry,” he said. “ e yel ow ones do wonders for my energy, but they give me some frightful indigestion.” “How did you learn this?” Edra asked, pointedly ignoring Denithal. Ather raised an eyebrow. “Did none of you think to try and identify the properties of the talismans? You simply took Kenton at his word?” e predatory popinjay snorted. “And I suppose none of you thought it odd those amulets were a matched set? e rst thing I did was sit down and properly identify each artifact—but you were al too eager to play with your new toys. You didn’t stop to think that young Master Kenton might be trying to control us?” Neither Der nor Denithal could meet his gaze. Edra at least had enough steel not to look sheepish, but Ather’s words rang painful y true. How long had he spent admiring his new leather armor and marveling at his new weapons? He’d never once in that time thought to second-guess their properties. Let the boy identify the artifacts and assign them, he had thought, and I’l make use of them. e former Master of Arms met Ather’s eyes. “Aye,” Edra said. “Seems we were a bit hasty in trusting the boy. What should we do then? We can’t put the amulets back on or he’l know we’ve gured out his secret.” “I mean to get out of here,” Ather said, nodding toward the road. “To leave Chaenbalu for good. Even if Kenton were being straight with us, you saw what Annev did to Elder Tosan—how he blew up the Academy and damn near kil ed us al . If we’re smart, we’l stay far, far away from that.” “But where can we go?” Der asked, looking pensive. “ e Academy … the vault and the magic?” He looked between the others. “What else is there for us?” Ather gave a dramatic sigh, dusted o a fal en tree, then sat down. “We should cal Murlach over. If you haven’t guessed yet, we aren’t ambushing any caravans today. I just needed an excuse to get us al together.” “And Aog?” Edra asked. “Why didn’t you invite him?” Ather peeled o one of his magic gloves and waved the garment at him. “ ese don’t work on Aog. I thought it was because of his armor, but he didn’t even respond when I touched his face. It’s like he’s … not there.” “ at’s nothing new,” Denithal said, snorting. “No,” Ather objected. “ is was di erent. Kenton’s done something to him, I think. Got him wrapped tighter than the rest of us, I’d wager. Haven’t you noticed? He keeps the Master of Punishment like some sort of pet. Has him digging those tunnels beneath the Academy’s ruins or running an errand of some sort. Aog’s never real y been the sycophantic type, and this reeks of magic.” He tapped Der on the shoulder with his gloved hand. “Go fetch Murlach?” Der nodded and sped away to col ect the monstrous Master of Engineering.

chunks.title: Chapter 8
chunks.content: Edra gave him a pointed look. “You just manipulated Der,” he accused. “How is that any di erent than what Kenton’s doing?” “Because,” Ather said, smiling wickedly, “I’m me and he’s not.” Edra sni ed but didn’t argue the point. Murlach and Der were back a minute later, the former frowning from within the nest of cables and wires surrounding his face and neck. “What’s al this about Kenton?” “He’s been spying on us,” Edra said, before Ather could o er a more garrulous explanation—Keos, that man could talk. “Ather gured out the amulets were involved somehow,” he continued. “You stil wearing yours?” A tentacled arm sprang to life at Murlach’s side, the pronged tip slithering into his armor. ere was a loud hissing sound and then his exoskeleton split open. “So,” he said, “you nal y gured it out.” “Figured what out?” Edra said, a moment before Der. “ e talismans.” Murlach’s tentacle retreated from his armor, its pincers drawing the amulet over his head before displaying the artifact for al to see. “I wondered how long it would take. Which of you was it?” Down the road, one of Murlach’s twiddlesnap contraptions clanked shut, eliciting a squeal as some poor animal was snapped and snared—but the rest of them gave it no mind. Edra pointed to Ather, head shaking as he said to Murlach, “If you’ve known this whole time, why would you wear it?” Murlach spun the talisman in front of Edra’s face so that he saw a peculiar drop of silver clinging to the amulet’s ruby. “What’s that?” Der asked, stepping forward to examine the artifact. “Some kind of … metal spider?” Edra grunted in agreement. e addition to the amulet did look like some sort of metal ic arachnid, with eight tiny legs and a blood-red thorax that matched the ruby beneath it. Murlach let each man see it in turn. “When we were down in the vault, I saw another half-dozen of these talismans sitting on a shelf at the back of the chamber—al with these metal spiders attached to them. at got me wondering, so I started poking around and found six unattached spiders sitting on the lower shelf. Didn’t take a genius to gure Kenton had modi ed ours, so I snatched one of the spider-amulets and gave it a closer look. Tried to gure out what kind of tricks our cursed leader was trying to pul on us.” “And?” Murlach’s silvery tentacle dropped the amulet back over his neck. “ e spiders alter the magic a bit. Instead of al owing Kenton to always hear my thoughts, they let me choose which ones to share and which to keep to myself.” “Why not tel the rest of us?” Der asked, his brow furrowed. Murlach shrugged. “I wanted to see how things played out—and I didn’t trust you lot to keep my secret.” He gestured at Ather with his pincers. “ at’s al moot now that Ather’s played our hands for us, though … so what’s the new plan?” He eyed the Master of Lies with unmasked contempt. “You going to confront him?” “After what he did to Master Carbad?” Ather said, his eyes widening with just a hint of terror. “Hel s no. I thought we could just leave—but rst I wanted to col ect some insurance.” “Which is?” “Aqlumera,” Ather said, his grin returning as he smoothed the thin line of his mustache. “Tosan didn’t like us entering the vault because he didn’t want people knowing we were sitting on an emperor’s ransom. Just a bottle of that stu would make us rich as kings—and I know folks who’d be more than eager to buy it. So imagine this: we hurry back to Chaenbalu before Kenton realizes we’ve discovered his secret. Murlach stays up here and uses his amulet to convince Kenton we’re al stil with him. When Kenton comes to investigate— and see why we’ve taken o our amulets—the rest of us wil break into the vault. We can grab some more artifacts, steal a few bottles of aqlumera and meet up with Murlach at the old mil . We circle south to the Brake Road and then we go east, away from Luqura and Banok and anywhere else Kenton might think to look for us. If we go to Port Caer, we’l have mountains of gold before the end of the month and can live out our lives in peace. Or we can turn mercenary and sel our services to the highest bidder. e point is we’l have options.” e others watched Murlach, who seemed to have become the de facto alternative to Ather’s leadership. “I don’t think there’s any reason for me to wait here,” Murlach said. “I can choose which thoughts Kenton sees, and I can do that as easily with you in Chaenbalu. And no need to regroup at the mil . We can just grab the aqlumera and get the hel out of these woods.” Der and Denithal glanced at Edra then, surprising him with their deference. e former Master of Arms waited just long enough to acknowledge their unasked question. “It has a certain attractiveness to it. Much better than waiting for Kenton to gure out what to do with us. I’m in.” Der and Denithal nodded—and that was that. One last theft, one nal betrayal, and they would be free of Chaenbalu forever. Murlach went to retrieve the trap he’d left on the road, and Der and Denithal replaced their masks, the former disappearing into an amorphous cloud of black smoke. “Hey, fel as!” Murlach cal ed back to them a minute later, his voice projected by some ingenious artifact inside his suit. “You need to come and look at this!” “What is it?” Ather shouted back, his nimble knee-high boots dancing him out of the tree line and down the slope leading onto the road. “You remember those metal monsters that attacked the Academy?” Murlach asked, a tremor in his voice. “ e twisted ones that ran o into the forest?” “Yes,” Edra said, feeling a cold prickle of fear creep up his neck. “Why? Did you nd one?” “Not sure,” Murlach said, his speaker clicking o as the group approached him from behind. “It looks a lot like one … but also not.” Edra nal y saw the beast caught in the jaws of Murlach’s enormous twiddlesnap: unlike the feral, mutated monsters that had attacked Chaenbalu, this creature seemed . . . wel , not like a creature at al ; more like a man wearing ful plate armor, his body segmented by overlapping metal plates. Metal and stone, Edra amended, slowing. en he realized. at’s not armor … that’s the creature’s esh! “Gods,” Denithal rasped from behind his white mask. “It is one of them!” Ather’s slender rapier hissed from its scabbard and Edra drew his own leaf-bladed long sword. Denithal dipped his hands under his bandolier and popped a red vial from his pocket, and while Edra couldn’t see Der’s gure amidst the cloud of smoke, he assumed the Master of Stealth was similarly preparing for battle. “You can put your pricks away, boys,” Murlach shouted back. “It’s dead.” “From the twiddlesnap?” Der asked amidst his cloud of smoke. “ ose aren’t lethal.” “ ey are when they’re big enough to crush a wagon wheel.” Murlach used his pincers to prod the metal man’s iron head and neck. “How in the name of the Gods does this magic work?” he wondered aloud. “Made of metal and stone … but not a machine. Is it a man … or a golem?” He shook his head, apparently more impressed by the arti cery than concerned by the dark omen of the creature’s presence. “Should we be worried that it was skulking about the East Road?” Edra asked. “No,” Ather said, any fear in his tone concealed beneath his usual veneer of vanity. “ is changes nothing. We go back to Chaenbalu, get the aqlumera, and head to Port Caer.” Murlach dropped the creature’s iron head and stood straight, his mechanized body nearly a foot tal er than without his suit. “We should keep an eye out for more of these buggers, though. If this ferruman is anything like the ones we saw in Chaenbalu, there’l be more—lots more.” Edra was suddenly anxious to get back to the questionable safety of Chaenbalu’s familiar ruins. “Let’s move.” CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN “Does she live?” Kenton asked, leaning dangerously close to the edge of the aqlumera pool. “Show me again. I have to know if she survived.” “She lives, Cursed One. She lives and wil yet live. As I promised, her life is only truly in peril when she returns here. You should not trouble yourself with these visions.” “Show me again, Kiara! I need to know what has happened to her.” e witmistress rubbed her temples then clasped her hands together. “Magic is not free, Kenton. Even when we use the aqlumera instead of the shadepools, there is a cost for scrying, and I do not spend it lightly.” “But those demons nearly kil ed her!” “ ose demons failed—as I foretold.” e Master of Curses ripped his blindfold away and stared into Kiara’s eyes, his own aring with demonic re, their light ickering at the edge of his vision. “Show. Her. Again.” “No.” Kenton’s cheek twitched and his hands shook as if he were about to strangle the woman. Instead, he spun away from the aqlumera cistern and smashed his st against the nearest shelf of artifacts. Magic ared from his Glove of Indomitability and the wood exploded into splinters. A heartbeat later, a catalogue of magic stones toppled to the oor, the rocks and pebbles scattering in al directions. Kiara frowned. “Tantrums do not persuade or inspire obedience. ey are a sign of weakness. A demonstration that you are incapable of leading.” She tucked a lock of hair behind her ear, the rest rmly secured in a neat bun. Since the Academy’s col apse, the other masters and ancients had started to relax, not seeking to impress one another, much less Kenton. Kiara had gone the opposite way, though, becoming even more formal, acting like a teacher in the midst of lecturing a student; her skirts were always clean and ironed, her face was always washed, her hair was always neat. Kenton, by contrast, was a haggard shadow of his former self who cared little for the company of others. e only exceptions were Kiara, whose magic al owed him to watch Myjun in the shadow realm, and Master Aog, whose wil he had entirely dominated. At the moment, the former Master of Punishment was digging a new tunnel from Chaenbalu’s lowest dungeon to the abandoned bakery at the perimeter of the vil age square—a secret tunnel, in case Kenton was ever trapped beneath the Academy again. Kenton had not yet admitted to anyone, not even himself, that he no longer wished to leave the Academy’s ruins. Its tunnels and its magic had become familiar to him, and he was becoming obsessed with the aqlumera pool and watching Myjun. He had no reason or desire to leave—not to wash, not to sleep, not even to eat—and the vault’s artifacts meant he never had to. “I could make you show me,” he growled. “I could force you.” “You can’t and you won’t. Harming me wil ensure you never see Myjun again. So you wil let me rest. You wil see the visions again when I am ready, not when you command. Is that clear?” Kenton’s lips puckered, his skin tightening as he felt his scarred face struggle to contain his scowl. “Quite clear,” he whispered, his voice so low it was almost impossible to hear. “She is not dead, Kenton. She is resting, and it wil take time for her wounds to heal.” “How long?” “Hours. Days. Not long, I suspect. Time passes more swiftly there, but while she is resting, we should rest.” Kenton stroked his scraggly beard. “I don’t like that half man. What he does … what he’s doing to her. He’s kil ing her. Maybe not her body, but her spirit.” “I’m not certain that girl ever real y had a spirit.” Kenton’s eyes ashed, their bril iance almost blinding, their light swel ing to throw back the shadows in the corners of the room. “You know nothing of Myjun.” “Don’t I? She was best friends with my apprentice, and the daughter of the headmaster. I knew her al too wel . Her little schemes, her vanity. I knew her mother too, before she died. Hel s, I practical y raised that girl with the other witwomen. If the Academy had lasted a few more years and her father hadn’t been an obstacle, we would have indoctrinated her into the Brides of Fate.” “Did you know she had magic?” “I did.” “How?” Kiara raised an eyebrow, her cool gray eyes inspecting him. “Come with me.” *** e witmistress’s bedchamber lay two oors above the vault, completely undisturbed by either the Academy’s col apse or the feurog attack, save for the narrow tunnel hidden behind Kiara’s bed. She had already explained how that single tunnel had al owed the feurog to enter the Academy, but she had been less forthcoming about why. “A clean slate,” she’d told him. “No witnesses to pursue us when we left with Annev. No survivors to guide any others to the village.” It had al seemed very cold to Kenton. “What did you want to show me?” he asked, sitting down in a padded rocking chair. “ is.” Kiara handed him a smal black book and Kenton ri ed through its pages. He saw dates, names and numbers—a chart of some kind—and a short description beside each name. In most cases, it also mentioned the parents’ names, or potential strains of magic. “ is is a logbook,” he said, ipping to the end. “A log of . . . stolen children?” “It was our job to locate and monitor infants who might become the Vessel. We abducted them from al over Greater Luqura and brought them here to be trained. One-armed infants were our rst priority, but none of them ever possessed the talent—none until Annev—so instead we kidnapped those likely to inherit the talent, thinking one might lose an arm during their training or an artifact retrieval mission … but it never happened. It was very vexing.” “What’s this?” Kenton asked, showing her an asterisk next to one boy’s name and the bright red letters NM. “Sage Lenka. Is this the Academy’s cook?” “Yes. ‘NM’ means nonmagical. Not every child had magic. Some were taken for political reasons.” “Hold on. ‘Lenka.’ Is that supposed to be King Lenka? As in the King of Greater Luqura.” Kiara nodded. “He had three children. e youngest boy was supposedly stil born, but he’s actual y been cooking the Academy’s meals for the past decade or more.” “You stole a prince?” he breathed. “Damn me. What for?” “Politics, mostly. We had our reasons.” Kenton ipped forward a few more pages and saw his reap mates. “Fyunai Harth … son of Janak Harth?” He looked up. “ at’s the merchant we kil ed in Banok!” “Just a strain of Ironborn in that one—nothing major—but Janak’s mercenary exploits let him amass too much power too quickly. Taking his son was meant to keep the bastard in line … but something went wrong at the reaping. Janak fought back. His wife was kil ed and he was crippled—but we stil managed to steal his son.” “Fyn,” Kenton breathed, head shaking in disbelief. “He kil ed his own father. at prick of a headmaster sent him to kil his own bloody father.” “It was no accident. Tosan was aware of his students’ parental lineage.” Kenton ipped to another page and found his own name. “Reotan NM,” he read beside his nameless father—and beside his unnamed mother . . . “Terran Arti cer?” He looked up. “I’m bloody Terran?” “Of course you are. Al Arti cers are Terran.” “But … I don’t look Terran.” “You have your father’s looks—like a Tir Reotan pirate—and your mother’s magic. She was an Arti cer.” “ ere are no names written here.” “No. We tended not to record the rapists, pirates, or whores.” Kenton’s mouth twitched, but he held his anger in check. “And I was stolen?” “You? No. Your father didn’t want a brat on his ship. Witwoman Kelga purchased you from your mother on the streets of Luqura.” Kenton wanted to ask more but his throat closed up. His nger drifted down the page until he found Annev’s name. “Ainnevog … but no number. No origin, no parentage.” He looked up. “Why not?” “Infants have their heels inked with numbers—to help us keep track of you al . Annev had no such number. My best guess is Sodar smuggled him into your reap.” Kenton snorted, nding some dark humor in it al . “So why show me this?” Kiara took the book and ipped to a group of pages he had missed. “ ese are our notes on the witapprentices. Only a few are stolen each year, though sometimes a witwoman wil get pregnant—in the case of us Brides, we select a mate with an a nity for prophetic magic. Myjun and her mother were both witchildren, but Myjun’s grandmother was a proper Bride of Fate . . . who married this man.” Kiara ipped to another page and tapped a spidery inscription next to an infant from the thirty-seventh reap. “Edwin,” Kenton read, taking back the book. “Son of Donald the Bard. Strong a nity for Ilumite magic.” He looked up. “ is is how you knew. You had your prophecies and the Academy’s training … and this.” “Yes. at’s how we knew Myjun would probably have the talent, though it was impossible to guess which strands would become dominant. Terran, Ilumite, Yomad. We never know until you reach an age where the magic is potent. We try to bring the girls into the Brides of Fate around then. For the young men . . . there’s usual y no harm in having a little of the talent, particularly if they’re never taught to use it. It makes them better avatars. And if some stumble upon how to use their magic … wel , avatars have such a high mortality rate.” “Did Duvarek have it?” Kenton asked, his voice sounding hol ow. “Is that why he was kil ed?” “Duvarek had it and I think he knew—it’s probably why he drank so much. But we didn’t kil him. at was al Janak’s fault.” “But Tosan had me kil him … because he got caught. at wasn’t your doing?” “No.” Kenton relaxed, suddenly aware he’d been on the point of violence. “ at’s good,” he said, his heart thudding heavily in his chest. He passed the logbook back. “I need to check in on Aog and the other masters.” “Are they giving you trouble?” “Not Aog. e slave ring keeps him completely docile—though he needs new commands every few hours or he’s liable to sit down in one of the tunnels and wait to be told what to do next.” “And the others?” Kiara asked, her tone implying something she knew that he did not. Kenton frowned. “Ather’s being a pain. He may have gured out the amulets.” “And if he has?” “ en I’l kil him.” Kiara nodded as though she’d expected as much. “You’re sure this isn’t motivated by your history with him?” “My history?” Kenton asked, tense once again. “Your scar,” she said, gesturing to the band of mottled esh that was now almost entirely hidden by the leathery, cal oused skin surrounding his lidless eyes. “No lingering resentments for that?” “Oh, of course,” Kenton said, his gloved hand gently scratching the smal patch of scarred esh, “but Ather has some subtlety that the others lack, so I’l overlook our past—so long as he stays in line. He recently stopped wearing his amulet, though, and I don’t think that’s an accident.” “He’s testing you,” Kiara said, her eyes glinting. “I think so, yes. And he keeps asking about the vault—keeps lingering whenever I enter or leave.” “ en make an example of him.” “I think he wants the aqlumera.” Kiara’s coy smile transformed into a frown. “He can’t take any of it. In the wrong hands, that magic could be catastrophic . . . not to mention you’ve trapped a demon down there.” “He’s not trapped,” Kenton said, his lips pressed into a rm line. “He’s waiting for another chance to escape.” “ en why hasn’t he tried to possess me?” Kenton smiled. “ at pin you wear in your hair. Did you not guess its enchantment?” Kiara’s frown deepened. “Identifying enchantments is not one of my strengths, Master Kenton.” Kenton led that information away for the future. “It protects the wearer from spectral possession. So long as you wear it, Elder Tosan can’t use you as a conduit.” “And do you wear a similar artifact?” “I do,” Kenton said, tapping the cu s of his Gloves of Indomitability. “ ese protect my hands and my soul.” Kiara nodded, seeming impressed. “You real y are a marvel with artifacts. I doubt anyone in the Academy’s history was so wel suited to be their keeper.” Kenton’s smile slipped and he turned from her then, choosing to busy himself checking on the masters. His eyes grew distant, and he located Aog in the dark tunnels of the Academy’s lowest levels. e brute was sluggishly carving away at the soil, his enchanted shovel simultaneously softening and hardening the earth that he cut away. He didn’t even need to cart away the dirt he excavated—it was simply vaporized. Kenton mental y told the man to dig for another hour and then come and eat, and then he checked on the other Sons of Damnation. “Something’s wrong,” he said, his brow furrowing. “ ey’ve taken o their amulets—al except Murlach.” “And where is he?” Kenton tried to glean the master’s location. “ e East Road … I think. But it doesn’t feel right. His thoughts are … chatty. He never thinks aloud this much.” “What’s he thinking?” “Something about robbing a caravan. It sounds like the others are with him.” He concentrated. “Oh shit.” “What?” Kiara asked, a touch of dread creeping into her voice. “ ey found something on the road. One of those feurog.” “Oh,” Kiara said, visibly relaxing. “You needn’t worry about them. Without someone to drive them, they’re little more than animals. at’s why Cruithear’s priests cast them out—and why we snatched them up. I admit they make hardy soldiers, but they prefer to hide from men. Besides, there aren’t many of them left. I’ve tried to recal the survivors but none have responded.” “No,” Kenton said, frowning. “ is one isn’t like your monsters—not exactly. Murlach … he’s cal ing it a ferruman. It’s not mutated like those others —not half-human, half-monster. It looks … Wel , damn. It looks like Janak Harth, after he drank that vial of magic.” Kiara’s nonchalance suddenly vanished. “Where did Murlach spot this ferruman?” “On the East Road. e golem got caught in one of his traps.” “It’s not a golem,” Kiara said, scowling. “If it looks like Janak Harth, then it’s human. A real man or woman, not a construct.” Kenton studied her, his magic revealing the aura of fear she fought to hide. “What aren’t you tel ing me?” e witmistress pursed her lips. “ e feurog were monsters—failed experiments of Cruithear—but the God of Minerals had some successes. Cruithear made those lucky enough not to become monsters into his elite soldiers—his Ironborn warriors. I suspect one of those is the ferruman Murlach saw.” “Why would one of those be here?” “Without scrying, I can only guess—but Cruithear is jealous of his elites. He hoards them like a miser with his coins … so if one is here, he means to attack someone, or something.” “What would be worth it, to him?” Kiara swore. “I haven’t asked the spirits … but Cruithear needs aqlumera to forge his warriors. e only reason he hasn’t made an army of them is because aqlumera is expensive, extremely limited, and di cult to locate—especial y untainted.” “Except here,” Kenton nished. “In the Vault of Damnation.” Kiara nodded. “Most of the feurog are mutants because the aqlumera that formed them was tainted—but if Cruithear discovered the existence of our fountain, and if he found one of Chaenbalu’s survivors and persuaded them to act as his guide …” “ en he’d bring his best soldiers here,” Kenton nished. “An army of ferrumen could be on their way to Chaenbalu now. ey could be just outside the village. Surrounding us. Looking for a way into the tunnels.” “ at is a possibility.” “And the masters are al north of the Brake. Al except Aog.” Kenton felt his adrenaline rising. “Blood and lth. How can we be sure?” e answer suddenly came to him and he let his eyes unfocus, sweeping his vision beyond Kiara’s bedroom and across the landscape around the Academy. He turned in a ful circle, his magic eyes piercing rock and stone, air and earth, and saw nothing alarming within the bounds of the vil age. He gave up after a minute of searching. “It seems we’re safe from … wait.” Kenton stopped, his eyes locking on to four warm bodies skulking near the edge of the vil age. Myjun wiped her blood-spattered face, leaving long streaks of crimson along her golden cheeks, delicate brow and shining jawbone. Another arrow ew past, this time grazing her shoulder. She merely gritted her teeth. “ ey ee from you.” e voice came from the shadows of the trench the Yomads had abandoned. “As they should,” Myjun growled. She licked her cracked lips behind the mask and imagined the coppery taste of the blood on her face and the texture of the soldiers’ esh between her teeth. She was so hungry … yet her body felt ful . As always, their deaths had strengthened her. Oyru looked to the looming Harwal behind them, its length disappearing leagues into the distance, its ancient stones protecting the southeastern corner of the Terran Empire. “We should go. e archers wil keep ring so long as we stay in range. ey do not know you ght for them, even though you’ve kil ed a hundred of the Yomads.” As if to emphasize his point, an arrow plunged through the half man’s chest, and exited more slowly from his back. A plume of black vapor trailed the injury and the assassin’s esh knitted itself back together. He climbed from the shadows then beckoned Myjun to fol ow, and they moved away from the Terran soldiers on the great wal , strol ing toward the eeing Yomads. “I do not ght for them,” Myjun snapped, nodding back at the towering wal that blocked the other end of the isthmus. “I ght for myself. I would kil them, too, if you would let me.” Oyru’s nger rose to trace the black scar that marked his missing eye. “ ose soldiers belong to the Legions of Keos, which makes them our al ies.” “I have no al ies.” “Not even me? Not after I risked my own life and sacri ced this for you?” Oyru tapped the withered eye socket, its esh puckered tight in contrast to the wide, unblinking eye pinning her with its soul ess glare. “ at was months ago—and I didn’t ask you to save me, you half-demon bastard.” e words hissed from her like steam from a kettle. “You’re not a savior or a rotting martyr. You’re a conjurer, a kil er, and a bloody liar. Al you do is torture me and tel me to kil , and delay ful l ing your promises.” Oyru shrugged as if her words meant nothing, which only enraged Myjun further. “I wil ful l my promises,” the Shadow Reborn said, resuming their walk. “We have made good progress these past few weeks.” “Months,” Myjun corrected. “It’s been ve months.” “Only if you reckon time by the blinks of Dorchnok’s Eye. Barely three weeks of traveling in the physical realm, and we have already reached the last leg of our journey.” e assassin gestured to the eld of ivory towers dotting the narrow isthmus of Lubree, a no-man’s-land that separated the continents of New and Old Terra. “Terra Minora lies just beyond the Neck, protected by the endless towers and the Spear of Tacharan. Once you are sated, we wil cross back into the shadow realm here in Lubree—at the Noose of the Neck—and from here pass into Takarania and Terra Minora.” He pointed to a speck on the horizon that could barely be seen above the heads of the innumerable towers ahead of them. “You see that lone tower? It is the Spear of Tacharan. It marks the end of the Neck of Lubree and the beginning of Takarania. Powerful magics protect it and the land surrounding it, preventing entry. Even sailors must avoid the isthmus and its shores and travel to Al tara in the south or Krosera in the north. We wil avoid its curse, though, by crossing the Neck in the shadow realm.” “And how much farther to Al tara?” Myjun asked, unable to conceal the venom in her tone. “Terra Minora is the home of three peoples: the Shalgarns of Al tara, the Yomads of Takarania, and my people in Krosera.” Oyru gestured past the isthmus. “Takarania lies at the center of Terra Minora and borders the Neck. It is a bu er between the shadowlands of Krosera and wildlands of Al tara, which we must pass through to reach the Iron Mountains and the trol clans. Doing so wil also bring us close to the obelisks that guard the House of Brass at the center of Takarania—perilous in either realm.” “So we must stil avoid them? Even after traveling into the shadow realm?” “We must, but for separate reasons. In this world, the Brazen Towers mark the borders of Takarania and are abutted by the mountains of Al tara. East of the mountains is the House of Brass, home to the priests who worship the God of Death. In the shadow realm, their temple overlaps the Heart of the Void— the center of Reocht na Skah.” “I thought you said it’s dangerous to go to Reocht na Skah—that we could get trapped there for eternity.” “Just so. To avoid both, we wil enter the shadows and cross beyond the Neck. at wil take us beyond the reach of the Spear of Tacharan. We wil then remain in the shadow realm and skirt the edge of Takarania to avoid entangling ourselves with the magic of Reocht na Skah. If we turn immediately southwest, that wil take us directly into the Al taran mountains and trol territory.” “To get my rotting armor.” “Yes.” “And then you wil take me back to the Empire to kil Annev.” “Yes.” “Fine. Let’s go.” Oyru gestured at the soldiers who had nal y reached the safety of their ivory towers. “You have satis ed your bloodlust?” He asked the question as though he were o ering her a nibble of a scone instead of the lives of a half-dozen men and women. “We wil not return to the physical world again—not til we reach Al tara—so you should take your l now.” “My hunger is never satis ed,” Myjun said, not bothering to hide her bitterness, “but I wil survive the trip.” Oyru nodded. “ e distance between here and Al tara would take a week to traverse over land—assuming we were unmolested by the Yomads and their magics. In the shadow realm it wil take a month or more … but time wil distort even more as we cross into Takarania. e greatest eidola also concentrate there, near the borders of Reocht na Skah, and that wil slow our pace further. at means it wil likely take us considerably longer than ve weeks to reach the trol mountains—at least, so long as we are traveling in the shadow realm.” “How much time wil al of this take in the physical realm?” “Stil a week by standard time, but we wil be stuck in the shadows for two months at least. And if we choose to venture nearer to southern Takarania— toward the heart of Reocht na Skah—it could be even longer.” “So why not return to the physical world once we are past the dangers of the Spear of Tacharan?” Oyru eyed her with his remaining black eye, its stare penetrating her to the core. “Because I believe the extra time and training would bene t you. You have grown much over these past ve months, but you stil lack ful control of your powers. You have not learned to bend or re ect the light as Bladesingers and Lightslingers do. You’ve learned to channel its baser elements—to summon your soulblades and channel the light re—but it seems the subtler arts are beyond you.” “And what do you know of the light, half man? You’re a master of the shadows. You couldn’t even teach me to summon the light, much less shape it. I learned that myself.” “Only because I forced you to.” He raised a hand to scratch the corner of his empty eye socket. Myjun sni ed. Perhaps he regretted his decision to save her, though if he did, Oyru never expressed it—and the omission hurt her more than any accusation. “I wil not delay my vengeance forever,” she asserted. “We should go west, straight into the mountains of Al tara. Reocht na Skah can keep its monsters and its secrets—and I would prefer we keep our current pace. If we stay in the shadow realm but keep close to the shoreline, that could be the fastest route of al .” Oyru said nothing, looking east—past the towers along the isthmus and toward a green coast that was almost entirely shrouded in mist. “We are close to Krosera now. If we crossed the Neck and went northeast instead of southwest, we would be in my homeland.” He looked wistful—and then he raised his face scarf and it was hidden. Myjun stared at him as if she’d just been slapped across the face. e man had been frowning—actual y frowning. “You don’t fear the death priests or the eidolons,” she said, accusing. “You’re not even afraid of spending a thousand years in the shadow of Reocht na Skah … but you are afraid of going home—and even then you tease yourself with it. Your words imply we might go there, yet you clearly wish to stay away. Why? What terrors do Krosera’s shadowlands hold for you?” Oyru turned to face her, his scarf fal ing away, his normal y stoic demeanor replaced by one of hatred and fear. “ e Kroserans and their impotent Shadow God can go to hel ,” Oyru said, his words colder than they had ever been. “We are bound for Al tara. I wil hasten our journey as you’ve requested—and you wil not speak of my homeland again.” As he said these last words, he covered his mouth and nose more completely, though the black fabric could not hide the tiny tear that trickled from the corner of the assassin’s eye. He dabbed it with his scarf, erasing the proof that he did indeed have a soul—but not before Myjun saw it. CHAPTER FIFTY-EIGHT “Why do you serve Keos instead of Dorchnok?” ey were back in the shadow realm and long past the Neck of Lubree. In their crossing, she had seen no evidence of the endless ivory towers that protected the isthmus, nor any shadow of the lone and awful Spear of Tacharan. She had instead seen black waves of smoke that l ed the depths of the Sauthron and Estron Seas. When she had later asked what happened to those that tried to sail those dark waters in the shadow realm, Oyru snorted, shook his head, and muttered something unintel igible about Voidweavers. e reaction seemed entirely out of character for the usual y stoic assassin, and the adjustment in her relationship with the Shadow Reborn left Myjun feeling adrift. At the same time, the assassin’s odd mood seemed to invite a more personal connection—something Myjun felt open to now they had left the physical world and the perpetual rage of her mask had been dimmed and dul ed. “I do not serve Keos,” Oyru said, morose. “I serve Dortafola and he serves Keos.” “Which is the same thing—and you did not answer my question. Why did you abandon your worship of Dorchnok?” “Are you not equal y impious? Did you not abandon your worship of Odar to fol ow me?” “ at’s di erent. I was damned—marked by Keos—and I had no choice. Not if I want to kil Annev.” Oyru said nothing for a long, long time. When he nal y did speak, it was with the measured words of someone who was unused to speech—as if the person behind the mask were speaking to her for the rst time. “I was betrayed once. Like you, I loved someone and was betrayed by them. She wasn’t Kroseran. She came from an Ilumite clan in Faer Fen and sailed across the Estron Sea to Northern Krosera. She pledged herself to me and then she wooed another Kroseran warrior—a warlord named Gevul the Terrible— and helped him destroy my house and my family. I kil ed Gevul, but not before he kil ed her . . . the woman I stil loved.” Oyru stared at the black waters, his face unreadable. “I tried to save her, I tried to bring her back—but Dorchnok would not heed my prayers. He did not save my family, he did not save her, and he could not save me.” e assassin turned south and pointed to the smoky horizon. “I ventured into Reocht na Skah. I thought that if I could reach into the Spirit World, I might persuade Oraqui to come back to me.” He xed his eye on Myjun. “She was a dualist—an Auramancer and a Lightslinger —but she could only do two things with her magic: she could manipulate others’ emotions and she could project il usions—re ections of the people and things nearby her. You have similar powers … sometimes you remind me of her.” He looked back to the horizon. “You entered Reocht na Skah,” Myjun said, her voice quiet. “I did.” “To the Heart of the Void.” “To the very center, yes.” Myjun swal owed. “How long were you gone? How long did you search for her?” “A week or two.” “A week or … in the Heart of the Void? When a day here is a thousand years there?” Oyru’s single eye shifted back to her, his usual stoic look back in place. “What made you leave? Or did you just give up?” She hadn’t meant it as a jab, though it came out that way. Stil , if Oyru was o ended he did not show it. “Dortafola came looking for me. Gevul had been one of his Siänar and when the man was kil ed … wel , he needed a replacement. Who better than the man who kil ed Gevul? He tracked me through the shadow realm to Reocht na Skah and promised that if I served him—that if I forsook my worship of Dorchnok and fol owed him—he would return Oraqui to me.” “And did he?” Oyru stared at her, his face a mask. “Maybe,” he said—and a chil went up her spine. *** “So you learned about Ilumite magic from her?” Oyru said nothing. He hadn’t spoken since their last conversation, two antumbras ago. Not a word. ey had turned southwest toward Al tara, keeping the black mists of the Sauthron Sea to their right and the endless gray plains to their left, and Myjun was tired of the shared silence. “She taught you about her magic, maybe even her people, and in return you taught her about Krosera and your magic.” Silence. “What made you think your master could bring her back?” More silence. “ is was hers, wasn’t it? is mask.” She tapped her gilded temple and forehead. “Did Gevul give it to her?” “Do not speak his name,” Oyru breathed, his voice as cold as ice—as cold as death. “Or what?” Myjun demanded, both relieved he had broken his silence and angry he had kept it for so long. “Wil you beat me? I wil drink the pain. Kil me? I don’t think so.” “I would leave you here,” Oyru said, his tone stil apathetic, though Myjun wondered if even his apathy was a mask. “I would leave you in the shadows, trapped here forever, and return to the physical world without you. You may have grown stronger, but you cannot traverse the planes of existence. You would be doomed to waste away until al life had left you and you became an eidolon.” “Is that what happened to you?” Myjun demanded. “Because you stayed so long in Reocht na Skah?” “Yes.” Myjun was satis ed. “ en I wil not speak that name again.” Oyru focused on a black xture that blanketed the horizon. “We are approaching the shadows of the Al taran mountains,” he said. “We are almost to our nal destination.” “We made good time, then.” Myjun stepped beside him, sharing the view. ough it seemed the land had been at for these many miles, she saw now that they had been climbing a long, gently rising hil . Al around them the ground gradual y fel away, the decline slow and steady behind them, almost imperceptible. Ahead, the slope grew more abrupt, rst fal ing and then rising again with greater height and severity. is pattern continued until the ground erupted in the black wal of mountains that stained the distant horizon.

chunks.title: Final Section
chunks.content: Edra gave him a pointed look. “You just manipulated Der,” he accused. “How is that any di erent than what Kenton’s doing?” “Because,” Ather said, smiling wickedly, “I’m me and he’s not.” Edra sni ed but didn’t argue the point. Murlach and Der were back a minute later, the former frowning from within the nest of cables and wires surrounding his face and neck. “What’s al this about Kenton?” “He’s been spying on us,” Edra said, before Ather could o er a more garrulous explanation—Keos, that man could talk. “Ather gured out the amulets were involved somehow,” he continued. “You stil wearing yours?” A tentacled arm sprang to life at Murlach’s side, the pronged tip slithering into his armor. ere was a loud hissing sound and then his exoskeleton split open. “So,” he said, “you nal y gured it out.” “Figured what out?” Edra said, a moment before Der. “ e talismans.” Murlach’s tentacle retreated from his armor, its pincers drawing the amulet over his head before displaying the artifact for al to see. “I wondered how long it would take. Which of you was it?” Down the road, one of Murlach’s twiddlesnap contraptions clanked shut, eliciting a squeal as some poor animal was snapped and snared—but the rest of them gave it no mind. Edra pointed to Ather, head shaking as he said to Murlach, “If you’ve known this whole time, why would you wear it?” Murlach spun the talisman in front of Edra’s face so that he saw a peculiar drop of silver clinging to the amulet’s ruby. “What’s that?” Der asked, stepping forward to examine the artifact. “Some kind of … metal spider?” Edra grunted in agreement. e addition to the amulet did look like some sort of metal ic arachnid, with eight tiny legs and a blood-red thorax that matched the ruby beneath it. Murlach let each man see it in turn. “When we were down in the vault, I saw another half-dozen of these talismans sitting on a shelf at the back of the chamber—al with these metal spiders attached to them. at got me wondering, so I started poking around and found six unattached spiders sitting on the lower shelf. Didn’t take a genius to gure Kenton had modi ed ours, so I snatched one of the spider-amulets and gave it a closer look. Tried to gure out what kind of tricks our cursed leader was trying to pul on us.” “And?” Murlach’s silvery tentacle dropped the amulet back over his neck. “ e spiders alter the magic a bit. Instead of al owing Kenton to always hear my thoughts, they let me choose which ones to share and which to keep to myself.” “Why not tel the rest of us?” Der asked, his brow furrowed. Murlach shrugged. “I wanted to see how things played out—and I didn’t trust you lot to keep my secret.” He gestured at Ather with his pincers. “ at’s al moot now that Ather’s played our hands for us, though … so what’s the new plan?” He eyed the Master of Lies with unmasked contempt. “You going to confront him?” “After what he did to Master Carbad?” Ather said, his eyes widening with just a hint of terror. “Hel s no. I thought we could just leave—but rst I wanted to col ect some insurance.” “Which is?” “Aqlumera,” Ather said, his grin returning as he smoothed the thin line of his mustache. “Tosan didn’t like us entering the vault because he didn’t want people knowing we were sitting on an emperor’s ransom. Just a bottle of that stu would make us rich as kings—and I know folks who’d be more than eager to buy it. So imagine this: we hurry back to Chaenbalu before Kenton realizes we’ve discovered his secret. Murlach stays up here and uses his amulet to convince Kenton we’re al stil with him. When Kenton comes to investigate— and see why we’ve taken o our amulets—the rest of us wil break into the vault. We can grab some more artifacts, steal a few bottles of aqlumera and meet up with Murlach at the old mil . We circle south to the Brake Road and then we go east, away from Luqura and Banok and anywhere else Kenton might think to look for us. If we go to Port Caer, we’l have mountains of gold before the end of the month and can live out our lives in peace. Or we can turn mercenary and sel our services to the highest bidder. e point is we’l have options.” e others watched Murlach, who seemed to have become the de facto alternative to Ather’s leadership. “I don’t think there’s any reason for me to wait here,” Murlach said. “I can choose which thoughts Kenton sees, and I can do that as easily with you in Chaenbalu. And no need to regroup at the mil . We can just grab the aqlumera and get the hel out of these woods.” Der and Denithal glanced at Edra then, surprising him with their deference. e former Master of Arms waited just long enough to acknowledge their unasked question. “It has a certain attractiveness to it. Much better than waiting for Kenton to gure out what to do with us. I’m in.” Der and Denithal nodded—and that was that. One last theft, one nal betrayal, and they would be free of Chaenbalu forever. Murlach went to retrieve the trap he’d left on the road, and Der and Denithal replaced their masks, the former disappearing into an amorphous cloud of black smoke. “Hey, fel as!” Murlach cal ed back to them a minute later, his voice projected by some ingenious artifact inside his suit. “You need to come and look at this!” “What is it?” Ather shouted back, his nimble knee-high boots dancing him out of the tree line and down the slope leading onto the road. “You remember those metal monsters that attacked the Academy?” Murlach asked, a tremor in his voice. “ e twisted ones that ran o into the forest?” “Yes,” Edra said, feeling a cold prickle of fear creep up his neck. “Why? Did you nd one?” “Not sure,” Murlach said, his speaker clicking o as the group approached him from behind. “It looks a lot like one … but also not.” Edra nal y saw the beast caught in the jaws of Murlach’s enormous twiddlesnap: unlike the feral, mutated monsters that had attacked Chaenbalu, this creature seemed . . . wel , not like a creature at al ; more like a man wearing ful plate armor, his body segmented by overlapping metal plates. Metal and stone, Edra amended, slowing. en he realized. at’s not armor … that’s the creature’s esh! “Gods,” Denithal rasped from behind his white mask. “It is one of them!” Ather’s slender rapier hissed from its scabbard and Edra drew his own leaf-bladed long sword. Denithal dipped his hands under his bandolier and popped a red vial from his pocket, and while Edra couldn’t see Der’s gure amidst the cloud of smoke, he assumed the Master of Stealth was similarly preparing for battle. “You can put your pricks away, boys,” Murlach shouted back. “It’s dead.” “From the twiddlesnap?” Der asked amidst his cloud of smoke. “ ose aren’t lethal.” “ ey are when they’re big enough to crush a wagon wheel.” Murlach used his pincers to prod the metal man’s iron head and neck. “How in the name of the Gods does this magic work?” he wondered aloud. “Made of metal and stone … but not a machine. Is it a man … or a golem?” He shook his head, apparently more impressed by the arti cery than concerned by the dark omen of the creature’s presence. “Should we be worried that it was skulking about the East Road?” Edra asked. “No,” Ather said, any fear in his tone concealed beneath his usual veneer of vanity. “ is changes nothing. We go back to Chaenbalu, get the aqlumera, and head to Port Caer.” Murlach dropped the creature’s iron head and stood straight, his mechanized body nearly a foot tal er than without his suit. “We should keep an eye out for more of these buggers, though. If this ferruman is anything like the ones we saw in Chaenbalu, there’l be more—lots more.” Edra was suddenly anxious to get back to the questionable safety of Chaenbalu’s familiar ruins. “Let’s move.” CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN “Does she live?” Kenton asked, leaning dangerously close to the edge of the aqlumera pool. “Show me again. I have to know if she survived.” “She lives, Cursed One. She lives and wil yet live. As I promised, her life is only truly in peril when she returns here. You should not trouble yourself with these visions.” “Show me again, Kiara! I need to know what has happened to her.” e witmistress rubbed her temples then clasped her hands together. “Magic is not free, Kenton. Even when we use the aqlumera instead of the shadepools, there is a cost for scrying, and I do not spend it lightly.” “But those demons nearly kil ed her!” “ ose demons failed—as I foretold.” e Master of Curses ripped his blindfold away and stared into Kiara’s eyes, his own aring with demonic re, their light ickering at the edge of his vision. “Show. Her. Again.” “No.” Kenton’s cheek twitched and his hands shook as if he were about to strangle the woman. Instead, he spun away from the aqlumera cistern and smashed his st against the nearest shelf of artifacts. Magic ared from his Glove of Indomitability and the wood exploded into splinters. A heartbeat later, a catalogue of magic stones toppled to the oor, the rocks and pebbles scattering in al directions. Kiara frowned. “Tantrums do not persuade or inspire obedience. ey are a sign of weakness. A demonstration that you are incapable of leading.” She tucked a lock of hair behind her ear, the rest rmly secured in a neat bun. Since the Academy’s col apse, the other masters and ancients had started to relax, not seeking to impress one another, much less Kenton. Kiara had gone the opposite way, though, becoming even more formal, acting like a teacher in the midst of lecturing a student; her skirts were always clean and ironed, her face was always washed, her hair was always neat. Kenton, by contrast, was a haggard shadow of his former self who cared little for the company of others. e only exceptions were Kiara, whose magic al owed him to watch Myjun in the shadow realm, and Master Aog, whose wil he had entirely dominated. At the moment, the former Master of Punishment was digging a new tunnel from Chaenbalu’s lowest dungeon to the abandoned bakery at the perimeter of the vil age square—a secret tunnel, in case Kenton was ever trapped beneath the Academy again. Kenton had not yet admitted to anyone, not even himself, that he no longer wished to leave the Academy’s ruins. Its tunnels and its magic had become familiar to him, and he was becoming obsessed with the aqlumera pool and watching Myjun. He had no reason or desire to leave—not to wash, not to sleep, not even to eat—and the vault’s artifacts meant he never had to. “I could make you show me,” he growled. “I could force you.” “You can’t and you won’t. Harming me wil ensure you never see Myjun again. So you wil let me rest. You wil see the visions again when I am ready, not when you command. Is that clear?” Kenton’s lips puckered, his skin tightening as he felt his scarred face struggle to contain his scowl. “Quite clear,” he whispered, his voice so low it was almost impossible to hear. “She is not dead, Kenton. She is resting, and it wil take time for her wounds to heal.” “How long?” “Hours. Days. Not long, I suspect. Time passes more swiftly there, but while she is resting, we should rest.” Kenton stroked his scraggly beard. “I don’t like that half man. What he does … what he’s doing to her. He’s kil ing her. Maybe not her body, but her spirit.” “I’m not certain that girl ever real y had a spirit.” Kenton’s eyes ashed, their bril iance almost blinding, their light swel ing to throw back the shadows in the corners of the room. “You know nothing of Myjun.” “Don’t I? She was best friends with my apprentice, and the daughter of the headmaster. I knew her al too wel . Her little schemes, her vanity. I knew her mother too, before she died. Hel s, I practical y raised that girl with the other witwomen. If the Academy had lasted a few more years and her father hadn’t been an obstacle, we would have indoctrinated her into the Brides of Fate.” “Did you know she had magic?” “I did.” “How?” Kiara raised an eyebrow, her cool gray eyes inspecting him. “Come with me.” *** e witmistress’s bedchamber lay two oors above the vault, completely undisturbed by either the Academy’s col apse or the feurog attack, save for the narrow tunnel hidden behind Kiara’s bed. She had already explained how that single tunnel had al owed the feurog to enter the Academy, but she had been less forthcoming about why. “A clean slate,” she’d told him. “No witnesses to pursue us when we left with Annev. No survivors to guide any others to the village.” It had al seemed very cold to Kenton. “What did you want to show me?” he asked, sitting down in a padded rocking chair. “ is.” Kiara handed him a smal black book and Kenton ri ed through its pages. He saw dates, names and numbers—a chart of some kind—and a short description beside each name. In most cases, it also mentioned the parents’ names, or potential strains of magic. “ is is a logbook,” he said, ipping to the end. “A log of . . . stolen children?” “It was our job to locate and monitor infants who might become the Vessel. We abducted them from al over Greater Luqura and brought them here to be trained. One-armed infants were our rst priority, but none of them ever possessed the talent—none until Annev—so instead we kidnapped those likely to inherit the talent, thinking one might lose an arm during their training or an artifact retrieval mission … but it never happened. It was very vexing.” “What’s this?” Kenton asked, showing her an asterisk next to one boy’s name and the bright red letters NM. “Sage Lenka. Is this the Academy’s cook?” “Yes. ‘NM’ means nonmagical. Not every child had magic. Some were taken for political reasons.” “Hold on. ‘Lenka.’ Is that supposed to be King Lenka? As in the King of Greater Luqura.” Kiara nodded. “He had three children. e youngest boy was supposedly stil born, but he’s actual y been cooking the Academy’s meals for the past decade or more.” “You stole a prince?” he breathed. “Damn me. What for?” “Politics, mostly. We had our reasons.” Kenton ipped forward a few more pages and saw his reap mates. “Fyunai Harth … son of Janak Harth?” He looked up. “ at’s the merchant we kil ed in Banok!” “Just a strain of Ironborn in that one—nothing major—but Janak’s mercenary exploits let him amass too much power too quickly. Taking his son was meant to keep the bastard in line … but something went wrong at the reaping. Janak fought back. His wife was kil ed and he was crippled—but we stil managed to steal his son.” “Fyn,” Kenton breathed, head shaking in disbelief. “He kil ed his own father. at prick of a headmaster sent him to kil his own bloody father.” “It was no accident. Tosan was aware of his students’ parental lineage.” Kenton ipped to another page and found his own name. “Reotan NM,” he read beside his nameless father—and beside his unnamed mother . . . “Terran Arti cer?” He looked up. “I’m bloody Terran?” “Of course you are. Al Arti cers are Terran.” “But … I don’t look Terran.” “You have your father’s looks—like a Tir Reotan pirate—and your mother’s magic. She was an Arti cer.” “ ere are no names written here.” “No. We tended not to record the rapists, pirates, or whores.” Kenton’s mouth twitched, but he held his anger in check. “And I was stolen?” “You? No. Your father didn’t want a brat on his ship. Witwoman Kelga purchased you from your mother on the streets of Luqura.” Kenton wanted to ask more but his throat closed up.
