Once you’ve opened a connection to me, I can hear what you’re thinking.” “Is that so?” Kiara said, her thoughts re ecting her utter distaste at the notion. “I think I’l stick to speaking aloud.” “ ere are mages outside the Academy,” Kenton said, sensing Kiara’s thoughts re ected his own. “ ey’l use Stonesmiths and Forgemasters to break into the ruins and search for the vault.” “Yes,” Kiara said, picking up the thread of his thoughts, “and Brayan is with them. is high priestess seems to want to keep him close.” “Can they breach the vault?” “Yes. Brayan knows the way inside, even if the hal ways have been col apsed, and I suspect he knows of the trapdoor as wel .” “He does,” Kenton agreed, remembering a conversation between Elder Tosan and the former quartermaster. “He could point them to either entrance, and their Stonesmiths could bore a tunnel straight to the aqlumera pool. You should leave the vault. Get to higher ground.” “Higher … Kenton, what do you have planned?” “ ere are another thirty ferrumen down in the tunnels,” Kenton said, sprinting to the surface and ying like a bowshot toward the center of town, “and the mages are al converging on the vault, so you should get out. Let them al get underground. Hel , they can even try to breach the vault and steal the aqlumera. Long before they get there, Aog is going to open the tunnels beneath the mil pond.” “And al the water from it and the southern stream wil come crashing down on their heads,” Kiara nished. “ at . . . might work. But it wil almost certainly ood the vault and the Academy’s lower levels.” “I’m counting on it.” “You mean to bury them beneath a lake of water … and lose the aqlumera with it?” “Yes.” ere was only silence from the other end of the talisman. “Witmistress?” he asked, fearing the connection had been broken. “Aog wil likely be kil ed in the ood,” Kiara nal y said, though her thoughts were anywhere but on the man’s safety. “You’re wil ing to sacri ce him, and al of Chaenbalu’s treasures, to win this battle?” “Why reserve our strength for the next battle if we can’t survive this one?” “ at’s not an answer,” Kiara said, her tone at. “It is,” Kenton said, pul ing up short beside the vil age courtyard. “I wil sacri ce everything—every friend, every treasure—to get one step closer to my goal.” “I suppose that answers my next question. You would have let me drown in the vault?” “Yes.” e bluntness of his answer seemed to give the witmistress pause. “You’re not even going to pretend you would have saved me?” “No. I expected you to save yourself—or to contact me earlier.” “Mm. Very touching.” e thoughts and feelings that reverberated back to Kenton through the amulet were the opposite of what he felt in the woman’s tone. Was she … proud of him? Had his decision to sacri ce the witmistress paradoxical y made her more fond of him? “You are strange,” Kenton whispered through the bond of the amulet. “My decision to sacri ce your life should not engender such pride.” “I did the same when I sacri ced al of Chaenbalu’s inhabitants to nd Annev.” ey were both silent then, and Kenton felt he understood the cunning old witwoman better. “ ey are coming,” he said, sweeping the ruins with his vision. “ e mages are inside the ruins—and the ferrumen are approaching from the other tunnels.” “Yes,” Kiara said, her tone preoccupied. “I need to col ect some things from the vault before it oods. I’l meet you outside … if I can.” e connection broke o abruptly and Kenton assumed she had reentered the vault. With measured movements, Kenton removed his blindfold and set it on the ground. He stared into dark and watched the ferrumen in the tunnels beneath his feet. Nearly al of them and their mages were accounted for. is was good. ey’d tightened the noose, and then hanged themselves with it. Suddenly the ground beneath his feet shook and Kenton saw the whoosh of air and water push through the catacombs beneath Chaenbalu. He felt the connection to Aog’s amulet grow faint as the man su ocated beneath a ton of earth and water, and then their connection disappeared entirely. He watched the water roar through the tunnels beneath his feet and witnessed each life as it was drowned out. Two mages tried to open new tunnels—tried to nd a way to escape—but they were too slow. e current took their bodies and their spirits. With barely a thought, Kenton withdrew his Shadow Bow and nocked an arrow, expecting to see at least one of them claw their way back to the surface. Some came close, but not before the water claimed them. e pink-eyed messenger who had escaped Mercy’s blade and Aog’s spade lasted the longest, holding out several minutes in an air pocket inside the underground arena formerly used for Tests of Judgment. In the end, though, she too was drowned. He saw no sign of the witmistress, nor did he know how he felt about that absence. “Kenton.” e witwoman’s voice crackled at the other end of his talisman and he smiled. “You’re alive,” he said, surprised by the warmth he felt for her and her unconquerable spirit. “Where did you wash up?” “ e Brakewood,” she said, sounding exhausted. “You forgot to seal the tunnel in my private chamber—the one I used to bring the feurog into Chaenbalu.” “Ah,” Kenton said. “Of course.” “You didn’t forget, did you?” Silence. “You left it open on purpose.” “I stil need you, Kiara,” Kenton said, tucking the Shadow Bow back into his cloak without a hint of remorse. “You’re the only one who can show me Myjun’s progress in the shadow realm … and I’d miss your mentorship.” “Is that sentiment, young Master Kenton? And here I thought you were wil ing to sacri ce everything to achieve your goals.” “Oh, I am. But only a fool sacri ces something he does not need to lose.” “Wise words, Master Kenton. Meet me in the Brakewood then, near the old shadepool where we watched Myjun enter the shadow realm. Perhaps there we can continue your apprenticeship.” Kenton broke his mind-link with the witmistress and turned one last gaze on the ruins of the Academy and the surrounding vil age. He felt a queer sense of nostalgia for the old village, which was quickly dispel ed by his subsequent vision of the dead mages and monsters drowned in the ooded tunnels. Not one stirred there—not one had escaped the destruction—and that seemed good to him. Perhaps it meant the Academy’s ghosts had nal y been laid to rest. Perhaps it might even lay his own ghosts to rest. With ritualistic slowness, Kenton picked up the black bandage and covered his lidless eyes—then he strode into the darkness of the night, and the deeper darkness of the Brakewood. CHAPTER FIFTY-SEVEN Myjun danced between the lines of Yomad warriors laying siege to the great wal . Arrows ew like rain behind her, their ne Terran broadheads punching through chainmail and crashing into the exposed arms, loins, and faces of the men clustered about her. e shattered remnants of one arrow de ected o the breastplate of the man behind her and shot through her calf, shooting pain up her leg and spiking her body with a rush of adrenaline and magical strength. She slapped a hand to her leg and ripped the shaft from her esh, causing a second ash of pain and a rush of strength as her magic stitched her ruptured skin and muscle back together. A swarthy Yomad in a lthy beige tunic stepped ahead of his companions and stabbed the point of his spear toward Myjun’s side. She dodged, al owing its edge to nick her as she stepped in close. e weapon bounced o her hip and her soulblades plunged into the man’s chest. In the space of a heartbeat, his eyes burned to ash and his corpse dropped to the sand. A heavy long sword swung for Myjun’s neck. She sensed its weight as it moved through space, felt the air pushed ahead of the blade. She smel ed the tang of forged steel and the musk of the soldier’s sweat as he brought the weapon down to meet the base of her skul . Myjun rol ed forward, her momentum fol owing the direction of the sword. As she fel , she dispel ed her rst knife and extended the length of the second. Her empty left hand hit the ground, catching her fal just as the Yomad’s sword passed overhead. She exed, pushed herself back to her feet and spun. e soul re sword in her right hand clove through her attacker’s bracer and forearm and then she swept it backward to decapitate him. More arrows pounded the earth beside her feet and the Yomads clustered nearby began to scatter, their ragged battalion retreating to the tal ivory towers that dotted the length and breadth of the Neck. Myjun watched them go then al owed her sword to disappear in a ash of light. Arrows chased the soldiers til they pul ed out of range, but an insulting number stil pattered down around her, their feathered butts popping up from the soil like strange owers in a mud-churned garden of death and blood. Myjun wiped her blood-spattered face, leaving long streaks of crimson along her golden cheeks, delicate brow and shining jawbone. Another arrow ew past, this time grazing her shoulder. She merely gritted her teeth. “ ey ee from you.” e voice came from the shadows of the trench the Yomads had abandoned. “As they should,” Myjun growled. She licked her cracked lips behind the mask and imagined the coppery taste of the blood on her face and the texture of the soldiers’ esh between her teeth. She was so hungry … yet her body felt ful . As always, their deaths had strengthened her. Oyru looked to the looming Harwal behind them, its length disappearing leagues into the distance, its ancient stones protecting the southeastern corner of the Terran Empire. “We should go. e archers wil keep ring so long as we stay in range. ey do not know you ght for them, even though you’ve kil ed a hundred of the Yomads.” As if to emphasize his point, an arrow plunged through the half man’s chest, and exited more slowly from his back. A plume of black vapor trailed the injury and the assassin’s esh knitted itself back together. He climbed from the shadows then beckoned Myjun to fol ow, and they moved away from the Terran soldiers on the great wal , strol ing toward the eeing Yomads. “I do not ght for them,” Myjun snapped, nodding back at the towering wal that blocked the other end of the isthmus. “I ght for myself. I would kil them, too, if you would let me.” Oyru’s nger rose to trace the black scar that marked his missing eye. “ ose soldiers belong to the Legions of Keos, which makes them our al ies.” “I have no al ies.” “Not even me? Not after I risked my own life and sacri ced this for you?” Oyru tapped the withered eye socket, its esh puckered tight in contrast to the wide, unblinking eye pinning her with its soul ess glare. “ at was months ago—and I didn’t ask you to save me, you half-demon bastard.” e words hissed from her like steam from a kettle. “You’re not a savior or a rotting martyr. You’re a conjurer, a kil er, and a bloody liar. Al you do is torture me and tel me to kil , and delay ful l ing your promises.” Oyru shrugged as if her words meant nothing, which only enraged Myjun further. “I wil ful l my promises,” the Shadow Reborn said, resuming their walk. “We have made good progress these past few weeks.” “Months,” Myjun corrected. “It’s been ve months.” “Only if you reckon time by the blinks of Dorchnok’s Eye. Barely three weeks of traveling in the physical realm, and we have already reached the last leg of our journey.” e assassin gestured to the eld of ivory towers dotting the narrow isthmus of Lubree, a no-man’s-land that separated the continents of New and Old Terra. “Terra Minora lies just beyond the Neck, protected by the endless towers and the Spear of Tacharan. Once you are sated, we wil cross back into the shadow realm here in Lubree—at the Noose of the Neck—and from here pass into Takarania and Terra Minora.” He pointed to a speck on the horizon that could barely be seen above the heads of the innumerable towers ahead of them. “You see that lone tower? It is the Spear of Tacharan. It marks the end of the Neck of Lubree and the beginning of Takarania. Powerful magics protect it and the land surrounding it, preventing entry. Even sailors must avoid the isthmus and its shores and travel to Al tara in the south or Krosera in the north. We wil avoid its curse, though, by crossing the Neck in the shadow realm.” “And how much farther to Al tara?” Myjun asked, unable to conceal the venom in her tone. “Terra Minora is the home of three peoples: the Shalgarns of Al tara, the Yomads of Takarania, and my people in Krosera.” Oyru gestured past the isthmus. “Takarania lies at the center of Terra Minora and borders the Neck. It is a bu er between the shadowlands of Krosera and wildlands of Al tara, which we must pass through to reach the Iron Mountains and the trol clans. Doing so wil also bring us close to the obelisks that guard the House of Brass at the center of Takarania—perilous in either realm.” “So we must stil avoid them? Even after traveling into the shadow realm?” “We must, but for separate reasons. In this world, the Brazen Towers mark the borders of Takarania and are abutted by the mountains of Al tara. East of the mountains is the House of Brass, home to the priests who worship the God of Death. In the shadow realm, their temple overlaps the Heart of the Void— the center of Reocht na Skah.” “I thought you said it’s dangerous to go to Reocht na Skah—that we could get trapped there for eternity.” “Just so. To avoid both, we wil enter the shadows and cross beyond the Neck. at wil take us beyond the reach of the Spear of Tacharan. We wil then remain in the shadow realm and skirt the edge of Takarania to avoid entangling ourselves with the magic of Reocht na Skah. If we turn immediately southwest, that wil take us directly into the Al taran mountains and trol territory.” “To get my rotting armor.” “Yes.” “And then you wil take me back to the Empire to kil Annev.” “Yes.” “Fine. Let’s go.” Oyru gestured at the soldiers who had nal y reached the safety of their ivory towers. “You have satis ed your bloodlust?” He asked the question as though he were o ering her a nibble of a scone instead of the lives of a half-dozen men and women. “We wil not return to the physical world again—not til we reach Al tara—so you should take your l now.” “My hunger is never satis ed,” Myjun said, not bothering to hide her bitterness, “but I wil survive the trip.” Oyru nodded. “ e distance between here and Al tara would take a week to traverse over land—assuming we were unmolested by the Yomads and their magics. In the shadow realm it wil take a month or more … but time wil distort even more as we cross into Takarania. e greatest eidola also concentrate there, near the borders of Reocht na Skah, and that wil slow our pace further. at means it wil likely take us considerably longer than ve weeks to reach the trol mountains—at least, so long as we are traveling in the shadow realm.” “How much time wil al of this take in the physical realm?” “Stil a week by standard time, but we wil be stuck in the shadows for two months at least. And if we choose to venture nearer to southern Takarania— toward the heart of Reocht na Skah—it could be even longer.” “So why not return to the physical world once we are past the dangers of the Spear of Tacharan?” Oyru eyed her with his remaining black eye, its stare penetrating her to the core. “Because I believe the extra time and training would bene t you. You have grown much over these past ve months, but you stil lack ful control of your powers. You have not learned to bend or re ect the light as Bladesingers and Lightslingers do. You’ve learned to channel its baser elements—to summon your soulblades and channel the light re—but it seems the subtler arts are beyond you.” “And what do you know of the light, half man? You’re a master of the shadows. You couldn’t even teach me to summon the light, much less shape it. I learned that myself.” “Only because I forced you to.” He raised a hand to scratch the corner of his empty eye socket. Myjun sni ed. Perhaps he regretted his decision to save her, though if he did, Oyru never expressed it—and the omission hurt her more than any accusation. “I wil not delay my vengeance forever,” she asserted. “We should go west, straight into the mountains of Al tara. Reocht na Skah can keep its monsters and its secrets—and I would prefer we keep our current pace. If we stay in the shadow realm but keep close to the shoreline, that could be the fastest route of al .” Oyru said nothing, looking east—past the towers along the isthmus and toward a green coast that was almost entirely shrouded in mist. “We are close to Krosera now. If we crossed the Neck and went northeast instead of southwest, we would be in my homeland.” He looked wistful—and then he raised his face scarf and it was hidden. Myjun stared at him as if she’d just been slapped across the face. e man had been frowning—actual y frowning. “You don’t fear the death priests or the eidolons,” she said, accusing. “You’re not even afraid of spending a thousand years in the shadow of Reocht na Skah … but you are afraid of going home—and even then you tease yourself with it. Your words imply we might go there, yet you clearly wish to stay away. Why? What terrors do Krosera’s shadowlands hold for you?” Oyru turned to face her, his scarf fal ing away, his normal y stoic demeanor replaced by one of hatred and fear. “ e Kroserans and their impotent Shadow God can go to hel ,” Oyru said, his words colder than they had ever been. “We are bound for Al tara. I wil hasten our journey as you’ve requested—and you wil not speak of my homeland again.” As he said these last words, he covered his mouth and nose more completely, though the black fabric could not hide the tiny tear that trickled from the corner of the assassin’s eye. He dabbed it with his scarf, erasing the proof that he did indeed have a soul—but not before Myjun saw it. CHAPTER FIFTY-EIGHT “Why do you serve Keos instead of Dorchnok?” ey were back in the shadow realm and long past the Neck of Lubree. In their crossing, she had seen no evidence of the endless ivory towers that protected the isthmus, nor any shadow of the lone and awful Spear of Tacharan. She had instead seen black waves of smoke that l ed the depths of the Sauthron and Estron Seas. When she had later asked what happened to those that tried to sail those dark waters in the shadow realm, Oyru snorted, shook his head, and muttered something unintel igible about Voidweavers. e reaction seemed entirely out of character for the usual y stoic assassin, and the adjustment in her relationship with the Shadow Reborn left Myjun feeling adrift. At the same time, the assassin’s odd mood seemed to invite a more personal connection—something Myjun felt open to now they had left the physical world and the perpetual rage of her mask had been dimmed and dul ed. “I do not serve Keos,” Oyru said, morose. “I serve Dortafola and he serves Keos.” “Which is the same thing—and you did not answer my question. Why did you abandon your worship of Dorchnok?” “Are you not equal y impious? Did you not abandon your worship of Odar to fol ow me?” “ at’s di erent. I was damned—marked by Keos—and I had no choice. Not if I want to kil Annev.” Oyru said nothing for a long, long time. When he nal y did speak, it was with the measured words of someone who was unused to speech—as if the person behind the mask were speaking to her for the rst time. “I was betrayed once. Like you, I loved someone and was betrayed by them. She wasn’t Kroseran. She came from an Ilumite clan in Faer Fen and sailed across the Estron Sea to Northern Krosera. She pledged herself to me and then she wooed another Kroseran warrior—a warlord named Gevul the Terrible— and helped him destroy my house and my family. I kil ed Gevul, but not before he kil ed her . . . the woman I stil loved.” Oyru stared at the black waters, his face unreadable. “I tried to save her, I tried to bring her back—but Dorchnok would not heed my prayers. He did not save my family, he did not save her, and he could not save me.” e assassin turned south and pointed to the smoky horizon. “I ventured into Reocht na Skah. I thought that if I could reach into the Spirit World, I might persuade Oraqui to come back to me.” He xed his eye on Myjun. “She was a dualist—an Auramancer and a Lightslinger —but she could only do two things with her magic: she could manipulate others’ emotions and she could project il usions—re ections of the people and things nearby her. You have similar powers … sometimes you remind me of her.” He looked back to the horizon. “You entered Reocht na Skah,” Myjun said, her voice quiet. “I did.” “To the Heart of the Void.” “To the very center, yes.” Myjun swal owed. “How long were you gone? How long did you search for her?” “A week or two.” “A week or … in the Heart of the Void? When a day here is a thousand years there?” Oyru’s single eye shifted back to her, his usual stoic look back in place. “What made you leave? Or did you just give up?” She hadn’t meant it as a jab, though it came out that way. Stil , if Oyru was o ended he did not show it. “Dortafola came looking for me. Gevul had been one of his Siänar and when the man was kil ed … wel , he needed a replacement. Who better than the man who kil ed Gevul? He tracked me through the shadow realm to Reocht na Skah and promised that if I served him—that if I forsook my worship of Dorchnok and fol owed him—he would return Oraqui to me.” “And did he?” Oyru stared at her, his face a mask. “Maybe,” he said—and a chil went up her spine. *** “So you learned about Ilumite magic from her?” Oyru said nothing. He hadn’t spoken since their last conversation, two antumbras ago. Not a word. ey had turned southwest toward Al tara, keeping the black mists of the Sauthron Sea to their right and the endless gray plains to their left, and Myjun was tired of the shared silence. “She taught you about her magic, maybe even her people, and in return you taught her about Krosera and your magic.” Silence. “What made you think your master could bring her back?” More silence. “ is was hers, wasn’t it? is mask.” She tapped her gilded temple and forehead. “Did Gevul give it to her?” “Do not speak his name,” Oyru breathed, his voice as cold as ice—as cold as death. “Or what?” Myjun demanded, both relieved he had broken his silence and angry he had kept it for so long. “Wil you beat me? I wil drink the pain. Kil me? I don’t think so.” “I would leave you here,” Oyru said, his tone stil apathetic, though Myjun wondered if even his apathy was a mask. “I would leave you in the shadows, trapped here forever, and return to the physical world without you. You may have grown stronger, but you cannot traverse the planes of existence. You would be doomed to waste away until al life had left you and you became an eidolon.” “Is that what happened to you?” Myjun demanded. “Because you stayed so long in Reocht na Skah?” “Yes.” Myjun was satis ed. “ en I wil not speak that name again.” Oyru focused on a black xture that blanketed the horizon. “We are approaching the shadows of the Al taran mountains,” he said. “We are almost to our nal destination.” “We made good time, then.” Myjun stepped beside him, sharing the view. ough it seemed the land had been at for these many miles, she saw now that they had been climbing a long, gently rising hil . Al around them the ground gradual y fel away, the decline slow and steady behind them, almost imperceptible. Ahead, the slope grew more abrupt, rst fal ing and then rising again with greater height and severity. is pattern continued until the ground erupted in the black wal of mountains that stained the distant horizon.

chunks.content: Edra gave him a pointed look. “You just manipulated Der,” he accused. “How is that any di erent than what Kenton’s doing?” “Because,” Ather said, smiling wickedly, “I’m me and he’s not.” Edra sni ed but didn’t argue the point. Murlach and Der were back a minute later, the former frowning from within the nest of cables and wires surrounding his face and neck. “What’s al this about Kenton?” “He’s been spying on us,” Edra said, before Ather could o er a more garrulous explanation—Keos, that man could talk. “Ather gured out the amulets were involved somehow,” he continued. “You stil wearing yours?” A tentacled arm sprang to life at Murlach’s side, the pronged tip slithering into his armor. ere was a loud hissing sound and then his exoskeleton split open. “So,” he said, “you nal y gured it out.” “Figured what out?” Edra said, a moment before Der. “ e talismans.” Murlach’s tentacle retreated from his armor, its pincers drawing the amulet over his head before displaying the artifact for al to see. “I wondered how long it would take. Which of you was it?” Down the road, one of Murlach’s twiddlesnap contraptions clanked shut, eliciting a squeal as some poor animal was snapped and snared—but the rest of them gave it no mind. Edra pointed to Ather, head shaking as he said to Murlach, “If you’ve known this whole time, why would you wear it?” Murlach spun the talisman in front of Edra’s face so that he saw a peculiar drop of silver clinging to the amulet’s ruby. “What’s that?” Der asked, stepping forward to examine the artifact. “Some kind of … metal spider?” Edra grunted in agreement. e addition to the amulet did look like some sort of metal ic arachnid, with eight tiny legs and a blood-red thorax that matched the ruby beneath it. Murlach let each man see it in turn. “When we were down in the vault, I saw another half-dozen of these talismans sitting on a shelf at the back of the chamber—al with these metal spiders attached to them. at got me wondering, so I started poking around and found six unattached spiders sitting on the lower shelf. Didn’t take a genius to gure Kenton had modi ed ours, so I snatched one of the spider-amulets and gave it a closer look. Tried to gure out what kind of tricks our cursed leader was trying to pul on us.” “And?” Murlach’s silvery tentacle dropped the amulet back over his neck. “ e spiders alter the magic a bit. Instead of al owing Kenton to always hear my thoughts, they let me choose which ones to share and which to keep to myself.” “Why not tel the rest of us?” Der asked, his brow furrowed. Murlach shrugged. “I wanted to see how things played out—and I didn’t trust you lot to keep my secret.” He gestured at Ather with his pincers. “ at’s al moot now that Ather’s played our hands for us, though … so what’s the new plan?” He eyed the Master of Lies with unmasked contempt. “You going to confront him?” “After what he did to Master Carbad?” Ather said, his eyes widening with just a hint of terror. “Hel s no. I thought we could just leave—but rst I wanted to col ect some insurance.” “Which is?” “Aqlumera,” Ather said, his grin returning as he smoothed the thin line of his mustache. “Tosan didn’t like us entering the vault because he didn’t want people knowing we were sitting on an emperor’s ransom. Just a bottle of that stu would make us rich as kings—and I know folks who’d be more than eager to buy it. So imagine this: we hurry back to Chaenbalu before Kenton realizes we’ve discovered his secret. Murlach stays up here and uses his amulet to convince Kenton we’re al stil with him. When Kenton comes to investigate— and see why we’ve taken o our amulets—the rest of us wil break into the vault. We can grab some more artifacts, steal a few bottles of aqlumera and meet up with Murlach at the old mil . We circle south to the Brake Road and then we go east, away from Luqura and Banok and anywhere else Kenton might think to look for us. If we go to Port Caer, we’l have mountains of gold before the end of the month and can live out our lives in peace. Or we can turn mercenary and sel our services to the highest bidder. e point is we’l have options.” e others watched Murlach, who seemed to have become the de facto alternative to Ather’s leadership. “I don’t think there’s any reason for me to wait here,” Murlach said. “I can choose which thoughts Kenton sees, and I can do that as easily with you in Chaenbalu. And no need to regroup at the mil . We can just grab the aqlumera and get the hel out of these woods.” Der and Denithal glanced at Edra then, surprising him with their deference. e former Master of Arms waited just long enough to acknowledge their unasked question. “It has a certain attractiveness to it. Much better than waiting for Kenton to gure out what to do with us. I’m in.” Der and Denithal nodded—and that was that. One last theft, one nal betrayal, and they would be free of Chaenbalu forever. Murlach went to retrieve the trap he’d left on the road, and Der and Denithal replaced their masks, the former disappearing into an amorphous cloud of black smoke. “Hey, fel as!” Murlach cal ed back to them a minute later, his voice projected by some ingenious artifact inside his suit. “You need to come and look at this!” “What is it?” Ather shouted back, his nimble knee-high boots dancing him out of the tree line and down the slope leading onto the road. “You remember those metal monsters that attacked the Academy?” Murlach asked, a tremor in his voice. “ e twisted ones that ran o into the forest?” “Yes,” Edra said, feeling a cold prickle of fear creep up his neck. “Why? Gevul had been one of his Siänar and when the man was kil ed … wel , he needed a replacement. Who better than the man who kil ed Gevul? He tracked me through the shadow realm to Reocht na Skah and promised that if I served him—that if I forsook my worship of Dorchnok and fol owed him—he would return Oraqui to me.” “And did he?” Oyru stared at her, his face a mask. “Maybe,” he said—and a chil went up her spine. *** “So you learned about Ilumite magic from her?” Oyru said nothing. He hadn’t spoken since their last conversation, two antumbras ago. Not a word. ey had turned southwest toward Al tara, keeping the black mists of the Sauthron Sea to their right and the endless gray plains to their left, and Myjun was tired of the shared silence. “She taught you about her magic, maybe even her people, and in return you taught her about Krosera and your magic.” Silence. “What made you think your master could bring her back?” More silence. “ is was hers, wasn’t it? is mask.” She tapped her gilded temple and forehead. “Did Gevul give it to her?” “Do not speak his name,” Oyru breathed, his voice as cold as ice—as cold as death. “Or what?” Myjun demanded, both relieved he had broken his silence and angry he had kept it for so long. “Wil you beat me? I wil drink the pain. Kil me? I don’t think so.” “I would leave you here,” Oyru said, his tone stil apathetic, though Myjun wondered if even his apathy was a mask. “I would leave you in the shadows, trapped here forever, and return to the physical world without you. You may have grown stronger, but you cannot traverse the planes of existence. You would be doomed to waste away until al life had left you and you became an eidolon.” “Is that what happened to you?” Myjun demanded. “Because you stayed so long in Reocht na Skah?” “Yes.” Myjun was satis ed. “ en I wil not speak that name again.” Oyru focused on a black xture that blanketed the horizon. “We are approaching the shadows of the Al taran mountains,” he said. “We are almost to our nal destination.” “We made good time, then.” Myjun stepped beside him, sharing the view. ough it seemed the land had been at for these many miles, she saw now that they had been climbing a long, gently rising hil . Al around them the ground gradual y fel away, the decline slow and steady behind them, almost imperceptible. Ahead, the slope grew more abrupt, rst fal ing and then rising again with greater height and severity. is pattern continued until the ground erupted in the black wal of mountains that stained the distant horizon.

chunks.title: Chapter 9
chunks.content: “How can these exist here?” Myjun asked, her eyes xed on the mountain range. “Near as I can tel , it re ects their proximity to Reocht na Skah. e power of the shadow realm lies thick on the mountains in the physical world, so their re ection in this world is more solid. It is the reason Al tara’s ironwood trees can be seen here and why another species grows in the hil s of Krosera—and why they cannot be cultivated anywhere else.” “Ironwood?” Myjun sni ed. “We have bushes of the stu in Western Daroea.” “A mongrel subspecies, no doubt transplanted by the Druids in Fertil Hedge. ey are not the same. Even the ironwood trees in Krosera are di erent from those here. Not worse—not mutated like your own shrubs—but di erent.” Myjun rol ed her eyes and let it drop, ready to move on. Oyru wasn’t. He pointed at the gray ring above their heads. “It is time to meditate. Also …” He tilted his head. “Something is hunting us.” Myjun spun, her eyes searching the horizon in every direction. From her vantage point, though, the plains looked empty. “Is there another waste nearby? I would have spotted—” “No waste. What hunts us is not so easily seen, nor is it attracted to the dreams and nightmares that bubble up from the cognitive realm.” “What is it then? An eidolon?” Oyru stood in silence for a long while, his eyes stil locked on the mountain range ahead of them. “You recal I said someone who was trapped here in the shadow realm would waste away and become eidola?” “Yes.” “ at was an oversimpli cation. People do not become shadow demons— not truly—they become something worse.” “Worse than shadow demons?” “Flesh wraiths … and witherkin.” “Wraiths and witherkin,” Myjun said, tasting the words. “Some kind of ghost? Something that eats our esh?” “Yes … and yes.” “And what hunts us?” “It is too soon to tel .” Myjun’s skin prickled with fear, and she found herself responding with anger. “So what the hel does it want? Why is it hunting us?” “Because,” Oyru said, his eye turning to face her, “I sent it here. I trapped it in the shadow realm when I attacked your vil age.” Myjun met Oyru’s gaze and the blood slowly drained from her face. “You mean a ghost is trying to kil us, and it’s somebody from Chaenbalu?” Oyru nodded. “It could not have fol owed us here without my noticing, but it might have used the aqlumera as a dimensional gate to Reocht na Skah.” “We can do that?” Oyru shook his head. “Not us. A Voidweaver or a Dark Lord could, but I am only a Shadowcaster.” “ en how … “ “I don’t know, tabibito. I only know it is someone from your vil age. A man, I think, or he was a man once.” “How long has he been fol owing us?” “Since the last umbra.” “And where is he now?” “Hiding. He seems to favor the deeper darkness of the umbra, so he stays out of sight of Dorchnok’s Eye. at is why we should meditate now, before the antumbra passes. Because when the umbra is here, I think we wil have a visitor—one that might crave our esh in addition to our spirits.” *** Myjun stared up at the black sky and wondered how any kind of light existed in this endless world of shadows. ere were no stars overhead, yet she felt as if she stood beneath the starlight of a moonless sky. And when the gray ring of Dorchnok’s Eye rose on the horizon, that starlight became more akin to moonlight. At the peak of the antumbra, when the eye stood directly above their heads, it was almost as bright as dawn or dusk in the physical world—yet there was no sun, moon, or star: the light simply was. Myjun had come to think of it as shadowlight, which softened the darkness of the shadow realm’s deeper blackness. Now, with Dorchnok’s Eye absent from the sky and the shadowlight faded to darkness, the umbral night possessed an alien intensity. Strangely, though, the black smoke of the Sauthron Sea seemed to sparkle more brightly during the umbra, as if its own luminescence increased when it did not have to compete with shadowlight or the Dorchnok’s antumbral eye. ey were camped near those shimmering waters now, its black vapors lapping at the gray land. Yet as Myjun turned her gaze across the wide, nethereal sea, it seemed more like a veil of stars. “He is coming,” Oyru said, rising from his meditative trance. “ e esh wraith?” Myjun asked. “Or the witherkin, yes. I glimpsed his form at the last umbra. I meant to kil him then, before he could hunt us, but he disappeared.” He pointed into the black vapors of the ocean. “And now he has returned.” Myjun stared into the night-black vapors and saw that where most of the waters stil sparkled with light, a space near the shore had lost its luminescence. Not long after that, she realized the darkness had the shape of a man and was coming toward them. “Do you know … before he was taken …” “Who he was?” Oyru shook his head. “I do not know the names nor do I recal the faces of the people the eidola stole from your vil age. I only wanted Annev.” e darkness drew closer and, as it did, Myjun saw more of the shade’s features revealed by the shadowlight: the broad forehead, the long nose and narrow eyes. It took her another moment, but then she knew the wraith’s identity for herself. “ at’s Yohan … the village chandler.” “A candlemaker. Interesting. His wil must have been strong to survive al this time.” Myjun remembered the chandler’s forceful personality, her anxiety rising. “Have you determined what he wants?” Oyru stared at the shade, his single eye squinting into the darkness. “Flesh wraiths crave life and take it in the form of esh. Witherkin want vengeance. ey have un nished business and won’t rest til it is ful l ed.” Oyru summoned his twin yssas and stepped purposeful y forward. “And this one is … ?” Myjun took a step back as the chandler’s ghost drew nearer. Oyru’s twin swords passed through the chandler’s shade, cutting the ghost neatly through the neck and chest. e blades passed through Yohan’s body without any resistance and then emerged out the other side. en the ghost’s eyes opened wide and shifted from night-black to pure white. “Witherkin!” Oyru said, dispel ing the blades. “Run!” Matching words to actions, the assassin bolted from their camp by the waters and ew straight as an arrow toward the dark mountains on the horizon. Myjun fol owed a heartbeat later, her soulblades screaming into existence in her hands. “Why are we running from a chandler’s ghost!” she shouted, not looking back to see if the witherkin was fol owing them. “ at is a spirit trapped in the cognitive realm,” Oyru bel owed. “ ey are to the shadow realm what the eidola are to the physical world: abominations. Nightmares. Void blades do not harm them, and they wil devour your mind and your somnumbra. ey are the wandering death of this land!” “You could have told me this before!” “Flesh wraiths are rare. Witherkin are almost nonexistent.” “Wel , this one seems pretty damn existent!” ey ran on in silence, their eet pace carrying them swiftly over the rol ing hil s toward the mountains. “Wil my soulblades kil it?” “Not likely. is stupid candlemaker is only partial y here. is is an echo of him; the rest has perished or moved on to the Spirit World.” “So how do we kil him?” “We don’t. He is dead already—but his mind wil not relent. If we give him what he wants, he may pass over.” Myjun ventured a glance back and saw the black ocean shore recede into the distance. ere was no sign of the witherkin. “Can we stop? I can’t see him.” “No. Witherkin are not tethered to this space, just as we are not temporal y tethered to space in the physical realm.” “Speak sense!” “He is not behind us because he is not actual y here.” “I said sense!” Oyru stopped abruptly and Myjun had to pivot to avoid crashing into him. He gestured at the rol ing hil s ahead of them and the sloping shores at their backs. “He is a shadow of the cognitive realm. His wil is causing him to manifest here, but he is not actual y here.” “ en why are we running from him!” Myjun shouted, her temper aring. As if in response to her question, a black shadow began to coalesce beside them, its glaring white eyes burning like the wrath of the sun. “Because of that,” Oyru said, and then he resumed his sprint. “How in the ve hel s can he do that!” “Nine Hel s,” Oyru said, not breaking stride. “But your question is stil valid. He’s not tethered to this plane, so as soon as we stop moving, he can shift to wherever we’ve run to.” “So,” Myjun said, gulping for breath, “we have to keep moving inde nitely?” “Until Dorchnok’s Eye rises and antumbra dawns … yes.” “Shit.” ey ran on in silence, neither one daring to look back, until Myjun slowed to a walk. Oyru ran on for a dozen paces, then turned. “What are you doing?” “If al we have to do is keep moving, we can walk. We don’t need to run.” Oyru stared at her blank-faced. en, as if realizing he had stopped moving, he jogged to catch up with Myjun and then kept pace beside her. ey walked in silence for a hundred paces, then Myjun snorted aloud. “I can’t believe you never thought to walk.” “ ey are not something I encounter often,” Oyru said, his voice strained. “What did you do last time? Run like an idiot?” e assassin peered sideways at her. “I am not usual y toting around a tabibito, much less one who cannot shift themselves to the physical world.” “So you run away … to another plane. You go to the physical world and hope it forgets about you?” Oyru exhaled. “Basical y.” Myjun laughed, her tone ful of spite. “You’re pathetic. You’re supposed to be this terrible, undying kil er who can pop out of the shadows and murder you—and here you are running from the ghost of a candlemaker.” “Witherkin,” Oyru said, his tone just shy of sul en. “He is not just a ghost. He is a witherkin.” Myjun slowed her pace even further then stopped. Oyru walked two more steps then stopped too. “What are you doing?” he asked. “Testing something.” She concentrated and summoned her soulblades. A moment later, the chandler’s shade appeared beside them, his black mouth yawning open in a silent scream. Myjun took a cautious step toward the specter and then rammed her daggers of light into the ghost’s eyes. e witherkin’s face contorted into a look of shock, then rage. His eyes ared, growing wider, brighter, and the chandler’s black hands reached out for her. Myjun stepped away, out of reach, then started walking. Oyru was just a step behind and, behind them, the witherkin’s eyes grew dim and his black form faded into the shadowlight. “I had to try,” Myjun said, dispel ing her soul re blades. “Obviously—and now you see why witherkin are not so easily vanquished.” Myjun grunted. “So are you witherkin?” “No. Maybe. Perhaps if I al owed one of the eidola to consume my soul, I would become one.” “Or a esh wraith?” “No. My body has grown too accustomed to somnumbra. I can survive on that alone … but that means I cannot stay in the physical world for too long. I am dependent on this world. I have become one of its denizens.” Myjun nodded, piecing it al together. “You had un nished business with Oraqui. You searched Reocht na Skah for her, for seven thousand years. Time warped and stretched and you became dependent on somnumbra … and you became a half shadow, half man.” Oyru kept pace beside her. “Annumbra,” he said. “Years in the shadow realm are cal ed annumbra … and I spent ten or twelve thousand of them in Reocht na Skah. Waiting. Searching. Praying for her to return to me.” “Do you regret it?” Myjun asked. “Sometimes,” he said, that single eye xed on the horizon, “I regret that I did not wait longer.” CHAPTER FIFTY-NINE Having passed their Tests of Ascendancy, erin and Titus established new routines with the journeymen and Dionachs from their respective castes. e most notable of these was Titus receiving instruction on the more nuanced arts of mindwalking, including how to enter an unguarded person’s mind and browse their dormant memories. e former steward was innately better at it than every journeyman in his caste, and that talent a rmed Dionach Holyoak’s decision to elevate him to ful Dionach. With that promotion, Brother Tym also began teaching Titus the principles of mind-leeching: drawing on another person’s thoughts and absorbing them, as if one’s own. Mind-leeching could also erase memories from a subject’s mind, but Dionach Holyoak and Brother Tym both agreed it would be prudent to master one aspect of the skil at a time. For erin, life at the Enclave had become far more interesting as a journeyman Breathbreaker. e skil s he practiced with Dionach Honeycutt and his fel ow journeymen weren’t altogether new, but their application required a new level of complexity, nuance, and creativity. He used vacuum bubbles to scale sheer wal s, cling to ceilings, and run up vertical surfaces. With the application of air and sound bubbles, he learned how to silence himself and those around him, how to create explosions with displaced air and how to propel himself with almost no friction or loss of momentum. He described his training in detail to Titus and Annev, thril ed by each new discovery and excited about combining them with the martial skil s he’d learned at the Academy. For Annev’s part, life at the Enclave had changed just as drastical y since the theft of the booby-trapped painting. Before the attack, he’d been determined to leave—to do anything except wait for Reeve to decide his future. But now he had a purpose again. He had a suspect, and he was tired of running from people who meant him harm. He’d tried to hide in Chaenbalu and they had sent the feurog and the Shadow Reborn. He’d gone to Banok and an assassin with a crossbow had tried to murder him. He’d ed to Luqura and been chased in turn by Elar Kranak and Saltair. Enough running. No longer content with simply leaving Quiri and returning to Luqura, Annev decided to go on the o ensive and begin hunting the people who were secretly hunting him. He told himself it would be cowardly to run and leave his friends to fend for themselves, and he had no intention of making them targets to save himself. Yet Annev held no il usions about what that meant for his own safety. Every day he took additional precautions against future attacks, and against any attempts to interfere with his belongings or his quarters. When his friends invited him to lunch, he was careful to eat food he had prepared himself. When he entered a new room or walked down a corridor, he slowed to study the wal s and furniture for subtle glyphs or wards. At night, he stopped sleeping in his room and instead rotated between the many empty chambers of the Enclave’s lowest oor. And then there were his experiments with the Rod of Arti cing. Once he had discovered that the Inquisitor ring al owed him to see the hundreds of invisible glyphs covering the wal s of the Enclave, Annev began to experiment, dismantling them. When he saw a rune or ward that looked potential y threatening, he took out his rod and tried to uncover which Dionach or journeyman had cast it. Sometimes the threads fel apart in his hands, but more often he was able to fol ow the ribbon of magic back to the caster. Sometimes Annev would then interrogate those Dionachs, using his codavora and Inquisitor rings, but his questions never yielded the answers he sought. at vigilance came with a cost, too, for as the days turned into weeks, he became increasingly morose, sleep-deprived, and paranoid. On the rare occasion that members of the Order came to speak with him, Annev refused to see them until he’d donned his entire arsenal of artifacts—including his dragonscale cloak and his amberge. He took the same precautions when walking around the Enclave, leading to some Dionachs whispering behind his back. He overheard himself described as Sodar’s unfortunate project—an oddity, a curio. Some brothers seemed to be afraid of him and his glowing golden hand—a fact con rmed by the auramancy of his codavora ring—which only pushed Annev further into depression. He struggled to be interested when his friends shared the exciting magics they were performing, and he convinced himself he couldn’t tel his friends what had happened. Gradual y, his silence transformed it into a secret. And Annev continued to search for his attacker. He recal ed Arnor warning Sodar about traitors amidst the brotherhood, and Annev became suspicious of every member of the Order save erin and Titus. Donning his Inquisitor ring, he endured the sanguine-red cloud that permanently misted his vision and counted it a smal sacri ce for having constant access to its magic, in particular its ability to sense the pulse of those nearest him. He became adept at discerning when someone was lying or, more often, when they were anxious or excited about something. e codavora ring likewise proved invaluable, as Brother Tym’s blood had layered a third ability atop the two magics already stored in the serpent shaped artifact. Now he could catch glimpses of the thoughts of whomever he scried. He had to be close for it to work, and he had to concentrate to activate the magic, but it let Annev hear whatever words or thoughts were running through that person’s mind. It’s also how he knew what the Dionachs whispered about him behind his back—and what had precipitated his depressive, downward spiral. During most of his investigations, Honeycutt was his primary target, and Annev frequently tried to talk to the man about his movements on the night of the attack. Each time he found Honeycutt alone, though, something interrupted their conversation. First Holyoak needed an urgent word with the caste leader; then Dionach Leskal did. On his third try, Honeycutt simply said he was too busy to chat. Insights from the Inquisitor ring showed him the man was agitated, perhaps even angry, but he got no con rmation of Honeycutt’s guilt. Even the mindwalking powers of the codavora ring were strangely silent, as if the man were deliberately shielding his thoughts. It might have seemed suspicious, but the other Dionachs took similar precautions around him. e same had not been true during his rst week using the codavora ring’s mindwalking powers, but something had changed since then. e mages had grown wary of him . . . colder and more suspicious. Leskal had inde nitely postponed their sparring sessions, and Holyoak had become mental y and emotional y closed o , his mind perpetual y guarded by an impenetrable psychic wal . Even Dionach McClanahan had begun to distance herself, though she tended to greet him warmly in the Enclave’s corridors. It was two weeks since the attack, including eight days of being treated like a pariah, when Annev had an unexpected encounter with Jayar Honeycutt. e caste leader had been approaching Annev in a corridor, and Annev had ful y expected the man to turn and walk the other way, but instead Honeycutt looked up from his musings, his eyes brightened and he waved Annev toward him. “Brother Annev! Might I have a private word with you?” Annev was completely taken aback by Honeycutt’s friendly demeanor. en he nodded, slow and uncertain. “Yes, Dionach Honeycutt.” He paused. “Is now convenient?” “Now would be perfect. In my chambers?” Annev fought to keep his expression neutral. “Lead the way,” he said, not trusting himself to say more. e caste leader did and soon Annev was walking beside him, erecting his own mental barriers and wondering why Honeycutt wanted to talk. He suspected a trap, and he began surreptitiously checking his artifacts. Honeycutt surprised him by taking Annev through the Breathbreakers’ wing and directly to his personal chambers. e room was unremarkable, as nondescript and impersonal as the many unoccupied rooms on Annev’s basement level, though when Honeycutt closed the door, Annev noticed a single glyph charred on its inside face—the ward for silence. en he saw the familiar cursed portrait, propped against the far wal . “You took it!” Annev exclaimed, staring wide-eyed at the damaged painting. Honeycutt showed neither guilt nor regret. “When I saw it was missing from the Breathbreaker testing room,” he said, “I tracked it to your bedchamber. I couldn’t fathom how it had got there, much less why you had defaced it. My initial guess was that you had taken it to help your friend erin . . . but that did not explain why you destroyed the painting or dispel ed its charm.” He eyed Annev closely, looking concerned. “You didn’t steal this painting. Someone put it in your room.” Annev nodded. “If I don’t miss my guess,” Honeycutt continued, “you were in there when the glyph was activated. Al the air was suddenly expel ed from your room, yes?” Annev nodded again and Honeycutt’s expression darkened. “I’m sorry, lad. I placed and activated those glyphs as part of the nal Breathbreaker trial. I had no idea someone had moved it to your quarters, and it must have been a shock when I activated the ward for erin’s test. I’m not sure who moved it, but it seems they did it with the intention of harming you.” Annev couldn’t believe what he was hearing. “So you’ve known about this since the test … and you didn’t tel me?” Honeycutt shrugged. “At rst I thought you took the painting to help erin. en I foolishly hoped you were absent when the ward was activated . . . though the damage to the painting implied otherwise. Your behavior convinced me too. You were present when the glyph was activated, and I fear it frightened you into thinking someone was trying to harm you. Perhaps you even realized I set the ward, and decided I was trying to scare you.” “Scare me?” Annev said, his voice rising. “It damn near kil ed me!” Honeycutt frowned. “ e air would have been pushed from your room, of course, and that’s frightening. But al you had to do was leave its sphere of in uence.” Annev’s temper was rising, though he began to see the puzzle pieces tting together. “I couldn’t leave, Jayar, because someone had sealed my room from the outside. I assumed …” “You assumed it was me.” Honeycutt’s face grew pale. “Someone tried to kil you, and they tried to make it look like I was the one responsible.” He frowned, his eyes growing misty with concern. “My boy … I’m so sorry. at must have been dreadful.” Annev slowly nodded, uncertain how to process this new revelation. As he watched, he saw Honeycutt’s eyes grow distant. e man tutted his tongue, his head shaking. “It must be one of our Dionachs, most likely a brother who lacks the skil for breathbreaking.” “What makes you think that?” “Because if they possessed the skil , your attacker could have conjured the shield wal and the vacuum sphere themselves. ey’d have no reason for this subterfuge with the painting.” “Or,” Annev said, picking up the direction of Honeycutt’s thoughts, “the attacker has the skil … but they needed an alibi. ey needed someone else to cast the spel so they could prove they had been elsewhere during the attack.” “Perhaps,” Honeycutt said, his thumb and fore nger stroking his beard. “But the attacker would stil need to stay close so they could lock you in your room and seal the chamber. at suggests we are looking for a Shieldbearer— or, at the very least, someone who possesses a talent for condensing skywater.” Annev could hardly believe he was nal y making some headway with the man he had most suspected of being his attacker. It took him a moment to adjust. “You don’t seem surprised that someone is trying to kil me.” “I’m not—at least, not entirely. Arnor was sent to check in with Sodar, in part to ensure your safety.” “You know Arnor?” e Dionach nodded. “He was my second. A natural Breathbreaker and a skil ed spy.” “Was?” “. . . yes,” Honeycutt said, looking distraught. “You see, he stil hasn’t returned from his mission … and you have. e implication is not good.” Annev vaguely remembered dreaming about Arnor’s death the night before his Test of Judgment. He had held his tongue because he couldn’t remember the details beyond its gruesome nature, and he had hoped nothing terrible had befal en the man, but on hearing Honeycutt’s words his hopes quietly died. He swal owed, feeling uncomfortable. “Arnor believed there were traitors within the Order. Do you?” Honeycutt nodded once, his eyes icking to his closed door. “Sàmhchair,” he said, gesturing with his hand. e glyph on the door ared white then cooled to a somber blue. “Does that answer your question? I am certain there are traitors in the Order, though I don’t know their motives. Some may be grasping for power, not realizing it further destabilizes the Order. Others may be working for a foreign power—perhaps more than one.” “But you have barely thirty brothers lodged here. You speak as if more than a third of them can’t be trusted.” “More like half, though I think most Dionachs remain uncorrupted by foreign powers.” He shook his head, his expression dour. “But I speak as if this is something new. Politics has always been rife within the Order, despite Reeve’s attempts to govern with neutrality. is attack on your life is a new development. Given Sodar’s unique mission and your golden hand, I can see two motives: either your attacker perceives you as a threat to the Order and plans to do us a service by eliminating you . . . or your attacker has al ied themselves with the Terran God-king, Neruacanta.” “Neruacanta?” Annev asked, recognizing the name from Sodar’s notes on the Siänar. “You think the ruler of the Terrans has in ltrated the Order?” “More than likely, yes.” Annev fretted at this new revelation but set it aside for later re ection. “How many Dionachs or journeymen would be capable of sealing my room and trying to su ocate me?” “Speaking strictly of shieldbearing, where I am quali ed to judge, I’d say at least half the brethren have enough skil to conjure an air wal , but not su cient skil to form an airtight seal. Probably half a dozen of those—maybe a few more when you include the journeymen.” “Al Shieldbearers?” “Al except myself, Dionach Holyoak and Arch-Dionach Reeve.” “Holyoak. But … he’s a Mindwalker? He manipulates quaire, not skywater.” “He’s a dualist, like me. His primary talent is mindwalking, which exerts an inward pul on quaire, but the adjacent skil s are stormcal ing and shieldbearing, the former because it uses the same physical form of magic and the latter because it uses the same inward-pul ing force. Holyoak can condense the air almost as wel as Leskal, whose only talent is shield bearing, but he’s also the best Mindwalker at the Enclave.” “And Brother Tym is his second.” “Yes.” Annev nodded, believing he understood. “And your own talents … you’re a Breathbreaker—you can push and expand the skywater—so your twin talent would either be pushing quaire as a Stormcal er or pul ing skywater as a Shieldbearer.” Honeycutt smiled. “As it happens, I have both those skil s.” “You mean … you have three blood-talents?” “One primary and two secondary, yes.” Annev digested this new information. “Were both your parents dualists?” “Yes,” Honeycutt said, stil smiling. “ en two of your grandparents were Mindwalkers,” Annev said, taking a guess, “and the other two were a Stormcal er and a Shieldbearer.” “My grandmothers,” Honeycutt said, nodding with enthusiasm. “You’re a bright young man, Annev.” His smile faded. “Bright … and in terrible danger. If we accept that a Shieldbearer tried to kil you, we should talk to Leskal. He knows the heart of every Dionach in his caste. He’l know if any of them have been acting suspiciously.” “Shouldn’t we take this to Reeve?” “If you trust him.” Annev’s already considerable paranoia spiked further. “Should I not trust him?” Honeycutt’s eyes shifted between the door, the painting and then back to Annev. “Reeve is blessed with a talent in al four of the Darite arts,” he said slowly, “but he’s always favored the Shieldbearer caste. If Reeve is above question, Leskal is not. He has a blunt martial mindset—always more likely to use a hammer when a chisel or a spade might be better. He’s a good Shieldbearer, and I doubt he would wil ingly betray the Order, but he’d also do dark things to protect it.
