Not unless …” He turned his single eye on Myjun. “What was your relationship to this chandler?” “Relationship?” Myjun laughed bitterly. “He was a mean old bastard with an eye for anyone younger than his wife. Never tried anything with the witgirls —he wasn’t stupid enough to do that—but he got away with preying on plenty of village girls.” “Mm. So it must be vengeance against me for summoning the eidola and his being trapped in the shadows.” Myjun sni ed. “In his defense, that was a rotten thing to do. You damned some of my friends to the shadows too.” Oyru shrugged. “Assassins aren’t in the business of making friends—or keeping them. You are better o without them.” “ en why are you training me? Why bring me here? Aren’t I a burden to you?” e assassin hesitated. “Yes.” “So why are we doing this? Why are we hunting trol s in these woods to steal ashes from their camp res? Why are you making armor and training me to be your apprentice?” Silence. Myjun felt the urge to prompt him again—to poke and prod and evoke some kind of angry response—but she held her tongue and watched as the largest trol s took turns sinking their sharp black nails into an ironwood tree the group had fel ed just before dusk. Until that point, the res had been fed by natural lumber, but now the trol s began peeling the impossibly tough ironwood into splinters of kindling and strips of tinder. She marveled at it, knowing from experience that ironwood bark was as hard and in exible as its namesake, and its heartwood was harder stil —closer to steel than iron. Yet the trol s of Al tara seemed to possess the strength to rip it into rewood. “ ey eat the ashes,” Oyru said, ignoring her questions. “ at’s why they make the res. When the coals die down, the trol s eat the ironwood ashes. It’s what makes their bones so dense and their teeth and nails so sharp. ey’re more than trol s. ey’re iron trol s. More, the magic of the shadow realm penetrates these old mountains and their dark forests. e trol s do not only eat ash, they consume their magic.” “I didn’t think trol s ate trees, much less ash.” “ e ones in Al tara do. ey’re omnivores, though. ey prefer meat—just as we might prefer a rich pastry or dessert—but it’s an indulgence. is”—he gestured at the old Al taran forest—“is their real food.” “And you brought me here to . . . what? Eat ashes?” she sco ed. “Even without the mask, there is no rotting way you’d make me eat that dreck.” “You’re not going to eat it,” Oyru said. “ en what the hel —” “Hush and prepare your weapons,” Oyru said, summoning his yssas. “Once they have nished gathering the ironwood, we wil slaughter the tribe. Take care, though. eir hide and bones are tough, even to my void shards and your soul re blades, so we wil have to attack strategical y.” “Our magic doesn’t work on them?” “Not wel , no. It is part of the enchantment of the ironwood. In addition to its mythical strength and exibility, it repels al but the most persistent magical attacks.” Myjun let loose a series of expletives, each more foul than the last. “You tel me this now? Seconds before we attack them?” “Try to avoid their claws and teeth, and focus your attacks on their eyes and mouth. If you see a chance to separate their head from their necks, you can try it … but don’t overcommit. Chances are high that your weapons won’t work on their hides—not even their necks—so stick to soft tissue and organs, like their mouths and eyes.” “Noted,” Myjun said, her anger beginning to rise. With battle imminent and the mask already working, she was eager to feel pain and cause pain. Eager to kil and feed on the lives of these monsters. It would be a chal enge, if Oyru was to be believed, and Myjun desired a chal enge. She hungered for it. Back in the clearing, the largest trol dumped his nal armload of dense ironwood amidst the embers of the smoking re. A moment later, some of the smal er strips of ironwood already lying there began to smoke and sizzle, its strange branches belching black soot and then popping like shots of thunder in the night. “Now?” Myjun asked, struggling not to race into the clearing and slash the throat of anything vaguely humanoid. “Now,” Oyru said, sliding into the shadows and stalking toward the nearest beast. Myjun let the rage pour into her. She inhaled deeply and tasted the smoky scent of ironwood resin on her tongue, almost syrupy sweet with a mel ow charcoal overtone. She smel ed the trol s’ feral musk. She stalked nearer and realized the one she had scented—a male—sat with his companion just outside the relight. He roared something Myjun did not understand, then rol ed his mate over and began to mount her. e magic of the mask awakened painful memories of Kenton . . . and Annev. She had tried to forget her seductions, her clumsy attempts to woo both boys, for it shamed her to think what they had later become. Now, with the fumes of the ironwood l ing her nostrils and the magic of the mask heightening her passions, Myjun felt the memories ood her thoughts. Closeted kisses. Secret trysts that had failed to come to fruition. Carnal thoughts she’d fought to suppress and later sought to forget. She’d been betrayed by them both, rst by her attraction to Kenton and then by her fascination with Annev. It l ed her with shame and anger, but also with a sense of longing and loss—with regret at what might have been if things had been di erent. ose re ections then fed back into her anger, and the tight control Myjun kept over her emotions threatened to slip free. She strengthened her grip, though, and rode the wave of her emotions—not al owing them to control her, nor ghting against them as she had in the past; instead, she bridled them, harnessing their strength and al owing their power to fuel her attacks. With a predatory snarl, Myjun leapt atop the two trol s, her twin blades slicing as she fought back the tears of hatred stinging her eyes, blinding her to the carnage she in icted. Al around her, Myjun could hear shouts of pain and the guttural cries of the frenzied trol clan. She became frenzied herself, her emotions further fueling her magic, speeding her beyond the reach of tooth and claw. She saw the anger in Kenton’s gaze and fought to dominate it. She saw the betrayal in Annev’s eyes after she’d discovered his missing limb, and she sought to blind him. Al around her, the trol s were fal ing, sprawling backward with their eyes burned out. One beast leapt atop her, surprising her as it wrestled her to the earth like an angry bear. It raked its claws down her back and she howled with both pleasure and pain. She twisted in his grasp, her sts slamming his armored skin, forcing the soul re blades into his chest. e iron trol convulsed … and died. Myjun gasped, crushed by the weight of the shaggy beast. With an e ort, she rol ed out from under the dead trol ’s bulk and blinked away the blood that stained her vision. ere were scores of monstrous corpses scattered about the clearing, and her body was already healing from the few wounds the trol s had in icted. She’d grown faster and stronger during their many months hunting eidolons—and though these trol s were fast, she was faster. Oyru stood over a trol that was stil moaning in the shadows. His yssas icked down, piercing its skul , and the thing shuddered and fel silent. With a grunt, the assassin yanked his narrow sword from the trol ’s eyes. e Shadow Reborn looked at her curiously. “You fought di erently tonight. Less angry. More . . . focused. It was almost a dance. Very beautiful.” He dispel ed his swords and walked close enough to her that Myjun could smel the hot blood on his clothes. “Have you gained control of your emotions, then?” he asked. “Have you discovered how to use the powers of the mask without letting it master you?” Myjun’s mind returned to her waking vision: she had never lain with Annev or Kenton, though she had come close with the latter, and the mask had centered her anger on that. She had been attracted to Kenton until the fool boy had been scarred. She’d never been able to look at him the same way after that. And then Annev had been worse. e deceptive one-armed bastard had been marked by Keos the whole time—and he’d kept it secret from her. He’d made her fal in love with him and then … What is wrong with me that everyone I love or care for is damaged or corrupted? Even my father. Even me. Everything I touch turns to ashes … and I am drawn to the darkness. She looked up and saw Oyru studying her, his pupil like a wide pool of inky blackness. He saw something in her and nodded his approval. “You are ready to face the test of ashes. Come with me to the re.” Myjun complied, feeling dazed and angry, only vaguely aware that she’d dispel ed her soulblades. She studied Oyru in turn, and when he beckoned her to sit, she did. Oyru extended his hand and wisps of smoke trailed behind his ngers. She half expected him to summon one of his yssas, but instead a pair of shadow-black tongs appeared in his hand. He stretched the tool into the re and plucked out one of the crumbling orange embers that glowed there. “Ironwood embers,” Oyru said, bringing the coal in front of him, “wil cool to resin and ash when they make contact with organic matter. e trol s eat them when there is only a touch of warmth remaining. To make your armor, though, the embers must be hot. Your blood wil cool them, and the mask wil heal your burns before they can scar … but it wil stil be painful.” Myjun nodded. “ e resin wil take about an hour to harden into plate armor. It wil be thin—like wearing a second skin—but it wil be tough as steel. Where you need more exibility, we wil use the residue from the ashes, which wil stil be stronger than any chainmail or leather you might wear—and protect you against magic, but it won’t be as strong as the resin. Even so, this is the most powerful and versatile armor in existence, and the best-kept secret of my long-dead family clan.” “Why do you not wear it then?” “ e magic does not bond with half-men.” “ en why didn’t you obtain it before you became a half man?” Myjun asked bluntly. Oyru hesitated, then placed the coal back in the re. “My father swore to bring me here and perform the ritual, but when he was kil ed that duty passed to my mother. She refused—for many years—because she disapproved of my choice of mate.” “Oraqui.” He nodded. “In the end, she won my mother over by o ering to take the test of ashes herself. She knew what it meant—both the pain, and that it would forever mark her as one of our clan. So my mother brought us both here, to these mountains. To the trol lairs. First she made me watch as she burned Oraqui’s esh … and then she made me help.” Oyru fel silent, no sign of emotion or weakness as he looked into the re. “I burned her with the ironwood resin and its ashes,” he continued, “but when it was my turn to take the test, there weren’t enough embers left. We swore to come back together—she would perform the ritual for me as I had for her—but then Oraqui betrayed me and brought Gevul down upon my household.” Myjun couldn’t hold her peace. “Why did you wait for her, after that? Why would you stil think she cared for you?” Oyru gestured to the re with his tongs. “Because Oraqui knew my family’s secret. She could have brought Gevul and his clan here and given our magic to them . . . but she never did. She kept her word. She helped Gevul kil my family, but she kept our greatest secret.” “Why would she do that?” He shrugged. “If I ever see her again, perhaps I wil ask.” “It makes no sense. She helped kil your family—why not betray that one secret?” Oyru hesitated. “Perhaps when we have hurt someone we love, it is natural to hold something in reserve, something to show we are not whol y monsters. Perhaps it is a cry for help or redemption.” e assassin plucked a fresh coal from its embers. “Or perhaps in a mad world, we cling to a single virtue so we can excuse the other atrocities we al ow ourselves to commit.” “I think it’s the latter.” e Shadow Reborn shrugged. “People are complicated.” “But you stil love her. Even though she kil ed your family, you stil love her.” “If you must ask that, you did not understand my story. Oraqui joined my family when I burned her with these coals. She became part of my clan.” He extended the ironwood ember toward Myjun. “I o er you the same.” Myjun stared at the orange coal then looked back to Oyru’s single eye. Without a word, she shed her clothes and stood, erce, before him. “I am ready.” “ en I wil bathe you in embers and ashes,” he whispered, and pressed the hot coal to her skin. Myjun hissed, just as the coal against her skin hissed, the latter glowing red with re and blood. e pain was bright and bril iant, almost overwhelming, and as it cooled it gave her clarity amidst the hazy vapors of charred ironwood. Oyru rol ed the ember over her and the pain ared anew, but when she looked down at her esh, she saw not bubbling burns, but a beautiful blue-black chitinous layer covering her esh. “ is wil transform me into a monster,” Myjun growled through gritted teeth. “I wil never be free of this—just like my mask.” “We are already monsters,” the assassin breathed in her ear, continuing the ritual, “and now our bodies match our hearts.” CHAPTER SIXTY-EIGHT Annev stared at Tym’s round face. “Dead?” he whispered. “But … I just saw him. He was alive.” Brother Tym’s eyebrows narrowed. “You mean . . . you saw him while mindwalking?” Annev nodded, earning a frown and a contemplative grunt from Misty and Tym respectively. “What did you see?” Tym asked, his expression neutral. Annev opened his mouth to answer, then he recal ed how his vision had ended: how blood had sprayed from Holyoak’s eyes, ears, and mouth. He remembered the mist. e gore. How it seemed he could taste the man’s blood on his lips. But none of that was real, Annev thought. We were mindwalking—we were in Holyoak’s mind, and I didn’t attack him. But was that true? Annev had used the Hand of Keos to break down Holyoak’s mind palace. Was that also an attack on the man’s literal mind? Had Annev’s actions inadvertently caused his death? “How did it happen?” Annev asked, reinforcing his own mental wal s. “You’d been under for a few hours,” Misty said, laying a hand on Tym’s shoulder. “Tym was monitoring you from outside the implanted memory and we were considering waking you but then something happened. You had … some kind of breakthrough?” “He found the quaire glyphs!” Tym interjected, unable to keep the excitement from his face. “It was bril iant. I never would have found them.” He turned to Annev. “But then you did something strange. You made the glyphs disappear … and then you disappeared.” “I dispel ed the quaire glyphs to see the trail of blood-talent and fol ow it to the traitor. Holyoak was at the other end—the forged memory must have led me into his mind. I spoke to him … and he admitted betraying the Enclave.” “We gathered that,” Misty said, her eyes ful of sympathy. “Tym couldn’t reach you, but you were mumbling. We caught pieces of what you were saying.” “I was talking in my sleep?” “Mindwalking is not sleep,” Tym corrected. “It looks near enough from the outside, though,” Misty said. “We heard enough of your accusations against Holyoak for Reeve to send some brothers to take him into custody.” “Did he ght back?” “He wasn’t even awake,” said Misty. Tym seemed about to say something, but a glare from her sti ed whatever objections he’d been about to raise. “ ere’s a time and a place for teaching mindwalking technique, dear.” Misty returned her gaze to Annev. “Holyoak was in a trance, like you, and nothing we did woke him. We worried that forcibly waking either of you might cause some mental or psychic damage, so we agreed not to wake either of you unless you became distressed. Holyoak was placed under close guard in a warded cel and you were kept in our bedroom.” Annev abruptly realized they were not currently in Misty and Tym’s bedchamber. e room was much smal er, and clearly unoccupied. He tensed when he noticed the tiny glyphs carved into the wal s. “ is is … one of the warded cel s?” Annev said, stating the obvious. Misty nodded then glanced sidelong at her husband. “Do you want to tel him?” “Might be better to show him,” Tym said, his hand gently fal ing on Annev’s shoulder. “Come on.” *** Not much was left in Tym and Misty’s bedroom: a badly charred bedspread, a soot-stained clothes chest, and scraps of smoky linens. e rest was gone—the bed, the books, the table and chairs—al burned to ash and cinders. Annev stood in the center of the room and swal owed, his throat dry from the lingering smoke and the bile that burned the back of his throat. His feet traced the curve of the melted stones beneath his feet and then he bowed his head in shame. “I’m sorry.” “It wasn’t your fault,” Misty said, immediately at Annev’s side. “You didn’t know what you were doing. You had no idea what was happening in the physical world.” “It’s my fault,” Tym said, his own head bowed with regret. “I should have moved you the moment you made contact with Holyoak— before then maybe— but I wanted to keep a close eye on you. I thought this was a good place, but . . . wel , it was my fault. I’m sorry.” e apology seemed as much for Misty as Annev. “It’s nobody’s fault,” Dionach McClanahan replied, her long arms draping over Tym’s shoulders. “It was an accident. No one could have predicted this.” Annev was less certain. He had wil ed the Hand of Keos to appear during his mindwalking trance: he had wanted it, summoned it—and then he had conjured its magic. He had brought the destructive ames into the cognitive realm, supposing they wouldn’t reach the physical world . . . and he’d been wrong. “How—” he croaked, his voice dry. He swal owed and tried again. “How did you stop it? How did you move me?” “As soon as the hand started glowing, we had some of the brothers come and try to contain the re with a shield spel ,” Tym said. “ at worked for a bit, until the ames . . . wel , they pushed the shield outward. I’m not sure how. I mean, it shouldn’t have been possible. But they couldn’t contain the re, and I couldn’t wake you, and the bed caught re and things were al a merry blaze for a bit. Reeve left Brother Honeycutt to watch Holyoak and dashed down here to help—he vented some of the re into that corner of the room, that’s how the bookcase caught ame—and things were stable enough that we were able to oat you down to the cel s. Got you tucked away nice and neat. Wel , mostly neat.” He looked around his ruined bedroom and shrugged. “It’s nothing that can’t be replaced. ere are copies of most of these books in the library—and the rest I can replace myself.” He tapped the side of his skul . “I’ve a pretty good memory.” Annev nodded, reminded of the chest of memories he’d recovered from Holyoak. “Did you get those memories back to Sraon? Wil he be okay?” “He’l be ne,” Misty said. “Tym passed me the stolen memories and I handled the transplant personal y. Reeve supervised. Sraon should make a ful recovery, but it wil stil take a few days before he feels like his old self.” Annev felt relieved until he returned his attention to the room’s destruction. “Al of this … How was I not injured?” “Good question,” Tym said. “Near as we can tel , the ames don’t harm you. Don’t understand why, but they don’t. Made our job a sight easier, in any case. We shielded you in a bal of skywater—ice, air, water—and that made the transport possible.” He chuckled. “Funny thing was, as soon as we got you to your cel , things began to quiet down. Turned the re o yourself, I think … but that’s when the trouble started up with Holyoak.” Annev studied the Mindwalker’s wary face. “What did happen to Holyoak?” Tym cleared his throat. “You remember how Honeycutt was left to watch Holyoak—when Reeve came dashing to help you?” “Yes,” Annev said, his eyebrows narrowing. “What happened?” “Honeycutt kil ed him.” Annev wasn’t sure he understood—then his eyes shot wide open. “Honeycutt kil ed Holyoak?” “Near as we can tel , yes.” “ e manner of death was consistent with a Breathbreaker attack,” Misty added. “And Brother Honeycutt has since ed the Enclave.” “But … why?” “We don’t know,” Misty said as Tym splayed his hands in the air. “ ere’s been some speculation that they were working together … and unfortunately that makes sense.” “If Honeycutt suspected Holyoak was talking to you,” Tym added, “he might have decided to eliminate him before he could be interrogated.” Annev nodded, imagining the Mindwalkers and Stormcal ers prying into Holyoak’s memories, sorting through his thoughts and exposing his secrets. “Has anyone else ed?” “No. Just him.” “Could there be other traitors hiding at the Enclave?” Tym sighed. “I had hoped you could answer that for us. I assume Holyoak didn’t tel you very much.” “No.” He gave a brief summary of what had transpired between him and Holyoak. When he had nished, both Tym and Misty seemed to be studying him with new eyes. “What is it?” Misty glanced at Tym, her eyes averted. “You pretended to be Keos?” “Wel … no, not exactly. I just intimidated him with the Hand and let him come to his own conclusions.” “So you pretended to be Keos,” she repeated, more forceful y. Annev winced. “I guess.” “And you told him to kneel?” is time there was no mistaking the look of disgust she tried to hide. “It seemed appropriate,” Annev said, wishing he’d omitted that detail. Tym’s eyes were twinkling. Misty shot him a look and he threw up his hands, defensive. “What? It was clever! He had to be convincing, didn’t he?” Dionach McClanahan sni ed then rol ed her eyes. “Men. Always quick to use the bluntest instrument in the room.” She turned back to Annev. “Did you get any inkling as to whether he had acted alone? Whether Honeycutt or anyone else had assisted him?” Annev thought about it. “He seemed surprised when I accused him of instigating the attack on my village and said he had only tried to kil me after I came to Quiri. But that can’t be true … can it?” “I don’t know, Annev. Why would he lie about that but admit being a servant of Keos? Why admit trying to kil you but deny the rest?” Annev thought for a long while. Final y, Tym broke the silence: “I worked closely with Holyoak, Annev—close enough to know when he left the Enclave. He was a bit of a recluse. He relied on messengers to communicate with distant members of our caste, and he rarely left Quiri.” “What about Saltair? Did Holyoak ever communicate with him?” “Not that I know of,” Tym said, chewing his lip, “but I doubt anyone at the Enclave would admit communicating with one of the Siänar.” “What about a merchant named Janak Harth?” “Janak who?” “Harth. He had a reputation for col ecting artifacts. Lived in Banok?” “I’ve heard of him,” Misty volunteered, “but how is he connected to the attack on your village?” “Honestly, I’m stil not sure, but he had planned to attack Chaenbalu. e feurog that nal y did destroy the village …” Annev shuddered, remembering them and the phantasmic shadow demons. “Maybe they weren’t connected— or maybe it was me. ey were al trying to get to me.” “ at may be true,” Tym said, “but so far as I know, Holyoak never had any contact with Janak Harth. In fact, the only suspicious thing I can identify is that he dispatched two of our Mindwalkers to visit the more distant Dionach chapter houses.” “Why is that suspicious?” “Because of those Dionachs who have traveled in the last year, al of them have been lost or kil ed, except for those two Dionachs—Chan and Davies, both Mindwalkers.” “And close associates of Brother Holyoak,” Misty said, her lips pursed. “ at does seem suspicious.” “Teiksim Chan and Rockford Davies? I can’t real y imagine any two Dionachs less suspicious. ey’re both dualists, like Holyoak, actual y.” Tym looked at Misty. “Do you think that’s signi cant?” She furrowed her brow. “Maybe … but we should be wary of prejudice. Mindcal ers and Stormpsychics have a history of being pro led as deviants. We can’t just assume their guilt, not even with Holyoak’s betrayal. And I doubt Rockford’s dualist nature is relevant. He’s a condenser, right?” “A Mindshear,” Tym supplied. “Half Mindwalker, half Shieldbearer.” Misty sni ed. “I can never keep those titles straight. Too many dualist names by half.” “One hundred and thirty-two among the prime mages,” Tym said, smiling, “and if you include the New Terran hybrids, you can have as many as—” “Please don’t.” “Four hundred and sixty-two,” he nished, stil grinning. “Makes my head hurt just thinking about it,” Misty said, pinching the bridge of her nose. “Anyway, I doubt it’s relevant. If Dionachs Chan and Davies are traitors, it wil be due to their proximity to Holyoak and his in uence, not because they are Mindwalker hybrids.” “So Chan and Davies are the only ones who survived recent trips abroad,” Annev pressed, not wanting to lose the thread of their discussion. “ ey’re both Mindwalkers with connections to Holyoak. at’s more than enough to investigate them.” “Dionach Chan’s proximity to the Empire’s border, on her mission, would have made her a perfect messenger, especial y since she and Holyoak were both Mindcal ers,” Misty added. “ ey could have passed messages freely between one another, and then Dionach Chan could have passed those messages on to their Terran al ies. She had the ability and the means to be invaluable to a spy network.” “What about Davies?” Annev asked. “Where was he stationed?” “His territory covered the southern half of the Empire,” Tym said, his expression darkening. “I don’t want to jump to any conclusions, but if Holyoak was orchestrating the assassinations of our missing members, Davies would have been perfect for the job. Mindwalking would have al owed him to spy on others, and his talents with skywater could make him a skil ed assassin.” He pursed his lips. “Blood and bile, I hope we’re wrong. Davies has always been a good friend to me. I can’t imagine him kil ing al those people. Dionach Kadmon, Brother Witherspoon, Sisters Rugebregt and Morgenstone . . . so many deaths, so many missing.” He clutched a hand to his mouth and muttered a quick apology before ducking out of the room. Annev and Misty both looked after him in sympathy, but when Misty turned back to Annev, he could see her steel. “We’ve tried to keep Holyoak’s death quiet, but with Honeycutt’s disappearance, rumors are going to spread. ey probably already have. If we’re going to track down Chan and Davies, we’l need to move fast.” “Agreed,” Annev said, grateful for the change in Misty’s attitude. “I don’t have much time to hunt down the traitors, and this recent debacle won’t encourage Reeve to extend my stay.” “Indeed not,” said a deep voice from the other end of the room. Annev turned and saw it was the Arch-Dionach himself, who entered with Brother Tym under his arm and a thunderous expression. “You wil leave the Enclave tomorrow.” “I hoped that—” “I am grateful for your work—but it doesn’t change this.” He gestured at the melted stones and charred furniture. “It’s too dangerous for you to stay here. at hasn’t changed, Annev. Holyoak is dead, so we have no one to question. Honeycutt is gone, and I can’t spare anyone to hunt him down with the threat of additional traitors hiding within the Order.” “We’ve been talking about that,” Annev said. “Dionachs Chan and Davies might be connected to Holyoak’s betrayal. Or even assisted him. If you quarantined them—” “Quarantined?” Reeve sni ed. “Boy, how many Dionachs do you think we have here at the Enclave? About two dozen. How many of those do you think I can trust? Odar’s beard, you think I’m worried about people running? I want them to run. I’m worried about whether I can keep control of the bloody place.” Annev blinked. “You’re worried about a coup?” Reeve nodded. “So . . . you’re not going to track him down? You’re going to let Honeycutt go?” “I don’t have a choice, Annev. e Order is in danger. e Enclave isn’t safe. I need to put my house in order before I start chasing down traitors and heretics. Frankly, I think we might have been overwhelmed already except we received some troubling news from the south just as this business with Holyoak happened.” He pul ed a creased letter from his robes, its seal broken. “Troubling news?” Annev said, his eyes brie y drawn to the letter. “Reeve, what could be more troubling than this? We need to act fast if we’re going to catch Honeycutt!” “You’re right … so take this.” He extended the letter to Annev. “Read it when you have the chance, and decide what you’d like to do.” Annev took it apprehensively. “What is it?”

chunks.title: Chapter 10
chunks.content: “For now, it’s just a distraction. Reports about a besieged city and a request from some traveling dreamers, when we need to focus on the traitors in our midst.” He nodded to the others. “Misty and Tym wil help me interrogate Davies and Chan, after we’ve questioned a few others of our brethren and con rmed their al egiance remains with Odar and the Dionachs Tobar.” “I could help, though,” Annev o ered, his st tightening. “I need to help. ese people . . . He’s not the one who has to check for lice every time he stops in Neahmar or who has to put up with … Anabo ung open the door and the sight within took her breath away: clean linens, a freshly made bed, scented candles, soap and a steaming tub of hot water. “Alan, you bastard,” she breathed, inhaling the scent of jasmine and juniper. “ ank the gods. ank stoic Odar and radiant Lumea and their bloody brother Keos.” She moaned with delight, already anticipating the warmth. “Ja a!” she cal ed down. “You can cancel the hot water! Alan did something right for once. I’l see you in the morning!” She slammed the door before her manservant could reply and began stripping o her travel cloak and skirts. She was half-naked before she realized the window was open and a gentle breeze was bil owing the curtains. She hu ed, strode over to the window and closed the shutters with a satisfying click. She could stil feel the breeze through the green-painted wooden slats, though, and it sent goose pimples up her esh. She shivered, more in anticipation of the bath than out of any chil —then she stripped o the rest of her clothes and slipped into the tub with a moan. “Yes,” she hissed, leaning back and closing her eyes. “ ank the ever-loving gods.” “You don’t real y strike me as the pious type.” Anabo shot up from the water, her left arm slapped across her breasts out of an instinct that thirty years in Innistiul had never quite driven from her. “Who the dreck are you?” she shouted, her head spinning to nd the speaker. “What are you doing in here? Get the hel out!” e young man stepped from the shadows behind the curtains and pul ed back the gray-white hood of his cloak. Had she real y not seen him before? Had she not noticed him while she stood so close to the window? e goose pimples returned again, now magni ed tenfold. “I’m here on behalf of Dionach Honeycutt.” Anabo frowned and she slowly eased back into the steamy water. “Are you now? at’s interesting. Jayar never told me you’d be coming.” “No?” Anabo looked at the stranger with fresh eyes. He was handsome enough— medium build, light brown hair, wide shoulders, and a youthful face. Yes, she was tempted to ask the Guildmaster for someone like this. Something about his eyes . . . dark blue and piercing. She broke her gaze, though she felt he should be the one looking away. “You’re a Breathbreaker then?” e candles in the room ickered and the young man rose to hover in midair. Anabo sni ed. “You’re just showing o . Stil , I could use a Breathbreaker tomorrow … and the day after. I’m taking a river barge south to Luqura and I’d kil for a favorable wind. ink you could arrange that?” “No.” “Why? Got somewhere better to be?” She raised her brow archly then leaned back until her chest peeked above the waters. “I could make it worth your while, and I promise Jayar won’t mind if you’re gone for a few days.” “My understanding … is that your promises aren’t worth very much.” “I’m a diplomat. I make a lot of promises and I’m prone to break a few now and then. I assure you, I can’t keep track of them al . Why are you here?” “Honeycutt asked you to pass a message to the mercenary Saltair—one about a boy named Annev de Breth.” “ e lizardman?” Anabo snorted. “ at’s hardly an o ense. If the Empire were a brothel, he’d be the bordel o’s favorite whore, at least here in the north —” e water in the tub suddenly felt ice-cold as she remembered the contents of Honeycutt’s message. e boy’s name and the memories it brought with it. Keos, she swore, if this one can read minds as wel as— “I can.” Anabo slapped the water, realizing she’d already given herself up. “Dammit! You should real y have to announce when you’re mindwalking. It’s not fair to the rest of us liars.” She squinted at the gray-garbed stranger who stil oated in the air, his cloak rippling softly about him. “What’s your interest in Annev de Breth?” the man asked. Anabo snorted. “Nothing—at least not for myself. Saltair was in charge of it.” “And what orders did you give him?” “ e ones Honeycutt paid me to pass along.” “No, you rescinded those and gave him a new set of orders. What were they?” Damn. “If you know I rescinded them, you’l know what the new orders were —or you could just read my mind.” “You’re blocking me—or trying to.” “And am I succeeding?” e stranger shrugged. “You’re right. I already know your replacement orders. I just wanted you to con rm them.” Anabo narrowed her eyes. “No,” she said, cal ing the young man’s blu . “You only think you know. at’s why you want me to con rm it.” She smiled. “I may not read minds, but I can read people, and you … you don’t even work for Honeycutt, do you?” He averted his gaze—she had guessed correctly then—and now that she considered it, he seemed more a boy than a man. Eighteen or nineteen? Surely no more than twenty. His features were strange too. Ilumite? Darite? Hard to say. ere may even be some Terran blood mixed in there. And was his left hand larger than the right? Di cult to tel with the single black glove he wore. Probably a padded gauntlet. “Who are you real y?” she asked. “You’re a Breathbreaker, but not one of Jayar’s, and a Mindwalker … so you’re a dualist. Very interesting.” Her eyes suddenly grew at. “Now cut the shit. Holyoak sent you to check up on me, so I guess he wants to know why the boy is stil alive. Wel , you can tel him I’ve been in Innistiul and none of the keokum’s messages have reached me. So Saltair’s either neck-deep in one of his schemes or he’s dead. Elar has been keeping me updated, and I’l check on it myself when I get to Luqura.” She paused. “Which you could speed along if you decided to come with me.” e young man pretended to hesitate, but Anabo already knew which way the coin would fal . She had a talent for reading people, men especial y. Her mother had whispered it came from an Ilumite ancestor. is one had decided. He would come. She just needed to give him the right reasons. “My previous o er stil stands,” she said, arching her back enticingly and thinking lusty thoughts to prevent this Mindbreaker … this Breathwalker … from learning she had no way to pay him except information, favors and— “Blood.” Anabo sat up in the water. “Excuse me?” “Ten vials of blood. One from you. One from your manservant … and eight more of my choosing.” e consul blinked. “Blood?” she repeated. “Just blood. Nothing else?” She shrugged suggestively. e boy was young, true, but she’d had younger … and it was a long way to Luqura, even with magical assistance. She’d made her own decision, that she didn’t want to wait for a concubine from Guildmaster Whalen—not when she had the genuine article right in front of her. “Ten vials of blood,” he repeated, “and … some information.” Phoeba Ondina Anabo sighed. Information was her most prized asset outside of coin, and it always seemed to cost her more than she bargained. Sex was so much cheaper when people deigned to accept it in payment. Maybe she was losing her touch. Maybe she was just getting older—though forty hardly seemed old to her. She licked her lips. So bedding this one would be a chal enge. She had time, and he’d have to take breaks to regain whatever essence he tapped to use his arcane magic. She smiled seductively. “So you’l come with me then? We can talk to Saltair, and you can report back to Holyoak yourself?” “Yes,” he said. “I’l come.” “And you’l help speed our voyage with your wind magic. As much as you can? As much as you … are able?” Again that hesitation. “If you get me the blood I request, yes.” Anabo frowned. What in the name of Keos did he want with blood? She supposed it was cheaper than sex—if not nearly as much fun. “I’l get you the blood. One smal vial from me. One from Ja a.” She shook her head, knowing it would be di cult to explain to her manservant. Fortunately, she didn’t have to explain. She could simply command. “I can’t promise you the eight other vials without knowing whose you want.” “I understand. I stil want your word you’l do everything you can to get them.” Anabo gave the young man her most captivating smile. “Of course, of course.” He knew how little her word was worth. ey were just playing games now, and these were games she knew how to play. “What should I cal you?” “Magpie.” “Ah,” Anabo purred. “I thought that pattern looked familiar.” She nodded at Magpie’s cloak and he slowly oated back to the ground. She smiled again, more wickedly this time. at skil would be very useful on the voyage. She wondered what other skil s he had … “Do you have anywhere to be, Master Magpie? I could use some help scrubbing my—” “I’l see you tomorrow morning. Riverside wharf. e Crested Cormorant. Bring the vials of blood.” “Mm. I’l see what I can arrange.” She began soaping herself and could feel his eyes on her again. at was good. at was what she wanted. “Did you arrange al this?” she asked, her sudsy ngers gesturing at the candles, the linens, and the hot water. “Alan is not usual y so thoughtful. Were you hoping to catch me o my guard? Vulnerable?” Magpie didn’t answer. Anabo slowly stood then and, with a sultry smile, she turned to face the young man. It was then she saw the shutters stood open and Holyoak’s messenger had already gone. Anabo might have been disappointed by that, but instead she only felt the thril of a chal enge. is would be far more fun than another concubine—they never lasted long once things got interesting anyway. And if things went wel , who knew? Perhaps she’d even keep her promise about the blood. “Strange bird,” she muttered, easing herself back into the water. “Not like any of the ones Holyoak sent before.” She wondered what that meant. Surely nothing good, since he was asking about Saltair. at meant this one—this Magpie—was special. More dangerous, no doubt, and it made her second-guess her promise to give him her blood. Something about him gave her pause, as if his eyes could pierce into her soul and see the secrets buried there. She supposed that wasn’t her imagination either, not with a Breathwalker … or Mindbreaker. Damn, she hated dualists, especial y the ones who could read minds. It made her work so much harder. But then, the chal enge was part of the fun. She detested long boat rides and bumpy carriages, but the choppy waters and dusty roads were only half the bother. It was the boredom that made her want to claw out her eyes or cut out her manservant’s dry tongue. Give her an interesting companion, though— someone with a little charisma, a little mystery—and just about any voyage became tolerable, even enjoyable. She guessed that the next three days would be ful of surprises. PART SIX To Kryss Jakasen and the Keepers of the Flame, I pray that my letter nds you wel —whether in Banok or Luqura or wherever your travels take you. Likewise, I thank you for your kind request to join you and your companions in Banok later this season. I must decline. Noble though your quest may be, local troubles in the Brotherhood require my ful attention at this time. If I am able to reconcile the current issues in Quiri quickly, I may stil send another member of my order to join your council, but I would strongly urge against meeting in Banok. Recent reports suggest the township is besieged by a coordinated assault from local bandits. I have news regarding one of your companions, though it is not the pleasant kind. e soothsayer Jian Nikloss died shortly after joining my company. May it be some consolation to know his death was a valiant one, his life given in the defense of others. In regards to Annev, you are correct in guessing the young man was recently in my Enclave, but I am sorry to say he has since departed. I gave him your letter, so perhaps he wil decide of his own accord to aid you in your quest. If he does, I advise caution in his presence and recommend you be respectful of his personal traumas (as I’m certain you would be). To do otherwise might have disastrous consequences for both you and your companions. May the light of Lumea and the winds of Odar protect you, Arch-Dionach Reeve, High Order of the Dionachs Tobar CHAPTER EIGHTY-TWO Alcoran approached the embers of the fading re with al the trepidation of a dog begging for scraps. e summer night wasn’t al that cold, but he coveted much of what the smal caravan shared: companionship, warmth, a sense of peace. ere had been very little peace during the campaign in Borderlund— not among its commanders or the squabbling nobility, and certainly not along the front lines adjacent to the Kuar River and the Terran armies in Daogort. It had been madness. Greed and bloodlust and chaos. He’d lost most of his troops and his left eye on his rst run at the Black Wal , and the company had never recovered. Al the glory he’d envisioned, al the clever strategies he’d planned—it had al gone down the garderobe. Barely a handful of his men had held their ground, and al of them had been slaughtered. Alcoran had only escaped because he’d been smart enough to place his command at the back, and he’d been one of the rst to ee when the rock golem began hurling boulders at the scattered company. He stil wasn’t sure where the arrow had come from—probably one of his own gutless men—and having been shot, he’d reacted in fear and stabbed the rst person he’d stumbled into. As it turned out, that had been the company’s medic—an herbalist they’d conscripted just outside of Lochland—and he’d had no one to tend to the damaged organ after that. ere’d been no peace since then. Not from the injury, which was currently weeping pus beneath the bandage, and not from the other o cers in Borderlund’s conscript army. It had been a farce from the beginning, and now Alcoran just wanted a little peace from this sleepy caravan. Peace, and al of their possessions. “Evening, folks,” Alcoran drawled in an approximation of the local accent. “Sorry to disturb. Might I trouble you to share the warmth of your re?” He swept into a bow with a dramatic ourish, his broad-rimmed hat tilted to cover his missing eye. “It’s late, friend,” said an elderly man sitting on a stump close to the camp re. “We don’t know you. Might be better if you pushed on.” Alcoran straightened, having expected that. “I won’t share your company, then. But spare me some news from out west? I’ve just come from the east. e war with Daogort has spread al across Borderlund. e Terrans are making forays into any villages near the Kuar, and our valiant soldiers are hoping for aid from Greater Luqura or Lochland. Do you have news? Or have other a airs kept the Empire’s soldiers away from their sister kingdom?” e old man exchanged a look with the woman tending a pot of food banked in the coals—bacon and root stew by the smel of it. Alcoran fought the urge to lick his lips. “You’re from Borderlund then? Your accent … sounded like you were from the capital.” Damn, Alcoran thought. He was getting sloppy. Being hungry would do that to a man, not to mention being in constant pain. “Yes. Born in Banok but my business keeps me in Borderlund—at least it used to. Tel me. How fares the King’s Road?” e old man whispered something to the woman and slowly stood. She ran o to one of the four tents set up just beyond the re and soon two men and an older lad had joined them. “Do you know anyone in Banok?” the old man whispered, his quivering lips seeming to chew his words. “Any family there? Loved ones?” Cursed Keos. What did this old man expect? Was Alcoran going to have to make up a family there before he could sit at a re? Alcoran fought the urge to scowl and instead forced a disarming smile. He was used to getting his own way, and it pained him to be unable to order folks around. at had been the beauty of the army. Before he could think up a clever response, though, the old man continued. “If you do,” he said, looking apologetic, “then you should know they’re in a bad way right now. So bad Borderlund probably won’t see any soldiers coming to their aid—not till word gets to the capital and other parts of the Empire.” Alcoran hadn’t expected this answer. “In a bad way? How so?” e older man indicated a broad-chested fel ow who was of a height with Alcoran. He stood in his nightshirt and britches, he carried no weapons, and he had a haunted look about him. e man next to him was stockier, had hair so dark it seemed black, and an angry scar crossed his cheek and chin. e tal er man patted the scarred one on his shoulder and nodded in greeting to Alcoran, unembarrassed by his state of undress.

chunks.title: Final Section
chunks.content: “For now, it’s just a distraction. Reports about a besieged city and a request from some traveling dreamers, when we need to focus on the traitors in our midst.” He nodded to the others. “Misty and Tym wil help me interrogate Davies and Chan, after we’ve questioned a few others of our brethren and con rmed their al egiance remains with Odar and the Dionachs Tobar.” “I could help, though,” Annev o ered, his st tightening. “I need to help. ese people . . . Reeve, this conspiracy may have been responsible for the attacks on my village. For Sodar’s death. I won’t just leave this investigation now.” “What makes you think they’re responsible, Annev? Holyoak knew nothing about Chaenbalu or Sodar’s mission. I alone knew Sodar’s location, and I only shared it with Brother Arnor.” He paused. “And he’s dead.” Annev considered this. “Would Arnor have told anyone else?” “Only his caste leader.” e group was silent as Reeve’s indignant, instinctive words slowly sank in. “Dammit,” Reeve swore. “Honeycutt knew.” e Arch-Dionach tugged his goatee. “Damn, this is al my fault.” Annev felt his st clench tighter. “No,” he said, his voice icy. “ is is Honeycutt’s fault. You made a mistake, but he pro ted from it. He’s de nitely part of this.” “… probably. But I can’t send anyone after him, Annev.” Annev’s wandering compass suddenly pointed resolutely in one direction, and he knew what he had to do. He could nal y leave the Enclave and continue his pursuit of the people who had attacked him and the vil agers of Chaenbalu. e certainty of it felt good—it felt right. Like he’d nal y found his purpose. “I’l go. You want me to leave anyway, so I may as wel hunt Honeycutt down and get answers out of him.” Reeve tutted his tongue against his teeth, his eyes shifting between the two silent Dionachs at his side. “I don’t like it … but you’re right. I can’t keep you here, and I can’t stop you.” He glanced meaningful y at Annev’s golden hand, which had begun to glow with a dul red luminescence. “Blood and ashes,” Annev swore, tucking the hand behind his back and trying to calm his emotions. “I’m sorry.” Reeve nodded, accepting the apology without drawing attention to it. “I had this made for you.” He tossed a black felt glove to Annev, its cu stitched with silver thread and its palm and ngers padded with … something. Annev slipped it on to his left hand and was immediately impressed by its t. “It’s got a few quaire glyphs woven into the lining—shields of air and water, something that might help quench an unintentional ame …” “It’s great,” Annev said, grateful to Reeve for saving the moment. “ ank you.” He nodded again. “Gather your things and go after Honeycutt if you must … but be careful. You’re resourceful and brave—you’ve been trained as an assassin and a thief—but you’re going up against a ful Dionach with over a thousand years of experience, and that puts you at a serious disadvantage. He might kil you or you might kil him, but you’re just as likely to blow up half the city. I hope that, if it comes down to letting Honeycutt go or destroying Quiri, you’l do the smart thing and save your revenge for another day. Another time and place.” “I’m not looking for revenge,” Annev protested, his cheeks ushed with anger and embarrassment. Reeve was unconvinced. “I know that look, Annev. I’ve worn it myself. You think you’re looking for answers—and you might nd them—but consider the cost before you do anything you may regret.” Annev remembered how close he had come to destroying Luqura and nodded. “Good.” Reeve patted Tym on the back. “Brother McClanahan, I’m sorry you are becoming the Mindwalkers’ leader under such sad circumstances—but I need your help. I’d be pleased if you and Misty would help me root out any remaining heretics. It’s time we nal y rid ourselves of the rot that’s been hiding under our noses. May Odar protect us … and may the Order survive our investigation.” CHAPTER SIXTY-NINE Annev’s goodbyes with Tym and Misty were quick, and accompanied with a promise to reconnect once their missions were complete. Even as he said the words, though, Annev doubted he’d return to the Order. ere was nothing for him here—he’d come to that conclusion long ago—and his presence endangered not only the Enclave, but his friends. He hastened to Titus and erin’s quarters to say his goodbyes but didn’t see either boy in their rooms, so he headed back down to col ect his few unburned possessions in preparation for his departure. Just as he reached the basement, he found them. “Annev, we’ve been looking for you!” “Titus, erin! I was—” “You heard the news about Dolyn and Brayan?” Titus continued. “Dolyn and …” Annev’s heart fel into the pit of his stomach. Was this related to the letter Reeve had given him? Annev had completely forgotten about the Orvanish blacksmith and the burly quartermaster. He hadn’t even sent word to Banok to let Brayan know the party had moved on from Luqura to Quiri. And I promised to return for them. Blood and ashes, I’m a horrible friend. at wasn’t al he had promised and forgotten. With painful clarity, Annev remembered swearing to Red-thumb that he would introduce Jian Nikloss to Sodja Rocas in Luqura and look after the albino necromancer. Annev hadn’t kept a single promise: he hadn’t returned to Banok, he had never found Sodja, and Jian had died to save him. Annev smothered his wave of guilt and made himself ask: “What news?” “ e whole damn town has been taken hostage!” erin said, his tone near hysterical. “We’ve been searching for you ever since we heard.” “Sorry, I’ve been a bit occupied.” He stopped. “Wait … so Brayan has been taken hostage?” Titus nodded. “Annev, I’m worried. ey aren’t letting anyone out.” Annev had an uneasy feeling sinking in his gut. “ is is in Banok?” ey nodded. “Do you know who’s doing it?” “A group cal ed the Sons of Damnation,” Titus said, looking concerned. “ ey aren’t Terran,” erin added. “ at’s been con rmed by the few who escaped before the gates were sealed.” Annev swal owed back bile, beginning to fear what was coming next. “How many?” “Just a handful, Reeve heard. Annev …” Titus wetted his lips. “Annev, they used artifacts. ey used magic to control the vil agers, but they’ve also been saying horrible things about anyone who might have a talent for magic—even a little. And I think … wel , I think they may be looking for you.” Rotting blood and ashes. Annev knees suddenly felt weak and his mouth had gone dry at this con rmation of his fears. “Why do you think they want me?” e boys shared a look and erin spoke. “ ey’ve made it clear they’re looking for someone with one arm or someone with a giant golden hand.” at sealed it then. e few masters left alive at Chaenbalu were the only group whose agenda might match Titus and erin’s description. Annev let out a long, slow breath and shook his head. “ ey didn’t seem like a threat. I thought they’d leave us alone … but they must have found a way to plunder the vault and come after us. Dammit. We should have kil ed them—made a clean slate of things. We were merciful, and now this is happening.” Annev looked up to see erin looking thoughtful and Titus horri ed. “Kil ed them?” Titus said, practical y whispering. “You don’t mean that, Annev. Master Edra was with them—and Master Der and Master Carbad!” “Ather would’ve been no loss, though,” erin said. “Sweet as a viper, that one.” “Aye, and Master Aog was a brute kil er. Who does that leave? Denithal and Murlach? e alchemist and the engineer?” Annev almost sco ed. “ ose men loved their arts more than anything else. None of them deserved to survive when the rest had died.” “But Edra …” Titus protested weakly. “He wasn’t so bad? Rough as he was, he was stil fair.” Annev had to nod at that, remembering how the weapons master had chosen not to disqualify him from the Test of Judgment after nearly throwing Lemwich o the roof. “ e past is the past … why in the hel s did they decide to take over Banok? Even if they are looking for me, it makes no sense.” “It’s been almost a month since they seized the town,” Titus croaked. “Word was slow to get here.” “A month? Why hasn’t Lenka stopped them? Banok is the crossroad to the eastern kingdoms and he’s got a hostile force in control of his second largest city.” “I don’t know,” erin said, “but bandits have started to cluster around the town now it’s clear no aid is coming. Trade with the eastern kingdoms has slowed to a trickle, and merchants are avoiding Banok.” Annev reached the door to his latest room and, out of habit, checked for traps. “I hope Brayan and Dolyn made it out. e masters aren’t apt to treat a priestess of Cruithear kindly if they discover her.” He opened the door, satis ed it was safe. “Annev, we need to help them.” He laughed then—not because it was funny, but because it was al too much. He’d nearly destroyed the Enclave, which he had to leave anyway. Reeve was interrogating the remains of the Order in search of traitors—and now this business in Banok. It was al too absurd to feel real. “What are you going to do?” Annev said, sti ing another laugh. “ e godsdamned King of Greater Luqura can’t help Banok … and you want to rescue Brayan and Dolyn?” He began scooping up his possessions. Most could be squeezed into his green hiding sack, the rest he tossed into a smal but sturdy rucksack. “We can’t just leave them there, Annev.” “Why can’t we, Titus? No one else is in a hurry to help. Why is it our responsibility?” “Because no one else wil help, Annev. at’s why it has to be us. I can’t leave Brayan there, he took care of me when they made me a steward. He stood up for you when Tosan and the rest wanted to kil you—and now he needs our help. Dolyn was injured trying to help you, and now she’s trapped.” Titus’s words twisted his gut. It was true, of course. Every word of it. Brayan had fought alongside them when the feurog attacked. He had defended Annev when Tosan had tried to have him executed. And now he was in danger because Annev had let the Sons of Damnation live. Being merciful and letting those men work out their own fates was coming back to haunt him. “Dammit,” he breathed. He didn’t want this, the burden of responsibility; he wanted vengeance. He wanted to hunt Honeycutt down and drag answers from him. He wanted to punish those responsible for destroying the vil age and kil ing Sodar. He wanted to stop reacting to someone else’s plots and start making his own. He did not want this hopeless quest to Banok. Annev turned from the blank wal he’d been facing. “Maybe you haven’t heard yet, but … during your Tests of Ascendancy, Holyoak tried to kil me. I didn’t want to spoil your promotions by tel ing you about the attack at the time.” “Holyoak?” Titus breathed. “But . . . but he was so helpful with my training. I would have sensed something. At least, I think I would have.” “How did he try to kil you?” erin asked. “It doesn’t matter,” Annev said, waving his hand. “ e important thing is . . .” He wasn’t sure how much he should say, but decided his friends deserved the truth. “Holyoak was kil ed, probably by Dionach Honeycutt. ey may have been working together, and now Honeycutt has ed and Reeve, Leskal, and the Dionachs McClanahan are searching for other traitors hidden amongst the Order. I have to leave, but no one is being al owed in or out of the Enclave—did you know that?” e two boys shook their heads in silence. “I know you both want to help. I know we owe a debt to Brayan and Dolyn … but this isn’t the right time to be a hero. You should stay here and help the Order—they need your help. You’re among the few they can trust to put things in order here—and once things have quieted down, you can ask Reeve to send some Dionachs to Banok to toss out Aog, Ather, and the rest.” “What about you?” erin asked, his eyes suspicious. “Where are you going?” “I’m going after Honeycutt.” e wiry boy snorted. “ at’s funny. Weren’t you just saying to stay here and help—to not run o and be a hero?” “I’m not a hero. I’m too dangerous for that, and what I’m doing won’t be heroic.” Both boys paused at that, but in the end neither was swayed. “You should come with us,” Titus said. “We’d have a better chance of making it to Banok if you came along.” “Hold on,” erin interrupted. “Why are you leaving the Enclave when the rest of us are held here?” A sad smile tugged at Annev’s mouth. “Reeve asked me to leave.” “What! Why?” Annev removed the new glove from his hand, then wil ed the latter to brighten into a erce glow. “ is hand is dangerous,” he said. “I’m too dangerous to stay.” “And you think leaving wil make it any safer?” erin snorted. “Rot and dreck, Annev. Al the glory he’d envisioned, al the clever strategies he’d planned—it had al gone down the garderobe. Barely a handful of his men had held their ground, and al of them had been slaughtered. Alcoran had only escaped because he’d been smart enough to place his command at the back, and he’d been one of the rst to ee when the rock golem began hurling boulders at the scattered company. He stil wasn’t sure where the arrow had come from—probably one of his own gutless men—and having been shot, he’d reacted in fear and stabbed the rst person he’d stumbled into. As it turned out, that had been the company’s medic—an herbalist they’d conscripted just outside of Lochland—and he’d had no one to tend to the damaged organ after that. ere’d been no peace since then. Not from the injury, which was currently weeping pus beneath the bandage, and not from the other o cers in Borderlund’s conscript army. It had been a farce from the beginning, and now Alcoran just wanted a little peace from this sleepy caravan. Peace, and al of their possessions. “Evening, folks,” Alcoran drawled in an approximation of the local accent. “Sorry to disturb. Might I trouble you to share the warmth of your re?” He swept into a bow with a dramatic ourish, his broad-rimmed hat tilted to cover his missing eye. “It’s late, friend,” said an elderly man sitting on a stump close to the camp re. “We don’t know you. Might be better if you pushed on.” Alcoran straightened, having expected that. “I won’t share your company, then. But spare me some news from out west? I’ve just come from the east. e war with Daogort has spread al across Borderlund. e Terrans are making forays into any villages near the Kuar, and our valiant soldiers are hoping for aid from Greater Luqura or Lochland. Do you have news? Or have other a airs kept the Empire’s soldiers away from their sister kingdom?” e old man exchanged a look with the woman tending a pot of food banked in the coals—bacon and root stew by the smel of it. Alcoran fought the urge to lick his lips. “You’re from Borderlund then? Your accent … sounded like you were from the capital.” Damn, Alcoran thought. He was getting sloppy. Being hungry would do that to a man, not to mention being in constant pain. “Yes. Born in Banok but my business keeps me in Borderlund—at least it used to. Tel me. How fares the King’s Road?” e old man whispered something to the woman and slowly stood. She ran o to one of the four tents set up just beyond the re and soon two men and an older lad had joined them. “Do you know anyone in Banok?” the old man whispered, his quivering lips seeming to chew his words. “Any family there? Loved ones?” Cursed Keos. What did this old man expect? Was Alcoran going to have to make up a family there before he could sit at a re? Alcoran fought the urge to scowl and instead forced a disarming smile. He was used to getting his own way, and it pained him to be unable to order folks around. at had been the beauty of the army. Before he could think up a clever response, though, the old man continued. “If you do,” he said, looking apologetic, “then you should know they’re in a bad way right now. So bad Borderlund probably won’t see any soldiers coming to their aid—not till word gets to the capital and other parts of the Empire.” Alcoran hadn’t expected this answer. “In a bad way? How so?” e older man indicated a broad-chested fel ow who was of a height with Alcoran. He stood in his nightshirt and britches, he carried no weapons, and he had a haunted look about him. e man next to him was stockier, had hair so dark it seemed black, and an angry scar crossed his cheek and chin. e tal er man patted the scarred one on his shoulder and nodded in greeting to Alcoran, unembarrassed by his state of undress.
