chunks.content: “For now, it’s just a distraction. Reports about a besieged city and a request from some traveling dreamers, when we need to focus on the traitors in our midst.” He nodded to the others. “Misty and Tym wil help me interrogate Davies and Chan, after we’ve questioned a few others of our brethren and con rmed their al egiance remains with Odar and the Dionachs Tobar.” “I could help, though,” Annev o ered, his st tightening. “I need to help. ese people . . . Reeve, this conspiracy may have been responsible for the attacks on my village. For Sodar’s death. I won’t just leave this investigation now.” “What makes you think they’re responsible, Annev? Holyoak knew nothing about Chaenbalu or Sodar’s mission. I alone knew Sodar’s location, and I only shared it with Brother Arnor.” He paused. “And he’s dead.” Annev considered this. “Would Arnor have told anyone else?” “Only his caste leader.” e group was silent as Reeve’s indignant, instinctive words slowly sank in. “Dammit,” Reeve swore. “Honeycutt knew.” e Arch-Dionach tugged his goatee. “Damn, this is al my fault.” Annev felt his st clench tighter. “No,” he said, his voice icy. “ is is Honeycutt’s fault. You made a mistake, but he pro ted from it. He’s de nitely part of this.” “… probably. But I can’t send anyone after him, Annev.” Annev’s wandering compass suddenly pointed resolutely in one direction, and he knew what he had to do. He could nal y leave the Enclave and continue his pursuit of the people who had attacked him and the vil agers of Chaenbalu. e certainty of it felt good—it felt right. Like he’d nal y found his purpose. “I’l go. You want me to leave anyway, so I may as wel hunt Honeycutt down and get answers out of him.” Reeve tutted his tongue against his teeth, his eyes shifting between the two silent Dionachs at his side. “I don’t like it … but you’re right. I can’t keep you here, and I can’t stop you.” He glanced meaningful y at Annev’s golden hand, which had begun to glow with a dul red luminescence. “Blood and ashes,” Annev swore, tucking the hand behind his back and trying to calm his emotions. “I’m sorry.” Reeve nodded, accepting the apology without drawing attention to it. “I had this made for you.” He tossed a black felt glove to Annev, its cu stitched with silver thread and its palm and ngers padded with … something. Annev slipped it on to his left hand and was immediately impressed by its t. “It’s got a few quaire glyphs woven into the lining—shields of air and water, something that might help quench an unintentional ame …” “It’s great,” Annev said, grateful to Reeve for saving the moment. “ ank you.” He nodded again. “Gather your things and go after Honeycutt if you must … but be careful. You’re resourceful and brave—you’ve been trained as an assassin and a thief—but you’re going up against a ful Dionach with over a thousand years of experience, and that puts you at a serious disadvantage. He might kil you or you might kil him, but you’re just as likely to blow up half the city. I hope that, if it comes down to letting Honeycutt go or destroying Quiri, you’l do the smart thing and save your revenge for another day. Another time and place.” “I’m not looking for revenge,” Annev protested, his cheeks ushed with anger and embarrassment. Reeve was unconvinced. “I know that look, Annev. I’ve worn it myself. You think you’re looking for answers—and you might nd them—but consider the cost before you do anything you may regret.” Annev remembered how close he had come to destroying Luqura and nodded. “Good.” Reeve patted Tym on the back. “Brother McClanahan, I’m sorry you are becoming the Mindwalkers’ leader under such sad circumstances—but I need your help. I’d be pleased if you and Misty would help me root out any remaining heretics. It’s time we nal y rid ourselves of the rot that’s been hiding under our noses. May Odar protect us … and may the Order survive our investigation.” CHAPTER SIXTY-NINE Annev’s goodbyes with Tym and Misty were quick, and accompanied with a promise to reconnect once their missions were complete. Even as he said the words, though, Annev doubted he’d return to the Order. ere was nothing for him here—he’d come to that conclusion long ago—and his presence endangered not only the Enclave, but his friends. He hastened to Titus and erin’s quarters to say his goodbyes but didn’t see either boy in their rooms, so he headed back down to col ect his few unburned possessions in preparation for his departure. Just as he reached the basement, he found them. “Annev, we’ve been looking for you!” “Titus, erin! I was—” “You heard the news about Dolyn and Brayan?” Titus continued. “Dolyn and …” Annev’s heart fel into the pit of his stomach. Was this related to the letter Reeve had given him? Annev had completely forgotten about the Orvanish blacksmith and the burly quartermaster. He hadn’t even sent word to Banok to let Brayan know the party had moved on from Luqura to Quiri. And I promised to return for them. Blood and ashes, I’m a horrible friend. at wasn’t al he had promised and forgotten. With painful clarity, Annev remembered swearing to Red-thumb that he would introduce Jian Nikloss to Sodja Rocas in Luqura and look after the albino necromancer. Annev hadn’t kept a single promise: he hadn’t returned to Banok, he had never found Sodja, and Jian had died to save him. Annev smothered his wave of guilt and made himself ask: “What news?” “ e whole damn town has been taken hostage!” erin said, his tone near hysterical. “We’ve been searching for you ever since we heard.” “Sorry, I’ve been a bit occupied.” He stopped. “Wait … so Brayan has been taken hostage?” Titus nodded. “Annev, I’m worried. ey aren’t letting anyone out.” Annev had an uneasy feeling sinking in his gut. “ is is in Banok?” ey nodded. “Do you know who’s doing it?” “A group cal ed the Sons of Damnation,” Titus said, looking concerned. “ ey aren’t Terran,” erin added. “ at’s been con rmed by the few who escaped before the gates were sealed.” Annev swal owed back bile, beginning to fear what was coming next. “How many?” “Just a handful, Reeve heard. Annev …” Titus wetted his lips. “Annev, they used artifacts. ey used magic to control the vil agers, but they’ve also been saying horrible things about anyone who might have a talent for magic—even a little. And I think … wel , I think they may be looking for you.” Rotting blood and ashes. Annev knees suddenly felt weak and his mouth had gone dry at this con rmation of his fears. “Why do you think they want me?” e boys shared a look and erin spoke. “ ey’ve made it clear they’re looking for someone with one arm or someone with a giant golden hand.” at sealed it then. e few masters left alive at Chaenbalu were the only group whose agenda might match Titus and erin’s description. Annev let out a long, slow breath and shook his head. “ ey didn’t seem like a threat. I thought they’d leave us alone … but they must have found a way to plunder the vault and come after us. Dammit. We should have kil ed them—made a clean slate of things. We were merciful, and now this is happening.” Annev looked up to see erin looking thoughtful and Titus horri ed. “Kil ed them?” Titus said, practical y whispering. “You don’t mean that, Annev. Master Edra was with them—and Master Der and Master Carbad!” “Ather would’ve been no loss, though,” erin said. “Sweet as a viper, that one.” “Aye, and Master Aog was a brute kil er. Who does that leave? Denithal and Murlach? e alchemist and the engineer?” Annev almost sco ed. “ ose men loved their arts more than anything else. None of them deserved to survive when the rest had died.” “But Edra …” Titus protested weakly. “He wasn’t so bad? Rough as he was, he was stil fair.” Annev had to nod at that, remembering how the weapons master had chosen not to disqualify him from the Test of Judgment after nearly throwing Lemwich o the roof. “ e past is the past … why in the hel s did they decide to take over Banok? Even if they are looking for me, it makes no sense.” “It’s been almost a month since they seized the town,” Titus croaked. “Word was slow to get here.” “A month? Why hasn’t Lenka stopped them? Banok is the crossroad to the eastern kingdoms and he’s got a hostile force in control of his second largest city.” “I don’t know,” erin said, “but bandits have started to cluster around the town now it’s clear no aid is coming. Trade with the eastern kingdoms has slowed to a trickle, and merchants are avoiding Banok.” Annev reached the door to his latest room and, out of habit, checked for traps. “I hope Brayan and Dolyn made it out. e masters aren’t apt to treat a priestess of Cruithear kindly if they discover her.” He opened the door, satis ed it was safe. “Annev, we need to help them.” He laughed then—not because it was funny, but because it was al too much. He’d nearly destroyed the Enclave, which he had to leave anyway. Reeve was interrogating the remains of the Order in search of traitors—and now this business in Banok. It was al too absurd to feel real. “What are you going to do?” Annev said, sti ing another laugh. “ e godsdamned King of Greater Luqura can’t help Banok … and you want to rescue Brayan and Dolyn?” He began scooping up his possessions. Most could be squeezed into his green hiding sack, the rest he tossed into a smal but sturdy rucksack. “We can’t just leave them there, Annev.” “Why can’t we, Titus? No one else is in a hurry to help. Why is it our responsibility?” “Because no one else wil help, Annev. at’s why it has to be us. I can’t leave Brayan there, he took care of me when they made me a steward. He stood up for you when Tosan and the rest wanted to kil you—and now he needs our help. Dolyn was injured trying to help you, and now she’s trapped.” Titus’s words twisted his gut. It was true, of course. Every word of it. Brayan had fought alongside them when the feurog attacked. He had defended Annev when Tosan had tried to have him executed. And now he was in danger because Annev had let the Sons of Damnation live. Being merciful and letting those men work out their own fates was coming back to haunt him. “Dammit,” he breathed. He didn’t want this, the burden of responsibility; he wanted vengeance. He wanted to hunt Honeycutt down and drag answers from him. He wanted to punish those responsible for destroying the vil age and kil ing Sodar. He wanted to stop reacting to someone else’s plots and start making his own. He did not want this hopeless quest to Banok. Annev turned from the blank wal he’d been facing. “Maybe you haven’t heard yet, but … during your Tests of Ascendancy, Holyoak tried to kil me. I didn’t want to spoil your promotions by tel ing you about the attack at the time.” “Holyoak?” Titus breathed. “But . . . but he was so helpful with my training. I would have sensed something. At least, I think I would have.” “How did he try to kil you?” erin asked. “It doesn’t matter,” Annev said, waving his hand. “ e important thing is . . .” He wasn’t sure how much he should say, but decided his friends deserved the truth. “Holyoak was kil ed, probably by Dionach Honeycutt. ey may have been working together, and now Honeycutt has ed and Reeve, Leskal, and the Dionachs McClanahan are searching for other traitors hidden amongst the Order. I have to leave, but no one is being al owed in or out of the Enclave—did you know that?” e two boys shook their heads in silence. “I know you both want to help. I know we owe a debt to Brayan and Dolyn … but this isn’t the right time to be a hero. You should stay here and help the Order—they need your help. You’re among the few they can trust to put things in order here—and once things have quieted down, you can ask Reeve to send some Dionachs to Banok to toss out Aog, Ather, and the rest.” “What about you?” erin asked, his eyes suspicious. “Where are you going?” “I’m going after Honeycutt.” e wiry boy snorted. “ at’s funny. Weren’t you just saying to stay here and help—to not run o and be a hero?” “I’m not a hero. I’m too dangerous for that, and what I’m doing won’t be heroic.” Both boys paused at that, but in the end neither was swayed. “You should come with us,” Titus said. “We’d have a better chance of making it to Banok if you came along.” “Hold on,” erin interrupted. “Why are you leaving the Enclave when the rest of us are held here?” A sad smile tugged at Annev’s mouth. “Reeve asked me to leave.” “What! Why?” Annev removed the new glove from his hand, then wil ed the latter to brighten into a erce glow. “ is hand is dangerous,” he said. “I’m too dangerous to stay.” “And you think leaving wil make it any safer?” erin snorted. “Rot and dreck, Annev. Don’t you think you’re better o with people who can help you? Or do you think it’s wise to go running o into a crowded city with a cursed hand that glows like the aming sun? Blood and hel . You do remember what happened back in Chaenbalu, don’t you?” Before Annev knew what he was doing, he cu ed his friend across the face with the back of his right hand, the rings clawing into erin’s esh. erin stumbled backward into Titus, his hand clutching his bloody cheek, his eyes wide with shock. “I haven’t forgotten,” Annev growled, his temper hot, his blood pumping in his ears. “I can’t forget. While you’re practicing your little spel s with the Dionachs, I’m down here remembering what it was like to burn down a building l ed with friends, women, and children.” He took a step forward, the narrow con nes of the room forcing his friends to step back. “When you’re upstairs enjoying your views of the city,” he continued, “I’m down here in the dark, because staying underground is the only place I’m t to live.” Another step. “When you’re joking, enjoying your new life, and your new magic, I’m hiding from assassins.” He slammed his metal st against the doorframe, causing his friends to jump backward into the hal way. “And now you tel me to stay here, where people can help, when those same people have told me to leave.” “Annev,” Titus began, his voice pleading though it came out like a whine. “He didn’t mean—” “I know what he meant, Titus, don’t keep apologizing for him.” He fought o the sneer that tugged at his lips. “You two want to leave? Fine. Leave. Break your oaths to the Order and pretend to be heroes—but when it al goes to hel , when you get captured or raped or kil ed, I can’t come and save you. I’m ghting my own demons. Ones that don’t go away.” He waved his golden hand at them. “Ones I can’t get rid of … or forget.” He spun away then, his eyes barely registering the smoldering imprint his hand had left in the wood. Behind him, his friends were smal and frightened. I shouldn’t have said that, Annev thought, immediately regretful. ey didn’t deserve to have my frustrations taken out on them. Only he couldn’t take back the words—and he couldn’t deny that he had meant them. Titus and erin real y were safer here at the Enclave, and he had no more desire to run o to save Banok than he did to stay here at the Enclave. He had a lead on who was responsible for the attack on Chaenbalu and he meant to fol ow it. Every minute he spent here was another minute Honeycutt might elude him. “Fine,” erin said. “We wil go. We don’t need you, and we can take care of ourselves.” Annev heard him turn to go, but then the footsteps halted halfway down the corridor. A moment later, he was back. “One more thing,” he said, his tone ice. “You’re the one leaving us. You’ve decided we’re a burden.” He waited for Annev to respond, but he had nothing to say. erin’s words re ected what lay in his heart: Annev had outgrown his friends, and he was determined to nd his own path, not be fettered by others’ expectations. Annev didn’t say any of it. He didn’t have to. He was sure Titus could hear his thoughts—Annev wasn’t shielding them—and erin could see it in his face. “Figures.” erin spat at his feet. “You and Kenton are the exact same. As soon as you think you can get by without us, you drop us like so much rubbish. But we don’t need you, you know that? We’ve grown here—without you, despite you—and I bet that burns you up inside.” Annev spun and erin inched, hand raised to block another blow to his face—but Annev didn’t strike him. Instead, he pul ed his dragonscale cloak over his pack and shoulders, nodded to them, and pushed past into the hal way. erin watched him go in silence, and Titus reached out a hand to slow him. But Annev did not stop. He couldn’t, because if he did, they might see the tears staining his cheeks. ey might see the uncertainty in his eyes or realize how much erin’s words had stung him. He pushed on, not al owing himself to look back, no goodbyes or farewel s. It didn’t feel right, but Annev told himself this was how it had to be. It had to be a clean break. No ambiguity. No promises to see one another again. He told himself he was doing it for them—to keep his friends safe—but some quiet part of him was glad of the separation, and that same part knew his motives weren’t entirely altruistic. Annev wiped his cheeks, set his jaw, and calmed his emotions. “I’m coming for you, Honeycutt,” he whispered, climbing the steps toward Honeycutt’s chambers. “I’m coming for you, and you’re going to tel me every secret you know—every single thing that led to the attack on Chaenbalu—and then you’re going to pay for Sodar’s death … and the deaths of every man, woman, and child taken by Oyru, his eidolons, and the feurog.” Annev stopped in front of Honeycutt’s door then rested his ngertips on the wood: he felt the magic from the man’s Ward of Silence there, the glyph burned into the opposite side of the wood planks. He focused on it, gritted his teeth, and used the Rod of Arti cing to unmake it. When he was nished, his ngers clutched the ephemeral threads of blood-talent left behind by Honeycutt’s ward; at its opposite end, he felt the familiar hum and thrum of life. “I’m coming for you.” CHAPTER SEVENTY Using the ampli ed power of the Inquisitor ring, Annev found he could il uminate the faint ribbons of blood-talent until their woven strands of pink light glowed erce as a scarlet sunrise, a red streak that stood bright against the coppery mists l ing his vision. Annev had grown so accustomed to those mists that navigating them had become second nature. He fol owed the trail of blood-talent into the darkness, its strand humming with Honeycutt’s pulse, and when he reached a shuttered window that led out into the night, he knew Honeycutt had used it to make his unseen exit from the Enclave. A glance at the wal s outside told him much of what he needed to know. He used his Breathbreaker magic to oat down from here, Annev thought, searching for another glyph. He didn’t see any symbols at the window’s ledge, so he supposed it lay at the other end of the drop. To nd out, Annev would have to climb down—no smal task given the height of the Enclave’s wal s. e brickwork wasn’t sheer or wel maintained, which at least gave Annev’s clever hands a chance to nd purchase amidst the mortar, stones, and ledges. ough, the Hand of Keos might be a hindrance. It was strong, but its ngers might be too large to t into the cracks and crevices. Only one way to nd out. Annev wound the corded threads of blood-talent around his golden ngers, then eased himself over the window ledge. is is crazy, he thought, glancing down at the cobblestone street far below. I have no safety rope and I have no experience climbing with this prosthetic. I should leave through the front door, circle the building, and nd the place where Honeycutt landed. But he suspected the Enclave’s magical defenses wouldn’t al ow him to nd its eastern wal , and the Dionachs guarding the front door might not know they were supposed to let Annev leave. It’l be ne, he thought, trying not to think about slipping. If I need to, maybe I can use the Hand of Keos to create handholds in the stone. Fortunately, it never came to that. After his right hand found purchase amid the uneven stones, Annev eased his left hand down the wal and found it clung to the rocks with almost no e ort. He hadn’t melted the stones or reshaped the bricks to t his massive hand, yet he felt certain magic was somehow at play. Devilry, he thought. But he was grateful for it and used it to descend swiftly from the upper oors of the Enclave. e trouble came when he was halfway down the building. e brickwork there was much tighter, and Annev found himself relying more and more on the magical strength and dexterity of his left hand . . . and worrying that relying on it too much might break the delicate blood-talent threads leading to Honeycutt. As if in response to that fear, as Annev reached for another hand hold he felt the tension on the magic thread tighten unexpectedly around his ngers. He stopped, feeling it ease, then reached again. e threads of blood-magic strained further . . . and then they snapped. Annev cursed, lunging for the fal ing laments as they began to disintegrate, and felt his right hand slip from the weather-worn stones— —he was tumbling backward to the street below. He twisted in the air, clawing desperately to sink his magic hand into the stone, to slow his fal or assert any measure of control over his descent, and only managed to move so his face would hit the ground rst. He barely managed to get his hands beneath him before smashing into the stones. Bones broke on impact. He heard as wel as felt the sickening crunch and the wet thump of soft meat against cobblestones. It would have been worse—far worse, by his estimation—without the sudden woosh of air he’d felt just before hitting the street. It spread out beneath him like a mattress of straw and feathers, saving him from the worst of the fal , but his head stil rang like a bel on Seventhday. “Keos,” he coughed, winded, sputtering the curse he’d been unable to scream. He spat, dribbling saliva onto the street, and was relieved to see it did not contain his blood. He struggled to right himself, moving careful y in case his neck or spine had been injured. ey seemed intact, though—and even his hands and wrists were unbroken, despite being the rst to strike the cobblestones—but his right arm had snapped, the bone protruding from his skin at the elbow. “Blood and bones,” he moaned. en he grit his teeth, clutched his arm, and forced himself to his feet. Annev glared up at the window he’d fal en from and then back down at the stones that had caught him. How far had he fal en? He’d thought two stories, but now he wasn’t so sure. And what had broken his fal ? Had his magic prosthetic tried to save him? It wouldn’t have been the rst time, but he didn’t see how the Hand of Keos could have formed the shield that saved him from a worse fal . Shield. He stared at the ground again. It was a shield, wasn’t it? Some burst of wind … some pad of air? He might have wondered for longer, but then he glimpsed the blue-white glow coming from his codavora ring, saw a dark stain beneath the haze of magic and cautiously rubbed the wet smear away. As he did, the glow of magic disappeared and Annev’s golden ngers came away aked with blood. But not his blood. And then it came to him. is is erin’s . . . from when I slapped his face. is is Breathbreaker blood. A chil ran through Annev; remorse for injuring his friend, and elation that he might have accidental y performed Darite magic without possessing the skil himself. He had accidental y bonded Brother Tym’s Mindwalker blood to the silver-gold codavora ring, and this seemed similar, though erin’s blood did not appear to have permanently bonded with the artifact. He had stil exploited his friend’s blood-magic, though. How? Not by making a glyph or speaking a word of power … Had Annev simply burned out the magic in his friend’s blood? If so, that would explain why it was dry instead of wet or sticky: the quaire had been leeched from the liquid. e pain of his broken arm screamed for attention, and Annev realized he’d have to save that mystery for another time. He moved with the practiced caution of someone who had grown used to tending his own injuries. Sodar had once helped him, but those days seemed a distant memory now. e priest’s teachings remained, though, and Annev had one other artifact to assist his ministrations. e ngers of his left hand brushed his neck, the golden skin somehow warm to the touch, and Annev careful y untied the bloody rag he’d grown accustomed to wearing as a grisly neckerchief. e Shirt of Regeneration had de nitely seen better days. In its current state, no one would see anything more than a sweat-soaked, blood-stained rag —but it was stil potent. Once he’d unwound the scarf from his neck, he careful y tied the cloth around his bicep. He was about to shift the rag so it covered his broken bone and ruptured elbow, but then he hesitated. Would the artifact try to seal his esh with the bone stil protruding? e shirt had healed broken bones before, back in Chaenbalu when he had fought the feurog … but those bones hadn’t broken his skin—and hadn’t Reeve counsel ed him not to heal Sraon while the venom was stil in his body? Blood and piss. Annev braced himself against the wal of the al ey, held his right arm in the grip of the Hand of Keos . . . and pul ed. With a grinding pop, the broken bones shift back into place and an intense wave of agony threatened to wash over Annev. Before he could black out or the bones could shift again, he dragged the healing cloth over his injury and pul ed it tight. e magic took hold of Annev’s esh before he’d prepared himself, and he felt the twist and pop of bones resetting and then mending. He screamed a second time at the sudden agony, then choked back a cry as his skin burned hot beneath the rag, the esh fusing together and completing the healing process—six weeks of healing in one go. He felt sore and drained, and the light of his glowing left hand revealed that a pink scar now laced his skin, but the pain was greatly diminished. Am I becoming the thing I hate? he wondered, watching as the gray pool of matter trickled toward a drain in the corner of the warehouse. Am I kil ing monsters … or am I becoming one? Annev waited for his conscience to respond, but there was only silence. CHAPTER EIGHTY-ONE It took Consul Phoeba Ondina Anabo almost a ful day to travel from King Cheng’s court in central Innistiul to the island’s southern shores, and from there to the northern beaches of Odarnea. After navigating the channel’s choppy waters, she was usual y too sick to travel beyond the coastal town of Neahmar and so had to endure a room at the only inn that seemed not to be lice-ridden. After two more days in a carriage navigating the provinces, she was then obliged to spend a night in Quiri, before booking a river voyage south to Luqura. If King Cheng felt generous—which was not often—or if a diplomatic mission required haste, she would then secure the services of a hedge witch or water wizard to guarantee smooth currents and favorable winds for the nal leg of her journey. Such self-taught sorcerers lacked the formal training of the Dionachs, but a competent one could stil help her shave a day or more from the typical four-day voyage. Having a genuine Breathbreaker or Shieldbearer was even better, for if the boat were swift and the captain departed early, she could reach Luqura’s northern gate before nightfal on the second day—and traveling home with the current was even faster. Such extravagances were hard to arrange, though, and expensive besides. Especial y since King Cheng was as miserly as he was shrewd—and Magistrate Bliven seemed to take especial delight in underfunding her travels. “An entire rotten week,” she spat, her sea sickness already tickling at her as she contemplated boarding another vessel on the morrow. “Two days eating dust in that bloody carriage. I’l barely have time to bathe and sleep … and now Bliven is suggesting I skip the night in Quiri altogether? at’l be the day. If he advances the issue any more with King Cheng, I’l have Elar cut out the man’s tongue and put it in a jar next to his bal s.” “Magistrate Bliven,” Ja a asked, trotting behind with the two heavy bags. “He keeps his bal s in a jar?” Anabo stood on the street in front of their destination, her face screwed up in distaste. “Damned if I know, Ja a. What do they usual y do with a eunuch’s bal s?” e Ilumite manservant set the bags down in front of the sprawling two-story inn. “I was never told. I believe mine were fed to the pigs, though I can’t con rm that. I’m certain they were not kept in jars.” Anabo groaned. “It was a gure of speech, Ja —a joke. You have those in Ilumea, don’t you?” Ja a was half listening. “What would be the point of saving them, anyway? ey would spoil unless you pickled them, and that would be a waste of good vinegar.” “Ja a,” Anabo said, rubbing her temples, “Must you always take things so literal y? It’s infuriating.” “I’m certain it is, madame.” Anabo tucked a strand of black hair behind her ear and sighed. “Just take care of the rotting rooms, wil you? And have Alan send up hot water for the tub. I’m caked in dust.” “Dusted.” “Mm?” “You have been dusted with dust. Caked implies a thick layer, or perhaps mud, and since you’re not—” “Just pay for the rooms and bring up the damn hot water, Ja a—then I don’t want to see you again till morning.” “As you wish, Consul Anabo.” “You’re bleeding right, it is.” She ung open the door then and ew past the innkeeper’s desk, ignoring Alan’s courteous nod and inquiry about the nature of the roads to the north. Ja a stepped between them, his tal , heavily muscled body blocking the innkeeper behind his long, walnut-stained desk. e eunuch o ered some apologies on behalf of his mistress and then Phoeba was out of earshot, already focused on the glory of the forthcoming bathwater. e mainland was too cold for her liking here, and people were too formal besides. But then, that was her job, wasn’t it? To put up with the cooler weather and the colder pleasantries, so King Cheng didn’t have to leave the comforts of his palace and his concubines. Anabo gritted her teeth and breezed up the stairs to the second oor. Perhaps that was what she needed: a nice compliant concubine. It had been ages since her last one ran away, and she’d been so busy haggling with Bliven over travel and lodging that she’d forgotten to requisition another. She’d have to make that a priority when she returned. Perhaps Guildmaster Whalen would donate one to her in the interim. She kept a stately room further down the corridor on retainer at the Stag and Oak. And Keos take that damn treasurer if he thinks I’l give this up. He’s not the one who has to spend a week on dusty roads and shit- l ed rivers. He’s not the one who has to check for lice every time he stops in Neahmar or who has to put up with … Anabo ung open the door and the sight within took her breath away: clean linens, a freshly made bed, scented candles, soap and a steaming tub of hot water. “Alan, you bastard,” she breathed, inhaling the scent of jasmine and juniper. “ ank the gods. ank stoic Odar and radiant Lumea and their bloody brother Keos.” She moaned with delight, already anticipating the warmth. “Ja a!” she cal ed down. “You can cancel the hot water! Alan did something right for once. I’l see you in the morning!” She slammed the door before her manservant could reply and began stripping o her travel cloak and skirts. She was half-naked before she realized the window was open and a gentle breeze was bil owing the curtains. She hu ed, strode over to the window and closed the shutters with a satisfying click. She could stil feel the breeze through the green-painted wooden slats, though, and it sent goose pimples up her esh. She shivered, more in anticipation of the bath than out of any chil —then she stripped o the rest of her clothes and slipped into the tub with a moan. “Yes,” she hissed, leaning back and closing her eyes. “ ank the ever-loving gods.” “You don’t real y strike me as the pious type.” Anabo shot up from the water, her left arm slapped across her breasts out of an instinct that thirty years in Innistiul had never quite driven from her. “Who the dreck are you?” she shouted, her head spinning to nd the speaker. “What are you doing in here? Get the hel out!” e young man stepped from the shadows behind the curtains and pul ed back the gray-white hood of his cloak. Had she real y not seen him before? Had she not noticed him while she stood so close to the window? e goose pimples returned again, now magni ed tenfold. “I’m here on behalf of Dionach Honeycutt.” Anabo frowned and she slowly eased back into the steamy water. “Are you now? at’s interesting. Jayar never told me you’d be coming.” “No?” Anabo looked at the stranger with fresh eyes. He was handsome enough— medium build, light brown hair, wide shoulders, and a youthful face. Yes, she was tempted to ask the Guildmaster for someone like this. Something about his eyes . . . dark blue and piercing. She broke her gaze, though she felt he should be the one looking away. “You’re a Breathbreaker then?” e candles in the room ickered and the young man rose to hover in midair. Anabo sni ed. “You’re just showing o . Stil , I could use a Breathbreaker tomorrow … and the day after. I’m taking a river barge south to Luqura and I’d kil for a favorable wind. ink you could arrange that?” “No.” “Why? Got somewhere better to be?” She raised her brow archly then leaned back until her chest peeked above the waters. “I could make it worth your while, and I promise Jayar won’t mind if you’re gone for a few days.” “My understanding … is that your promises aren’t worth very much.” “I’m a diplomat. I make a lot of promises and I’m prone to break a few now and then. I assure you, I can’t keep track of them al . Why are you here?” “Honeycutt asked you to pass a message to the mercenary Saltair—one about a boy named Annev de Breth.” “ e lizardman?” Anabo snorted. “ at’s hardly an o ense. If the Empire were a brothel, he’d be the bordel o’s favorite whore, at least here in the north —” e water in the tub suddenly felt ice-cold as she remembered the contents of Honeycutt’s message. e boy’s name and the memories it brought with it. Keos, she swore, if this one can read minds as wel as— “I can.” Anabo slapped the water, realizing she’d already given herself up. “Dammit! You should real y have to announce when you’re mindwalking. It’s not fair to the rest of us liars.” She squinted at the gray-garbed stranger who stil oated in the air, his cloak rippling softly about him. “What’s your interest in Annev de Breth?” the man asked. Anabo snorted. “Nothing—at least not for myself. Saltair was in charge of it.” “And what orders did you give him?” “ e ones Honeycutt paid me to pass along.” “No, you rescinded those and gave him a new set of orders. What were they?” Damn. “If you know I rescinded them, you’l know what the new orders were —or you could just read my mind.” “You’re blocking me—or trying to.” “And am I succeeding?” e stranger shrugged. “You’re right. I already know your replacement orders. I just wanted you to con rm them.” Anabo narrowed her eyes. “No,” she said, cal ing the young man’s blu . “You only think you know. at’s why you want me to con rm it.” She smiled. “I may not read minds, but I can read people, and you … you don’t even work for Honeycutt, do you?” He averted his gaze—she had guessed correctly then—and now that she considered it, he seemed more a boy than a man. Eighteen or nineteen? Surely no more than twenty. His features were strange too. Ilumite? Darite? Hard to say. ere may even be some Terran blood mixed in there. And was his left hand larger than the right? Di cult to tel with the single black glove he wore. Probably a padded gauntlet. “Who are you real y?” she asked. “You’re a Breathbreaker, but not one of Jayar’s, and a Mindwalker … so you’re a dualist. Very interesting.” Her eyes suddenly grew at. “Now cut the shit. Holyoak sent you to check up on me, so I guess he wants to know why the boy is stil alive. Wel , you can tel him I’ve been in Innistiul and none of the keokum’s messages have reached me. So Saltair’s either neck-deep in one of his schemes or he’s dead. Elar has been keeping me updated, and I’l check on it myself when I get to Luqura.” She paused. “Which you could speed along if you decided to come with me.” e young man pretended to hesitate, but Anabo already knew which way the coin would fal . She had a talent for reading people, men especial y. Her mother had whispered it came from an Ilumite ancestor. is one had decided. He would come. She just needed to give him the right reasons. “My previous o er stil stands,” she said, arching her back enticingly and thinking lusty thoughts to prevent this Mindbreaker … this Breathwalker … from learning she had no way to pay him except information, favors and— “Blood.” Anabo sat up in the water. “Excuse me?” “Ten vials of blood. One from you. One from your manservant … and eight more of my choosing.” e consul blinked. “Blood?” she repeated. “Just blood. Nothing else?” She shrugged suggestively. e boy was young, true, but she’d had younger … and it was a long way to Luqura, even with magical assistance. She’d made her own decision, that she didn’t want to wait for a concubine from Guildmaster Whalen—not when she had the genuine article right in front of her. “Ten vials of blood,” he repeated, “and … some information.” Phoeba Ondina Anabo sighed. Information was her most prized asset outside of coin, and it always seemed to cost her more than she bargained. Sex was so much cheaper when people deigned to accept it in payment. Maybe she was losing her touch. Maybe she was just getting older—though forty hardly seemed old to her. She licked her lips. So bedding this one would be a chal enge. She had time, and he’d have to take breaks to regain whatever essence he tapped to use his arcane magic. She smiled seductively. “So you’l come with me then? We can talk to Saltair, and you can report back to Holyoak yourself?” “Yes,” he said. “I’l come.” “And you’l help speed our voyage with your wind magic. As much as you can? As much as you … are able?” Again that hesitation. “If you get me the blood I request, yes.” Anabo frowned. What in the name of Keos did he want with blood? She supposed it was cheaper than sex—if not nearly as much fun. “I’l get you the blood. One smal vial from me. One from Ja a.” She shook her head, knowing it would be di cult to explain to her manservant. Fortunately, she didn’t have to explain. She could simply command. “I can’t promise you the eight other vials without knowing whose you want.” “I understand. I stil want your word you’l do everything you can to get them.” Anabo gave the young man her most captivating smile. “Of course, of course.” He knew how little her word was worth. ey were just playing games now, and these were games she knew how to play. “What should I cal you?” “Magpie.” “Ah,” Anabo purred. “I thought that pattern looked familiar.” She nodded at Magpie’s cloak and he slowly oated back to the ground. She smiled again, more wickedly this time. at skil would be very useful on the voyage. She wondered what other skil s he had … “Do you have anywhere to be, Master Magpie? I could use some help scrubbing my—” “I’l see you tomorrow morning. Riverside wharf. e Crested Cormorant. Bring the vials of blood.” “Mm. I’l see what I can arrange.” She began soaping herself and could feel his eyes on her again. at was good. at was what she wanted. “Did you arrange al this?” she asked, her sudsy ngers gesturing at the candles, the linens, and the hot water. “Alan is not usual y so thoughtful. Were you hoping to catch me o my guard? Vulnerable?” Magpie didn’t answer. Anabo slowly stood then and, with a sultry smile, she turned to face the young man. It was then she saw the shutters stood open and Holyoak’s messenger had already gone. Anabo might have been disappointed by that, but instead she only felt the thril of a chal enge. is would be far more fun than another concubine—they never lasted long once things got interesting anyway. And if things went wel , who knew? Perhaps she’d even keep her promise about the blood. “Strange bird,” she muttered, easing herself back into the water. “Not like any of the ones Holyoak sent before.” She wondered what that meant. Surely nothing good, since he was asking about Saltair. at meant this one—this Magpie—was special. More dangerous, no doubt, and it made her second-guess her promise to give him her blood. Something about him gave her pause, as if his eyes could pierce into her soul and see the secrets buried there. She supposed that wasn’t her imagination either, not with a Breathwalker … or Mindbreaker. Damn, she hated dualists, especial y the ones who could read minds. It made her work so much harder. But then, the chal enge was part of the fun. She detested long boat rides and bumpy carriages, but the choppy waters and dusty roads were only half the bother. It was the boredom that made her want to claw out her eyes or cut out her manservant’s dry tongue. Give her an interesting companion, though— someone with a little charisma, a little mystery—and just about any voyage became tolerable, even enjoyable. She guessed that the next three days would be ful of surprises. PART SIX To Kryss Jakasen and the Keepers of the Flame, I pray that my letter nds you wel —whether in Banok or Luqura or wherever your travels take you. Likewise, I thank you for your kind request to join you and your companions in Banok later this season. I must decline. Noble though your quest may be, local troubles in the Brotherhood require my ful attention at this time. If I am able to reconcile the current issues in Quiri quickly, I may stil send another member of my order to join your council, but I would strongly urge against meeting in Banok. Recent reports suggest the township is besieged by a coordinated assault from local bandits. I have news regarding one of your companions, though it is not the pleasant kind. e soothsayer Jian Nikloss died shortly after joining my company. May it be some consolation to know his death was a valiant one, his life given in the defense of others. In regards to Annev, you are correct in guessing the young man was recently in my Enclave, but I am sorry to say he has since departed. I gave him your letter, so perhaps he wil decide of his own accord to aid you in your quest. If he does, I advise caution in his presence and recommend you be respectful of his personal traumas (as I’m certain you would be). To do otherwise might have disastrous consequences for both you and your companions. May the light of Lumea and the winds of Odar protect you, Arch-Dionach Reeve, High Order of the Dionachs Tobar CHAPTER EIGHTY-TWO Alcoran approached the embers of the fading re with al the trepidation of a dog begging for scraps. e summer night wasn’t al that cold, but he coveted much of what the smal caravan shared: companionship, warmth, a sense of peace. ere had been very little peace during the campaign in Borderlund— not among its commanders or the squabbling nobility, and certainly not along the front lines adjacent to the Kuar River and the Terran armies in Daogort. It had been madness. Greed and bloodlust and chaos. He’d lost most of his troops and his left eye on his rst run at the Black Wal , and the company had never recovered. Al the glory he’d envisioned, al the clever strategies he’d planned—it had al gone down the garderobe. Barely a handful of his men had held their ground, and al of them had been slaughtered. Alcoran had only escaped because he’d been smart enough to place his command at the back, and he’d been one of the rst to ee when the rock golem began hurling boulders at the scattered company. He stil wasn’t sure where the arrow had come from—probably one of his own gutless men—and having been shot, he’d reacted in fear and stabbed the rst person he’d stumbled into. As it turned out, that had been the company’s medic—an herbalist they’d conscripted just outside of Lochland—and he’d had no one to tend to the damaged organ after that. ere’d been no peace since then. Not from the injury, which was currently weeping pus beneath the bandage, and not from the other o cers in Borderlund’s conscript army. It had been a farce from the beginning, and now Alcoran just wanted a little peace from this sleepy caravan. Peace, and al of their possessions. “Evening, folks,” Alcoran drawled in an approximation of the local accent. “Sorry to disturb. Might I trouble you to share the warmth of your re?” He swept into a bow with a dramatic ourish, his broad-rimmed hat tilted to cover his missing eye. “It’s late, friend,” said an elderly man sitting on a stump close to the camp re. “We don’t know you. Might be better if you pushed on.” Alcoran straightened, having expected that. “I won’t share your company, then. But spare me some news from out west? I’ve just come from the east. e war with Daogort has spread al across Borderlund. e Terrans are making forays into any villages near the Kuar, and our valiant soldiers are hoping for aid from Greater Luqura or Lochland. Do you have news? Or have other a airs kept the Empire’s soldiers away from their sister kingdom?” e old man exchanged a look with the woman tending a pot of food banked in the coals—bacon and root stew by the smel of it. Alcoran fought the urge to lick his lips. “You’re from Borderlund then? Your accent … sounded like you were from the capital.” Damn, Alcoran thought. He was getting sloppy. Being hungry would do that to a man, not to mention being in constant pain. “Yes. Born in Banok but my business keeps me in Borderlund—at least it used to. Tel me. How fares the King’s Road?” e old man whispered something to the woman and slowly stood. She ran o to one of the four tents set up just beyond the re and soon two men and an older lad had joined them. “Do you know anyone in Banok?” the old man whispered, his quivering lips seeming to chew his words. “Any family there? Loved ones?” Cursed Keos. What did this old man expect? Was Alcoran going to have to make up a family there before he could sit at a re? Alcoran fought the urge to scowl and instead forced a disarming smile. He was used to getting his own way, and it pained him to be unable to order folks around. at had been the beauty of the army. Before he could think up a clever response, though, the old man continued. “If you do,” he said, looking apologetic, “then you should know they’re in a bad way right now. So bad Borderlund probably won’t see any soldiers coming to their aid—not till word gets to the capital and other parts of the Empire.” Alcoran hadn’t expected this answer. “In a bad way? How so?” e older man indicated a broad-chested fel ow who was of a height with Alcoran. He stood in his nightshirt and britches, he carried no weapons, and he had a haunted look about him. e man next to him was stockier, had hair so dark it seemed black, and an angry scar crossed his cheek and chin. e tal er man patted the scarred one on his shoulder and nodded in greeting to Alcoran, unembarrassed by his state of undress.

chunks.title: Chapter 11
chunks.content: “I’m John Stout and this is my brother, Jacob. We just came from Banok. Barely escaped with the shirts on our backs.” “Escaped?” Alcoran tilted his head, stil trying to make sense of the tale they were tel ing him. “Surely the Terrans haven’t come this far into the Empire?” John shook his head. “I don’t think so … but maybe? We were overrun by the Sons of Damnation—and they didn’t sound like foreigners. ey knew the city, knew our ways and our speech, but they were dressed strangely, and they said they’d come to liberate the village from evil. We didn’t know what to make of them, wrote them o as zealots from Quiri … but then they seized the Harth family’s keep and started making demands of the governor. Acted like they were running the village. Governor sent the town guard . . . and they didn’t come back. ey formed a militia, and they didn’t return either. Some folks went for help and . . . wel , we didn’t see them again, neither. When others nal y did come, it was more strangers and monsters—and they were there to help the Sons of Damnation. e whole place has gone to hel and the remaining townsfolk are being held hostage—forced to serve the man who leads the Sons.” “Strangers and monsters,” Alcoran repeated, forgetting for a moment why he had come to the smal encampment. “And … Sons of Damnation?” He scratched his short red beard, hunger receding to the back of his mind. “And you don’t know who they are?” e shorter man, Jacob, shook his head. “We weren’t keen on nding out. We decided to send for help—to sneak out of the vil age and nd someone who might help take back the city—but no one cares. Everyone’s concerned about their own problems, like the war in the east or the famine in the south. We heard no aid would be coming from the capital, so we’re taking our case to the king of Paldron.” Alcoran laughed—he couldn’t help it. e irony was too amusing. “King Alpenrose wouldn’t sel you his own piss, much less spare you a company of soldiers.” “But … the people are desperate. e soldiers are gone. e only folk left are shopkeeps and farmers. Merchants and artisans. ey aren’t warriors! And the people control ing the city … they’ve got magic. e Sons said they hate it, but they use it to keep people in line. Even the mercenaries they’ve hired— half of them use shadow magic and the others . . . they’re rotting demons. eir esh is more metal and stone than skin and bone!” “You have my sympathy—truly, you do—but no aid wil be coming. Borderlund has its sts ful on the Black Wal . Our numbers are thin. Conscripts are eeing, abandoning the war and seeking safety elsewhere. If they aren’t helped soon, the Terrans wil cross the Kuar and start sacking Paldron itself.” Alcoran hu ed. “If these men—these Sons of Damnation— aren’t harming you, you should count yourselves lucky. And if they aren’t friends of the Terrans, maybe they’l protect you from the war that’s about to come.” e old man’s face paled. “If that is the case, then we are truly in dark times.” You don’t know the half of it, Alcoran thought, feeling a tiny pang of guilt for what his band of soldiers was about to do to these folks. Times were tough al around, though, and only the ttest were going to survive. He tipped his hat low over his bandaged eye and made sure to stay out of the relight. His men should be in position now … yet something stayed his hand. “Lord Stout,” Alcoran said, addressing the elder of the two young men. “You said these Sons of Damnation aren’t letting folk in or out. How did you escape?” “We can’t take much credit for it,” the tal er man said. “ ese warlocks— the shadow men helping the Sons of Damnation—they wear gray and purple clothing and masks, and they spy on us townsfolk for the Sons of Damnation … but there’s a resistance forming. ey’ve got a leader too—one who uses magic—and she helped us waylay two of these warlocks and take their clothes.” Alcoran frowned. “She? ere’s a witch leading your militia?” “Not just one,” Jacob interrupted, “there are three! One who speaks to the plants, one who doesn’t speak at al , and one who charms the warlocks with her witching song.” John elbowed his younger brother, shushing him. “ ey aren’t witches. ey’re just . . . wel , they’re helping us. And we’re ghting back, with or without King Lenka and King Alpenrose.” Alcoran nodded, his tongue drawing across the bottom of his front teeth. “ ese mercenaries. Any notion why they’re helping these Sons of Damnation?” John and Jacob exchanged a look that suggested they knew exactly what Alcoran was asking, but they didn’t seem eager to share that information. Perhaps they weren’t as stupid as Alcoran hoped. “Only rumors,” John said, speaking for them both. “We heard about some kind of gold—liquid gold, I guess. I don’t know why that’d be so special, but word of it got out soon after the Sons came to Banok, and the mercenaries started appearing pretty quickly.” “Huh. Liquid gold.” Alcoran shrugged. “Seems like it’d be more valuable as simple coin. Easier to transport too. Stil … gold is gold. When folk o er it, others wil take it.” He hesitated. “Anyone else taking this gold? Any of your townsfolk helping these Sons?” “You mean has anyone turned traitor?” Jacob spat then ran his nger along the side of his savaged cheek. “Vilhelm Stenger decided he’d take some of that gold—he signed on to help the Sons keep order in the town—but we made an example of him. Forrest Bower and Josie Ladle too. Banok folks don’t take kindly to traitors.” Alcoran was satis ed. “Sounds like you folk have your a airs in order then. And this old ga er here … no relation to you?” e young men shook their heads as the old man spoke. “I can speak for myself. Me and Mirel a found the boys just before nightfal . ey were tired and needed help, so we took them in. We’l take them as far as Trizgard.” “I just came from there,” Alcoran said, grunting. “It hasn’t been touched by the war yet, that’s why I was surprised by trouble in Banok.” “Eh, that’s some good news at least. We’re from Luqura and don’t usual y trade beyond Banok—too many bandits on the King’s Road.” He sni ed. “But there’s no trade in Banok these days, so we’ve got to chance Trizgard.” Alcoran clucked his tongue. “Bandits, eh? Yes … that real y is a sad tale.” Alcoran took o his black felt hat and waved its wide brim in front of his face. “Hm?” e old man squinted at him in the pale glow of the re as John and Jacob stared aghast at the blood-soaked bandage wrapped around half of Alcoran’s face. “Here now, what’s—” An arrow blossomed from the ga er’s chest and he fel backward into the coals of the re. A heartbeat later, ve more arrows sprang from Jacob’s chest and John’s neck and groin. Mirel a opened her mouth to scream as the two young men fel —but Alcoran was faster. He dashed forward with his long knife in one hand, the other slipping over her mouth. She bit down hard on his palm, but he ignored the pain and slashed hard at her jugular, cutting her windpipe and spil ing her lifeblood down her dress. Alcoran waited, panting in the near-darkness, but no one else stirred from their tents. Slowly, the other soldiers began trickling in from the edge of the tree line and the ditch by the roadside. Fifteen soldiers in al . Not the best from his old company, but the toughest, the meanest, and the ones smart enough to stay alive. He nodded to al of them, his missing eye pulsing with savage agony beneath the lthy bandage. He hoped to the gods the infection didn’t spread … “Should be half a dozen more in those tents,” he whispered. “You know what to do.” e others slunk away, their short bows disappearing to be replaced by short swords and daggers. Alcoran tore a strip of cloth from the dead woman’s dress, used it to clean his knife, then ambled over to the simmering pot of stew. Using the same piece of bloody cloth, he eased the lid o the pot and sni ed at the boiling bacon, parsnips, and potatoes. While Alcoran searched for a spoon or a ladle, shouts went up along the cluster of tents behind him. Men, women, and at least one child. Alcoran tsk ed at that. e King’s Road was no place for children after dark. ere were bandits about, after al . “ ere it is,” Alcoran exclaimed, snatching the charred ladle from the shadows next to the camp re. He smacked it against his leg, shaking o the ash, then scooped up the stew. He raised it to his mouth, blowing to cool it, and savored the smel of the thick cottage bacon. It’d been so long since he’d had pork that wasn’t rancid, or salted, and he imagined the texture of it, the root vegetables mixing with the avor. He tested it with his tongue, then blew on the ladleful again. Just a little cooler. If he ate quickly, there’d be less to share with his men.
