Brayan . . . was kind. He helped me with my work.” “Brayan was always tender-hearted,” Kiara agreed, “and you took advantage of that.” Dolyn looked toward the bier. “I … did. I tried to convince him that only magic could heal my hands—Chaenbalu’s magic—but he refused to bring me here. ‘Only if it was a matter of life and death,’ he said … so I poisoned him, and convinced him the cure lay in Chaenbalu’s vault. I think he even believed me—and so he became our guide, and we passed through Chaenbalu’s circle of protection. I expected to nd the vil age abandoned. I had hoped … I had thought . . .” She shuddered. “What did you do, Kiara? What demons did you send to attack us?” “Just our Master of Curses—him and his brainwashed lapdog—but that was enough. Kenton decimated you and your precious ferrumen.” She sni ed, not hiding her disdain. “You should have stayed in Banok, Dolyn. With a little patience, you would have met with Annev when we came to forge the Sword of Seeking. We would have brought you to this very room.” She gestured at the shelves of artifacts and the churning pool of liquid magic. “You acted in haste —and Brayan paid for it with his life.” Dolyn’s head bowed in sorrow, but then she sneered. “You dare to lecture me about the cost of lives? You, who sacri ced your entire vil age to protect your dark secrets? Do not judge the blood I have spil ed or spent. Your hands are no cleaner than mine.” “On that, we can agree,” Kiara said, her demeanor stil cool. She frowned. “Why did you stay? Why not burrow your way out with your magic?” Dolyn gestured at the concave wal s and domed ceiling. “Magic protects this place. I can’t shape the stone here.” “But the trapdoor? Surely you could have swum out through one of the ooded tunnels?” “I tried. I swam in search of an escape, but every exit was sealed.” She lifted her dirty tunic to show her skin, scaled with white marble and akes of greenish-white platinum. “I lacked the strength to shape the stone wal s. I can’t even slow the transmutation without proper food to replace the minerals my body has lost,” she explained. “I need meat and milk, and other things that I can’t get locked underground in a ooded chamber.” “Of course—and you shal have them.” “You’re … letting me go?” “I need your help,” Kiara snapped, “to forge the Sword of Seeking—and so does Annev. He wil be in Banok soon, and we wil need to be ready to greet him.” Dolyn’s brow furrowed, suspicious. “Why would I do that? I tried to kil him!” “But he doesn’t know that,” Kiara said, completing the other woman’s thoughts. “And before you try to barter with me, you should know you cannot have the Hand of Keos, nor wil I al ow you to capture the Vessel. I have already promised him to Tacharan, and if you obstruct me in this, we wil become enemies.” “ en there is nothing you can o er me.” “Oh no?” Kiara gestured at the fountain and its rainbow-hued contents. “As much aqlumera as you can carry, in exchange for helping Annev forge the diamagus when it is time.” e high priestess of the Orvanes grunted, considering. “ at . . . is a tempting o er.” “Stop being coy. You know the value of what I o er.” “And what’s to stop me from kil ing you and escaping through the tunnel you just opened?” “Fate,” Kiara crooned, her voice sure. e smith frowned at Kiara’s cryptic answer, but eventual y she nodded. “Cruithear curse me, but … very wel .” “Good,” Kiara said. “ ere are some enchanted jars on that shelf. Take as many as you can. ey’l be needed to forge the sword.” She moved between the shelves, guided by a preternatural sense of intuition. Halfway down the third shelf, she squatted down and found a worn leather satchel containing the other item she sought—a brass lamp engraved with a thousand runes in Old Darite. “What’s that?” Dolyn asked, drawing close to peer over the witmistress’s shoulder. “A lamp,” Kiara said, dropping it into her apron pocket. “Anything signi cant about it?” “ e Dionachs Tobar think it houses the Oracle of Odar.” “ ey think it does? What does it actual y hold?” Kiara smiled, her eyes sparkling with the secrets that only a High Priestess of Tacharan could know. “My sweet Dolyn, you wouldn’t believe me if I told you—and this is a secret I’l take to my grave.” ACKNOWLEDGMENTS I am so grateful to the many people at Blackstone who made this book possible —from the words on the page, to the layout of the gorgeous cover, to publicizing the book and sharing it with others—these people made my book the best version of itself. ank you Lauren Maturo, Megan Wahrenbrock, Deirdre Curley, Kathryn G. English, Zena Co man, Rick Bleiweiss, Je rey Yamaguchi, Josie Woodbridge, and the rest of the Blackstone team. Please al ow me to also heap an unseemly amount of praise on my UK editor, Gil ian Redfearn, whose keen eye, sage advice and uncanny wisdom helped me shape this rough story into something special. When I worried that Master Arti cer was getting too long, she was the person who assured me the story was good and that I should stay the course. It takes an immense amount of trust to do that, and I feel uniquely blessed to be al owed that privilege—so thanks again to the people at Blackstone, Gol ancz, and al my other foreign publishers who have believed in me, my writing, and this series. e next person I’d like to thank is my wonderful wife Col ette, whose sacri ces have enabled me to be an author and to sneak away from my kids long enough to write my darn books. I have said before that Co doesn’t much like anything to do with SFF—but she does believe in my writing; she knows it makes me happy, and it makes a lot of other people happy to read it. anks for the cheerleading, Coco. Which leads me back to those amazing kids—I love you guys! Hopeful y when you are older, you’l be able to read these books and appreciate why your dad locked himself in his o ce al those times. And to Tord—who is old enough to read these books now—please know that I love and support you, and I treasure our time exploring other people’s fantasy stories together. I’d also like to thank three of the people in the background whose unrecognized contributions make my storytel ing al the more epic. If you are reading the ebook, hardback, or paperback for Master Arti cer, you should know that most of the handwritten maps, symbols, and ephemera in this book were il ustrated by my good friend Jared Sprague—and we spent a lot of hours discussing and re ning those illustrations so they could accurately represent the world I imagined. Special attention should also be given to Jen El iott—who, at the time of this acknowledgment, is the lead artist for the Forgotten Realms TTRPG; Jen il ustrated the phenomenal diagram in the appendix that explains the rules and categories for the Prime and New Terran magic systems in e Silent Gods. If you haven’t seen it, please al ow your eyes to feast on her talents (and go check out her other amazing artwork). e third unsung hero I’d like to thank is Peter Kenny, my absolutely amazing audiobook narrator. If you are listening to his narration, you may lack the ability to see the maps and appendix graphics I previously mentioned, but in exchange you get to hear Peter’s incredible vocal talents as he brings my characters, my world, and my story to life. In addition to his legendary narrative skil s, Peter is also one of the kindest people I’ve met in the publishing industry (or anywhere else for that matter), and I’m delighted to cal him my friend. Lastly, I’d like to thank my agent Danny Baror. If it weren’t for Danny, no one would have heard these stories—either domestical y or international y— and his belief in my talents as a storytel er is invaluable. Cheers and thanks to al . APPENDIX e Luquatran Magic System

chunks.title: Final Section
chunks.content: “I’m John Stout and this is my brother, Jacob. We just came from Banok. Barely escaped with the shirts on our backs.” “Escaped?” Alcoran tilted his head, stil trying to make sense of the tale they were tel ing him. “Surely the Terrans haven’t come this far into the Empire?” John shook his head. “I don’t think so … but maybe? We were overrun by the Sons of Damnation—and they didn’t sound like foreigners. ey knew the city, knew our ways and our speech, but they were dressed strangely, and they said they’d come to liberate the village from evil. We didn’t know what to make of them, wrote them o as zealots from Quiri … but then they seized the Harth family’s keep and started making demands of the governor. Acted like they were running the village. Governor sent the town guard . . . and they didn’t come back. ey formed a militia, and they didn’t return either. Some folks went for help and . . . wel , we didn’t see them again, neither. When others nal y did come, it was more strangers and monsters—and they were there to help the Sons of Damnation. e whole place has gone to hel and the remaining townsfolk are being held hostage—forced to serve the man who leads the Sons.” “Strangers and monsters,” Alcoran repeated, forgetting for a moment why he had come to the smal encampment. “And … Sons of Damnation?” He scratched his short red beard, hunger receding to the back of his mind. “And you don’t know who they are?” e shorter man, Jacob, shook his head. “We weren’t keen on nding out. We decided to send for help—to sneak out of the vil age and nd someone who might help take back the city—but no one cares. Everyone’s concerned about their own problems, like the war in the east or the famine in the south. We heard no aid would be coming from the capital, so we’re taking our case to the king of Paldron.” Alcoran laughed—he couldn’t help it. e irony was too amusing. “King Alpenrose wouldn’t sel you his own piss, much less spare you a company of soldiers.” “But … the people are desperate. e soldiers are gone. e only folk left are shopkeeps and farmers. Merchants and artisans. ey aren’t warriors! And the people control ing the city … they’ve got magic. e Sons said they hate it, but they use it to keep people in line. Even the mercenaries they’ve hired— half of them use shadow magic and the others . . . they’re rotting demons. eir esh is more metal and stone than skin and bone!” “You have my sympathy—truly, you do—but no aid wil be coming. Borderlund has its sts ful on the Black Wal . Our numbers are thin. Conscripts are eeing, abandoning the war and seeking safety elsewhere. If they aren’t helped soon, the Terrans wil cross the Kuar and start sacking Paldron itself.” Alcoran hu ed. “If these men—these Sons of Damnation— aren’t harming you, you should count yourselves lucky. And if they aren’t friends of the Terrans, maybe they’l protect you from the war that’s about to come.” e old man’s face paled. “If that is the case, then we are truly in dark times.” You don’t know the half of it, Alcoran thought, feeling a tiny pang of guilt for what his band of soldiers was about to do to these folks. Times were tough al around, though, and only the ttest were going to survive. He tipped his hat low over his bandaged eye and made sure to stay out of the relight. His men should be in position now … yet something stayed his hand. “Lord Stout,” Alcoran said, addressing the elder of the two young men. “You said these Sons of Damnation aren’t letting folk in or out. How did you escape?” “We can’t take much credit for it,” the tal er man said. “ ese warlocks— the shadow men helping the Sons of Damnation—they wear gray and purple clothing and masks, and they spy on us townsfolk for the Sons of Damnation … but there’s a resistance forming. ey’ve got a leader too—one who uses magic—and she helped us waylay two of these warlocks and take their clothes.” Alcoran frowned. “She? ere’s a witch leading your militia?” “Not just one,” Jacob interrupted, “there are three! One who speaks to the plants, one who doesn’t speak at al , and one who charms the warlocks with her witching song.” John elbowed his younger brother, shushing him. “ ey aren’t witches. ey’re just . . . wel , they’re helping us. And we’re ghting back, with or without King Lenka and King Alpenrose.” Alcoran nodded, his tongue drawing across the bottom of his front teeth. “ ese mercenaries. Any notion why they’re helping these Sons of Damnation?” John and Jacob exchanged a look that suggested they knew exactly what Alcoran was asking, but they didn’t seem eager to share that information. Perhaps they weren’t as stupid as Alcoran hoped. “Only rumors,” John said, speaking for them both. “We heard about some kind of gold—liquid gold, I guess. I don’t know why that’d be so special, but word of it got out soon after the Sons came to Banok, and the mercenaries started appearing pretty quickly.” “Huh. Liquid gold.” Alcoran shrugged. “Seems like it’d be more valuable as simple coin. Easier to transport too. Stil … gold is gold. When folk o er it, others wil take it.” He hesitated. “Anyone else taking this gold? Any of your townsfolk helping these Sons?” “You mean has anyone turned traitor?” Jacob spat then ran his nger along the side of his savaged cheek. “Vilhelm Stenger decided he’d take some of that gold—he signed on to help the Sons keep order in the town—but we made an example of him. Forrest Bower and Josie Ladle too. Banok folks don’t take kindly to traitors.” Alcoran was satis ed. “Sounds like you folk have your a airs in order then. And this old ga er here … no relation to you?” e young men shook their heads as the old man spoke. “I can speak for myself. Me and Mirel a found the boys just before nightfal . ey were tired and needed help, so we took them in. We’l take them as far as Trizgard.” “I just came from there,” Alcoran said, grunting. “It hasn’t been touched by the war yet, that’s why I was surprised by trouble in Banok.” “Eh, that’s some good news at least. We’re from Luqura and don’t usual y trade beyond Banok—too many bandits on the King’s Road.” He sni ed. “But there’s no trade in Banok these days, so we’ve got to chance Trizgard.” Alcoran clucked his tongue. “Bandits, eh? Yes … that real y is a sad tale.” Alcoran took o his black felt hat and waved its wide brim in front of his face. “Hm?” e old man squinted at him in the pale glow of the re as John and Jacob stared aghast at the blood-soaked bandage wrapped around half of Alcoran’s face. “Here now, what’s—” An arrow blossomed from the ga er’s chest and he fel backward into the coals of the re. A heartbeat later, ve more arrows sprang from Jacob’s chest and John’s neck and groin. Mirel a opened her mouth to scream as the two young men fel —but Alcoran was faster. He dashed forward with his long knife in one hand, the other slipping over her mouth. She bit down hard on his palm, but he ignored the pain and slashed hard at her jugular, cutting her windpipe and spil ing her lifeblood down her dress. Alcoran waited, panting in the near-darkness, but no one else stirred from their tents. Slowly, the other soldiers began trickling in from the edge of the tree line and the ditch by the roadside. Fifteen soldiers in al . Not the best from his old company, but the toughest, the meanest, and the ones smart enough to stay alive. He nodded to al of them, his missing eye pulsing with savage agony beneath the lthy bandage. He hoped to the gods the infection didn’t spread … “Should be half a dozen more in those tents,” he whispered. “You know what to do.” e others slunk away, their short bows disappearing to be replaced by short swords and daggers. Alcoran tore a strip of cloth from the dead woman’s dress, used it to clean his knife, then ambled over to the simmering pot of stew. Using the same piece of bloody cloth, he eased the lid o the pot and sni ed at the boiling bacon, parsnips, and potatoes. While Alcoran searched for a spoon or a ladle, shouts went up along the cluster of tents behind him. Men, women, and at least one child. Alcoran tsk ed at that. e King’s Road was no place for children after dark. ere were bandits about, after al . “ ere it is,” Alcoran exclaimed, snatching the charred ladle from the shadows next to the camp re. He smacked it against his leg, shaking o the ash, then scooped up the stew. He raised it to his mouth, blowing to cool it, and savored the smel of the thick cottage bacon. It’d been so long since he’d had pork that wasn’t rancid, or salted, and he imagined the texture of it, the root vegetables mixing with the avor. He tested it with his tongue, then blew on the ladleful again. Just a little cooler. If he ate quickly, there’d be less to share with his men. He hoped it would take them a while to loot the tents, wagon, and corpses. “Banok’s under siege or something, lads. ey’ve got mercenary work if you’re up for it, though.” He turned an ear toward his men as he blew on the stew and slurped noisily at its thick gravy. Damn, it was good. Too hot by half, but burning his tongue was a smal price to pay for the delicious broth. “Or we can stay on the road,” Alcoran continued, his body huddled over the pot, the steaming ladle raised to his lips. “Lots of folk wil be coming this way now Banok is o -limits to traders. Easy pickings.” Alcoran stopped. Why had it gone so quiet? He peered over his shoulder and spied the rent and tattered oil cloth, the tents shredded and dismantled. None of his men were in sight, though: only the dead, their voices as silent as the grave. So where were his men? Alcoran squinted into the darkness. e bodies … there were too many bodies. Almost a score of them. On instinct, Alcoran spun around and splashed the hot stew into his silent attacker’s face. e young man hissed, his short sword swinging wide. e stranger didn’t blink, though—in fact, he didn’t close his eyes at al ; instead, the steaming liquid glistened on the hard leather skin of his scarred cheekbones, evaporating under the heat of the man’s ery, unblinking eyes. “Gods,” Alcoran breathed. e short sword swung again and Alcoran raised his long knife to parry. Instead of blocking the sword, though, the silvery blade seemed to pass right through it, striking Alcoran on the shoulder and severing his arm at the clavicle. “Keos,” Alcoran swore, his left hand dropping the wooden ladle and clutching at the pulsing artery beneath his armpit. He’d seen wounds like this on the battle front—kil ing wounds. e young man’s blade bit into his neck, its edge as cold as winter’s ice. Alcoran tried to raise his hand to staunch the ow of blood but neither of his limbs responded. Instead, the world seemed to spin around him, as though he were tumbling through the air. His head crashed into the coals of the dying camp re and he watched, confused, upside down, dying, as his headless body toppled to the ground in front of him. CHAPTER EIGHTY-THREE “ ey’ve gone to Banok,” Kenton said, appearing like a wraith in the gloom of the Brakewood. “Worse, they’ve put my original plan into action, though I can’t fathom why. None of them were keen on pursuing it to begin with. Without a leader, that lot would bicker inde nitely.” Kiara looked as if none of that was news to her. “ e masters and ancients of Chaenbalu were never very good at improvising. ey’re just bandits. Al they know is theft and living o the labor of others.” “ is is di erent,” Kenton said, hanging his Cloak of Secrets from the branch of a nearby spruce. “ ey’re stil cal ing themselves the Sons of Damnation—as if they want people to know who they are and what they’re doing—and they’ve taken the whole town hostage.” “Hmm.” Kiara looked up from the shadepool she’d been studying. “ at is di erent. But ve men are keeping the town hostage? How?” Kenton frowned in response and Kiara’s eyes narrowed. “Whose help have they secured to do it?” “ ey’ve hired mercenaries. Strange ones with shadow magic, like that assassin who visited Chaenbalu with his demons.” Kiara hu ed. “ ere is a smal faction of Dorchnok’s warriors in Luqura. ey’re servants of one of the noble houses. I can’t see why they’d help the Sons of Damnation seize control of a township, though. ere’s no pro t in it.” “It gets worse,” Kenton said. “I think they have ferrumen helping them.” “Ferrumen? ” Kiara jumped up from her stump and strode over to Kenton. “You’re certain?” “Reasonably certain. ey could be golems . . . but I think not. eir descriptions are too similar to the monsters that attacked Chaenbalu.” “But these are ferrumen. Not feurog?” Kenton nodded. “It seems that, like the shadow-warriors, the ferrumen have been persuaded to help the Sons of Damnation take control of Banok.” “Could they be fugitives from the failed attack on Chaenbalu?” “No,” Kenton said, his gaze turning to take in the dead vil age at the heart of the Brake. “ ey were al kil ed—al those who joined the attack on the village, anyway. ese other ferrumen must be a separate force from the one that attacked.” “But they wil stil be servants of Cruithear,” Kiara mused. She slowly turned and stared into the trees behind him, her attention unfocused, thinking before she turned her gray eyes on Kenton. “You have guessed what this means.” “Mercenaries don’t work for free, and I can only think of one thing that would persuade the ferrumen to help the Sons. e men on the road even said the soldiers are being paid in liquid gold.” “Aqlumera,” Kiara said, frowning. “Yes, and I’m sure that would convince the shadow assassins to help too. Ather and the rest must have stolen it before the ferrumen attacked, which also explains why we’ve been unable to locate them. Blood of Tacharan! We spent al that e ort protecting the vault from Cruithear’s minions and then your entourage just went ahead and handed it to them.” “Not my entourage—not anymore, anyway. If Ather went into the vault to steal aqlumera, then I would bet Tosan is leading them now. And he liked the idea of possessing Banok.” “I don’t fol ow your logic.” “Tosan’s spirit was stil guarding the aqlumera pool,” Kenton said, replacing the black wrapping that covered his glowing eyes. “He would have attacked anyone who approached the pool without protection, and I doubt any of them could have fought him o .” “A sensible explanation, though I wish there were another one. If Tosan has begun sel ing the liquid in exchange for mercenary services, it wil make it that much harder to reclaim the substance.” “Reclaim it?” Kenton tilted his head in confusion, then he realized the implication in Kiara’s words. “You want me to go and steal it back. Before it’s distributed to the mercenaries.” “Easier than trying to steal it back from the Cult of Cruithear or these shadowmen.” Kiara nodded. “It’s one target. One task. One mission. Go to Banok and retrieve the aqlumera from the Sons of Damnation.” “And what if Tosan is control ing them?” “So what if he is? e aqlumera is al that matters. Annev wil be drawn to it and Myjun wil be drawn to him. When he gets his hands on it, Annev wil use the aqlumera to forge a new artifact—a powerful one, almost as strong as the diamagi.” “ e what?” “ e Hammer of Keos, the Flute of Lumea, and the Sta of Odar. e three most powerful artifacts in existence. Many times more powerful than the Hand of Keos—and you’ve seen the destruction that wrought on the Academy.” “So Annev wil have the Hand of Keos … and this new artifact. Which wil make him magnitudes stronger.” “Yes, but you have grown stronger too. Both in your magic and your inventory of artifacts.” e witmistress smiled. “Besides, you do not need to concern yourself with Annev. He is my a air and no longer your enemy—but if he dies, so does Myjun.” “How is she? Have you seen her recently?” Kiara tilted her hand as if sensing the wind or weighing the balance of fate on her palm. “ e shadepools here do not o er the same clarity as the fountain of aqlumera. I can sometimes see her … but not wel . Not often.” “Does she persist in her desire to enter the World of Dreams?” Kiara nodded and Kenton cursed. “If she does enter, wil your magic stil work? Wil I stil be able to track her progress?” “Probably not. If I could access the vault, perhaps. But with this?” She gestured at the smoky black surface pooling about her ankles. “Aqlumera pierces al veils and touches al realms, but the shadepools are tied directly to the shadow realm. It only borders the Dream World, so the shadepools might provide a few glimpses, but they would be indistinct and infrequent.” “But her armor … the ironwood skin. You said it was imbued with shadow magic. Would that not make it easier to observe her through the shadepools?” “It is and it does—but that is the only reason we have not lost sight of her entirely. She is more than a continent away, and in another realm. You are lucky I am able to glimpse her at al . Once Oyru takes her to the World of Dreams, I expect we wil be entirely blind to her.” Kenton clenched his st, brooding. What if he lost her? What if she didn’t come back? e thought sickened him, not so much because of his love for the girl-turned-assassin, but because she was his single remaining purpose in life. e thought of losing that frightened him more than he dared acknowledge, and so he persisted in this obsession. If he could save her, perhaps al his su ering would be for something. “So how can we view them?” he asked, his eyes aring, betraying his emotions. “Short of dreamwalking?” Kiara shrugged. “I suspect your Cloak of Secrets could take you there, if you trusted its magic to transport yourself to other realms—but I cannot accompany you. My a airs tie me to this world—and without a guide, such risks seem unwise.” She hesitated. “Do you carry anything that would al ow us to look into another’s dreams?” Kenton consulted his memory ring for any such artifacts. He shook his head. “I have no such thing. If there was one in the vault, I did not encounter it.” “Mm. en we must content ourselves with the glimpses we steal from the shadepools.” “You mentioned dreamwalking,” Kenton pressed, pacing around the black pool of placid shadows. “Can you teach me?” “It is not a skil I cared to learn. A few Seers and Shadowcasters have been known to dreamwalk, but it is mainly practiced by Kroseran Voidweavers and the Darite mind-mages: the Stormcal ers and the Mindwalkers. Beyond those three castes, it is a dangerous skil to hone, whose reward rarely outweigh the risks.” “ en I wil assume Myjun is in danger,” Kenton snapped, though he fought to remain calm. “If they have traveled to the World of Dreams, Oyru’s magic wil be less potent there … and he’l be less capable of protecting her.” Kiara snorted. “Don’t worry about Myjun. She is more than capable of protecting herself—at least until she attempts to kil Annev, and that is why you wil be here to stop her.” “But she wil be in danger,” Kenton pressed. “More so than in the shadow realm.” Kiara sighed. “Yes, but she wil survive. She may not be the same woman when she returns, but she wil survive. Put yourself at ease. She wil stil return here to confront Annev.” “But only if the aqlumera is here.” “Yes.” Kenton grunted. “I only have your word on that—your word and this prophecy. And what is that exactly?” Kiara seemed to have been waiting for Kenton to ask that question. “Before a year has passed, Annev wil be enlisted to build an artifact—a sword—but forging it wil require a certain quantity of aqlumera. If he nds it anywhere except Chaenbalu, he wil not return to the vil age . . . and neither wil Myjun. However, if he can nd no other aqlumera, he wil return to the Vault of Damnation. He wil forge the sword, and Myjun wil come there to kil him. You must be there to stop her, or her life wil be forfeit.” “And if the sword is forged elsewhere?” he asked, staring into the rippling shadepool. “What wil happen then?” “ en she wil be taken the Gods only know where … beyond your reach, I suspect.” Kenton stared into darkness, hoping his supernatural vision might pierce the mists of shadow without the witmistress’s aid—but they refused to yield to him. “She kil s Annev, doesn’t she? In your prophecy? If she nds him, they both die.” Kiara hmm ed beside him. “Your eyes are beginning to see more than this world, Cursed One. Soon you wil be able to prophesy too.” Kenton shook his head. “I’ve enough curses. I do not care to burden myself with more.” He paused. “But that is something you could teach me, isn’t it? You could show me how to see more than this world. Perhaps even peer into the shadow realm.” “I suspect I could teach you more than that, even. Peering into shadows is only the beginning. With the proper training and the aid of your altered sight, I expect you could see the patterns of Fate himself.” “Himself?” “ e plots of Tacharan. e God of Death. e God of Doom. He works the loom of fate to weave the pattern of our lives.” Kenton snorted. “You don’t real y believe that, do you?” “I do.” Kenton and the iron-haired woman were of a height, and he fancied he could almost peer into the woman’s soul. Final y he made up his mind. “I wil learn your magics then, witch. Teach me what you can . . . but I wil not worship your God. I wil not chant his prayers or sacri ce lives to him.” “Nor does he ask for them—not yet. We can begin your training when you return from Banok.” “And you are certain Myjun wil not return before then?” “As certain as I can be, when the future is never clear. By my estimations, it wil be a month or more before either Annev or Myjun returns to Chaenbalu. Annev surveyed the wreckage of the Crested Cormorant once more, pushing himself as high as the cloak would take him—almost seven feet above the river. From that vantage and using the supernatural vision of his Inquisitor ring, Annev could just make out the sunken barge resting at the bottom of the Tocra. e bodies had cooled in the river’s waters—al except Ja a’s, which was bobbing face-down in the current. ere would be no witnesses sharing news of the consul’s fate with anyone in Luqura. e wreck was far enough from the capital that no homes or villages dotted the shores of the wide river. No one had seen anything. For once, fate seemed to be aiding Annev, no matter how dark his actions might be. Annev dropped down to hover just above the river and the spray from the water and wind began to mist his boots. He angled himself until the bulk of his magic was propel ing him forward, sending him upstream toward Luqura. Freed of having to propel the massive river barge, Annev ew across the water at a breakneck pace. Drops of water beaded around his magpie mask and ew along the lacquered feathers carved into the bone artifact. Not an artifact, Annev reminded himself, not yet. Not until I fuse it with the Terran mage’s blood. en again, Annev thought, perhaps that wouldn’t be necessary. e mask had been carved from the Bloodlord’s skul . A trace of the man’s blood-talent might stil reside in the core of the mask. Perhaps that would be enough to manipulate the magic threads and form something more … permanent. But he could worry about that later. For now, he had to reach Luqura before dawn—a task he felt con dent he could achieve at his current pace. He’d gain admittance as Master Magpie, an enigmatic lord from . . . somewhere. Innistiul? at would explain the writ he carried on his back. Or perhaps he should continue pretending to be an agent of the God-king Neruacanta. Annev wasn’t sure, but he had no intention of entering the city as himself. In fact, his best option might be to levitate over the city wal and enter Luqura unannounced. Once inside I can seek out Tiana and Dante, and nd out where Saltair is hiding. And if they can tel me anything about who hunts me, I’l pursue those leads too, until none of my enemies remain behind me. en I can go on to Banok and clean up the mess I left there. Hel s, I could go to Daogort and roust out the God-king himself, and nal y put an end to this madness. And it was madness—Annev had no il usions about that; even his own plans for retribution had a taste of insanity about them—but Annev no longer feared the people he was facing or the lengths he might need to go to stop them. If I must be a monster, he thought, then I wil be the kind that hunts the others. I wil be the vil ain that destroys al other vil ains. e cold knot resting in his stomach seemed to untwist then, and he felt at peace with the decisions he had made over the past week. He was not a hero, nor would he try to be one. He was not a virtuous savior, or even the prophesied descendant of Breathanas. He was just … himself. Annev de Breth. Ring-snake. Magpie. Phoenix. He was the Master of Sorrows: a savior and a destroyer. And he was not afraid of the fate that awaited him. Whether in darkness or light, life or death, he would fol ow his heart and never waver from what needed to be done. And right now, Annev needed to go to the capital and hunt out some monsters. EPILOGUE Kiara knelt beside the altar she had built in the heart of the Brakewood, her strong ngers clutching the ceremonial knife she carried for exactly this occasion. Lying on the gray stone in front of her was one of Cruithear’s fal en children—an abomination, a twisted one. A feurog. is creature had been a man once, and the magic that strengthened him had also crippled and deformed him: scabs of stone grew like scales across his chest and abdomen; soft veins of steel threaded his muscles like glimmering bands of silver sinew. In time, those would harden and petrify the poor creature, paralyzing him until Death himself claimed him. Such a waste. Such a shame. Fortunately, Kiara was here to give that death a purpose; it would no longer be meaningless, and it was coming much, much sooner. e abomination’s eyelids began to utter. Before it could regain control of the rest of its muscles, Kiara sliced her blade deep into the monster’s abdomen. e feurog tried to scream, but only managed a strangled whimper. Kiara paid him no heed, her attention focused on its intestines, liver, and spleen. She poked, prodded, and twisted, her ngers entwining with the bloody entrails as her Yomad magic seeped into the dying monster’s bowels. Some of the organs had a metal ic sheen to them, though they stil yielded to the edge of her magical y honed knife. Final y, Kiara felt the blood-magic reach out to her, as light and cool and potent as the touch of a wraith as it traveled up her arms, through her heart and up to the sclera of her eyes. If she looked into a mirror just then, she knew her pupils would appear cloudy white—a temporary side e ect of her Seer magic. Kiara felt her skin tighten too, her esh losing some of its elasticity, and her face becoming ever more skeletal. is was another unfortunate side e ect and one that would be regrettably permanent. Such were the costs of peering into Fate’s owing rivers, particularly without a pool of aqlumera to aid in her scrying. As soon as her eyes were ful y saturated, Kiara drew out a damp rag. Until a few minutes ago, the cloth had been stained with Kenton’s dried blood— which she had been circumspect about obtaining. Kiara placed the bloody scrap in her mouth and sucked until she tasted the familiar tang of rust and iron. Images ashed across her eld of vision. Imagined scents l ed her nose, replacing the coppery smel of Kenton’s dried blood and the foul odor of whatever the feurog had recently digested. She caught fragments of thoughts— words and sentences, rhymes and riddles. Despite her years of experience interpreting the whispers of Fate, Kiara grappled with the prophecy, wrestling with its meaning, attempting to bind it to her wil and her memory. Kenton, she thought, then asked her question aloud: “Has the boy reclaimed the aqlumera?” e answer came almost immediately. e Cursed Leader has failed to reclaim what was lost. Kiara bowed in gratitude to Tacharan. e Younger God of Fate had answered her swiftly—and with uncharacteristic clarity—and though she did not like the answer she received, she knew better than to express her ire. She considered inquiring after the boy’s fate, but it would be a di cult subject to navigate. Much better to keep her questions speci c. “Where is Kenton now?” He has lost himself in turn and nds himself where al things go that are lost. Damn. at was as vague an answer as she’d ever received—or perhaps it was very speci c. It was hard to tel , with Fate. Kiara slipped another loop of intestines between her ngers and sifted through the blood-magic, searching for clarity. “When wil he return?” Yes. Blood and ashes. e augury was already degrading. Kiara had feared as much, and while she had three more unconscious feurog lying on separate stone tables, she had a limited quantity of Kenton’s blood and a similarly limited quantity of Annev’s. She had tasted a good deal of it since the boy’s imprisonment, but it wouldn’t last forever. Sooner rather than later, she’d be unable to divine anything related to the Vessel … and she would be as blind to his presence as she had been for these past seventeen years. Kiara moved to the second table, her bloody knife already separating esh and muscle in her attempt to divine Annev’s future. When Kiara placed this second rag in her mouth, she knew this would be the last augury she would divine regarding Annev’s fate; she’d taken the bloody rag from Brayan and Titus after they had tended to the boy’s wounds and placed him in the Academy’s dungeons, and the blood-magic was nearly spent. She sucked and chewed, mixing the blood with water and saliva, trying to awaken a sense of the boy’s fate in her mind. Final y, something kindled, and she latched onto the magic, using the dying feurog in front of her as a focal point. e witmistress opened her mouth, prepared to ask her questions—then hesitated. ere might only be enough magic for one question. Best to make it a good one. “What must I do to help Annev forge the Sword of Seeking?” Kiara’s past auguries had told her the boy would forge the sword using the aqlumera from Chaenbalu’s vault, and that her aid would be critical if she were to gain his trust—but some of that aqlumera had been stolen, and the matter of Annev’s involvement was now in doubt. If Kiara was to help him, she would need to know where to nd him. And if she was to help him forge the artifact and earn his trust, she would need to o er invaluable aid. Open the Vault of Damnation, Fate whispered. Inside its ooded chamber, you wil nd the help you seek. Bring it to Banok and the Vessel wil construct the diamagus. Another imperfect answer. Of the thousands of artifacts inside the vault, Kiara could barely guess what might aid Annev and bind his wil to her own. But the instruction to open the vault was clear enough. Perhaps knowing the answers would be inside would prove enough. More concerning was the omission of Annev’s location and Kiara’s involvement in his prophesied creation. If I go to Banok, wil Annev be there? ere is no mention of where the sword wil be forged. Must I lead him back to the fountain of aqlumera— assuming he does not come here on his own? But Kiara could work with this information. She understood, better than any, how to manipulate Fate’s web. If she could open the vault, Kiara could take a portion of the aqlumera for herself and take it to Banok. If she encountered the Vessel, she could o er him the aqlumera as an act of good wil along with the pledge of her al egiance. Perhaps that was even what the prophecy intended. Perhaps … but probably not. Fate rarely made any task easy for her. Kiara looked down the line at the two remaining feurog. It had been di cult to nd any after their attack on Chaenbalu, but Kiara knew their burrows and the creatures were slowly returning to their network of tunnels beneath the Brakewood. Even so, it had taken two days to nd these four sacri ces, and she would need to use these last two careful y so that she did not delay her trip to Banok hunting for more. But what to ask? She needed to know which items to take from the vault, and she needed a way to open it—with the connecting tunnels al ooded, it would be dangerous to attempt any sort of digging. e nechraict, Kiara thought with a sigh. e cost for using her necromancy would be high—she had been very careful not to dabble in its usage while at the Academy—but she couldn’t waste time hunting for more feurog to aid her. Resurrecting their dead bodies would be much easier, despite the cost. It must be done. She moved to the third feurog— a female whose stone tumors had transformed her body into a misshapen lump of hardened esh and crystal ized bone. Her eyes were open, and she watched Kiara with undisguised horror. “Shhh,” she whispered. “I’ve severed your spinal cord to keep you from moving. It’l be over soon.” Once she had the woman’s bowels wrapped between her ngers, Kiara studied them with her next question held rmly in her mind. “What must I take from the Vault of Damnation and bring to Banok … ?” She considered being more speci c—mentioning her intent to help Annev forge the Sword of Seeking—but that often back red. When you were dealing with Fate, you had to walk the line between being too vague and getting an answer you couldn’t use, or being too speci c and getting no answer at al . e air that hissed between the feurog’s paralyzed lips matched the cadence of Tacharan’s eventual answer: Take the lamp marked by Odar … the smith marked by Keos … and the essence of life and death. It was never an easy answer … but it was good enough. Kiara looked down at the fourth feurog, intending to ask when she needed to go to Banok, only to realize the creature had bled to death while she’d been studying the rst three auguries. Wel , she consoled herself, at least I have four fresh bodies to help with the digging. *** Kiara ignored the water pulsing from the mouth of the excavated tunnel and instead examined her skeletal hands: before that summer they’d held the beauty and strength of life, but her use of magic over these past few months had drained away that vitality; Kiara looked thin, almost sickly, and her hands were an ashen gray tone in place of their usual healthy pink. It was the cost of her magic, which she’d managed to stave o for many, many years. e cost of using her necromancy had been much worse: white bones now showed beneath the translucent skin covering her thin ngers, and her eyes had sunken into her skul . She was a far cry from the striking Gray Lady, as her witgirls and witwomen had once cal ed her. Her magic was twisting her, revealing her to be like the necromancers and lich lords of Takarania and Terra Majora. But she had chosen to pay the price. Once the water had drained away, Kiara stepped around the enslaved corpses that had dug her path into the Vault of Damnation. ey had been the rst bodies to spew out of the tunnel mouth, with the rst violent blast of draining water, and a stream of bloated corpses had soon fol owed—a grisly reminder of how Kenton had won his campaign against the ferrumen and their mage-priests. Using the light of a single torch, Kiara navigated the sodden warren until she found the secret entrance Kenton had used to enter the otherwise impenetrable Vault of Damnation. *** “Hel o, High Priestess Ciarán.” “You!” Kiara hissed in shock, recognizing the voice that greeted her from within the Vault of Damnation. “How are you alive? After al these weeks … how have you survived?” Dolyn Smith climbed down from the bier she’d been sitting on and gestured at the pewter and limestone jars sitting at the foot of the aqlumera fountain. “ e metal one makes barley cakes—palatable, but dry—and the stone one generates water.” She gestured behind her. “ ere’s a black one back there I’ve been using to relieve myself. Not sure where it goes, but it keeps the stink out of the chamber.” e priestess stretched and walked over to Kiara. “Do I have you to thank for trapping me in here?” “Our Master of Curses. He said the leader of the ferrumen was dead—that he had eliminated everyone who had attacked the vil age—but hiding inside the vault would have hidden you from his magic.” “So you didn’t know it was me? You didn’t guess … or use your magic?” “I guessed Cruithear might send his high priestess—and that if he had, you were certainly dead. I don’t bother to divine the answer to every question, Dolyn. You know the costs of our magic as wel as anyone.” Dolyn shrugged, her hands rising to show Kiara the scars burned there— the marks from where Annev had burned her with the Hand of Keos. “I am wel acquainted with the cost of our magics, Ciarán.” Kiara stared at the red scars burned into the woman’s open palms. “You touched it, then … the Hand of Keos.” “I did. e Vessel came to me and asked if I could assist him in removing the Hand. I tried, and failed. is was my punishment.” She lowered her hands. “I would have kil ed him right there and harvested it from his corpse … but Cruithear’s spirit stayed me.” Kiara chuckled. “You mean you were afraid he might destroy you, and Banok too.” Dolyn nodded. “It did not seem wise to attack him directly. I tried to assassinate him instead, but using a crossbow proved di cult with my injuries … and he had companions with him. Other servants of the gods.” Kiara had foreseen this. e priests of the Younger and Elder Gods would be drawn to the Vessel of Keos. “Of course you failed. e prophecies state he must forge the Sword of Seeking—he must end the Silence of the Gods.” “Him or his hand, Ciarán? We do not believe as you do—and I answer to Cruithear, not Tacharan. I wil not be conned into helping your master achieve his goals.” “And how are Cruithear’s plans working out for you?” Kiara snapped, her patience at an end. “First you siphon the tainted aqlumera from beneath our village and try to make your perverse ferrumen—and then you abandoned your failures.” “ ey were imperfect—and they knew the risks.” “You turned Janak Harth against us and attempted to start a war between Banok and Chaenbalu,” Kiara continued, her anger rising, “… and for what? For this?” She gestured at the glowing pool of liquid magic. “You know it is forbidden to forge with it.” “And yet you claim the Vessel wil use the aqlumera to forge the Sword of Seeking!” Dolyn sco ed. “Hypocrite.” “ e Vessel bears the Hand. He is the only one who can safely risk its dangers. You’ve seen what the aqlumera can do. You’ve seen how it can corrupt and kil .” “And I have seen how it can heal—I’ve seen it can transform mundane soldiers into living golems! I wil not be denied its power, nor wil Cruithear.” “Bah!” Kiara waved a hand, dismissing the iron-headed fool. “You’re as stubborn as your Ironborn.” She frowned, her attention momentarily drawn back to the corpse on the bier at the center of the room. “Is that Brayan?” “He … was my guide,” Dolyn admitted. “You tricked him into bringing you here.” “I had no choice,” Dolyn protested, sounding anguished. “When the Vessel left Banok, he left the quartermaster to help me. Brayan . . . was kind. He helped me with my work.” “Brayan was always tender-hearted,” Kiara agreed, “and you took advantage of that.” Dolyn looked toward the bier. “I … did. I tried to convince him that only magic could heal my hands—Chaenbalu’s magic—but he refused to bring me here. ‘Only if it was a matter of life and death,’ he said … so I poisoned him, and convinced him the cure lay in Chaenbalu’s vault. I think he even believed me—and so he became our guide, and we passed through Chaenbalu’s circle of protection. I expected to nd the vil age abandoned. I had hoped … I had thought . . .” She shuddered. “What did you do, Kiara? What demons did you send to attack us?” “Just our Master of Curses—him and his brainwashed lapdog—but that was enough. Kenton decimated you and your precious ferrumen.” She sni ed, not hiding her disdain. “You should have stayed in Banok, Dolyn. With a little patience, you would have met with Annev when we came to forge the Sword of Seeking. We would have brought you to this very room.” She gestured at the shelves of artifacts and the churning pool of liquid magic. “You acted in haste —and Brayan paid for it with his life.” Dolyn’s head bowed in sorrow, but then she sneered. “You dare to lecture me about the cost of lives? You, who sacri ced your entire vil age to protect your dark secrets? Do not judge the blood I have spil ed or spent. Your hands are no cleaner than mine.” “On that, we can agree,” Kiara said, her demeanor stil cool. She frowned. “Why did you stay? Why not burrow your way out with your magic?” Dolyn gestured at the concave wal s and domed ceiling. “Magic protects this place. I can’t shape the stone here.” “But the trapdoor? Surely you could have swum out through one of the ooded tunnels?” “I tried. I swam in search of an escape, but every exit was sealed.” She lifted her dirty tunic to show her skin, scaled with white marble and akes of greenish-white platinum. “I lacked the strength to shape the stone wal s. I can’t even slow the transmutation without proper food to replace the minerals my body has lost,” she explained. “I need meat and milk, and other things that I can’t get locked underground in a ooded chamber.” “Of course—and you shal have them.” “You’re … letting me go?” “I need your help,” Kiara snapped, “to forge the Sword of Seeking—and so does Annev. He wil be in Banok soon, and we wil need to be ready to greet him.” Dolyn’s brow furrowed, suspicious. “Why would I do that? I tried to kil him!” “But he doesn’t know that,” Kiara said, completing the other woman’s thoughts. “And before you try to barter with me, you should know you cannot have the Hand of Keos, nor wil I al ow you to capture the Vessel. I have already promised him to Tacharan, and if you obstruct me in this, we wil become enemies.” “ en there is nothing you can o er me.” “Oh no?” Kiara gestured at the fountain and its rainbow-hued contents. “As much aqlumera as you can carry, in exchange for helping Annev forge the diamagus when it is time.” e high priestess of the Orvanes grunted, considering. “ at . . . is a tempting o er.” “Stop being coy. You know the value of what I o er.” “And what’s to stop me from kil ing you and escaping through the tunnel you just opened?” “Fate,” Kiara crooned, her voice sure. e smith frowned at Kiara’s cryptic answer, but eventual y she nodded. “Cruithear curse me, but … very wel .” “Good,” Kiara said. “ ere are some enchanted jars on that shelf. Take as many as you can. ey’l be needed to forge the sword.” She moved between the shelves, guided by a preternatural sense of intuition. Halfway down the third shelf, she squatted down and found a worn leather satchel containing the other item she sought—a brass lamp engraved with a thousand runes in Old Darite. “What’s that?” Dolyn asked, drawing close to peer over the witmistress’s shoulder. “A lamp,” Kiara said, dropping it into her apron pocket. “Anything signi cant about it?” “ e Dionachs Tobar think it houses the Oracle of Odar.” “ ey think it does? What does it actual y hold?” Kiara smiled, her eyes sparkling with the secrets that only a High Priestess of Tacharan could know. “My sweet Dolyn, you wouldn’t believe me if I told you—and this is a secret I’l take to my grave.” ACKNOWLEDGMENTS I am so grateful to the many people at Blackstone who made this book possible —from the words on the page, to the layout of the gorgeous cover, to publicizing the book and sharing it with others—these people made my book the best version of itself. ank you Lauren Maturo, Megan Wahrenbrock, Deirdre Curley, Kathryn G. English, Zena Co man, Rick Bleiweiss, Je rey Yamaguchi, Josie Woodbridge, and the rest of the Blackstone team. Please al ow me to also heap an unseemly amount of praise on my UK editor, Gil ian Redfearn, whose keen eye, sage advice and uncanny wisdom helped me shape this rough story into something special. When I worried that Master Arti cer was getting too long, she was the person who assured me the story was good and that I should stay the course. It takes an immense amount of trust to do that, and I feel uniquely blessed to be al owed that privilege—so thanks again to the people at Blackstone, Gol ancz, and al my other foreign publishers who have believed in me, my writing, and this series. e next person I’d like to thank is my wonderful wife Col ette, whose sacri ces have enabled me to be an author and to sneak away from my kids long enough to write my darn books. I have said before that Co doesn’t much like anything to do with SFF—but she does believe in my writing; she knows it makes me happy, and it makes a lot of other people happy to read it. anks for the cheerleading, Coco. Which leads me back to those amazing kids—I love you guys! Hopeful y when you are older, you’l be able to read these books and appreciate why your dad locked himself in his o ce al those times. And to Tord—who is old enough to read these books now—please know that I love and support you, and I treasure our time exploring other people’s fantasy stories together. I’d also like to thank three of the people in the background whose unrecognized contributions make my storytel ing al the more epic. If you are reading the ebook, hardback, or paperback for Master Arti cer, you should know that most of the handwritten maps, symbols, and ephemera in this book were il ustrated by my good friend Jared Sprague—and we spent a lot of hours discussing and re ning those illustrations so they could accurately represent the world I imagined. Special attention should also be given to Jen El iott—who, at the time of this acknowledgment, is the lead artist for the Forgotten Realms TTRPG; Jen il ustrated the phenomenal diagram in the appendix that explains the rules and categories for the Prime and New Terran magic systems in e Silent Gods. If you haven’t seen it, please al ow your eyes to feast on her talents (and go check out her other amazing artwork). e third unsung hero I’d like to thank is Peter Kenny, my absolutely amazing audiobook narrator. If you are listening to his narration, you may lack the ability to see the maps and appendix graphics I previously mentioned, but in exchange you get to hear Peter’s incredible vocal talents as he brings my characters, my world, and my story to life. In addition to his legendary narrative skil s, Peter is also one of the kindest people I’ve met in the publishing industry (or anywhere else for that matter), and I’m delighted to cal him my friend. Lastly, I’d like to thank my agent Danny Baror. If it weren’t for Danny, no one would have heard these stories—either domestical y or international y— and his belief in my talents as a storytel er is invaluable. Cheers and thanks to al . chunks.content: “I’m John Stout and this is my brother, Jacob. We just came from Banok. Barely escaped with the shirts on our backs.” “Escaped?” Alcoran tilted his head, stil trying to make sense of the tale they were tel ing him. “Surely the Terrans haven’t come this far into the Empire?” John shook his head. “I don’t think so … but maybe? We were overrun by the Sons of Damnation—and they didn’t sound like foreigners. ey knew the city, knew our ways and our speech, but they were dressed strangely, and they said they’d come to liberate the village from evil. We didn’t know what to make of them, wrote them o as zealots from Quiri … but then they seized the Harth family’s keep and started making demands of the governor. Acted like they were running the village. Governor sent the town guard . . . and they didn’t come back. ey formed a militia, and they didn’t return either. Some folks went for help and . . . wel , we didn’t see them again, neither. When others nal y did come, it was more strangers and monsters—and they were there to help the Sons of Damnation. e whole place has gone to hel and the remaining townsfolk are being held hostage—forced to serve the man who leads the Sons.” “Strangers and monsters,” Alcoran repeated, forgetting for a moment why he had come to the smal encampment. “And … Sons of Damnation?” He scratched his short red beard, hunger receding to the back of his mind. “And you don’t know who they are?” e shorter man, Jacob, shook his head. “We weren’t keen on nding out. We decided to send for help—to sneak out of the vil age and nd someone who might help take back the city—but no one cares. Everyone’s concerned about their own problems, like the war in the east or the famine in the south. We heard no aid would be coming from the capital, so we’re taking our case to the king of Paldron.” Alcoran laughed—he couldn’t help it. e irony was too amusing. “King Alpenrose wouldn’t sel you his own piss, much less spare you a company of soldiers.” “But … the people are desperate. e soldiers are gone. e only folk left are shopkeeps and farmers. Merchants and artisans. ey aren’t warriors! And the people control ing the city … they’ve got magic. e Sons said they hate it, but they use it to keep people in line. Even the mercenaries they’ve hired— half of them use shadow magic and the others . . . they’re rotting demons. eir esh is more metal and stone than skin and bone!” “You have my sympathy—truly, you do—but no aid wil be coming. Borderlund has its sts ful on the Black Wal . Our numbers are thin. Conscripts are eeing, abandoning the war and seeking safety elsewhere. If they aren’t helped soon, the Terrans wil cross the Kuar and start sacking Paldron itself.” Alcoran hu ed. “If these men—these Sons of Damnation— aren’t harming you, you should count yourselves lucky. And if they aren’t friends of the Terrans, maybe they’l protect you from the war that’s about to come.” e old man’s face paled. “If that is the case, then we are truly in dark times.” You don’t know the half of it, Alcoran thought, feeling a tiny pang of guilt for what his band of soldiers was about to do to these folks. Times were tough al around, though, and only the ttest were going to survive. He tipped his hat low over his bandaged eye and made sure to stay out of the relight. His men should be in position now … yet something stayed his hand. “Lord Stout,” Alcoran said, addressing the elder of the two young men. “You said these Sons of Damnation aren’t letting folk in or out. How did you escape?” “We can’t take much credit for it,” the tal er man said. “ ese warlocks— the shadow men helping the Sons of Damnation—they wear gray and purple clothing and masks, and they spy on us townsfolk for the Sons of Damnation … but there’s a resistance forming. ey’ve got a leader too—one who uses magic—and she helped us waylay two of these warlocks and take their clothes.” Alcoran frowned. “She? ere’s a witch leading your militia?” “Not just one,” Jacob interrupted, “there are three! One who speaks to the plants, one who doesn’t speak at al , and one who charms the warlocks with her witching song.” John elbowed his younger brother, shushing him. “ ey aren’t witches. ey’re just . . . wel , they’re helping us. And we’re ghting back, with or without King Lenka and King Alpenrose.” Alcoran nodded, his tongue drawing across the bottom of his front teeth. “ ese mercenaries. Any notion why they’re helping these Sons of Damnation?” John and Jacob exchanged a look that suggested they knew exactly what Alcoran was asking, but they didn’t seem eager to share that information. Perhaps they weren’t as stupid as Alcoran hoped. “Only rumors,” John said, speaking for them both. “We heard about some kind of gold—liquid gold, I guess. I don’t know why that’d be so special, but word of it got out soon after the Sons came to Banok, and the mercenaries started appearing pretty quickly.” “Huh. Liquid gold.” Alcoran shrugged. “Seems like it’d be more valuable as simple coin. Easier to transport too. Stil … gold is gold. When folk o er it, others wil take it.” He hesitated. “Anyone else taking this gold? Any of your townsfolk helping these Sons?” “You mean has anyone turned traitor?” Jacob spat then ran his nger along the side of his savaged cheek. “Vilhelm Stenger decided he’d take some of that gold—he signed on to help the Sons keep order in the town—but we made an example of him. You know the costs of our magic as wel as anyone.” Dolyn shrugged, her hands rising to show Kiara the scars burned there— the marks from where Annev had burned her with the Hand of Keos. “I am wel acquainted with the cost of our magics, Ciarán.” Kiara stared at the red scars burned into the woman’s open palms. “You touched it, then … the Hand of Keos.” “I did. e Vessel came to me and asked if I could assist him in removing the Hand. I tried, and failed. is was my punishment.” She lowered her hands. “I would have kil ed him right there and harvested it from his corpse … but Cruithear’s spirit stayed me.” Kiara chuckled. “You mean you were afraid he might destroy you, and Banok too.” Dolyn nodded. “It did not seem wise to attack him directly. I tried to assassinate him instead, but using a crossbow proved di cult with my injuries … and he had companions with him. Other servants of the gods.” Kiara had foreseen this. e priests of the Younger and Elder Gods would be drawn to the Vessel of Keos. “Of course you failed. e prophecies state he must forge the Sword of Seeking—he must end the Silence of the Gods.” “Him or his hand, Ciarán? We do not believe as you do—and I answer to Cruithear, not Tacharan. I wil not be conned into helping your master achieve his goals.” “And how are Cruithear’s plans working out for you?” Kiara snapped, her patience at an end. “First you siphon the tainted aqlumera from beneath our village and try to make your perverse ferrumen—and then you abandoned your failures.” “ ey were imperfect—and they knew the risks.” “You turned Janak Harth against us and attempted to start a war between Banok and Chaenbalu,” Kiara continued, her anger rising, “… and for what? For this?” She gestured at the glowing pool of liquid magic. “You know it is forbidden to forge with it.” “And yet you claim the Vessel wil use the aqlumera to forge the Sword of Seeking!” Dolyn sco ed. “Hypocrite.” “ e Vessel bears the Hand. He is the only one who can safely risk its dangers. You’ve seen what the aqlumera can do. You’ve seen how it can corrupt and kil .” “And I have seen how it can heal—I’ve seen it can transform mundane soldiers into living golems! I wil not be denied its power, nor wil Cruithear.” “Bah!” Kiara waved a hand, dismissing the iron-headed fool. “You’re as stubborn as your Ironborn.” She frowned, her attention momentarily drawn back to the corpse on the bier at the center of the room. “Is that Brayan?” “He … was my guide,” Dolyn admitted. “You tricked him into bringing you here.” “I had no choice,” Dolyn protested, sounding anguished. “When the Vessel left Banok, he left the quartermaster to help me. Brayan . . . was kind. He helped me with my work.” “Brayan was always tender-hearted,” Kiara agreed, “and you took advantage of that.” Dolyn looked toward the bier. “I … did. I tried to convince him that only magic could heal my hands—Chaenbalu’s magic—but he refused to bring me here. ‘Only if it was a matter of life and death,’ he said … so I poisoned him, and convinced him the cure lay in Chaenbalu’s vault. I think he even believed me—and so he became our guide, and we passed through Chaenbalu’s circle of protection. I expected to nd the vil age abandoned. I had hoped … I had thought . . .” She shuddered. “What did you do, Kiara? What demons did you send to attack us?” “Just our Master of Curses—him and his brainwashed lapdog—but that was enough. Kenton decimated you and your precious ferrumen.” She sni ed, not hiding her disdain. “You should have stayed in Banok, Dolyn. With a little patience, you would have met with Annev when we came to forge the Sword of Seeking. We would have brought you to this very room.” She gestured at the shelves of artifacts and the churning pool of liquid magic. “You acted in haste —and Brayan paid for it with his life.” Dolyn’s head bowed in sorrow, but then she sneered. “You dare to lecture me about the cost of lives? You, who sacri ced your entire vil age to protect your dark secrets? Do not judge the blood I have spil ed or spent. Your hands are no cleaner than mine.” “On that, we can agree,” Kiara said, her demeanor stil cool. She frowned. “Why did you stay? Why not burrow your way out with your magic?” Dolyn gestured at the concave wal s and domed ceiling. “Magic protects this place. I can’t shape the stone here.” “But the trapdoor? Surely you could have swum out through one of the ooded tunnels?” “I tried. I swam in search of an escape, but every exit was sealed.” She lifted her dirty tunic to show her skin, scaled with white marble and akes of greenish-white platinum. “I lacked the strength to shape the stone wal s. I can’t even slow the transmutation without proper food to replace the minerals my body has lost,” she explained. “I need meat and milk, and other things that I can’t get locked underground in a ooded chamber.” “Of course—and you shal have them.” “You’re … letting me go?” “I need your help,” Kiara snapped, “to forge the Sword of Seeking—and so does Annev. He wil be in Banok soon, and we wil need to be ready to greet him.” Dolyn’s brow furrowed, suspicious. “Why would I do that? I tried to kil him!” “But he doesn’t know that,” Kiara said, completing the other woman’s thoughts. “And before you try to barter with me, you should know you cannot have the Hand of Keos, nor wil I al ow you to capture the Vessel. I have already promised him to Tacharan, and if you obstruct me in this, we wil become enemies.” “ en there is nothing you can o er me.” “Oh no?” Kiara gestured at the fountain and its rainbow-hued contents. “As much aqlumera as you can carry, in exchange for helping Annev forge the diamagus when it is time.” e high priestess of the Orvanes grunted, considering. “ at . . . is a tempting o er.” “Stop being coy. You know the value of what I o er.” “And what’s to stop me from kil ing you and escaping through the tunnel you just opened?” “Fate,” Kiara crooned, her voice sure. e smith frowned at Kiara’s cryptic answer, but eventual y she nodded. “Cruithear curse me, but … very wel .” “Good,” Kiara said. “ ere are some enchanted jars on that shelf. Take as many as you can. ey’l be needed to forge the sword.” She moved between the shelves, guided by a preternatural sense of intuition. Halfway down the third shelf, she squatted down and found a worn leather satchel containing the other item she sought—a brass lamp engraved with a thousand runes in Old Darite. “What’s that?” Dolyn asked, drawing close to peer over the witmistress’s shoulder. “A lamp,” Kiara said, dropping it into her apron pocket. “Anything signi cant about it?” “ e Dionachs Tobar think it houses the Oracle of Odar.” “ ey think it does? What does it actual y hold?” Kiara smiled, her eyes sparkling with the secrets that only a High Priestess of Tacharan could know. “My sweet Dolyn, you wouldn’t believe me if I told you—and this is a secret I’l take to my grave.” ACKNOWLEDGMENTS I am so grateful to the many people at Blackstone who made this book possible —from the words on the page, to the layout of the gorgeous cover, to publicizing the book and sharing it with others—these people made my book the best version of itself. ank you Lauren Maturo, Megan Wahrenbrock, Deirdre Curley, Kathryn G. English, Zena Co man, Rick Bleiweiss, Je rey Yamaguchi, Josie Woodbridge, and the rest of the Blackstone team. Please al ow me to also heap an unseemly amount of praise on my UK editor, Gil ian Redfearn, whose keen eye, sage advice and uncanny wisdom helped me shape this rough story into something special. When I worried that Master Arti cer was getting too long, she was the person who assured me the story was good and that I should stay the course. It takes an immense amount of trust to do that, and I feel uniquely blessed to be al owed that privilege—so thanks again to the people at Blackstone, Gol ancz, and al my other foreign publishers who have believed in me, my writing, and this series. e next person I’d like to thank is my wonderful wife Col ette, whose sacri ces have enabled me to be an author and to sneak away from my kids long enough to write my darn books. I have said before that Co doesn’t much like anything to do with SFF—but she does believe in my writing; she knows it makes me happy, and it makes a lot of other people happy to read it. anks for the cheerleading, Coco. Which leads me back to those amazing kids—I love you guys! Hopeful y when you are older, you’l be able to read these books and appreciate why your dad locked himself in his o ce al those times. And to Tord—who is old enough to read these books now—please know that I love and support you, and I treasure our time exploring other people’s fantasy stories together. I’d also like to thank three of the people in the background whose unrecognized contributions make my storytel ing al the more epic. If you are reading the ebook, hardback, or paperback for Master Arti cer, you should know that most of the handwritten maps, symbols, and ephemera in this book were il ustrated by my good friend Jared Sprague—and we spent a lot of hours discussing and re ning those illustrations so they could accurately represent the world I imagined. Special attention should also be given to Jen El iott—who, at the time of this acknowledgment, is the lead artist for the Forgotten Realms TTRPG; Jen il ustrated the phenomenal diagram in the appendix that explains the rules and categories for the Prime and New Terran magic systems in e Silent Gods. If you haven’t seen it, please al ow your eyes to feast on her talents (and go check out her other amazing artwork). e third unsung hero I’d like to thank is Peter Kenny, my absolutely amazing audiobook narrator. If you are listening to his narration, you may lack the ability to see the maps and appendix graphics I previously mentioned, but in exchange you get to hear Peter’s incredible vocal talents as he brings my characters, my world, and my story to life. In addition to his legendary narrative skil s, Peter is also one of the kindest people I’ve met in the publishing industry (or anywhere else for that matter), and I’m delighted to cal him my friend. Lastly, I’d like to thank my agent Danny Baror. If it weren’t for Danny, no one would have heard these stories—either domestical y or international y— and his belief in my talents as a storytel er is invaluable. Cheers and thanks to al .
